key_facts.value: Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm, on 01252 367 200

key_facts.label: Regulator
key_facts.value: None. Airport parking sits outside the FCA, and no ombudsman or ADR scheme covers it

sections.heading: The eight names behind the results
sections.html:
Type a date into any airport page and the ladder that comes back is assembled from eight wholesalers. The FAQ lists them plainly — "APH, BCP, Essential Travel, Holiday Extras, FHR, Park and Go, Purple Parking & Skyparksecure" — and the homepage repeats the eight under the heading "8 Parking Providers". That is the whole product. Each of those firms has its own inventory, its own deals with the car parks and its own price for the same tarmac, and putting the eight in one column is a job none of them will do for you.

Two of the eight are the same business. Holiday Extras bought Purple Parking's brand and website in November 2017 and the Purple Parking privacy policy has said so ever since, so a reader comparing those two rows is comparing two price lists from one Kent company rather than two competitors. That is not concealment — both names are correct and the prices genuinely differ — but it thins the field by one, and nothing on Airport Parking Shop mentions it.

The discrepancy worth knowing is smaller and stranger. The terms and conditions, which are the document that governs what you are agreeing to, say the site searches "7 of the largest parking brokers in the UK: APH, BCP, Essential Travel, FHR, Holiday Extras, Park and Go and Purple Parking". SkyParkSecure is missing from that sentence and present everywhere else, including the cookie policy, which lists a Cloudflare cookie set on www.SkyParkSecure.com. Eight is the live number; seven is what the contract page still says. Worth asking about if a SkyParkSecure booking goes wrong, because the cancellation terms for it are the outlier of the set.

sections.heading: What the price on the tile actually is
sections.html:
Every listing carries a per-day figure before you have entered anything, and the small print under the Gatwick and Heathrow ladders explains exactly how it is built: "The lowest price recorded in the past week for a week's parking, divided by 7 to show the daily equivalent." So the number is a historic floor, not an offer. It is the best price anyone was shown for a seven-night stay in the previous seven days, spread across the days. Change your dates to a half-term Friday and it will not be that.

That is a fairer way of advertising than a bare "from" price, because it is a price somebody actually got rather than a rate that exists once a year. It is still not your price, and the site does not say so in those words. Treat the ladder as a ranking — which broker is cheapest for which car park — and read the real number after the dates go in.

The ranking is where the site earns its place. At Gatwick on 24 September 2026 the top of the list was The Gatwick Valet Parking Company at £7.20 a day on-airport, then Gatwick Noble Parking meet and greet at £7.22, AVPS park and ride at £8.09 and Gatwick Airparks at £10.38 with a twelve-minute transfer. Cophall came in at £11.61, Purple Parking's own Gatwick site at £11.74 and APH at £13.82 — the two best-known names in the trade sitting sixth and eighth on a list built by a company with no stake in either.

Heathrow ran from Heathrow Car Park Ltd at £7.60 a day with a ten to fifteen minute transfer, through ParkInn meet and greet at £9.41 and Purple Parking's Terminal 5 park and ride at £10.75, up to MBW meet and greet at £15.63. Manchester was the cheapest of the three airports by a distance: Avian at £4.82, Vacationcare premium self-park at £5.06, Red Rose park and ride at £5.16, Hunters at £6.34 with an eight-minute transfer, and the airport's own JetParks Ringway at £7.91. A week at Avian is roughly £34; the same week at the airport's own Drop & Go P16, at £9.94 a day, is nearer £70.

sections.heading: The cancellation table nobody links to from the booking page
sections.html:
The single most useful document on the site is buried in the footer under "Amend / Cancel", and it sets out what each of the eight charges to change or scrap a booking. Nothing else in this trade publishes the comparison, because nobody else has eight sets of terms to compare.

APH takes nothing for a cancellation made more than 24 hours before arrival, and nothing for an amendment; inside 24 hours there is no refund. BCP, Essential Travel, Holiday Extras and Purple Parking all run to 23:59 on the day before departure and charge £10.50 on parking and lounge bookings, £15 on hotels. FHR charges £10.00 per reservation with 24 hours' notice. Park and Go charges £7.50, and an amendment inside 24 hours costs "£7.50 or 50% of the cost of parking (whichever is smaller)". SkyParkSecure is the one to watch: its deadline is 72 hours rather than 24, the fee is £10.00, and it is the only one of the eight that charges for an amendment at all — £5.00, even with more than a day's notice.

Set that beside the general terms and conditions, which say flatly: "All cancellations are subject to a cancellation fee of £10.50 for car park and lounge bookings and £15 for hotel bookings." Both are the same company's words on the same site, and they cannot both be right — a cancelled APH booking is free and a SkyParkSecure one has to be cancelled three days out. Work to whichever of the two documents is worse for you and you will not be caught out. Promotional rates, super savers and anything sold as non-flexible cannot be cancelled at all, which is the usual rule in this trade and the reason the cheapest tile is not always the one to buy.

sections.heading: Who is actually on the hook when the car park lets you down
sections.html:
There is no financial regulator here. Airport parking is not a regulated activity, so there is no FCA permission to look up, no firm reference number, no Financial Ombudsman Service and no compensation scheme — and this site is a step further back again, because it is not even the party you pay. Its terms disclaim the data itself: "We do not guarantee the accuracy of the information and accept no liability for any error or omission", with the reader made responsible for reading everything before travelling.

In practice that leaves three parties and a clear order. The car park owes you reasonable care and skill under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, and from the moment a member of staff takes your keys it is holding your car as a bailee, which is an older and in some ways stronger duty. The broker — whichever of the eight took the payment — owes you the booking it sold and handles the refund. Airport Parking Shop sits outside both, which is why its own FAQ tells you to take a complaint about a car park "directly" to the provider rather than to itself.

It does answer the phone, though, which several larger sites in this trade no longer do. The number is 01252 367 200, staffed Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm, with booking@airport-parking-shop.co.uk for email and a self-service portal for resending a voucher. The terms add that cancellation requests by phone or email are not accepted outside those hours, so a Sunday-morning change of plan before a Monday departure has to go through the portal or wait — and waiting can cost the whole fare.

sections.heading: A twenty-six-year-old publisher, and the question its own terms never answer
sections.html:
Fubra Limited was incorporated on 7 April 2000 and registered for VAT as 733667024. Its filed purpose is SIC 63990, "other information service activities not elsewhere classified", which is the register's way of saying it publishes websites. Alongside this one it runs an airport guides network and AffJet, a dashboard that pulls a publisher's earnings together from, in its own words, "over 100 affiliate networks". Accounts were last made up to 30 September 2025, with the next set due by 30 June 2027.

The people have been stable for five years. Joanne Elizabeth Gutteridge and Thomas Hamilton Nunn were appointed directors on 22 and 23 June 2021, and Dr Paul Martin McCormick — a director from 2011 to 2021 — came back on 26 September 2022. The only person with significant control is Brendan McLoughlin, notified on 6 April 2016 as holding more than 25% but not more than 50% of the shares. Twelve officers have come and gone since 2000, which for a company of this age is an ordinary number.

One administrative snag is worth a footnote. The registered office is c/o Rock Tax & Accounting, Elm House, Tanshire Park, Shackleford Road, Elstead, Godalming GU8 6LB. The terms and conditions give the same building under a different accountancy name, "C/O Chamberlains" — the sort of thing that happens when a firm rebrands and a footer does not follow. Same address, older label.

The question the site never answers is how it is paid. The about page says "We are truly independent, not affiliated with or owned by any one particular brand", which is a statement about ownership and is true: Fubra is not a subsidiary of any of the eight. It is not a statement about money, and there is no page anywhere on the site explaining what the eight brokers pay when a reader clicks through. Given what AffJet does for a living, commission is the obvious inference — but it is an inference, and it should be confirmed with Fubra rather than assumed. A line disclosing it would cost the site nothing and would settle the point.

sections.heading: Eighty thousand reviews, and how much to trust them
sections.html:
The site has collected more than 80,000 car park reviews from its own customers, and they are attached to individual car parks rather than to the site — which is the useful way round. Cophall at Gatwick carries 4.5 stars from 1,133 people, Purple Parking's Gatwick site 4.0 from 665, APH Gatwick 4.5 from 779 and Heathrow's 5 Star meet and greet 4.5 from 587. They are gathered by an email after the trip, scored one to five, and the published policy promises that "We will not exclude a comment if it contains negative feedback on a service". It keeps that promise visibly: Manchester JetParks Ringway sits at 2.0 stars from 63 reviews and Purple Parking's Heathrow meet and greet at 3.0 from 48, both still listed and sold.

Three things temper them. Reviewers are entered into a competition, and the policy's own sanction for breaking the rules is that a comment "will not be published and they will be refused entry into our competition" — an incentive that tends to lift averages a little wherever it is used. The policy does not say how the star average is calculated, whether old scores drop out, or how long a review stays up, so a 4.5 could be last month's or a decade's worth. And the counts are wildly uneven: Maple Parking at Heathrow shows 3.5 stars from two reviews, which is not a rating at all. Read the number of reviews before the number of stars, and ignore anything under about fifty.

pros: Compares eight booking companies at once, including APH, Holiday Extras, Purple Parking and SkyParkSecure, so you see one car park's price from several sellers side by side
No booking fee at present, and the terms say so in as many words
660 car parks at 32 airports, plus Dover, Dublin and Shannon — including small airports such as Inverness, Teesside and Humberside that larger sites skip
Publishes a per-broker cancellation and amendment table, which no other site in this trade does
More than 80,000 customer reviews tied to individual car parks, with poor scores left up: JetParks Ringway at 2.0 stars is still listed
The advertised daily figure is defined openly as the lowest recorded week divided by seven, rather than an unexplained "from" price
A staffed telephone line on 01252 367 200 and a named email address, which several bigger sites no longer publish
Run by a company on the register since 7 April 2000, with a stable board and a single person with significant control
cons: The terms and conditions name seven brokers; the homepage, the FAQ and the cookie policy all name eight. SkyParkSecure is missing from the one document that governs the booking
Those terms also state a blanket £10.50 cancellation fee, while the amend page shows APH charges nothing and SkyParkSecure wants 72 hours' notice plus £10 — two of the company's own pages disagreeing
The price on every tile is a trailing seven-day low for a seven-night stay, not a quote for your dates, and the ladder can reorder once the dates go in
Nothing on the site explains how it is paid. "Truly independent" describes ownership, not money, and no commission disclosure appears anywhere
Reviewers are entered into a competition, and the review policy does not say how the star average is worked out or how long a score stays published
Cancellations and amendments cannot be taken by phone or email outside Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm, although the deadline for most brokers is 23:59 the day before departure
Two of the eight brokers, Holiday Extras and Purple Parking, have been the same company since November 2017, and the site does not say so
verdict: Airport Parking Shop is the only site in British airport parking that compares the sellers rather than the car parks, and after twenty-three years it does that job well: eight brokers, 660 car parks, 32 airports, no booking fee, and a cancellation table that is more honest than anything the brokers publish themselves. Use the ladder to find out which of the eight is cheapest for the car park you want, then read the real price once your dates are in, because the headline figure is last week's low rather than your quote. Check which broker took the money before you need to change anything — a free APH cancellation and a SkyParkSecure one needing 72 hours are both sold from the same results page.

faqs.q: Who do I actually book with?
faqs.a: One of eight parking brokers: APH, BCP, Essential Travel, FHR, Holiday Extras, Park and Go, Purple Parking or SkyParkSecure. Airport Parking Shop's own terms say it is "a comparison website and do not provide the Car Park Service itself", so your payment, confirmation and voucher all come from whichever of the eight you clicked through to, and a complaint about the car park goes to them.

faqs.q: Is there a booking fee?
faqs.a: Not at the moment. The terms say: "We currently do not require a booking fee but we reserve the right to charge one at any time." The broker you book with may add its own charges, and the lowest price guarantee specifically excludes "booking fees, card processing fees and additional charges" from any comparison, so check the total at the broker's checkout rather than the figure on the tile.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between nothing and £10.50, depending which broker sold it. APH charges nothing more than 24 hours out; BCP, Essential Travel, Holiday Extras and Purple Parking charge £10.50 on parking up to 23:59 the day before departure, and £15 on a hotel; FHR charges £10.00; Park and Go £7.50; and SkyParkSecure £10.00 but with a 72-hour deadline. Super saver, non-flexible and promotional bookings cannot be cancelled at all.

faqs.q: How does the lowest price guarantee work?
faqs.a: If you find the same car park cheaper on another UK parking website, the site will refund the difference. The claim has to be made after payment but before the first day of the booking, with proof of purchase and a screen grab showing the same car park, the same airport, the same start date and the same duration, quoted on the same day. Special offers and fees are excluded, and the terms state that whether to honour a claim is "at the sole discretion of Airport Parking Shop".

faqs.q: Are the prices on the listings the price I will pay?
faqs.a: No. Each tile shows "the lowest price recorded in the past week for a week's parking, divided by 7 to show the daily equivalent" — a historic floor rather than a live quote. On 24 September 2026 that put Manchester at £4.82 a day, Gatwick at £7.20 and Heathrow at £7.60. Enter your own dates to see what is actually available, and expect school holidays and short stays to price differently.

faqs.q: Is airport parking covered by an ombudsman?
faqs.a: No. It is not a regulated financial activity, so there is no FCA authorisation, no Financial Ombudsman Service and no compensation scheme behind any of this. What you have instead is the Consumer Rights Act 2015, which requires the car park to perform with reasonable care and skill, the law of bailment once staff take your keys, and the county court. Photograph the car at handover and raise damage before you leave the site.

title: Aldermore Savings Accounts: The Fixed-Term Specialist
meta_title: Aldermore Savings: 7 Fixed Terms, 9 Months to 5 Years
meta_description: Seven fixed bonds from 9 months to 5 years, a £1,000 minimum, a Defaqto 2026 fixed-ISA award, Which? Recommended status and only 74 FOS cases.
intro:
Nine months, one year, eighteen months, two years, three, four and five: Aldermore runs the deepest fixed-term ladder of any provider in this comparison, and it is the only one here offering a four-year bond at all. That four-year bond pays 5.17% AER, read from Aldermore's own product page on 7 October 2026. Choosing a term precisely — rather than rounding to whatever a bank happens to offer — is the reason to be here.

The cash ISA range is stronger still. The three-year Fixed Rate Cash ISA pays 5.03% AER, the best three-year fixed ISA rate across the five providers reviewed in this cluster, and Aldermore holds the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 for Fixed Term Cash ISAs. It is also a Which? Recommended Provider, cited with an above-average customer score and five-star online banking.

Where it falls away is instant money. The Easy Access Account pays 2.25% against Close Brothers' 3.85%, and against the 4.15% Cynergy pays on an easy access account it has now closed to new customers. Aldermore is a place to lock money up, not to leave it loose.

sections.heading: Seven fixed terms, and the only four-year bond here
sections.html:
Aldermore's Fixed Rate Savings range starts at a £1,000 minimum and covers:

  • 5 years — 5.25% AER
  • 4 years — 5.17% AER
  • 3 years — 5.16% AER
  • 2 years — 4.97% AER
  • 18 months — 4.93% AER
  • 1 year — 4.88% AER
  • 9 months — 4.57% AER

The value of that granularity is easy to miss. If you know money is needed in roughly eighteen months, an 18-month product at 4.93% beats parking it in a one-year bond at 4.88% and then dropping to an easy access rate for six months. The nine-month option does the same job for short, dated commitments — a tax bill, a completion date — that a twelve-month bond would strand.

The ladder spans 68 basis points from the nine-month to the five-year, but nearly all of it is earned in the first three years: three years to five adds just nine basis points (5.16% to 5.25%), which argues for keeping the term short unless you have a specific reason not to. Aldermore charges an interest deduction for early access to any fixed product — there is no free exit.

sections.heading: Cash ISAs from nine months to three years
sections.html:
The Fixed Rate Cash ISA range, also £1,000 minimum, runs:

  • 3 years — 5.03% AER tax-free
  • 2 years — 5.01%
  • 1 year — 4.79%
  • 15 months — 4.70%
  • 9 months — 4.50%

The three-year at 5.03% is the best three-year fixed ISA rate in this comparison, ahead of Nationwide's 4.65% and Santander's 4.85%. Over five years Close Brothers now pays more, at 5.12%. Note the shape of the curve: the 15-month sits below the one-year, so pay attention to the specific term rather than assuming longer means better.

Elsewhere in the tax-free range, the 60 Day Notice Cash ISA pays 3.51% and the Easy Access Cash ISA 2.25%. The 45 Day Notice Account, outside the ISA wrapper, pays 4.05% — a reasonable middle ground for money you can plan six weeks ahead for.

The Defaqto Banking Award 2026 for Fixed Term Cash ISAs is a consistency measure rather than a single-day snapshot: qualifying products have to hold a top-fifteen position for ten of twelve months, and only 29 products out of 2,114 assessed won across all categories.

sections.heading: Withdrawals counted per year, not per month
sections.html:
Aldermore's access accounts use a different clock from its rivals. Nationwide and Santander count withdrawals per calendar month; Aldermore counts them per year.

  • Reward ISA Single Access — 4.00% if you make one withdrawal or fewer a year, dropping to 2.00% thereafter. £100 minimum
  • Reward ISA Double Access — 3.75% for up to two withdrawals a year, then 2.00%. £100 minimum
  • Double Access Account — 3.75% for up to two withdrawals a year, then 1.50%. £1,000 minimum
  • Regular Saver — 4.20%, £25 minimum, maximum £300 a month
  • Easy Access Account — 2.25%, £100 minimum

An annual allowance suits savers whose money moves rarely but unpredictably; a monthly allowance suits regular, small drawdowns. Neither is better in the abstract — match it to your actual behaviour. The cliff-edges are real: breach the count on the Double Access Account and the rate halves to 1.50% for the remainder.

The Regular Saver takes £300 a month, a 50% higher cap than Santander's or Nationwide's £200, but at 4.20% rather than 8.00% or 6.50%. Over a year, the larger cap does not compensate for the rate gap unless you have already filled the better accounts.

sections.heading: Independent recognition and the complaints record
sections.html:
Aldermore is one of only two providers in this cluster holding both a Which? Recommended Provider badge and a Defaqto Banking Award 2026. Which? cites an above-average customer score and five-star online banking.

The complaints data is the strongest signal in the set. The Financial Ombudsman Service recorded 74 new cases against Aldermore between 1 July 2025 and 31 March 2026 — the lowest volume of all five providers, and a genuinely notable figure given the size of its deposit base. Per-firm uphold percentages are published only in an FOS spreadsheet we could not access and remain unverified. At firm level, FCA data for 2025 H2 shows 1,445 complaints opened — 754 in banking and credit cards, 691 in home finance, so a substantial share relates to mortgage lending rather than savings.

Aldermore holds its own banking licence, not shared with any other retail brand, so the £120,000 FSCS limit applies cleanly without the aggregation problem that affects Nationwide/Virgin Money and Santander/cahoot savers.

sections.heading: Where Aldermore is beaten
sections.html:
Instant access is the weak flank. At 2.25%, the Easy Access Account is roughly half what Cynergy advertises and well behind Close Brothers' bonus-free 3.85%. If a large part of your savings needs to stay liquid, that money should sit elsewhere and only your term deposits should come here.

There is also no branch network — everything runs online or by phone. That is unremarkable for a specialist savings bank, but worth knowing if you expect to sort a problem face to face. Aldermore does at least keep entry costs low: £25 on the Regular Saver and £100 on the Reward ISAs and Easy Access, against the £10,000 that Close Brothers demands on every single product.

pros: The widest fixed-term ladder here — 9 months, 1 year, 18 months, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years
The only 4-year bond in this comparison, at 5.17% AER
Best three-year fixed cash ISA in the set, at 5.03%
Defaqto Banking Award 2026 winner for Fixed Term Cash ISAs
Which? Recommended Provider with an above-average customer score and five-star online banking
Just 74 new FOS cases from July 2025 to March 2026 — the lowest of the five providers
Annual rather than monthly withdrawal allowances on the Reward and Double Access range
Low entry points: £25 on the Regular Saver, £100 on Reward ISAs and Easy Access
Own banking licence, so the £120,000 FSCS limit is not shared with a sister brand
cons: Easy Access at 2.25% is well behind Close Brothers (3.85%), and behind the 4.15% Cynergy pays on an account closed to new customers
Steep cliff-edges: the Double Access Account halves to 1.50% and the Reward ISAs fall to 2.00% if you overstep
Early access to any fixed product costs an interest deduction — there is no free exit
£1,000 minimum on all fixed bonds and fixed cash ISAs
The Regular Saver's 4.20% is far below Santander's 8.00% and Nationwide's 6.50%, despite a higher £300 monthly cap
The 15-month cash ISA (4.70%) pays less than the 1-year (4.79%) — check the specific term, not the length
No branch network; online and telephone servicing only
verdict: Aldermore is the right answer for a saver with a known time horizon and a lump sum of £1,000 or more to commit — especially anyone whose horizon is awkward, at nine months, eighteen months or four years, where most banks force you to round up or down. The 5.03% three-year cash ISA, the Defaqto award for exactly that product type and the lowest FOS complaint volume in this group make a coherent case. It is not the place for your emergency fund: 2.25% on easy access money, with a 1.50% penalty rate lurking behind the Double Access allowance, means liquid savings should live with Close Brothers or elsewhere while Aldermore takes the money you can genuinely tie up.

faqs.a: Because matching the term to the date you need the money avoids a gap. An 18-month bond at 4.93% beats a one-year bond at 4.88% followed by six months at an easy access rate. Aldermore is the only provider in this comparison offering a four-year term at all.

title: Alfred Household Bills Membership
meta_title: Alfred: What £195 a Year Actually Buys You
meta_description: Alfred bundles energy, mobile, broadband and insurance for £195 a year, no mark-up. Who it suits, who it doesn't, and how it compares to Utility Warehouse.
disclosure: we are on Alfred's waitlist ourselves and the link on this page is our personal invite. We do not earn commission from Alfred — there is no affiliate programme. If you join through it we get Founding Member benefits: priority access and our membership price frozen.

headline.label: Membership
headline.value: £195 a year — services sold at cost, no mark-up

intro: Alfred charges £195 a year and then sells you energy, mobile, broadband and insurance at the price it pays for them. No margin on the units, no loyalty penalty, no annual switching ritual. It is the Costco model pointed at household bills, and the company is unusually open about the catch: if your household does not use much, the membership can cost more than it saves. Everything below was checked against what Alfred has published as of 4 October 2026.

sections.heading: One provider for six things you currently buy from six companies
sections.html:
Alfred replaces the separate accounts most households keep for electricity, gas, mobile, broadband, home insurance, car insurance and breakdown cover. The membership is £195 a year, plus £125 a year for each additional home.

That fee is the whole of Alfred's margin. Everything else is sold on at the price Alfred pays, which is what the phrase "members pay what we pay" is describing.

You do not have to move everything at once. Alfred's own answer is direct: "You can start with one service and Alfred can remind you as your contract ends on the others." The £195 does not change whether you take one service or all six, so the arithmetic improves with every service you bring across.

Services are billed individually under a single direct debit, with one view of them in the app. It is not one combined bill, which is what most people picture when they hear "one provider".

sections.heading: Who actually supplies it
sections.html:
Alfred is not building power stations or laying fibre. It buys wholesale and resells:

  • Energy — British Gas
  • Mobile — EE, as an MVNO
  • Broadband — BT Openreach and Vodafone infrastructure
  • Insurance — brokered, with Aviva, AXA and Allianz named on the panel

That is a point in its favour. The coverage, the speeds and the claims handling are the same ones you would get buying direct from those brands. Alfred is a buying club sitting in front of them, not an untested new network.

On regulation, in Alfred's own words: "Alfred is a regulated provider of energy, mobile and broadband… However, for insurance we're both." The insurance arm operates as an appointed representative of PHL Insurance Brokers Ltd, firm reference 301732. If you claim on a policy, the insurer handles it, not Alfred.

sections.heading: What £195 has to beat
sections.html:
This is the only question that matters, and Alfred answers it more honestly than most companies would:

"Alfred sells energy at the price it costs to supply, with no margin added. Instead, membership costs £195 a year. So the more energy your household uses, the more you save compared with a supplier who adds a margin to every unit. Use less, and the membership might cost more than it saves you."

So this is a volume play. A four-bedroom house with two cars, several mobiles and a family's worth of hot water is the household it is built for. A single person in a one-bed flat who already switches every year is not.

Alfred's published estimates are up to £1,000 a year for busy households, and the calculator on its own site returns £949 for a three-bed detached taking British Gas energy, two EE mobiles, BT broadband and two cars insured. The launch coverage put more than £2,000 on the largest households. Those are Alfred's figures for specific profiles, and Alfred itself labels them illustrative estimates for a service still in development. They are not quotes.

Before you commit, Alfred says it will show you a projected price based on your actual usage, and refund the membership if the savings disappoint.

sections.heading: Alfred and Utility Warehouse
sections.html:
If the idea sounds familiar, it should. Utility Warehouse, part of FTSE-listed Telecom Plus, has bundled energy, broadband, mobile and insurance onto one bill for years, has over a million customers, and charges no membership fee at all. Its discounts grow as you add services.

The difference is where the money comes from. Utility Warehouse makes its margin on the services and hands some of it back as a multi-service discount. Alfred takes its margin up front as a flat fee and says it adds nothing to the services themselves.

Which is better depends entirely on how much you use. A flat fee is excellent for a heavy user and poor for a light one, while a percentage discount scales with your bill whichever way your usage goes. Until Alfred publishes unit rates nobody can settle it with a calculator, and that includes us. What can be said is that Utility Warehouse is a known quantity with a service record you can look up, and Alfred is not one yet.

You can read our Utility Warehouse Dual Fuel and Utility Warehouse Gas pages for the comparison from the other side.

sections.heading: Where it does not work
sections.html:
Light users can lose money. Alfred says so itself. £195 is roughly £16 a month before you have saved a penny, and a low-usage flat may never make it back.

You cannot see a single price. There is no pence per kWh, no standing charge, no broadband speed or monthly cost, no mobile allowance and no insurance excess published anywhere. You are being asked to join a waitlist for a deal you cannot inspect. That is unusual, and it is a legitimate reason to wait.

The membership stops being refundable if you take insurance. Leave early and Alfred refunds the unused months — its own example is "if you leave after 8 months, we'll pay you back £65 (4/12 × £195)". Take out a 12-month insurance policy and that refund goes away for the term.

There is an exit fee on fixed energy. £50 if you leave the Wholesale Fixed tariff early. None on Wholesale Variable, mobile or broadband.

No heating oil. Homes off the mains gas grid are not served.

And it has not launched. Alfred Wholesale Limited was incorporated on 5 March 2025, the waitlist opened on 25 August 2026, and the app is in private beta. There are no customers to ask, no complaints record and no service history. The company has raised £5m at a £27.5m valuation from Liberty Global and others and is aiming at 50,000 members within three years, which is real money and a real plan. It is still a plan.

pros: The membership fee is the only margin Alfred takes — services are sold at cost
Supplied by British Gas, EE, BT Openreach and Vodafone, so the underlying service is not experimental
You can start with a single service and move the rest as contracts end
No annual switching to stay on the best rate, and no loyalty penalty
Unused membership refunded pro-rata if you leave, and refunded in full if you are unhappy with your savings
Alfred states plainly that light users may not save, which is rare and worth something
cons: Light users can pay more — £195 is roughly £16 a month before any saving
No unit rates, speeds, allowances or excesses published anywhere yet
Membership becomes non-refundable for the term if you take a 12-month insurance policy
£50 exit fee on the Wholesale Fixed energy tariff
Heating oil is not covered, so homes off the mains gas grid are excluded
Not launched: no customers, no complaints record and no service history to check

faqs.q: Can I join if I cannot switch everything yet?
faqs.a: Yes. Alfred's answer is "You can start with one service", and it will prompt you as your other contracts end. The £195 membership does not change, so your savings improve with every service you move across.

faqs.q: Is it all on one bill?
faqs.a: No. There is one direct debit, but each service is billed separately so you can see what each one costs. The app gives you a single view of them.

faqs.q: Who handles an insurance claim?
faqs.a: The insurer, not Alfred. Alfred brokers the policy as an appointed representative of PHL Insurance Brokers Ltd, with Aviva, AXA and Allianz named on its panel.

faqs.q: How is this different from Utility Warehouse?
faqs.a: Utility Warehouse charges no membership fee and makes its margin on the services, discounting them as you add more. Alfred charges £195 a year and says it adds no margin at all. Heavy users should prefer Alfred's shape, light users Utility Warehouse's.

faqs.q: Can I leave whenever I want?
faqs.a: Yes, with no exit fee unless you are on the Wholesale Fixed energy tariff, which carries £50. Unused membership is refunded pro-rata, unless you have taken out a 12-month insurance policy.

faqs.q: When does Alfred launch?
faqs.a: Alfred opened its waitlist on 25 August 2026 and says it will launch later in 2026. No date has been published. We check this page weekly and will update it when that changes.

verdict: Alfred is the most interesting thing to happen to household bills in a while, and the candour of its own FAQ does it credit — a company that tells you in writing that its product might cost you money is not trying to fool anybody. But there is nothing to buy yet and no price to check. If you have a big house, several cars, a family's worth of mobiles and no appetite for switching every year, the waitlist costs nothing and is worth joining. If you are a light user, or you already switch annually and rather enjoy it, wait for the rates and judge it then. We will update this page when Alfred publishes prices.

title: Amazon Children's Fashion
meta_title: Amazon Kids' Clothes: Prices, Delivery and Returns
meta_description: Children's clothes on Amazon start at £1 on Amazon Haul. What you pay, how long you get to send it back, and the two safety rules that apply only to kids.

headline.label: Cost of free delivery
headline.value: £15 minimum order on Amazon Haul, or £95 a year for unlimited one-day delivery with Prime — checked 25 September 2026

intro:
Children's clothes on Amazon start at £1. Amazon Haul, the budget storefront that opened in the UK on 6 May 2025, prices everything at £20 or less and most of it under £10, and delivery is free once the basket reaches £15. Those figures come from Amazon's own UK newsroom and were checked on 25 September 2026.

The main store is a different shop with different economics. Prime costs £8.99 a month or £95 a year, £4.49 and £47.49 for students, and in 2025 Amazon delivered more than 1.6 billion items to UK addresses on the same or the next day. Around 100,000 UK small and medium-sized businesses sell through it; roughly 60% of Amazon's sales come from small businesses, and in 2024 they sold more than a billion products and booked over £3.8 billion in export sales.

Two practical things follow from that, and both are worth knowing before you click. Most children's clothing on Amazon is sold by one of those independent businesses rather than by Amazon, so the contract for the garment is with the seller whose name sits under the buy button. And the two storefronts run on different clocks: Haul orders are quoted at up to two weeks to arrive and carry a 15-day window to ask for a return, which is a tighter pair of numbers than the main store's next-day delivery.

sections.heading: What a pound buys, and what it costs to get it to the door
sections.html:
Amazon now runs two children's clothing shops under one roof and they price in opposite directions. Amazon Haul, launched in the UK on 6 May 2025 after a late-2024 debut in the United States, caps everything at £20, puts most of the range under £10 and keeps a section of items at £1. Delivery is free on orders of £15 or more and £2.99 below that, and Amazon quotes the majority of Haul orders as arriving in two weeks or less.

The main store buys speed instead. Prime is £8.99 a month or £95 a year — £4.49 and £47.49 on the student rate for 18 to 24-year-olds and those in higher education — and it carries unlimited one-day delivery, same-day delivery on more than a million items across 80-plus UK towns and cities, and a year of Deliveroo Plus Silver. Amazon says more than 1.6 billion items reached UK customers the same or the next day during 2025.

The arithmetic for a parent is not complicated. A £95 annual Prime fee is six Haul baskets brought up to the £15 free-delivery threshold with change to spare, or it is 31 separate £2.99 delivery charges avoided. If you buy school polo shirts twice a year, Haul plus patience is cheaper; if you are replacing a coat the week the weather turns, the two-week quote makes the decision for you.

One number to check on the day rather than take from here. Amazon's two newsroom articles about Haul give different multi-buy thresholds — one says 5% off orders over £30 and 10% over £50, the other says 5% over £50 and 10% over £75. Both are Amazon's own pages. Read the basket total at checkout and believe that.

sections.heading: Who actually sells the dress
sections.html:
Around 100,000 UK small and medium-sized businesses sell on Amazon. Roughly 60% of Amazon's sales come from small businesses, they sold more than a billion products in 2024, and their export sales through the platform passed £3.8 billion in the same year. Amazon employs about 75,000 people in the UK, has invested more than £75 billion here between 2014 and 2024, announced a further £40 billion of planned UK investment in June 2025, and runs more than 30 fulfilment centres, sort centres and delivery stations.

For a shopper, the consequence sits in one line of grey text on the listing. Where the seller is an independent business, the sale contract is with that business. Amazon's role is the shop window, the payment rail and, where the item is held in its warehouses, the packing and posting. That matters when a jacket arrives with a cord where a cord should not be: the Consumer Rights Act claim and the 14-day distance cancellation right under regulation 30 of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 both run against the seller named on the order, and regulation 30 starts that 14-day clock on the day the last of the goods physically reaches you, not the day you ordered.

The position of Amazon's own retail arm inside its own marketplace has been examined by the competition regulator. In case 51184, decided on 3 November 2023, the Competition and Markets Authority accepted binding commitments from Amazon.com, Inc., Amazon UK Services Ltd, Amazon Europe Core SARL, Amazon Services Europe SARL and Amazon EU SARL. The CMA's published reasoning contains the figures nobody else prints: more than 75% of UK Marketplace purchases go through the Featured Offer — the box with the buy button in it — and Amazon Retail was selected as the Featured Offer in more than 80% of cases where both Amazon and a third-party seller were eligible. Prime subscribers accounted for over 80% of total sales value in 2021. Under the commitments, which run until 20 June 2028, Amazon must apply objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria when choosing the Featured Offer and may not use Prime eligibility or Prime labelling as one of them.

sections.heading: The economics behind a £6 T-shirt
sections.html:
Amazon publishes what it charges the businesses selling on it, and on clothing the numbers are unusually low. A seller pays either £25 a month excluding VAT on the Professional plan or 75p per item sold on the Individual plan, then a referral fee on each sale. For Clothing and Accessories that fee is tiered: 5% on items priced at or below £15, 10% between £15 and £20, and 15% above £20, with a minimum of 25p per item. Amazon cut clothing referral fees in its European stores on 5 January 2026.

Children's clothing sits almost entirely in the bottom band. A £6 babygrow carries a 30p referral fee; a £12 pack of school socks carries 60p. Most categories on Amazon run at a flat 8% to 15%, so a seller of infant clothes keeps a larger share of a small price than a seller of almost anything else on the site — which is a large part of why the cheap end of this category is as deep as it is.

Sellers using Fulfilment by Amazon or Seller Fulfilled Prime on items over £40 pay 15% on the first £40 and 7% on the rest. Those sellers are also enrolled automatically in prepaid returns: they must supply a prepaid return label or a returnless refund on every request, and respond to any request that falls outside Amazon's own returns policy within 24 hours.

sections.heading: Two rulebooks that apply to children's clothes and nothing else
sections.html:
Most clothing in Britain is sold under the general duty in the General Product Safety Regulations 2005 that a product be safe in normal or reasonably foreseeable use, and nothing more specific. Children's clothing is one of the few exceptions, and the first of the two extra rulebooks is about fire.

The Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985 came into operation on 1 March 1987 and cover anything designed for and normally worn by a person under 13 years old. Children's nightwear must meet the flammability performance of BS 5722, tested after washing to BS 5651 — with three exceptions: pyjamas, cotton terry-towelling bath robes, and infants' garments for children up to three months with a chest measurement of 53cm or less. The regulations also cut off at size: a nightdress with a chest over 91cm or a length over 122cm, or a robe with a chest over 97cm or a sleeve over 69cm, falls outside the children's definition.

The labelling is the part a parent can actually use. A garment that does not meet BS 5722 must carry KEEP AWAY FROM FIRE in red. One that does may carry LOW FLAMMABILITY TO BS 5722 in black. Where the fabric has been treated with a flame-retardant chemical, the label must add DO NOT WASH AT MORE THAN 50 °C. CHECK SUITABILITY OF WASHING AGENT, because a hot wash strips the treatment out. The label belongs inside the neck or next to the size label, on durable material with enough colour contrast to be legible. BS EN 14878 is the recommended standard for the exempted pyjamas, robes and infants' garments. Enforcement sits with local Trading Standards under these regulations and the 2005 regulations together.

Open the parcel, look inside the neck, and read what is printed there. That is a thirty-second check and it is the only one in this article that requires nothing but the garment.

sections.heading: Cords, hoods and the 7.5 centimetre rule
sections.html:
The second rulebook is BS EN 14682:2014, on cords and drawstrings, and it exists because children strangle on them. It splits childhood into two bands: young children from birth to 7 years, taken as heights up to 134cm; and older children and young persons from 7 to 14, up to 182cm for boys and 176cm for girls. It then divides the garment into zones.

In the head, neck and upper chest zone, drawstrings and functional cords are prohibited outright on young children's clothing, and decorative cords may not appear on hoods or at the back of the neck, with no knots or three-dimensional embellishments. For older children the same zone allows a drawstring with no free ends, a protruding loop no more than 15cm in circumference measured at the smallest opening, functional cords limited to 7.5cm, no elastic in a functional cord, and toggles fixed to the garment.

Lower down, the limits loosen and stay precise. On trousers, shorts and skirts, drawstring free ends may run to 20cm each; on shirts, coats and dresses, 14cm each with the garment open and flat. A tied belt or sash is capped at 36cm from the tying point. Below the hip, no cord may hang below the lower edge of the garment, and fringes count as a series of decorative cords. At the back, drawstrings and functional cords are banned and decorative cords are held to 7.5cm. On long sleeves, free ends stop at 7.5cm and nothing below the elbow may extend past the cuff; on short sleeves the limit is 7.5cm for young children and 14cm for older ones. A drawstring must be bar-tacked at its middle so it cannot be pulled out in one piece.

None of that is a legal requirement in the way the nightwear labelling is. A standard of this kind creates a presumption: a product that meets the relevant standard is presumed safe. It is still the best single test a parent can apply to a hooded top bought online, and the numbers are short enough to remember — nothing at the neck under seven, nothing hanging past a hem, 7.5cm anywhere at the back.

sections.heading: What the recall register shows, and what it does not
sections.html:
The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes every UK product recall, safety report and safety alert in one free database on GOV.UK. It held 3,730 reports when this page was written, and it is filtered by product category, so a parent can look up a brand before buying and a recall after.

Search it for nightwear and four recalls come back across five years: Lipsy girls' jersey nightwear on 9 July 2021, Shein children's sleepwear sets on 8 October 2021 marked high risk, an Asda older girls' leopard print pyjama set on 11 November 2022, and a La Redoute Alanis printed bathrobe on 15 September 2026. All four were recalls from end users, which is the strongest corrective action the register records. None of the four is an Amazon own-brand product.

Read that carefully in both directions. Four recalls in the whole register is a small number for a category with a mandatory flammability standard, and it says something reassuring about how rarely the rule is broken by businesses large enough to be traced. It is also a register of what was caught. A listing from a seller with no UK presence, taken down before anyone tested the garment, never reaches it. The categories most relevant to a parent — clothing, textiles and fashion items, and childcare articles and children's equipment — are both there to be browsed, and the most recent entry on the day of checking was a baby side sleeper wedge flagged as a serious risk on 21 September 2026.

sections.heading: Sending it back when it does not fit
sections.html:
Children's clothes are bought against a moving target, so the returns terms matter more here than in almost any other category. Amazon offers free return shipping on eligible items in Clothing, Shoes and Handbags, and charges sellers a returns processing fee on customer returns in those categories — a fee that does not apply to other fashion lines such as jewellery or luggage. Sellers who fulfil their own orders are automatically enrolled in prepaid returns labels and must provide a label or a returnless refund on every request, with 24 hours to respond to anything outside Amazon's standard policy.

Underneath all of that sits the statutory right, and it is narrower than most people assume. Regulation 30 of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 gives 14 days to cancel a distance sale, counted from the day the goods come into your physical possession; where an order is split into several deliveries, the clock starts when the last of them arrives. A retailer may give you longer and many do. None may give you less.

Haul is the exception worth planning around. Its return window is 15 days from delivery — one day past the statutory floor — and the item must be new, unused and unaltered. Set that against a delivery quoted at up to two weeks and the practical position is stark: a Haul coat ordered on the first of the month may not arrive until the fourteenth, leaving a fortnight in which a growing child must try it on, fail to fit it, and have it dropped at a Post Office, Asda or Morrisons collection point. Refunds are typically processed within seven days after that.

sections.heading: The rules for marketplaces are being rewritten
sections.html:
Until recently, British product safety law was built around manufacturers, importers and distributors — three roles that a website connecting a Chinese workshop to a Bolton doorstep does not obviously occupy. The Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025 changes that. Section 2(2)(e) expressly allows product regulations to cover the marketing of products through an online marketplace, and section 2(3) lists the people on whom requirements may be imposed: manufacturers, anyone who markets a product in the UK, importers, anyone controlling access to or the contents of an online marketplace, anyone acting as an intermediary, authorised representatives, and anyone carrying out monitoring, assessment, verification or certification.

The Act is a framework: it grants the powers, and the regulations made under it will decide what marketplaces have to do. Until they arrive, the General Product Safety Regulations 2005 and the sector rules above are what apply, and the practical burden of checking sits with the buyer.

OPSS has effectively said as much. Its online marketplaces safety campaign ran in two phases, November to December 2025 and February to March 2026, and its stakeholder toolkit sets out five checks to make before buying: look up the seller's name, location and how long they have been trading; read the detailed reviews rather than the star average, looking for comments about safety; check the description for instructions, warnings and material information; look for a UKCA or CE mark; and search GOV.UK for product recalls. The campaign's one published statistic is that nearly one in four people had bought a counterfeit electrical product online.

sections.heading: How Amazon scores against the shops it competes with
sections.html:
Which? surveys shoppers on baby and children's retailers and publishes the results, which is the nearest thing this category has to an independent rating. The most recent survey drew on 2,317 members of the public with fieldwork in July and August 2025, and set a category average customer score of 80%.

Amazon scored 81% — above the average and below most of its direct rivals in children's clothing. Next took 83%, Marks & Spencer and John Lewis 82% each, and JoJo Maman Bébé 76%. The best score in the survey went to UK Baby Centre on 86%, with Baby City and iCandy World on 85%; The Range came last on 74%. Seven retailers were named Which? Recommended Providers — Joie Baby, Maxi Cosi, Next, Smyths Toys, The Nursery Store, Bugaboo and John Lewis. Amazon was not among them.

A single percentage point above a category average is a fair summary of the Amazon children's clothing experience: it works, it is cheap, it arrives quickly, and the people who scored it did not love it the way they loved a specialist. Most retailers in the survey took four or five stars for customer service and delivery, with value for money typically at four.

sections.heading: What Which? found when it went looking for unsafe listings
sections.html:
Two pieces of Which? research sit behind the safety sections above, and both are specific about Amazon.

On 21 November 2025 Which? published research that took all 702 OPSS safety reports issued between 1 August 2024 and 11 August 2025, extracted 1,036 product images from them and reverse-image-searched 17 online marketplaces. It found close to 800 products matching items that regulators had already declared unsafe, more than 200 of them with immediately verifiable safety risks; 31% of the OPSS reports had a matching product still on sale; 98% of the matches related to reports graded serious or high risk; and 95% of the products had been available for at least 28 days after the warning. Among them were 71 baby sleeping bags with suffocation hazards. Amazon initially declined to remove sleeping bags reported to it and subsequently took down eight of the twelve products flagged.

On 8 July 2026 Which? published a follow-up covering 150 unsafe products across Alibaba, AliExpress, Amazon, eBay, Etsy, OnBuy, TikTok Shop and Wish. Nearly a quarter of the 150 were found on Amazon, including six dangerous sleeping bags, some of them fulfilled by Amazon itself. One example was a swaddle blanket for babies aged nought to six months with a hooded design and no arm holes, sold for nursery use — the same product Which? had reported to Amazon in January. Sue Davies, the organisation's head of consumer protection policy, said the lives of babies were at risk because the platforms would not stop dangerous products reaching their customers. Amazon removed the flagged listings while it investigated and pointed to its controls and its requirement for third-party laboratory testing; eBay, Etsy, TikTok Shop, AliExpress, Alibaba and OnBuy also removed items, and Wish did not respond.

Neither study is a study of children's clothing, and neither is a reason to avoid the shop. Both are a reason to treat the safety label as the thing you buy on, rather than the listing copy.

pros: Prices start at £1 on Amazon Haul, with most of the range under £10 and nothing above £20
Free return shipping on eligible Clothing, Shoes and Handbags items, and sellers must supply a prepaid label
Prime at £8.99 a month or £95 a year covers unlimited one-day delivery, with same-day on over a million items in 80-plus UK towns and cities
Around 100,000 UK small and medium-sized businesses sell through the site, which is where the depth of the cheap end comes from
Clothing referral fees of 5% to 15% are among the lowest Amazon charges, and were cut again on 5 January 2026
Competition and Markets Authority commitments running to 20 June 2028 bar Amazon from using Prime eligibility as a Featured Offer criterion
cons: Amazon Haul gives 15 days from delivery to request a return while quoting up to two weeks for the parcel to arrive, which is a tight window for a garment a child has to try on
Amazon's own two newsroom articles about Haul print different multi-buy thresholds — 5% over £30 and 10% over £50 on one, 5% over £50 and 10% over £75 on the other

Its 81% score in the Which? baby shops survey (2,317 respondents, July and August 2025) trails Next on 83% and Marks & Spencer and John Lewis on 82%, and it was not named a Which? Recommended Provider
Which? found nearly a quarter of 150 unsafe baby products on Amazon in its 8 July 2026 investigation, including six sleeping bags and one swaddle it had already reported in January
Where the seller is an independent business, the 14-day cancellation right under regulation 30 and any Consumer Rights Act claim run against that seller rather than against Amazon

Amazon's consumer terms — the conditions of sale, the store's A-to-z Guarantee wording and the clothing returns window — are published only on amazon.co.uk, which refuses automated access, so none of it could be read or quoted here and needs confirming on the site itself
verdict: Amazon is the cheapest broad children's clothing range in Britain and the fastest, and the numbers behind that are published rather than claimed: £1 entry prices on Haul, £95 a year for unlimited one-day delivery, referral fees of 5% on anything under £15 that keep small sellers in the category. It scores 81% with Which? shoppers against a category average of 80%, which is about right — competent rather than cherished. The reasons to be careful are structural rather than commercial. Most of what you buy comes from an independent seller, so that is who your legal rights run against; Haul's 15-day return window sits awkwardly beside its two-week delivery quote; and Which? has twice found unsafe baby goods listed on the site, once after flagging them. Buy on the label rather than the listing: children's nightwear must carry its BS 5722 wording inside the neck, and nothing should hang from the hood of anything made for a child under seven.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from on Amazon?
faqs.a: The trading entity behind Amazon.co.uk is Amazon EU S.à r.l., UK Branch, registered in the UK on 2 February 2015 under FC032354 and incorporated in Luxembourg; the main UK operating company is Amazon UK Services Ltd, company 03223028, incorporated on 10 July 1996 and registered at 1 Principal Place, Worship Street, London EC2A 2FA. Where a listing names an independent seller, however, your sale contract is with that business, not with Amazon.

faqs.q: How long do I have to send children's clothes back?
faqs.a: On the main store, eligible Clothing, Shoes and Handbags items carry free return shipping and sellers must provide a prepaid label. On Amazon Haul the window is 15 days from delivery and the item must be new, unused and unaltered. Underneath both sits regulation 30 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, which gives 14 days from the day the goods reach you — a floor no retailer may go below.

faqs.q: What should I check on a child's pyjamas?
faqs.a: Look inside the neck. Under the Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985 anything designed for a child under 13 must carry either KEEP AWAY FROM FIRE in red or LOW FLAMMABILITY TO BS 5722 in black, and a flame-retardant-treated garment must add DO NOT WASH AT MORE THAN 50 °C. Pyjamas, cotton terry-towelling robes and infants' garments up to three months with a chest of 53cm or less are exempt from the BS 5722 performance requirement but not from the labelling regime.

faqs.q: Are hooded tops with drawstrings allowed for young children?
faqs.a: BS EN 14682:2014 prohibits drawstrings and functional cords in the head, neck and upper chest zone of clothing for children from birth to seven years, and bars decorative cords on hoods or at the back of the neck. For children of seven to fourteen the same zone allows a drawstring with no free ends and a protruding loop of no more than 15cm, with functional cords capped at 7.5cm.

faqs.q: Is Amazon Prime worth it for buying children's clothes?
faqs.a: That depends on how often you order. Prime is £95 a year or £8.99 a month, which is the equivalent of 31 separate £2.99 Haul delivery charges, or a little over six Haul baskets brought up to the £15 free-delivery threshold. If your orders are planned and infrequent, Haul plus the two-week wait is cheaper; if you buy in small quantities at short notice, the annual fee pays for itself quickly.

faqs.q: Where do I report something unsafe?
faqs.a: The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes UK product recalls, safety reports and safety alerts at gov.uk — 3,730 reports as at 25 September 2026, filtered by product category, including clothing, textiles and fashion items. Enforcement against a seller is carried out by local Trading Standards, which consumers reach through Citizens Advice rather than directly.

title: Amazon Computers: What You Get, What Renewed Means and Who Pays the VAT
meta_title: Amazon Computers: Renewed Cover, Warranty and VAT
meta_description: Amazon Renewed computers carry a one-year guarantee and a battery floor of 80%. Seller fees, VAT invoices and the safety register, checked 25 September 2026.
intro:
Amazon takes 7% of the sale price when a seller lists a computer, against 15% on most other categories, and every refurbished machine sold through Amazon Renewed carries a guarantee of one year from the day it arrives. Both figures were checked on 25 September 2026 against Amazon's own seller pricing schedule and its published Renewed quality policy, not against any comparison site.

Those two numbers explain most of what a buyer sees. The low referral fee is why the computer listings run so deep — a reseller keeps 93p in the pound here and 85p in most other departments — and the one-year guarantee is why Amazon is now one of the larger refurbished-computer shops in the country without owning a single refurbishment workshop. The scale behind it is real: Amazon's second quarter of 2026, the three months to 30 June, produced net sales of $200.6 billion, of which $46.8 billion came from third-party seller services alone.

One thing is worth knowing before you start comparing listings. A computer on Amazon can reach you three different ways — sold by Amazon itself, sold by an independent seller, or sold as Renewed by an approved refurbisher — and the guarantee, the VAT invoice and the condition of the battery are different in each case. None of that is hidden, but none of it is on the listing in one place either.

headline.label: Warranty included in the price
headline.value: 1 year on every Amazon Renewed computer, backed by Amazon itself — a new machine carries only the manufacturer's own cover

key_facts.label: Amazon Renewed Guarantee
key_facts.value: One year from the customer receiving the product, in the UK, France, Germany, Spain and Italy

key_facts.value: Capacity must exceed 80% of the new equivalent

key_facts.label: Cosmetic standard
key_facts.value: No scratches or dents visible with the product held 30 centimetres away

key_facts.label: Who may sell Renewed
key_facts.value: £20,000 of qualifying refurbished purchase invoices in the previous 90 days, and an order defect rate of 0.8% or less

key_facts.label: Data on a used machine
key_facts.value: Forensic destruction of personally identifiable information to NIST standards

key_facts.label: A-to-z Guarantee
key_facts.value: Extended in the UK in May 2024 to cover property damage and personal injury from a defective product

sections.heading: The word Renewed has a written specification behind it
sections.html:
Most shops that sell refurbished computers describe the grading in their own words. Amazon publishes a quality policy that applies across the UK, France, Germany, Spain and Italy, and it is unusually specific about the physical object rather than the paperwork.

A Renewed product must be "inspected, repaired (if applicable), cleaned and tested to function and look like new". The cosmetic test is a measured one: no signs of cosmetic damage such as scratches or dents should be visible when the product is held 30 centimetres away. Any markings already on the outside — the maker's logo, for instance — have to be intact, and no new markings may be added. Batteries must have a capacity that exceeds 80% of the new equivalent. The machine has to come with every accessory a new one would include, and those accessories must themselves be original parts or refurbished to like-new condition.

Two further requirements matter more on a computer than on a kettle. Personally identifiable information must be destroyed forensically, to NIST standards — that is the previous owner's data, and it is the thing a private buyer of a second-hand laptop has no way of auditing. And the box has to do its job: original packaging or a new cardboard box, clean and free of damage, markings and unrelated labels, with the product and accessories compartmentalised so they are not in direct contact, and the whole thing has to pass drop tests based on widely adopted standards.

The guarantee sitting on top of that is one year after the customer receives the product. That is Amazon's own promise, separate from anything the original manufacturer may or may not still honour on a machine that has already had one owner.

sections.heading: Not every seller is allowed near the programme
sections.html:
The entry requirements are the part of Renewed that a shopper never sees, and they do more work than the branding does.

To be approved, a seller has to supply invoices showing a total value of £20,000 in qualifying refurbished purchases in the previous 90 days. For Apple smartphones the bar is £1 million in Apple refurbished products, which gives a sense of how the thresholds are calibrated to the fraud risk in each brand. The seller's refurbishment process has to include a diagnostic test, replacement of any defective parts, a cleaning and inspection process and repackaging where applicable, and they must submit a minimum of ten images of a sample unit so that the product and its packaging can be reviewed before anything is listed. Running performance is policed too: an order defect rate of 0.8% or less across a trailing 90 days.

Personal computers and tablets are both named categories in the programme, alongside phones, cameras, headphones, kitchen appliances, power tools, televisions and games consoles. A Professional selling account is the baseline for any of it.

Set that against a private sale or a general auction listing and the difference is not the warranty, it is the audit. Someone has checked the invoices, seen photographs of a sample machine and is watching the defect rate. That is a genuine consumer protection and it is not advertised anywhere on the product page.

sections.heading: Seven per cent, and why the listings run so deep
sections.html:
Amazon publishes what it charges sellers, and the schedule is the clearest explanation of why the computer aisle looks the way it does.

The referral fee on Computers is 7% of the sale price with a minimum of 25p. Consumer Electronics is also 7%. Electronic Accessories is 15% up to £100 and 8% on anything above that, and the default rate on categories with no specific listing is a flat 15%. A seller moving a £600 laptop therefore hands over £42; the same £600 spread across accessories would cost roughly twice that. A Professional selling plan costs £25 a month excluding VAT, or an Individual plan charges 75p per item sold.

Amazon's own accounts show the scale that margin operates at. In the second quarter of 2026 — the three months to 30 June — total net sales were $200.6 billion, up 20%. North America contributed $116.2 billion, International $42.2 billion and AWS $42.2 billion. Split by activity rather than geography, online stores produced $70.4 billion and third-party seller services $46.8 billion, with advertising at $19.8 billion and subscription services at $13.7 billion. Segment operating income ran to $27.5 billion in the quarter. Net income of $62.6 billion, or $5.75 a diluted share, is not a like-for-like trading figure: $53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income sits inside it, chiefly from Amazon's investments in Anthropic.

What none of that tells you is anything about Britain, or about computers. Amazon reports International as one line. There is no published UK computer sales figure, no UK unit count and no published count of how many machines are listed, so any such number a reader meets elsewhere has been estimated by somebody.

sections.heading: Buying through a company account, and the invoice underneath it
sections.html:
Computers are the category where the buyer is most likely to be a business, and Amazon Business exists for exactly that. It reports 11 million customers worldwide and $60 billion in annualised global sales, counts 97 of the Fortune 100 among its customers, and says B2B customers order 75% more units per order and make 30% fewer returns than consumer buyers. Business sellers offer VAT-exclusive prices and downloadable VAT invoices, and the quantity-discount and business-only pricing tools are offered to sellers at no additional charge.

The useful feature is a defensive one. Amazon Business lets an account display a "restricted" or "blocked" flag in search results and on product pages for items without an automatically downloadable VAT invoice. That flag matters most on exactly the machines this page has been discussing.

A refurbished computer is often sold under the VAT margin scheme, and HMRC's rules on it are unambiguous. The scheme covers goods on which the seller could not claim back any VAT when buying them. On a margin-scheme sale the seller "must not show VAT separately" on the invoice, and the invoice has to carry the words "Margin Scheme — second-hand goods". HMRC is equally clear the other way: if a purchase invoice shows a separate VAT amount, the item is not eligible to be sold under the scheme at all. The consequence for a VAT-registered buyer is simple and easy to miss — there is no VAT to reclaim on that laptop, so a £600 margin-scheme machine really costs £600, while a £600 machine bought with a full VAT invoice costs £500 net. That is a 20% difference in the true price of two listings that look identical in a search result.

sections.heading: Second-hand electricals come with their own rulebook
sections.html:
Selling used electrical goods in Great Britain is governed by the General Product Safety Regulations 2005 and the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994, and the trading standards guidance on it is more demanding than most sellers realise.

Before a used electrical item is offered for sale, a competent person should examine it for access to live parts, the adequacy of the insulation, and creepage and clearance. Test reports have to be kept and produced to enforcement officers on request. A dated portable appliance testing label alongside a UKCA or CE mark is treated as best practice rather than as proof — the guidance is explicit that such testing will not identify every hazard on its own. Any appliance must be supplied with an approved plug complying with BS 1363, carrying BSI or ASTA approval marks, with sleeved live and neutral pins and the correct fuse. Three-core mains leads must use the standard colours — green and yellow for earth, blue for neutral, brown for live — and leads have to be checked for fraying, breaks, kinks and exposed wires. A seller who supplies unsafe goods that go on to cause injury or damage may be liable to pay compensation, and enforcement sits with local trading standards.

Amazon's own remedy moved in the same direction in May 2024, when the A-to-z Guarantee was extended in the UK to cover customers where a defective product bought in its store causes property damage or personal injury — a step Amazon describes as going beyond its legal obligation. Under the broader A-to-z policy a seller has five business days to respond once a claim is opened.

sections.heading: The machine is regulated; the listing is the weak point
sections.html:
Computers sold in Great Britain still fall under the retained ecodesign regime for computers and computer servers, Commission Regulation (EU) No 617/2013. Its scope is drawn widely: desktop computers, integrated desktops, notebooks — including tablets, slate computers and mobile thin clients — desktop thin clients, workstations, mobile workstations, small-scale servers and computer servers. Blade systems, server appliances, multi-node servers, servers with more than four processor sockets, games consoles and docking stations are outside it. The substantive requirements applied from 1 July 2014, with a second tranche from 1 January 2016.

The register of things that have actually gone wrong tells a narrower story, and it is about the box in the bag rather than the machine. Searching the government's product safety alerts, reports and recalls database for "laptop" on 25 September 2026 returns 21 reports, and almost every one of them is a charger, an AC adapter or a power supply rather than a computer. Among them: a Lenovo USB-C laptop power bank recalled from end users on 30 November 2023; Toshiba AC adapters for laptops recalled from end users on 11 February 2025; a counterfeit USB-C laptop charger on 18 November 2025 where the outcome recorded is removal of the listing by the online marketplace; and a GEU 45W laptop charger rated high risk on 15 September 2026, stopped at the border. Several other entries record the same marketplace-removal outcome, and a handful end in destruction of the product.

Read that in both directions. Twenty-one reports across the whole register is a small number, and the fact that marketplaces are removing listings means the reporting chain works. It also means the hazard was on sale first, and that the replacement charger — the cheapest, most anonymous thing in the category — is where the risk concentrates rather than in the laptop itself.

sections.heading: What an independent survey will and will not tell you
sections.html:
For reliability rather than retailing, Which? surveys laptop owners directly. Its most recent work on which brands develop the fewest faults was an online survey carried out in February and March 2026, covering 15,755 people who own tech products, of whom 6,971 were laptop owners. A brand receiving a one-star reliability rating is automatically excluded from Which? recommendations.

The headline finding it makes public is a warning rather than a ranking: more than a third of Toshiba laptops developed some sort of fault within seven years of purchase. The brand-by-brand table itself sits behind a Which? membership, so a non-subscriber can see the method and one example and not the answer. That is worth saying plainly rather than working around, and it is a limit on this page as much as on any other.

The practical reading is that brand reliability and retailer choice are separate questions. Buying from Amazon does not change how a given laptop is built; what it changes is the paperwork behind the purchase and the route to a remedy if something fails.

pros: A published one-year Amazon Renewed Guarantee backed by Amazon itself, separate from any manufacturer cover left on a used machine
The Renewed quality policy sets measurable standards — 80% battery capacity, a 30-centimetre cosmetic test, NIST-grade data destruction and drop-tested packaging
Approved refurbishers must show £20,000 of qualifying purchase invoices over 90 days and hold an order defect rate of 0.8% or less
A 7% referral fee on computers, against 15% in the default category, keeps a very deep field of sellers in the aisle
Amazon Business flags listings that cannot produce an automatic VAT invoice, and its quantity-discount tools cost sellers nothing extra
The A-to-z Guarantee was widened in May 2024 to cover property damage and personal injury from a defective product, which Amazon itself calls more than the law requires
cons: A Renewed computer can arrive with a battery at 80% of a new one's capacity and still meet Amazon's own written standard — that figure is the floor, not the target, and it is the component most likely to decide when the machine is retired

The quality policy sets a single uniform standard and defines no condition grades, so the word Renewed describes the same test on a £200 machine and a £900 one, with no published way to tell a lightly used return from a heavily repaired unit

The substance of the guarantee lives in a quality-policy document rather than on the product page, and Amazon's consumer help pages are closed to automated readers, so the consumer-facing wording could not be checked line by line against the seller-facing policy. Treat the customer-side detail as needing confirmation from Amazon direct

A search of the government safety register for "laptop" returns 21 reports, and the outcome recorded again and again is removal of the listing by the online marketplace — which means the item had already been on sale

A margin-scheme refurbished machine can never produce a reclaimable VAT invoice, so a VAT-registered buyer comparing two identical-looking listings can be 20% out on the real cost unless they check every offer individually

Amazon publishes no UK figures for computers at all — no sales, no units, no listing count — so every scale number available is global or group-wide, and the International segment is reported as a single line covering dozens of countries
verdict: Amazon is the most heavily documented place to buy a used computer in Britain, which is not the same as the safest or the cheapest. The Renewed programme has a written specification, an audited entry bar and a one-year guarantee, and those are worth real money against a private sale. The two things to hold onto are the battery floor and the invoice: 80% of original capacity satisfies the policy, and a margin-scheme machine costs a VAT-registered buyer a fifth more than an identical listing with a full VAT invoice. Check both before comparing prices, and buy the charger from the manufacturer rather than from the cheapest listing.

faqs.q: How long is the Amazon Renewed guarantee?
faqs.a: One year, running from the day the customer receives the product. Amazon's Renewed quality policy applies that same period in the UK, France, Germany, Spain and Italy. It is Amazon's own guarantee and sits separately from whatever remains of the original manufacturer's warranty on a machine that has already had an owner.

faqs.q: Will a Renewed laptop have a worn-out battery?
faqs.a: It should not be worn out, but it need not be new. The policy requires a capacity exceeding 80% of the new equivalent, which is the minimum the machine has to meet rather than what it is expected to deliver. On a laptop whose usefulness is measured in hours away from a socket, that is the single figure worth asking the seller about before ordering.

faqs.q: Can I reclaim the VAT on a refurbished computer bought on Amazon?
faqs.a: Often not. Second-hand goods are frequently sold under HMRC's VAT margin scheme, and on a margin-scheme sale the seller must not show VAT separately and the invoice carries the words "Margin Scheme — second-hand goods". There is no VAT for the buyer to reclaim. An Amazon Business account can flag listings that cannot produce an automatically downloadable VAT invoice, which is the quickest way to spot the difference before ordering.

faqs.q: Who is allowed to sell as Amazon Renewed?
faqs.a: Sellers approved for the programme, which requires invoices showing £20,000 of qualifying refurbished purchases in the previous 90 days, a refurbishment process covering diagnostic testing, parts replacement, cleaning and repackaging, at least ten photographs of a sample unit for review, and an order defect rate of 0.8% or less over a trailing 90 days. Apple smartphones carry a much higher bar of £1 million in refurbished Apple stock.

faqs.q: What does Amazon charge a seller to list a computer?
faqs.a: A referral fee of 7% of the sale price with a minimum of 25p, the same rate as consumer electronics. Most categories without a specific rate pay 15%, and electronic accessories pay 15% up to £100 and 8% above it. On top of the referral fee a seller pays either £25 a month excluding VAT on the Professional plan or 75p per item sold on the Individual plan.

faqs.q: Are laptop chargers bought on a marketplace safe?
