faqs.a: They are the part of the category where problems cluster. A search of the government's product safety alerts, reports and recalls register for "laptop" returns 21 reports, and nearly all of them concern chargers, AC adapters and power supplies rather than computers — including a counterfeit USB-C charger whose listing an online marketplace removed in November 2025 and a 45W charger rejected at the border in September 2026. Buying the power supply from the machine's manufacturer avoids the whole question.

title: Amazon Fitness Wearables: The Fees, The Cover and What the Sensor Is Allowed to Claim
meta_title: Amazon Fitness Trackers: Accuracy, Cover and Safety
meta_description: Which? put wrist heart-rate error at 1.1% to 2.58% across 58 devices. Amazon's watch fees, Renewed cover and two Fitbit notices, checked 25 September 2026.
intro:
A fitness tracker sold on Amazon can cost anything from about £2 to close to £250, and the sellers crowding the cheap end are there partly because of the fee: Amazon takes 15% of a watch's price up to £225 and 5% of anything above that, against a flat 7% in Consumer Electronics. Those rates come from Amazon's own seller pricing page, read on 25 September 2026; the price band is Which?'s, from its fitness tracker buying guide.

Breadth is what the shop is for. Every serious wearable brand lists there alongside a long tail of £20 bands, and the marketplace machinery behind them is more visible than most shoppers realise. Amazon says it identified, seized and disposed of more than 15 million counterfeit products worldwide in 2025, and that its Counterfeit Crimes Unit has pursued more than 32,000 bad actors through litigation and criminal referrals since it was set up in 2020. Sellers using Fulfilment by Amazon have to label CE-marked goods with the contact details of a Responsible Person, which is the one piece of paperwork a buyer can check on the parcel.

One thing is worth knowing before you read a single product description. Nothing a wearable does under the heading of fitness is a regulated medical device. The MHRA's own guidance on stand-alone software says that "the monitoring of general fitness, general health and general wellbeing is not usually considered to be a medical purpose", and that apps and software monitoring sport or fitness, heart rate included, "are not considered to be medical devices". That is not a complaint about Amazon or about any brand. It is the frame the whole category sits in, and the rest of this page follows from it.

headline.label: Guarantee behind the device
headline.value: 1 year on an Amazon Renewed product — but traditional wristwatches are excluded from the Renewed Guarantee, so a refurbished watch rests on the seller's own terms (checked 25 September 2026)

key_facts.label: Seller referral fee on watches
key_facts.value: 15% of the price up to £225, then 5%, minimum 25p

key_facts.label: Referral fee on sports and outdoors
key_facts.value: 15% flat, minimum 25p

key_facts.label: Amazon Renewed Guarantee
key_facts.value: 1 year from receipt — traditional wristwatches excluded

key_facts.label: Regulatory status of fitness features
key_facts.value: Not a medical device: fitness heart-rate monitoring is not a medical purpose (MHRA)

key_facts.label: Best wrist heart-rate accuracy measured
key_facts.value: 1.1% error, Apple, across 58 devices tested by Which? (3 February 2026)

key_facts.label: Fitbit notices on the OPSS register
key_facts.value: 2 — Ionic recall 4 March 2022, Sense and Versa 3 report 20 January 2025

key_facts.label: Fitbit security update promise
key_facts.value: At least 2 years after a model is last sold on Fitbit.com or the Google Store

key_facts.label: Refund window after cancelling
key_facts.value: 14 days from the day Amazon receives the goods back (reg 34, Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013)

key_facts.label: Amazon's own wearable
key_facts.value: Halo switched off 31 July 2023; purchases in the preceding 12 months refunded

sections.heading: What a wrist sensor is allowed to say it does
sections.html:
Medical devices in Great Britain run on the Medical Devices Regulations 2002 (SI 2002 No 618, as amended), which still carries the old European directives rather than the EU's 2017 regulations. Anything that counts as a device has to be registered with the MHRA before it is placed on the Great Britain market, has to carry a UKCA mark or a still-accepted CE mark, and, where the manufacturer sits outside the UK, has to have a UK Responsible Person who holds written authority from that manufacturer and keeps the declaration of conformity and technical file available for inspection. CE-marked devices under the old directives are accepted in Great Britain until 30 June 2028; devices carrying EU MDR or IVDR marks, and in vitro diagnostics under the old IVD directive, until 30 June 2030.

Almost none of that touches a step counter. The MHRA's software guidance (version 1.10f) puts general fitness, general health and general wellbeing outside the definition, and says heart-rate monitoring for sport or fitness is not a medical device — with one exception, "where the intention is to investigate the physiological processes". Its newer guidance on digital mental health technology, updated on 3 July 2025, applies the same two-step test: does the product have a medical purpose, and does it do enough computationally to count, rather than merely storing, archiving, communicating or searching. A product aimed at sub-clinical or wellbeing-level symptoms stays outside; the same product aimed at clinically relevant ones comes inside, and most software that supplies diagnostic information lands in class IIa.

The practical consequence for a shopper is narrow and worth holding on to. A resting heart rate, a sleep score, a stress reading and a step count on a tracker bought from Amazon have been assessed by nobody. No regulator has looked at them, no approved body has signed anything, and the number on the screen is the manufacturer's own claim about its own sensor.

sections.heading: Apple publishes an error rate for its ECG app; the fitness features have none
sections.html:
The exception in the paragraph above is where the regulated features live, and Apple's ECG app is the clearest example a buyer can actually read about. Apple's own support documentation gives the trial figures: in a clinical study of roughly 600 subjects the app showed 99.6% specificity for sinus rhythm classification and 98.3% sensitivity for classifying atrial fibrillation, with the caveat that "real world use of the ECG app may result in a greater number of strips being deemed inconclusive and not classifiable".

The limits are published in the same place, and they are blunt. The app runs on Apple Watch Series 4 or later and all Apple Watch Ultra models, not on Apple Watch SE. It "is not intended for use by people under 22 years old". It "cannot detect a heart attack", "cannot detect blood clots or a stroke", and cannot detect high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, high cholesterol or other forms of arrhythmia.

Set those numbers against the rest of the category and the asymmetry is the useful finding. A feature that went through a conformity assessment publishes a sensitivity figure, a minimum age and a list of things it cannot do. A feature sold as fitness publishes a marketing figure and nothing else. On a listing page the two sit a centimetre apart in the same bullet list.

sections.heading: Fifteen per cent to £225, and why the watch aisle is so deep
sections.html:
Amazon's referral fees are published openly and they shape what a category looks like. Watches pay 15% of the portion of the total price up to £225 and 5% of any portion above it, with a 25p minimum. Jewellery pays 20% then 5% at the same £225 line. Sports and Outdoors pays a flat 15%. Electronic Accessories pays 15% up to £100 and 8% above. Consumer Electronics and Computers both pay 7%. On top of the referral fee a seller pays either £25 a month excluding VAT on the Professional plan or 75p per item sold on the Individual plan.

Those rates do real work. A £180 watch hands Amazon £27; the same £180 spent on a device classified as consumer electronics hands over £12.60. A £400 watch pays £33.75 — 15% of the first £225 plus 5% of the remaining £175 — so the marginal cost of selling an expensive watch falls away sharply above that line, while the cost of selling a cheap one does not. That is the commercial logic behind a category that is thick at £20 and thick again at £300, with less between.

It also explains something a shopper sees without being told. Where the same physical product can plausibly be listed as a watch, an accessory or consumer electronics, there is an eight percentage point incentive to pick the cheapest classification, and the category a listing sits in is chosen by the seller.

sections.heading: Renewed is a written standard that stops at the wristwatch
sections.html:
Amazon Renewed is the strongest consumer protection Amazon operates in hardware, and it is a proper specification rather than a badge. The Renewed Guarantee "will be valid for one year after a customer's receipt of a Renewed product". Batteries, "when present, must have a capacity that exceeds 80% of the new equivalent". Sellers cannot enter the programme casually: £20,000 of qualifying refurbished purchase invoices in the previous 90 days (£1 million for Apple smartphones), an order defect rate of 0.8% or less on a trailing 90 days, and a minimum of 10 images of a sample unit.

Read the quality policy for a wearable, though, and it runs out. The document's appendices cover wireless devices, personal computers, printers, small kitchen appliances, power tools and lawn and garden equipment, and softlines. It explicitly excludes "traditional wristwatches" from the Renewed Guarantee, and it does not mention smartwatches or fitness bands at all. Amazon's seller-facing page lists phones, cameras, headphones, kitchen appliances, power tools, personal computers, tablets, televisions and video game consoles as examples and points to programme policies for the full list, which is not published to shoppers.

So the sentence a refurbished-laptop buyer relies on cannot be relied on for a refurbished watch, and the exact position of a smartwatch under the policy could not be established from the documents that are public. That needs confirming with Amazon rather than assuming either way. What is certain is that the 80% battery floor is Amazon's own number, and on a wearable it would matter more than on anything else: a tracker whose selling point is multi-day battery life can meet the standard having already lost a fifth of it.

sections.heading: Two Fitbit notices sit on the public register
sections.html:
The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes every UK recall and safety report free, and a search for the word smartwatch on 25 September 2026 returned three entries. Two are Fitbit and one is a recall of Dorland 'Intrinsically Safe' electronic equipment sold via Amazon, published 7 April 2025 and rated serious.

The first Fitbit entry is case 2203-0041, dated 4 March 2022 and published on 9 March 2022: a recall from end users of the Fitbit Ionic, model FB503, made between January 2017 and December 2020 in Taiwan and China. The battery "can overheat, presenting a risk of burns when the product is in use", and the notice records the product as breaching the General Product Safety Regulations 2005. Owners were told to stop using it and register for a refund.

The second is case 2509-0315, a product safety report dated 20 January 2025 covering the Fitbit Sense and Versa 3, manufactured between August 2020 and September 2022 and sold from September 2020 to September 2023. The risk is again burns from batteries overheating in normal use, rated low. The remedy is the interesting part: Fitbit LLC deployed a remote firmware update in January 2025 that reduces battery capacity to mitigate the overheating, pushed by email, device notification and the app, with factory resets applied to devices that had not taken it. Owners may qualify for what the notice calls an appeasement; neither the OPSS notice nor the UK-facing support pages state a sterling amount, so what it is worth needs confirming with Fitbit.

One search tip, because the register rewards precision and punishes vagueness. Smartwatch returns three results and fitbit returns two, but fitness tracker returns 576, because the search treats the words as alternatives and matches every fitness machine and every fitting on the database. Read a small number carefully in both directions: two notices on the best-known brand in the category is reassuring about a business that can be found and made to act, and says nothing at all about a £19 band from a seller nobody has tested.

sections.heading: Support ends before the strap does
sections.html:
A wearable is a computer, and its useful life is decided by software as much as by the case. Google publishes the security update commitment for Fitbit devices in one table, and the promise is "security updates for at least two years after the applicable device is last sold on Fitbit.com or the Google Store".

The dates in that table are worth reading next to the safety notice above. Support for the Fitbit Sense ended in September 2025 and for the Versa 3 in December 2025 — the two models named in the January 2025 report are both out of security support now, while stock of them still turns up for sale. The Charge 5 also ended in December 2025, the Inspire 2 in April 2026 and the Luxe in June 2026. Current models run longer: the Charge 6, Inspire 3, Sense 2 and Versa 4 are listed to February 2028, and the Fitbit Air to May 2028.

Amazon has been on the other side of this. Its own wearable was withdrawn: Amazon stopped supporting Halo on 31 July 2023, and from 1 August 2023 "Amazon Halo devices, and the Amazon Halo app, will no longer function". It refunded purchases of the Halo View, Halo Band, Halo Rise and accessory bands made in the preceding 12 months, plus unused prepaid subscription fees, and gave customers until 1 August 2023 to download or delete their health data before the rest was deleted. A 12-month refund window is a reasonable gesture and it is also the measure of the risk: a wearable bought 13 months earlier was worth nothing the day the servers went off.

sections.heading: Sending back something you have already worn
sections.html:
Buying online carries a cancellation right that a shop does not have to give, and the money side of it is set out in regulation 34 of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013. The trader "must reimburse all payments, other than payments for delivery, received from the consumer", within 14 days of receiving the goods back where it has not offered to collect them, or 14 days after being told of the decision to cancel where it has.

Regulation 34(9) is the part that bites on a wearable. Where "the value of the goods is diminished by any amount as a result of handling of the goods by the consumer beyond what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods, the trader may recover that amount from the consumer, up to the contract price". Trying a watch on and checking that the sensor lights up is establishing how it works. Wearing it for a fortnight of training, showering in it and scuffing the bezel is not, and the deduction is lawful. The protection in regulation 34(11) is that no deduction may be made at all if the trader failed to give the cancellation information in the first place.

Amazon's own returns window and its rules on worn goods could not be quoted here. Every path on www.amazon.co.uk refuses automated retrieval under its robots file, re-tested on a help page on 25 September 2026, so the store's published terms are readable by a person in a browser and not by anything else. Read them yourself before you buy a watch you may send back, and treat the statutory position above as the floor rather than the whole answer.

sections.heading: Independent testing, and the point at which it goes behind a paywall
sections.html:
Which? published the most useful comparison in this category on 3 February 2026, and it is about the one thing every wearable claims. It measured 58 devices against medical-grade chest straps, counting how often the watch disagreed with the strap. Apple came out lowest overall at 1.1% error, then Oppo at 1.47% and Google at 1.79%; Garmin sat at 2.5% and Samsung at 2.58%. The spread within a brand was wider than the gap between brands in places — Google managed 0.74% at rest and 3.08% while walking.

Two caveats belong with those figures. The brand samples are uneven: Oppo was represented by a single model, Google and Polar by two each, so a brand average is not a model verdict. And error against a chest strap is a measure of agreement, not of clinical accuracy — the strap is the reference, not the truth.

The same testing programme is unsparing about the cheap end. One tracker recorded 10,000 steps when 3,400 had been taken, out by 66%, which is the sort of result that turns a health target into a number. Which? says good trackers commonly cost £80 to £150 while the category runs from as little as £2 to close to £250, and it rates comfort, distance, blood oxygen where claimed, battery life and day-to-day consistency alongside steps and heart rate. The individual test scores and the model-by-model table are members-only; the brand accuracy figures above are the part published openly. Saying so is more honest than working around it.

sections.heading: The rules tightened in June 2025, and again in June 2026
sections.html:
Two changes have landed since these devices became mainstream, and both point the same way. The Medical Devices (Post-market Surveillance Requirements) (Amendment) (Great Britain) Regulations 2024, SI 2024 No 1368, were made on 16 December 2024 and came into force six months later. They oblige a manufacturer to run a post-market surveillance plan that is "clear, organised and searchable" for the life of the device, to report a serious incident no later than 15 days after becoming aware of it, a serious public health threat within 2 days and a death or unanticipated serious deterioration within 10 days, to report significant increases in the frequency or severity of incidents as a trend, and to produce a periodic safety update report within a year of the device going on sale and then at least annually. Records are kept for 15 years for an implantable device and 10 years for anything else. None of that applies to a device that is not a medical device, which is the point: the rules that produce a public paper trail stop exactly where the fitness label starts.

The other change came from the advertising regulator, and it is recent. On 17 June 2026 the ASA upheld four complaints against Hume Health LLC over adverts for its smart scales and its wearable band, which had been promoted as "YOUR 2026 STROKE DETECTOR", as "like wearing an ICU monitor on your wrist" and as giving "the same data as those DEXA scans". The ASA found breaches of CAP Code rules 12.1 and 12.2 — medical claims for products with no MHRA registration or applicable conformity marking, and claims liable to discourage people from seeking essential treatment — as well as rules 3.1, 3.7 and 3.11 on misleading and exaggerated claims. On the same day it upheld a ruling against HealthTracker Apps, trading as Blood Pressure Monitor App, where a colour-coded chart "implied the app could analyse users' blood pressure readings to indicate whether they were normal, borderline or high" when the app only logged what was typed into it.

Neither ruling is about Amazon, and neither is about the established brands. They are about the wording used to sell wrist sensors, which is the wording a marketplace listing is written in, and they set out plainly what a product with no conformity marking may not claim.

pros: The widest selection in the category, from roughly £2 bands to premium watches, with the brands and the long tail in one place
Seller costs are published rather than hidden: 15% to £225 then 5% on watches, 7% on consumer electronics, 25p minimum, £25 a month or 75p an item
Fulfilment by Amazon requires CE-marked goods to carry the Responsible Person's contact details on the product, packaging, parcel or an accompanying document
Amazon reports seizing more than 15 million counterfeit products in 2025 and pursuing more than 32,000 bad actors since 2020
Where Renewed does apply, it is a written standard: one-year guarantee, batteries above 80% of new capacity, a £20,000 invoice bar and a 0.8% order defect ceiling for sellers
Amazon refunded Halo purchases made in the 12 months before the product was switched off, and let customers export their health data first
cons: The Renewed Guarantee excludes traditional wristwatches and says nothing about smartwatches, so the one-year cover a refurbished laptop carries may not exist on a refurbished watch — and the full permitted-product list is published only to sellers
A watch pays 15% referral fee to £225 where the same sensor sold as consumer electronics pays 7%, and the seller chooses the category the listing sits in

No fitness feature on any of these devices has been assessed by a regulator: the MHRA treats fitness heart-rate monitoring as outside the medical device rules, so the numbers on screen are the manufacturer's own claim

Amazon's own store pages refuse automated retrieval, re-tested 25 September 2026, so its returns window, its rules on worn goods, its delivery promises and its prices could not be quoted or checked here
Which?'s model-by-model scores are behind membership; only the brand-level accuracy figures are public, and the brand samples are as small as one model
Security support on Fitbit's Sense ended in September 2025 and on the Versa 3 in December 2025 — the two models in the January 2025 safety report — while stock still appears for sale
Amazon Halo shows the platform risk in the category: devices and app stopped working on 1 August 2023 and refunds reached only purchases made in the previous 12 months
verdict: As a place to buy a fitness wearable Amazon is hard to beat on range and on price, and it is more transparent about its own economics than most retailers: the 15% referral fee to £225, the 7% on consumer electronics and the £25 monthly plan are all published. The gap is cover rather than choice. Renewed's one-year guarantee, the strongest thing Amazon offers on hardware, excludes traditional wristwatches and is silent on smartwatches, and the store's own returns terms cannot be read by anything but a browser. Buy the brand's warranty as much as the device — Polar publishes two years, and Fitbit publishes the date its security updates stop — check the model against the free OPSS register before you pay, and treat every fitness number on the box as a claim nobody has audited. The one figure on this page that came from a regulated feature, Apple's 98.3% sensitivity for atrial fibrillation, exists precisely because that feature was assessed and the fitness ones were not.

faqs.q: Is a fitness tracker bought on Amazon a medical device?
faqs.a: No. The MHRA's guidance on stand-alone software says the monitoring of general fitness, general health and general wellbeing is not usually a medical purpose, and that monitoring heart rate for sport or fitness is not a medical device. Specific features can be regulated separately — Apple's ECG app is the clearest example — and those carry a UKCA or accepted CE mark and an MHRA registration. Everything else on the device has been assessed by nobody.

faqs.q: Does the Amazon Renewed one-year guarantee cover a refurbished smartwatch?
faqs.a: The Renewed quality policy explicitly excludes traditional wristwatches from the guarantee and does not mention smartwatches or fitness bands, and the full list of permitted products is published only to sellers. So the answer could not be established from public documents and is worth asking Amazon before buying refurbished. Where Renewed does apply the guarantee runs for one year from receipt and batteries must exceed 80% of the capacity of a new equivalent.

faqs.q: How accurate is wrist heart-rate measurement?
faqs.a: Which? measured 58 devices against medical-grade chest straps and published the results on 3 February 2026: Apple 1.1% error, Oppo 1.47%, Google 1.79%, Garmin 2.5% and Samsung 2.58%. Accuracy varies by activity more than by brand in places — Google was 0.74% out at rest and 3.08% out while walking. Brand samples were small, with one Oppo model and two each from Google and Polar, so treat the figures as brand averages rather than model verdicts.

faqs.q: Can I return a fitness tracker I have already worn?
faqs.a: Distance selling gives you a cancellation right, and regulation 34 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 says the trader must reimburse all payments other than delivery within 14 days of getting the goods back. But regulation 34(9) lets it deduct for any loss of value caused by handling beyond what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods. Trying it on is fine; two weeks of training in it is not, and the deduction can run up to the contract price. No deduction is allowed if you were never given the cancellation information.

faqs.q: Have any fitness wearables been recalled in the UK?
faqs.a: Yes. The OPSS register holds a recall from end users of the Fitbit Ionic, model FB503, dated 4 March 2022, over a battery that can overheat and cause burns, and a product safety report of 20 January 2025 on the Fitbit Sense and Versa 3 for the same risk, rated low, remedied by a firmware update that reduces battery capacity. Searching the register is free at gov.uk; use a single tight keyword, because smartwatch returns three results while fitness tracker returns 576.

faqs.q: How long will a tracker keep getting software updates?
faqs.a: Google commits to security updates for Fitbit devices for at least two years after the model is last sold on Fitbit.com or the Google Store, and publishes the end date for every model. The Sense ended in September 2025, the Versa 3 and Charge 5 in December 2025, the Inspire 2 in April 2026 and the Luxe in June 2026, while the Charge 6, Inspire 3, Sense 2 and Versa 4 run to February 2028. Other brands do not all publish an equivalent table, so check before you buy an older model cheaply.

faqs.q: What can a wearable legally claim in its advertising?
faqs.a: Less than some listings suggest. On 17 June 2026 the ASA upheld complaints against Hume Health LLC for advertising a wearable band as a stroke detector and as being like wearing an ICU monitor on the wrist, finding breaches of CAP Code rules 12.1 and 12.2 because the products had no MHRA registration or applicable conformity marking, as well as rules 3.1, 3.7 and 3.11 on misleading and exaggerated claims. A separate ruling the same day went against an app whose colour-coded chart implied it could analyse blood pressure readings when it only logged what was typed in.

title: Amazon Furniture
meta_title: Amazon Furniture: Delivery, Returns and the Fire Label
meta_description: Amazon takes 15% on furniture to £175 and 10% above. What that buys: room-of-choice delivery, a 30-day return window, and a label worth checking.

headline.label: Return window on a large item
headline.value: 30 days to start the return, with the seller's courier due within 15 calendar days — checked 26 September 2026

key_facts.label: Seller referral fee, Furniture
key_facts.value: 15% of the first £175, then 10% on the rest, minimum 25p

key_facts.label: Counts as heavy or bulky
key_facts.value: Over 23kg, or any packed side longer than 175cm

key_facts.label: Room-of-choice delivery
key_facts.value: Included with Scheduled Delivery; Standard Delivery stops at the front entrance for items under 31.5kg and under £250

key_facts.label: Marketplace cover
key_facts.value: A-to-z Guarantee, claimable up to 90 days after the last delivery date

key_facts.label: Statutory cancellation right
key_facts.value: 14 days from receipt, extended voluntarily to 30 days for unused goods

key_facts.label: Fire label to look for
key_facts.value: A permanent label headed CARELESSNESS CAUSES FIRE, required since the 1988 Regulations

key_facts.label: Ombudsman membership
key_facts.value: None — Amazon is absent from the Furniture & Home Improvement Ombudsman's 2026 member list

key_facts.label: FBA heavy and bulky handling
key_facts.value: £15.43 up to 20kg, rising to £44.25 at 50–60kg and 39p per kg beyond

intro:
Amazon takes 15% of a furniture sale up to £175 and 10% of everything above that line, which makes furniture the cheapest large category on its published rate card — kitchenware and mattresses both pay a flat 15%, and tools 13%. Those rates were read from Amazon's own seller pricing page on 26 September 2026, and they explain a great deal about why the aisle looks the way it does.

What Amazon has built behind that rate card is a genuine bulky-goods operation rather than a parcel service pretending to handle wardrobes. Anything over 23kg, or with a packed side longer than 175cm, is routed through a separate network: Scheduled Delivery lets you pick a date and a slot, carriage into the room of your choice is part of it, and eligible items can be bought with unpacking, assembly and removal of the old one added at checkout. Sellers using Amazon's own warehouses can put items of up to 140kg and 300cm through the same pipes.

Most furniture on the site is sold by third-party businesses rather than by Amazon, and that is worth knowing before you click rather than after. It is not a warning: purchases from those sellers carry the A-to-z Guarantee, which you can claim on for up to 90 days after the last delivery date, and which also reaches property damage and personal injury caused by a product bought on the site. It does change who turns up if a sofa has to go back, and that is covered further down.

sections.heading: The rate card, and what it tells you about the aisle
sections.html:
Amazon publishes what it charges the businesses selling on it, and for furniture the schedule is tiered rather than flat: 15% of the first £175 of the sale price, 10% of the portion above it, with a 25p minimum on any item. Sit that beside the neighbouring categories and the shape of the shop becomes clear. Home Products pay 8% at or below £20 and 15% above it. Kitchen pays 15%. Mattresses pay 15%. Tools and Home Improvement, along with door, window and shower accessories, pay 13%. Amazon reduced a number of these rates across its European stores on 5 January 2026.

On top of the commission a seller pays either 75p per item sold on the Individual plan or £25 a month excluding VAT on the Professional plan. If they also store the goods in Amazon's warehouses under the heavy and bulky programme, handling is charged per item: £15.43 up to 20kg, £18.48 from 20 to 30kg, £19.16 from 30 to 40kg, then a sharp step to £42.98 at 40 to 50kg and £44.25 at 50 to 60kg, with anything heavier at 39p per kilogram. The eligibility band for that programme in the UK runs from 31.5kg to 140kg, with a length of 175cm to 300cm or a girth of at least 360cm.

The arithmetic matters to a buyer for one reason. A three-piece suite at £900 hands Amazon £26.25 on the first £175 and £72.50 on the rest — £98.75, or about 11% — before a penny of handling. A £90 flat-pack chest of drawers hands over £13.50, a full 15%. The tapering fee is a deliberate invitation to list expensive furniture, and it is the reason the upper end of the range on Amazon is deeper than most people expect it to be.

sections.heading: Getting a wardrobe through your front door
sections.html:
Amazon treats an item as heavy or bulky once it passes 23kg or has any side longer than 175cm when packed, and from that point the delivery behaves differently from a parcel. On Scheduled Delivery you choose the date and time window at the checkout and placement in the room you want is included. On Standard Delivery you get an estimated date, the driver will normally ring around 30 minutes before arriving, and — this is the detail people miss — an item under 31.5kg priced below £250 is only carried as far as the entrance to your home. Getting it upstairs is either a Scheduled Delivery or a paid add-on.

Where a service is offered it is bought at the point of purchase and not afterwards: unpacking with removal of all the packaging, installation and assembly, wall mounting where that applies, and recycling of the item being replaced. Amazon does not take payment for any of it until the work is finished, though the card is authorised at the time of the order. An adult has to be there, appointments can be changed up to 24 hours beforehand, and a signature may be required on the delivery itself. Availability is regional, and some postcodes simply cannot be served.

Sellers who fulfil their own heavy and bulky orders either have the carrier telephone to agree a date, or publish a calendar of slots for the buyer to choose from. That is a materially different experience from Amazon's own network, and nothing on a listing page makes the distinction obvious before you order.

sections.heading: The label sewn inside the sofa
sections.html:
Upholstered furniture sold in the UK has to satisfy the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, and there is no version of the rules that applies less strictly because the seller is on a marketplace. Four things have to be true: filling materials must meet the ignition requirements in Schedule 1 for foam or Schedule 2 for non-foam fillings, the upholstery composite must pass the cigarette test in Schedule 4, the cover must pass the match test in Schedule 5 or sit over a compliant interliner, and a permanent label must be attached to every item apart from mattresses and bed bases.

That label is the one thing on this entire subject a buyer can check with nothing but the delivered item. It is headed CARELESSNESS CAUSES FIRE and it carries the supplier's name and postcode, a batch or identification number, the date of manufacture or import, a description of the filling and the covering, and whether a Schedule 3 interliner is present. It has to be durable and securely fixed to an external surface, usually beneath a seat cushion or behind a loose cover. Trading Standards guidance treats a stitched label as a better sign than a stapled one, because stapling suggests it was added after the fact. Mattresses are labelled instead against BS 7177.

Second-hand upholstery is caught by the same regime, with one exemption: furniture made before 1 January 1950, and upholstery materials for it, falls outside the Regulations. Anything newer that arrives without a legible permanent label should not have been sold, and that applies to a private resale as much as to a shop.

sections.heading: What changed on 30 October 2025
sections.html:
The 1988 Regulations were amended by SI 2025/531, made on 28 April 2025, laid before Parliament on 30 April and brought into force on 30 October 2025 after a six-month deferral to meet World Trade Organization obligations. The changes followed a public consultation held between August and October 2023 and announced in January 2025.

Three things moved. The display label — the swing ticket that used to hang off new furniture in a showroom — was abolished outright, with regulation 10 omitted and its schedules deleted, on the reasoning that the permanent label already carries the compliance information. Stock still bearing an accurate display label may go on being sold. A long list of baby and child products came out of the definition of furniture altogether, including prams, pushchairs, buggies and strollers, cots, cribs, cradles, carry cots, Moses baskets, travel cots and bedside sleepers, cot bumpers, play pens, play mats, changing mats, baby nests, rockers and bouncers, highchairs, booster seats, baby walkers and children's car seats, along with children's mattresses under 170cm long and 75cm wide. Those products are now governed by general product safety law instead. And the window for prosecuting a breach was extended from six months to twelve months from the date the offence was committed, across all four UK nations, with no retrospective effect on anything done before 30 October 2025.

For anyone buying online the practical consequence of the first change is small but real: the ticket that a shopper in a showroom could once read at a glance no longer exists, so the permanent label is now the whole of the evidence, and it cannot be seen until the thing is in the house.

sections.heading: Why the fire rules are written the way they are
sections.html:
Home Office figures for the year ending March 2026 put the case better than any argument about regulation could. Fire and rescue services in England attended 26,180 dwelling fires in that year, up 2.8% on the 25,465 of the year before. There were 184 fire-related fatalities in dwellings, 72% of all fire deaths, and that figure fell 14% from 214.

Inside those numbers, textiles, upholstery and furnishings were the item first ignited in 27% of primary dwelling fires and were mainly responsible for the spread of the fire in 22% of them. They were associated with 48% of the deaths. Cooking appliances start far more fires — 42% — and kill far fewer people. A sofa is not usually what starts a house fire; it is very often what turns one into a fatal one. That asymmetry is the entire reason a piece of upholstered furniture carries a label and a toaster does not.

sections.heading: Sending it back, and the clause that stops you
sections.html:
Two separate rights run in parallel. The statutory one gives 14 days from receipt to cancel a distance purchase for any reason at all. Amazon's own policy is more generous and gives 30 days from receipt for unused, undamaged goods, which is the number most people are working from without realising the two are different.

For a heavy or bulky marketplace item — 31.5kg or more, or a longest packed side over 175cm — the process is its own thing. The return has to be started within 30 days of delivery, after which collection cannot be guaranteed and the matter becomes a negotiation with the seller. Once started, the seller has 48 hours to supply carrier details and a collection date through the messaging service, and collection is due within 15 calendar days in the UK or 22 for an international seller. An adult has to be present, and the item should be taken apart and packed, ideally in what it arrived in. If it turned up damaged or faulty, a free replacement or a full refund with home collection can be asked for instead.

Where the buyer simply changed their mind, return postage is charged from £1.99 in the UK and £8.09 internationally unless the item was both sold and dispatched by Amazon and flagged as eligible for free return. On Global Store orders the site automatically refunds return postage up to £20 for a US seller and £15 for an EU one.

The clause that catches furniture buyers is regulation 28(1) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, which removes the cancellation right entirely for goods made to the consumer's specifications or clearly personalised. A sofa ordered in a chosen fabric, a wardrobe cut to a stated width, a bed built to order: none of those has to be taken back because the buyer has changed their mind, and Amazon's own policy records customised products as not returnable, refundable only where they arrive damaged or defective. The fault-based rights survive; the free trial of the purchase does not.

sections.heading: Two recalls with an order number attached
sections.html:
The Office for Product Safety and Standards runs a free, searchable register of product safety alerts, reports and recalls, and it is the most useful thing a furniture buyer can look at before ordering. A search on the word furniture returned 83 reports on 26 September 2026, and a search on sofa returned 16.

Two of them name a product sold on Amazon. On 27 November 2025 a Yaheetech recliner armchair, model 610887 in grey, batches 202507 and 202508, was recalled from end users at serious risk of fire for failing to meet the requirements of the 1988 Regulations; the register records the Amazon ASIN, B0BDKX966B, as the sales channel, and names Monumart Ltd as the distributor handling returns. On 15 May 2026 a Yaheetech velvet convertible sofa bed, model 615825 in modern grey, batch Y02058B-202511, sold between January and April 2026 and made in China, was recalled on the finding that the foam filling could catch fire and continue to flame. Both were notified by local authority Trading Standards, and both offered a full refund including postage.

Read that in both directions. The system worked: a national regulator published the model number, the batch and the marketplace identifier, and a refund route exists. It also means a fire-risk armchair reached British living rooms through the site, and a buyer who does not think to search a government database before ordering will never know.

sections.heading: Who hears the complaint
sections.html:
Furniture retailing in the UK has its own ombudsman. The Furniture & Home Improvement Ombudsman closed 6,832 cases in 2025, handled 19,520 telephone enquiries and 10,028 emails, settled 99% of cases by conciliation at an average of 37 days, and sent the remaining 1% to adjudication with an expert inspection. Of those adjudicated, 45% were upheld in full for the consumer and 23% in part, with 32% not upheld. It awarded £1.2 million in settlements. Upholstery was the largest single complaint category at 37%, ahead of home improvement at 36%, with beds and mattresses and furniture and cabinetry at 5% each.

Membership is voluntary and paid for on a scale set by turnover. B&Q, DFS, Furniture Village, Marks & Spencer, Wickes and Wren Kitchens are all on the scheme's published member list. Amazon is not, and neither is any Amazon entity — checked against that list on 26 September 2026. A buyer with a dispute about a sofa bought on Amazon therefore has the A-to-z Guarantee, the seller, their card provider and the small claims track, but not an ombudsman with a code of practice behind it.

The A-to-z Guarantee is a reasonable substitute in most cases and a poor one in a few. It runs for 90 days from the last delivery date, requires three days to have elapsed since the latest estimated delivery before an undelivered-item claim, and gives the seller 48 hours to respond. It does not cover refused deliveries, chargebacks already raised, Amazon Global Store purchases, or Prime-delivered marketplace items, which are handled under a different route.

sections.heading: The company taking the commission
sections.html:
Amazon.com reported net sales of $200.6 billion for the quarter to 30 June 2026, up 20% year on year, with operating income of $27.5 billion, a 43% increase. AWS contributed $42.2 billion of sales and grew 37%. Net income of $62.6 billion, or $5.75 a diluted share, was inflated by $53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income arising principally from the company's investment in Anthropic, so the operating line is the one to read.

The segment that contains the UK is International, and it is the thin one: $42.2 billion of sales produced $1.7 billion of operating income, a margin of 4.1%, against $9.1 billion on $116.2 billion in North America. Retail outside the United States is not where this company makes its money, which is worth holding in mind when reading any claim about how much Amazon can afford to spend on handling a damaged wardrobe.

Amazon has also stepped back from selling furniture under its own labels, having cut most of its private-label lines in 2023 as costs and antitrust scrutiny mounted. Its second-hand operation continues: Amazon Resale sells returned and open-box stock graded Like New, Very Good, Good or Acceptable, and Amazon Renewed sells refurbished goods graded Premium, Excellent, Good or Acceptable, with savings quoted at up to 50% off recommended retail prices. Buying used upholstery still puts the fire label question squarely back on the buyer.

pros: A tiered furniture commission — 15% to £175, then 10% — that is cheaper than the flat 15% on kitchenware and mattresses, and encourages sellers to list higher-value pieces
A real heavy and bulky network rather than a parcel service: Scheduled Delivery with a chosen date and slot, and room-of-choice placement included
Unpacking, assembly, wall mounting and recycling of the item being replaced can be bought at the checkout, and are not charged until the work is done
A voluntary 30-day return window that more than doubles the 14 days the law requires
The A-to-z Guarantee covers third-party purchases for 90 days and extends to property damage and personal injury
Sellers can put items of up to 140kg and 300cm through Amazon's own warehouses, so large furniture is not confined to seller-fulfilled listings
Free, checkable recall data exists for the exact products sold here, published by the OPSS with model numbers and ASINs
cons: Amazon is not a member of the Furniture & Home Improvement Ombudsman, unlike DFS, B&Q, Furniture Village, Marks & Spencer, Wickes and Wren Kitchens, so there is no ombudsman route for a sofa dispute
On Standard Delivery an item under 31.5kg priced below £250 is only carried to the entrance of your home; getting it to the right room costs extra or requires Scheduled Delivery
Returning a heavy or bulky marketplace item depends on the seller, not on Amazon: 48 hours for them to respond and up to 15 calendar days before anyone collects, with an adult required to be present

Regulation 28(1) of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 removes the cancellation right for made-to-specification and personalised goods, which covers a large share of sofas and fitted furniture ordered online

Two Yaheetech items — a recliner armchair in November 2025 and a velvet sofa bed in May 2026 — were recalled at serious fire risk for breaching the 1988 Regulations, one with its Amazon ASIN recorded on the register
The permanent fire label cannot be inspected until the furniture is in the house, and since the display label was abolished on 30 October 2025 there is nothing else to read
Services, availability and even whether a delivery is possible vary by postcode, and cannot be added after the order is placed
verdict: Amazon is a serious place to buy furniture rather than an accident of scale: the tiered 15%/10% commission pulls expensive pieces onto the site, and the heavy and bulky machinery behind it — dated slots, room-of-choice carriage, assembly, recycling, items to 140kg — is closer to a furniture retailer's operation than to a parcel network. The 30-day return window beats the statutory 14 days, and the A-to-z Guarantee gives 90 days of cover on third-party purchases. The gaps are structural rather than accidental. There is no ombudsman behind a dispute, because Amazon has not joined the one its competitors use. A large item returned to a marketplace seller moves at that seller's pace. Made-to-specification furniture is outside the cancellation right altogether under regulation 28(1). And on a category where textiles and upholstery are the item first ignited in 27% of dwelling fires but are associated with 48% of the deaths, the only compliance evidence a buyer can see is a label they cannot read until the thing is already in the room. Buy from it with the OPSS register open in another tab, and check the label under the cushion the day it arrives.

faqs.q: Does furniture sold on Amazon have to meet UK fire safety law?
faqs.a: Yes. Upholstered furniture supplied in the UK must comply with the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988 regardless of who sells it or where they are based. Fillings must meet Schedule 1 for foam or Schedule 2 for non-foam, the composite must pass the Schedule 4 cigarette test, the cover must pass the Schedule 5 match test or sit over a compliant interliner, and a permanent label headed CARELESSNESS CAUSES FIRE must be attached to everything except mattresses and bed bases, which are labelled against BS 7177 instead.

faqs.q: How long do I have to return a sofa bought on Amazon?
faqs.a: The statutory right is 14 days from receipt; Amazon's own policy extends that to 30 days for unused, undamaged goods. For a heavy or bulky marketplace item — 31.5kg or over, or a longest packed side over 175cm — the return must be started within 30 days of delivery. The seller then has 48 hours to give you carrier details, and collection is due within 15 calendar days in the UK or 22 days for an international seller. An adult must be at home for it.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a made-to-order sofa?
faqs.a: Not on a change of mind. Regulation 28(1) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 excludes goods made to the consumer's specifications or clearly personalised from the cancellation right, and Amazon records customised products as not returnable. If the item arrives damaged or defective your rights are unaffected and a refund is available within 30 days.

faqs.q: Will the driver take the furniture upstairs?
faqs.a: Only on a Scheduled Delivery, which includes placement in the room of your choice, or where you have paid for a service at the checkout. On Standard Delivery an item under 31.5kg priced below £250 is delivered to the entrance of your home. Unpacking, assembly and removal of the old item are separate paid options on eligible products and cannot be added after the order is placed.

faqs.q: Is there an ombudsman if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: Not for Amazon. The Furniture & Home Improvement Ombudsman closed 6,832 cases in 2025 and awarded £1.2 million, but it only takes disputes about member businesses, and Amazon is absent from its member list — checked on 26 September 2026 — while B&Q, DFS, Furniture Village, Marks & Spencer, Wickes and Wren Kitchens are all on it. Your routes are the seller, the A-to-z Guarantee within 90 days of the last delivery date, your card provider and the small claims track.

faqs.q: How do I check whether a piece of furniture has been recalled?
faqs.a: Search the OPSS product safety alerts, reports and recalls register on GOV.UK by keyword. On 26 September 2026 a search on furniture returned 83 reports and a search on sofa returned 16, and individual entries carry the model number, the batch codes, the country of manufacture and, in at least one case, the Amazon ASIN. It is free, it takes a minute, and no marketplace listing will tell you.

title: Amazon Gaming and Accessories
meta_title: Amazon Gaming: Luna from £8.99 and What PEGI 18 Means
meta_description: Amazon gaming and accessories checked against its own seller and help pages: 15% fees, Luna at £8.99, PEGI ratings that are law, and the opened-software rule.

headline.label: Cheapest way into the gaming range, delivered
headline.value: £8.99 — one month of Prime, which carries Luna Standard cloud gaming and more than 50 titles with nothing to deliver at all; Amazon's own Luna Controller is £59.99 (checked 26 September 2026)

key_facts.label: Seller referral fee
key_facts.value: 15% on video games and gaming accessories, 8% on video game consoles — and no minimum fee on either, where nearly every other Amazon category floors at 25p

key_facts.label: UK games market, 2025
key_facts.value: £8.76 billion, up 7.4% — but console game accessories fell 9% to £420 million while console hardware rose 12% to £811 million (Ukie, published April 2026)

key_facts.label: Boxed games
key_facts.value: £319 million in 2025, down 1.0%, inside £6.03 billion of game software

key_facts.label: Age ratings that are law
key_facts.value: PEGI 12, 16 and 18 — enforceable in the UK from 30 July 2012 under the Video Recordings (Labelling) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012 No. 1767)

key_facts.label: Penalty for an underage sale
key_facts.value: Up to a £5,000 fine or six months' imprisonment, or both; supplying an unclassified game carries an unlimited fine or two years

key_facts.label: Rating symbol on the case
key_facts.value: White, minimum height 5 millimetres, red background at 18 and orange below 18, displayed on two of the largest faces

key_facts.label: Opened software
key_facts.value: Not returnable — Amazon's own wording is "We won't accept the return of any software returned to us if it's been opened"

key_facts.label: Published age-verification check
key_facts.value: UK or international passport or UK driving licence plus a selfie, taking 30 to 45 seconds — named for bladed items; video games are not named at all

key_facts.label: Luna subscriptions
key_facts.value: Standard included with Prime, Premium £8.99 a month, Ubisoft+ £14.99, Jackbox £3.99; a sustained 10Mbps recommended

key_facts.label: Games rated by PEGI
key_facts.value: 39,930 in total to the end of 2023, of which 1,666 were rated in 2023 alone and 207 of those — 12.4% — came out at PEGI 18

intro:
Amazon's cheapest way into gaming costs £8.99. One month of Prime carries Luna Standard, Amazon's own cloud gaming service, with more than 50 titles included and nothing at all to be delivered; the Luna Controller, if you want the hardware, is £59.99. Both prices come from Amazon's UK newsroom and were checked on 26 September 2026.

The catalogue sitting behind that is the deepest in British gaming, and the reason is printed on Amazon's own seller price list rather than in its advertising. It takes 15% of the sale price on video games and gaming accessories and 8% on video game consoles — and, unusually, applies no minimum fee to either, where nearly every other category on that list floors at 25p. A seller shipping a £3 thumbstick cover keeps more of the money here than almost anywhere else in Amazon's catalogue, and that is why the cheap end of the accessories shelf runs as deep as it does.

One thing worth knowing before you click: Amazon's product pages refuse automated access, so no figure on this page has been taken from a listing or from another comparison site. Everything below comes from Amazon's seller, newsroom, payments and customer-help hosts, from Ukie's own market valuation, or from a regulator — the Office for Product Safety and Standards, the Games Rating Authority, the Advertising Standards Authority and the Chartered Trading Standards Institute.

sections.heading: Where the 15% goes, and what it does to the shelf
sections.html:
Amazon publishes what it charges the people selling on it, and for this category the numbers are worth reading before the prices are. Video games and gaming accessories carry a 15% referral fee. Video game consoles carry 8%. Both are recorded with the minimum referral fee shown as not applicable — there is no 25p floor, which there is on Consumer Electronics at 7%, on Electronic Accessories at 15% up to £100 and 8% above it, on Toys and Games at 15% and on Computers at 7%. On top of that a seller pays either 75p an item on the Individual plan or £25 a month, excluding VAT, on the Professional plan.

Removing the floor matters more than the headline percentage. On a £1.50 cable clip, 15% is 23p; with a 25p minimum it would be 25p. The difference is two pence, and two pence is the whole margin at that price. It is the clearest single explanation for why a search for a controller grip or a console stand on Amazon returns pages of sub-£5 listings that no high-street shop carries.

Set that against the market Ukie measured. Its UK Games Market Valuation for 2025, published in April 2026, puts the consumer market at £8.76 billion, up 7.4% on £8.158 billion. Game software took £6.03 billion of it, with digital console at £2.49 billion, mobile at £2.07 billion, digital PC at £1.15 billion and boxed games down 1.0% at £319 million. Hardware took £2.17 billion: consoles £811 million and up 12%, gaming PCs £790 million and up 11%, VR £151 million and down 26%.

The line that should shape how you shop is console game accessories: £420 million, down 9%, in a year when the consoles themselves grew 12%. More people bought machines and spent less on the things that plug into them. A falling accessories market with a rising installed base is the condition in which cheap, unbranded, high-volume listings multiply — which is exactly the shape of Amazon's own fee schedule for the category.

sections.heading: The number on the box that Trading Standards can enforce
sections.html:
Most retail categories have no rating system at all. Video games are one of the very few consumer products in Britain where an age label on the packaging is a legal instrument, and it has been since 30 July 2012, when the Video Recordings (Labelling) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012 No. 1767, made 4 July 2012) came into force. Sections 40 and 41 of the Digital Economy Act 2010 removed the general exemption video games had enjoyed and allowed the Video Standards Council — now operating as the Games Rating Authority — to be designated the classification authority for games, with the British Board of Film Classification keeping R18 material and small games carried on discs containing film.

The underlying statute is the Video Recordings Act 1984, revived by the Video Recordings Act 2010 after the original was found never to have been properly notified. It bites on physical media sold, hired, exchanged or lent in England, Scotland and Wales. PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are the enforceable ratings; PEGI 3 and 7 are advisory. Exemptions survive for educational works and for games about sport, religion or music, provided they do not depict to any significant extent violence, sexual content, genital imagery, excretory functions or criminal technique.

The penalties are not nominal. Selling an age-classified game to someone below the rated age carries a fine of up to £5,000 or imprisonment of up to six months, or both. Supplying a game that should have been classified and was not carries an unlimited fine or up to two years. A due diligence defence exists for a trader who took all reasonable precautions, and who can show the breach was down to another person's act or default — which on a marketplace is a sentence worth rereading.

The labelling rules give you a test you can run with nothing but the parcel in your hands. The classification symbol must be white and at least 5 millimetres high, on a red background where the rating is 18 and an orange background where it is lower, and it must appear clearly on one of the largest faces of the case and again on another face. Content descriptor icons may sit beside it, white on black or black on white. Everything must be clearly legible, indelible and not hidden or obscured. Turn the case over. If the symbol is missing, undersized, or printed on the wrong colour, the game in your hands was not labelled the way the law requires, whoever sold it.

For scale: PEGI has rated 39,930 games in total to the end of 2023, and 1,666 in 2023 alone — 435 at PEGI 3 (26.1%), 268 at 7 (16.1%), 488 at 12 (29.3%), 268 at 16 (16.1%) and 207 at 18 (12.4%). Roughly three in five new games carry a rating the law will enforce. One limit worth stating plainly: the Video Recordings Act reaches physical copies, so a download of the same title is outside it entirely.

sections.heading: A wireless controller is electrical equipment before it is a gaming product
sections.html:
The accessories half of this category is governed by safety law rather than content law, and the rules are the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 and the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994. A mains-powered console charger, a plug-in headset base or a docking station has to meet them regardless of which seller's name is on the listing. Anything that transmits — a wireless controller, a Bluetooth headset — also falls under the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 (SI 2017 No. 1206), which carry across the requirements of Directive 2014/53/EU.

The GOV.UK product safety register is free, searchable and shows how those rules are actually used. Searching it for the single word console returned 6 reports on 26 September 2026, and two of them are gaming power supplies rather than consoles. A Games Console Charger, model USG-002, made in China and sold through an online marketplace under listing ID 1054467868, was recalled from end users on 14 August 2023: creepage and clearance distances were insufficient and the product failed the electrical strength test, so accessible metal parts could become live. The Office for Product Safety and Standards notified it and the marketplace removed the listing. An AC Adapter for Xbox One, model PE-2121-03M1, barcode 6900214000121, also made in China, was reported on 12 February 2024 as a serious fire risk: insufficiently earthed, poorly constructed, no fuse, and a clover-leaf plug whose live pins the user can touch while plugging it in. That import was rejected at the border and destroyed, on a notification from local authority Trading Standards.

A note on searching that register yourself, because the search is an OR and small numbers mean more than large ones. The keyword gaming returns 90 reports, almost all of them wooden fishing games and toy sets, and tells you nothing. The keyword console returns 6 and is worth reading line by line. Among the wider gaming results is one piece of furniture: a Trust GXT 705R Ryon gaming chair, recalled on 2 July 2021.

Read six notices in both directions. It is reassuring that so few gaming products have been formally recalled, and it says nothing about listings taken down before anyone tested them. The recurring hazard is not the console or the controller — it is the third-party power supply sold to sit beside it, which is the cheapest item in the transaction and the only one carrying mains voltage.

There is also a duty on the seller that almost nobody claims. Under the WEEE rules, a retailer of electrical and electronic equipment must give customers a way to dispose of the old equivalent item when it sells them a new one, and that applies “regardless of how you sell the products, whether direct or by internet, mail order or telephone”. It can be met in store, by a free alternative take-back service, or by joining the Distributor Take Back Scheme, and the seller must publish on its website which service it offers, how to reuse and recycle, and what the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol means. If you are replacing a controller or a headset, that take-back route exists and is free to use.

sections.heading: Break the seal and the refund goes with it
sections.html:
The general shape of Amazon's returns policy is generous and well known: a statutory 14 days from receipt under regulation 30 of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, extended voluntarily to 30 days on most things. This category is where the exceptions bite hardest, and Amazon states them in its own words on its customer help pages.

“We won't accept the return of any software returned to us if it's been opened.” Sealed audio or video recordings, and sealed software, are non-returnable “if unsealed by you after delivery”. Digital content that is not supplied on a tangible medium — apps, digital software, eBooks, MP3 — is outside the cancellation right altogether. Amazon.co.uk gift cards are listed as non-returnable items. And the policy reserves the right to refuse a return or charge its fees and expenses where a product is not received in new, unopened condition.

None of that is Amazon being difficult. Regulation 28 of the same 2013 Regulations sets out the exceptions to the 14-day right, and sealed audio recordings, video recordings and computer software unsealed after delivery are on that list, alongside goods made to the customer's specification. The law hands the retailer this one, and every game shop in the country uses it.

The arithmetic is worth doing before you order. A full-price console game at £69.99 that turns out to be the wrong platform, the wrong region or simply the wrong game is worth £69.99 while the cellophane is intact and nothing once it is not. On a marketplace where the seller is often not Amazon, that is a harder position than it looks, because the person you would be negotiating with is a third party with a 48-hour response window rather than a shop with a returns desk. Buy the disc you meant to buy, and open it last.

sections.heading: A rating tells you about the content, not the cost
sections.html:
An age rating answers one question — what is in this game — and is silent on the one that increasingly decides what a game costs. A game rated at any PEGI level may also contain in-game purchases, and where it does, the Games Rating Authority's own explanation is that this “will be indicated by an icon on the box”. The rating itself does not rise because the game sells things. A PEGI 3 title with an open wallet behind it is still a PEGI 3 title.

What exists instead is a voluntary regime. On 18 July 2023 the video games industry agreed 11 principles on paid loot boxes, drawn up by a Technical Working Group of international platforms, publishers and developers that met over ten months from September 2022 to June 2023, alongside a £1 million, three-year public awareness campaign. The principles commit signatories to “make available technological controls to effectively restrict anyone under the age of 18 from acquiring a Loot Box, without the consent or knowledge of a parent, carer or guardian”, to “give clear probability disclosures” so players can see the odds of receiving a given item, to improve access to spending controls, and to take a lenient line on refunds where a child has spent money without a parent knowing. They are commitments, not law.

Advertising is the one part of this with teeth, and the enforcement is recent. The Advertising Standards Authority's guidance on advertising in-game purchases was published in September 2021 and reviewed in May 2024. On 24 June 2026 it upheld a complaint against Microsoft over two digital posters for Xbox Game Pass seen on 13 December 2025, which showed identifiable gameplay from Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 + 4 and Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 without saying those games contained in-game purchasing. The ruling breached CAP Code rules 3.1 and 3.3, and its reasoning was that the omission “was material to a consumer's transactional decision”. The complaint came from a single academic researcher in game regulation.

That ruling is about a publisher's advertising, not a retailer's, and it is here because it is the clearest available statement of what the label on a box is not doing. If a game in a child's basket carries the in-game purchases icon, the useful next step is the platform's family spending controls, not the age rating.

sections.heading: The age check Amazon publishes — and the one it does not
sections.html:
Selling an 18-rated game online raises a question the Chartered Trading Standards Institute answers bluntly through its Business Companion guidance: a seller “must have effective systems in place for preventing sales to customers who are underage”, and the things that do not count as such a system are named. Relying on the purchaser confirming they are over the minimum age does not count. Asking the purchaser simply to provide a date of birth does not count. Tick boxes, disclaimers and payment-method checks do not count on their own. What is expected is a risk analysis of the business to find the weak points, measures against them, and monitoring to keep them working. The guidance also states that age-restricted products “must not be delivered to self-service lockers, as it would affect the due diligence defence”. The old reference point, PAS 1296, has been withdrawn in favour of BS ISO/IEC 27566-1:2025 on age-assurance systems.

Amazon does publish an age-restricted items policy, and what it contains is specific. The items it names are “alcoholic beverages, such as beer and wine, e-cigarettes and bladed items”, with a threshold of 18 or over. For bladed items the check is a UK passport, an international passport or a UK driving licence together with a selfie, a process it says usually takes 30 to 45 seconds. At the door, “the delivery driver is required to request and record a year of birth and record that the customer is visibly over 25 years old”, with photo ID required if they are not, and age-restricted items cannot be left with a neighbour.

Video games are not mentioned on that page, and neither is PEGI. That is a gap in what is published rather than proof of a gap in practice, and it should be read that way: Amazon may well apply a check at checkout that it has not described on the help page this review could reach, and its own product pages are closed to automated access. What can be said is that the page a customer is pointed to lists three categories of goods and not the fourth that Parliament made criminal to sell to a child. If it matters to you — if you are buying a PEGI 18 game on an account a teenager can reach, or having one delivered to a locker — that is worth a question to customer services before the order, and the answer would be worth having in writing.

sections.heading: Renting instead of owning: what Luna actually includes
sections.html:
Amazon's own gaming product is Luna, and it is the cheapest way into the category because the entry tier is bundled. Luna Standard is included with a Prime membership and carries more than 50 titles, among them Fortnite, Hogwarts Legacy, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II and TopSpin 2K25. Above it, Luna Premium is £8.99 a month, a Ubisoft+ channel with more than 45 Ubisoft games is £14.99 a month, and a Jackbox Games channel with more than 50 party titles is £3.99 a month. GameNight is a separate collection of more than 25 local multiplayer games, and the only part of Luna that does not need a controller or a mouse and keyboard.

It runs on supported Windows PCs, Macs, Fire TV, Fire tablets, Chromebooks, iPhone, iPad, Android devices and selected Samsung and LG smart televisions, and Amazon recommends a sustained 10Mbps for the best experience. The Luna Controller costs £59.99, which makes it the most expensive single item in the cheapest route into Amazon's gaming range — the subscription is free with Prime and the hardware is not.

Two things follow. A cloud library is a rental: nothing in Luna Standard belongs to the player, the list changes, and a title that goes leaves with it. And a 10Mbps sustained connection is a real requirement rather than a suggestion, which for a household on a congested evening connection is the difference between the service working and the money being wasted. Against a £69.99 disc that keeps its value until it is opened, a bundled subscription at no extra cost is an easy first step and a poor place to build a collection.

pros: The cheapest entry point in the category costs nothing extra on top of Prime: Luna Standard and more than 50 titles are included, with no delivery and no hardware needed for the GameNight collection
No minimum referral fee on video games or gaming accessories, against 25p on most Amazon categories, which keeps sub-£5 accessories commercially viable and the catalogue unusually deep
Consoles carry the lowest fee in the category at 8%, half the 15% on the games and accessories that sit beside them
A voluntary 30-day change-of-mind window on most goods, against the statutory 14 days under regulation 30 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013

Amazon's published age-verification process for the categories it does name is documented and quick — passport or driving licence plus a selfie in 30 to 45 seconds, with a driver check recording a year of birth and visible age over 25
A free WEEE take-back route exists for a replaced controller, headset or console, and distance sellers are covered by the same duty as shops
Luna's paid channels are priced separately and clearly — £8.99, £14.99 and £3.99 a month — rather than bundled into one unavoidable fee
cons: Open a game and the refund goes with the cellophane. Amazon's own wording is "We won't accept the return of any software returned to us if it's been opened", and a £69.99 disc bought for the wrong platform is worth nothing the moment it is unsealed. The law permits this under regulation 28 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, but on a marketplace the seller you have to argue with is a third party, not a returns desk

The age-restricted items page names alcohol, e-cigarettes and bladed items, and does not mention video games or PEGI anywhere — even though PEGI 12, 16 and 18 have been legally enforceable since 30 July 2012 and an underage sale carries up to a £5,000 fine or six months' imprisonment. Whether a check is applied at checkout could not be established from any page open to automated access, and it needs confirming with customer services

Business Companion states that age-restricted products must not be delivered to self-service lockers because it would undermine the due diligence defence. Locker delivery is a standard Amazon option and nothing on the pages this review could read says PEGI-rated games are excluded from it

No price is published anywhere reachable for the cheapest gaming accessory or game on the site, because amazon.co.uk refuses automated access. The cheapest-item figure other retailers in this category can be checked on cannot be checked here, and the honest answer is that it is unknown rather than low

Two of the six safety notices on the GOV.UK register for the keyword console are third-party power supplies, one of them recalled from end users for live accessible metal parts on 14 August 2023 and the other stopped at the border on 12 February 2024 for having no fuse and touchable live pins. Both were sold as gaming accessories and neither came from the console manufacturer

Luna Standard is a rental, not a library: the titles are Amazon's to remove, the entry tier depends on keeping Prime, and the controller that most of it requires is £59.99 — more than many full-price games

An age rating says nothing about spending. In-game purchases are flagged only by an icon and never raise the rating, and the controls around them rest on 11 voluntary industry principles agreed on 18 July 2023 rather than on any enforceable rule
verdict: As a place to buy gaming hardware and accessories, Amazon's advantages are structural rather than promotional: a 15% referral fee with no minimum on games and accessories, 8% on consoles, and no price floor at all, in a category where console accessories sales fell 9% to £420 million in 2025 while console sales rose 12%. That combination is why the shelf is deep and why so much of it is cheap, and it is also why the mains-powered end of it deserves a look at the plug: both of the gaming power supplies on the GOV.UK safety register were third-party accessories, not manufacturer parts. For games themselves the decisive facts are legal rather than commercial. PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are enforceable ratings, the symbol has to be white, at least 5 millimetres high and on two of the largest faces of the case, and opening the seal ends the right to a refund. Turn the case over before you open it, and check the rating is printed the way the 2012 Regulations require. The one thing this review could not settle is how Amazon verifies age on a PEGI 18 game — its published age-restriction page names alcohol, e-cigarettes and bladed items and stops there — so if that matters in your household, ask before you order rather than after.

faqs.q: Is a PEGI rating legally binding in the UK?
faqs.a: PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are. They became enforceable on 30 July 2012, when the Video Recordings (Labelling) Regulations 2012 came into force under powers in sections 40 and 41 of the Digital Economy Act 2010, on top of the Video Recordings Act 1984 as revived in 2010. Selling a game to someone under the rated age carries a fine of up to £5,000 or six months' imprisonment, or both, and supplying a game that should have been classified and was not carries an unlimited fine or up to two years. PEGI 3 and 7 are advisory. The Act covers physical copies, so a download of the same game sits outside it.

faqs.q: Can I return a game or a piece of software to Amazon once I have opened it?
faqs.a: No. Amazon's own policy says “We won't accept the return of any software returned to us if it's been opened”, and sealed audio recordings, video recordings and sealed software are non-returnable once unsealed after delivery. Digital content not supplied on a disc, and Amazon.co.uk gift cards, are non-returnable as well. This follows regulation 28 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, which lists those exceptions to the 14-day cancellation right that regulation 30 otherwise gives you. Unopened, the ordinary window applies — 14 days by statute and 30 days by Amazon's own policy on most goods.

faqs.q: How can I tell whether a game has been labelled properly?
faqs.a: Look at the case. The classification symbol must be white and at least 5 millimetres high, set on a red background where the rating is 18 and an orange background for every lower rating, and it has to appear clearly on one of the largest faces of the case and again on another face. Content descriptor icons may sit alongside it, white on black or black on white. All of it must be legible, indelible and not hidden or obscured. A missing, undersized or wrongly coloured symbol means the copy in front of you was not labelled the way the 2012 Regulations require.

faqs.q: What does Luna cost, and do I own the games?
faqs.a: Luna Standard is included with Prime and carries more than 50 titles. Luna Premium is £8.99 a month, a Ubisoft+ channel with more than 45 games is £14.99 a month and a Jackbox Games channel with more than 50 titles is £3.99 a month. The Luna Controller is £59.99, and most of the service needs a controller or a mouse and keyboard — the exception is the GameNight collection of more than 25 local multiplayer games. Amazon recommends a sustained 10Mbps. Nothing is owned: the library is Amazon's to change, and access depends on the subscription continuing.

faqs.q: Who checks that a gaming accessory is safe?
faqs.a: Mains-powered accessories fall under the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 and the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994, and anything that transmits also falls under the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017. Enforcement is by the Office for Product Safety and Standards and local authority Trading Standards, and their notices are published free on GOV.UK. Searching that register for the word console returned 6 reports on 26 September 2026, two of them third-party gaming power supplies — one recalled from end users on 14 August 2023 because accessible metal parts could become live, the other stopped at the border on 12 February 2024 with no fuse and touchable live pins.

faqs.q: Does Amazon verify age when you buy an 18-rated game?
faqs.a: Its published age-restricted items page names alcoholic drinks, e-cigarettes and bladed items, and does not mention video games or PEGI. For bladed items the check is a passport or UK driving licence plus a selfie, taking 30 to 45 seconds, and at delivery the driver records a year of birth and that the customer is visibly over 25, with photo ID required otherwise and no leaving the parcel with a neighbour.
