Nothing reachable states whether an equivalent check applies to a PEGI 18 game, and Trading Standards guidance is explicit that self-declaration and a date-of-birth box are not enough on their own. It is worth asking customer services before ordering.

title: Amazon Groceries Review: Delivery Fees, Date Codes and Who You Are Buying From
meta_title: Amazon Groceries: Delivery Fees, Dates and the Small Print
meta_description: Amazon grocery delivery is free for Prime members over £20 and £5.99 otherwise. We read the help pages, the food labelling law and the supplier survey.

headline.label: Delivery: what it costs and the basket that makes it free
headline.value: Free over £20 for Prime members on same-day grocery delivery, £5.99 for everyone else — Amazon's figures, 4 June 2026

intro:
Prime members pay nothing to have fresh groceries delivered the same day on an Amazon order over £20, and everyone else pays £5.99 whatever the basket is worth. Those are Amazon's own figures, published on 4 June 2026 and checked on 26 September 2026. Behind them sits a grocery range Amazon puts at more than two million lines, delivered in one-hour windows, and a category the company says now accounts for roughly one in every three units sold on Amazon.co.uk.

What you are actually shopping is five shops in one search box. Amazon Fresh is Amazon's own range, and alongside it sit Morrisons, Iceland, Co-op and Gopuff, each selling as itself. That matters more than it sounds, because the contract for a Morrisons basket is with WM Morrison Supermarkets PLC of Hilmore House, Bradford, company number 358949, and an Iceland basket is with Iceland Foods Ltd of Deeside, company number 01107406. Amazon publishes all four entities, with company numbers, VAT numbers and telephone numbers, which is more than most marketplaces bother to do — and it decides which number you ring when a delivery goes wrong.

The shops themselves have gone. On 23 September 2025 Amazon set out a proposal to close all 14 of its Amazon Fresh stores in the UK, with five of them converting to Whole Foods Market by the end of 2026. Anyone searching for an Amazon grocery shop to walk into, or for click-and-collect from one, is looking for something that no longer exists; this is a delivery business now.

key_facts.label: Amazon's cut on a grocery sale
key_facts.value: 5% on items up to £10, 15% above — and no minimum referral fee at all

key_facts.label: Grocery range
key_facts.value: More than 2 million grocery and household lines (Amazon, 11 February 2026)

key_facts.label: Who you buy from
key_facts.value: Amazon Fresh, Morrisons, Iceland, Co-op and Gopuff — four separate legal entities besides Amazon

key_facts.label: Delivery windows
key_facts.value: 1 hour on Amazon Fresh and Co-op for everyone; 1 hour on Morrisons and Iceland for Prime members; Gopuff from 15 minutes

key_facts.label: Refunds on fresh items
key_facts.value: 7 days to report a spilled or damaged item, with no return required; Amazon Fresh purchases refundable within 30 days

key_facts.label: Unattended delivery
key_facts.value: Amazon Fresh only, orders under £500, and never for chilled, frozen or age-restricted items

key_facts.label: Supplier compliance ranking
key_facts.value: 68.6% — bottom of 14 designated retailers in the Groceries Code Adjudicator's 2026 survey

key_facts.label: Prime membership
key_facts.value: £8.99 a month or £95 a year, which is what the free delivery is priced into

sections.heading: Five per cent on a tin of beans, and no floor under it
sections.html:
Amazon's published referral fee for Grocery and Gourmet is 5% on any item priced up to £10 and 15% above it, and the minimum referral fee is recorded as not applicable. Read that second half carefully, because almost nothing else on Amazon's fee schedule works that way. Pet Supplies is a flat 15% with a 25p minimum. Beauty, Health and Personal Care is 8% up to £10 and 15% above, again with a 25p minimum. Home Products is 8% at or below £20 and 15% above, with the same 25p floor.

On an 89p tin, 5% is 4p. If the 25p minimum applied, Amazon would be taking 28% of the sale, and nobody would list it. Removing the floor is the single decision that makes a cheap grocery line worth putting on the site at all, and it explains why the range runs to millions of items rather than the few thousand a delivery-only grocer normally carries. It also explains the shape of what you find: the depth is in ambient and household goods, where a seller keeps 95p in the pound, rather than in the fresh food the category is named after.

Selling costs sit on top. A Professional selling plan is £25 a month excluding VAT, or 75p an item on the Individual plan. For a seller shifting 400 jars of sauce a month, the plan is 6p a jar; for someone shifting twelve, it is more than £2 each, which is the arithmetic behind a marketplace grocery listing priced oddly high.

sections.heading: The date on the packet is the one thing the law lets them leave off
sections.html:
Buy food in a shop and the label is in your hand before you pay. Buy it online and the law splits the label in two. Article 9(1) of assimilated Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 lists twelve mandatory particulars, from (a) the name of the food and (b) the list of ingredients through to (l) the nutrition declaration. Article 14, the distance selling article, requires all of them to be available before the purchase is concluded, free of charge — with one exception, point (f), the date of minimum durability or the 'use by' date. That one need only be available at the moment of delivery.

So an online grocer is under no obligation to tell you how much life is left on the chicken before you pay for it, and a legal obligation to tell you when it arrives. The enforcement sits in the Food Information Regulations 2014 and the Food Safety Act 1990, policed by local authority Trading Standards rather than by any financial regulator.

The distinction between the two dates is worth knowing before the box is open. A use-by date goes on highly perishable food, and it is an offence to sell or offer for sale food after it — after midnight on the stated day, that item cannot lawfully be sold. Best before is a quality marker: the food may still be sold and eaten after it, and the retailer carries the responsibility for its condition if it is. Fresh fruit and vegetables that have not been peeled or cut carry no date mark at all, along with vinegar, cooking salt, solid sugar confectionery and chewing gum.

There is one thing to do on the doorstep, and it takes ten seconds. Read the dates on the chilled items while the driver is still there, because that is the moment the law gives you the information, and the mandatory particulars have to be legible when they reach you: the minimum x-height for the text is 1.2mm, dropping to 0.9mm only where the largest surface of the pack is under 80cm².

sections.heading: Two Amazon pages, two free-delivery thresholds, four days apart
sections.html:
Amazon's own pages do not agree on what free grocery delivery costs, and both were current within the same week. The newsroom announcement of 4 June 2026, which launched fresh groceries inside an ordinary Same-Day order in parts of central and east London, gives free delivery for Prime members on orders over £20 and £5.99 for non-members regardless of basket size. Amazon's Prime membership page, last modified on 31 May 2026, gives Prime members free two-hour deliveries on Amazon Fresh orders above £60.

Both are true, because they are different services: one is a dedicated Amazon Fresh slot, the other is fresh food dropped into the same basket as everything else. The practical point for a shopper is that the number depends on which route you happen to be in, and the help pages add that temporary promotions on delivery fees are not shown, so the fee is not something you can establish in advance. Assume you will see it at checkout and check it there.

The free delivery is also priced in elsewhere. Prime is £8.99 a month or £95 a year, with an 18-to-24 student rate of £4.49 a month or £47.49 a year. At £5.99 a delivery, sixteen grocery orders a year come to £95.84 — so if groceries are the only reason to hold Prime, the membership starts paying for itself at roughly one delivery every three weeks, and below that it does not.

sections.heading: 8°C, and what happens when the bag arrives warm
sections.html:
Chilled food in England is governed by Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013, SI 2013/2996. Paragraph 2 is blunt: a person who keeps food that needs temperature control at a temperature above 8°C commits an offence. There are tolerances — a period of less than four hours for service or display, and limited periods for unavoidable transfer — and general exemptions for food that is safe at ambient temperature throughout its shelf life, for canned and dehydrated goods before opening, and for cooked food held at or above 63°C.

Amazon says perishable items are stored, picked and packed in temperature-controlled conditions with checks at several points, and that temperature-sensitive products travel in insulated, recyclable packaging under a freshness guarantee. The delivery mechanics carry the rest of the answer. Unattended delivery, where the driver leaves the order without you, is available on Amazon Fresh only, for orders under £500, and is not available at all for chilled, frozen or age-restricted items — which is the right rule, and it means a chilled grocery order is an appointment rather than a drop-off.

If something arrives spilled or damaged, you have seven days from delivery to report it through Your Orders, and Amazon states it will not ask for the item back. Amazon Fresh purchases are refundable within 30 days, though the returns policy is explicit that most Fresh food is not returnable — perishables and goods that deteriorate or expire rapidly are excluded outright, as are items unsuitable for return on hygiene grounds once unsealed. On a grocery order, the remedy is a refund and nothing else.

sections.heading: Since 6 April 2026 the price per 100g has had to be there too
sections.html:
The rule that lets you compare a 400g jar with a 680g jar changed this spring, and it is the most useful change to grocery pricing law in twenty years. The Price Marking (Amendment) Order 2024, SI 2024/1055, was made on 21 October 2024. The Price Marking (Amendment) Order 2025, SI 2025/592, made on 14 May 2025, pushed its commencement from 1 October 2025 to 6 April 2026. Two changes matter to anyone filling an online basket: a new Article 7A requires a trader offering a product at more than one price — a loyalty price and a shelf price, say — to show each selling price and each unit price together with the conditions for getting them; and the amendment to Article 9 requires a price reduction to show the reduced selling price and the reduced unit price.

That was written because the old rules were not working. The Competition and Markets Authority reviewed unit pricing across the sector in July 2023, covering 11 nationwide supermarkets and 7 variety store retailers, visiting 22 supermarket and 24 variety stores and analysing more than 4,000 photographs of shelf labels. The supermarkets came out of it reasonably well, with one or two isolated errors each; the variety stores did not, and the CMA's worst example was a 250ml handwash priced at £1.19 and unit priced at £476.00 per 100ml. The review also recorded that the same product could be unit priced per litre in one shop, per 100ml in the next and per wash in a third, and noted that by December 2022 an estimated 94% of UK shoppers belonged to at least one loyalty scheme — which is why a promotional price with no unit price attached had become a hole worth closing.

Use it. On a multi-seller listing the pack sizes rarely match, and the unit price is the only number that survives the comparison.

sections.heading: What Amazon's own suppliers report, and the investigation that is still open
sections.html:
Amazon is a designated retailer under the groceries code, and it did not volunteer. The Competition and Markets Authority designated Amazon.com, Incorporated on 9 February 2022 under Article 4(1)(b) of the Groceries (Supply Chain Practices) Market Investigation Order 2009, which catches any retailer whose UK grocery retail turnover exceeds £1 billion. The obligations began on 1 March 2022, and the practical effect is that Amazon's dealings with its direct grocery suppliers are measured every year by the Groceries Code Adjudicator against the same yardstick as Tesco's and Waitrose's.

It measures badly. In the GCA's 2026 annual survey, conducted by YouGov and published on 16 April 2026, the proportion of direct suppliers saying a retailer consistently or mostly complies with the code put Waitrose top on 97.8% and Amazon bottom of all 14 designated retailers on 68.6% — a gap of 29 percentage points, with Co-op the next lowest on 89.1% and the rest of the field between 90% and 97%. Amazon accounted for 11.2% of the retailer mentions when suppliers were asked which retailer their issue concerned, and 52% of direct suppliers reported an issue of some kind, up from 51%. It is an improvement on 2024, when 3,000-plus responses gathered between 15 January and 25 February put Amazon on 47% against Co-op's 98% and the then Adjudicator, Mark White, said that the survey showed clearly that many suppliers did not believe Amazon was complying with the code.

On 20 June 2025 the GCA went further and opened a formal investigation into Amazon under the Groceries Code Adjudicator Act 2013, on reasonable grounds to suspect breaches of paragraph 5 of the code, No delay in Payments, which requires a retailer to pay a supplier within a reasonable time of the invoice. The investigation covers 1 March 2022 to 20 June 2025 with particular attention to the period since 1 January 2024, and examines Amazon's goods receipt and payment processes, how it handles supplier concerns, and its use of settlement deductions in commercial negotiations. Mark White's stated reason was that the alleged delays could expose Amazon's suppliers to excessive risk and unexpected costs, affecting their ability to invest and innovate. The call for evidence closed on 8 August 2025 and the investigation was still open as at the GCA's annual report of 16 July 2026.

Be fair about what this is and is not. The code protects suppliers, not shoppers, and nothing in it says a delivery will arrive cold or on time. It is still the only independent, annual, published measurement of how a grocery retailer behaves, and on that measurement Amazon has been last every year it has been measured.

sections.heading: Five shops, five contracts, and nobody to appeal to
sections.html:
Mixing Amazon Fresh items with ordinary Amazon items splits your shopping into separate baskets with separate checkouts and separate order confirmations, and the same is true across the partner merchants. That is a mechanical nuisance rather than a scandal, but it has a consequence worth knowing before something goes wrong: each order sits with a different company. Co-op orders are with Co-operative Group Food Limited, 1 Angel Square, Manchester, customer services 0800 068 6727. Morrisons is WM Morrison Supermarkets PLC on 0345 611 6111. Iceland is Iceland Foods Ltd on 0800 328 0800. Gopuff is GoBrands UK Holdings Ltd, company number 12793914, contactable only by email.

There is no ombudsman above any of them. A grocery order is not a regulated financial product, so there is no Financial Ombudsman Service to escalate to and no compulsory alternative dispute resolution scheme covering food retail. If a refund is refused, the routes are the merchant's own complaints process, then the local authority — Trading Standards for labelling and pricing, environmental health for temperature and hygiene — and then the small claims track. That is worth knowing in advance precisely because Amazon's own service is usually quick: the escalation path behind it is short.

Coverage is the other limit. Amazon's grocery partners are postcode-by-postcode rather than national, and the target Amazon has set itself is that more than 80% of UK Prime members will have access to at least one grocery partner by the end of 2026 — a target, not a present state. The Iceland tie-up reached Belfast, Cardiff, Edinburgh and Nottingham on 11 February 2026, having started in selected Greater Manchester postcodes; Gopuff and Co-op are narrower still. Check your own postcode before assuming any of the figures on this page apply to you.

pros: Free same-day grocery delivery for Prime members on orders over £20, and one-hour windows on Amazon Fresh and Co-op for members and non-members alike
More than two million grocery and household lines, far deeper than a single supermarket's online range
The 5% referral fee with no minimum makes cheap ambient and household lines viable, so the long tail is genuinely long
All four partner merchants are published with their legal entity, company number, VAT number and a direct phone number
Chilled, frozen and age-restricted items cannot be left unattended, which is the right rule and is stated plainly
Damaged or spilled fresh items are refunded without a return, reported through Your Orders within seven days
Morrisons, Iceland and Co-op ranges sit behind one search box and one payment method
cons: Amazon publishes no minimum life on delivery. Neither the grocery help pages nor the freshness guarantee state how many days are left on a chilled item when it arrives, which is the one figure several rival grocers do publish — we could not find it and it needs confirming with customer services before a first order.

Two different free-delivery thresholds appear on Amazon's own pages within four days of each other, £20 on 4 June 2026 and £60 on the Prime page modified 31 May 2026, and the help pages add that temporary delivery-fee promotions are not shown. The delivery cost cannot be established before checkout.

Amazon has come bottom of the Groceries Code Adjudicator's supplier compliance table every year it has been measured — 68.6% against Waitrose's 97.8% in 2026 — and has been under formal investigation for late payment to suppliers since 20 June 2025, unresolved as at 16 July 2026.

Most food cannot be returned at all. Perishables and rapidly deteriorating goods are excluded from the returns guarantee outright, so a refund is the only remedy and the window for reporting damage is seven days.

All 14 Amazon Fresh shops were put forward for closure on 23 September 2025, five of them becoming Whole Foods Market by the end of 2026, so there is no Amazon grocery store to collect from or return to.

Coverage is postcode-by-postcode and incomplete. Amazon's own target is that more than 80% of UK Prime members will reach at least one grocery partner by the end of 2026, which means a significant minority still will not.

Mixing fresh items with the rest of an Amazon order creates separate baskets, separate checkouts and separate confirmations, and each merchant is a different company with its own customer service line.
verdict: Amazon's grocery business is now a delivery service with five shopfronts, and it is at its strongest on the ambient and household end of a basket, where a 5% referral fee with no minimum has pulled in a range no single supermarket matches. For a Prime member in a covered postcode, free same-day delivery over £20 alongside the rest of an Amazon order is a genuinely good offer, and the temperature and unattended-delivery rules are sensible and clearly stated. The gaps are all in what is not published: no minimum life on a chilled item, two different free-delivery thresholds four days apart, and a fee you only see at checkout. Read the use-by dates at the door, because Article 14 of the food information rules means that is the first moment anybody has to show them to you, and compare on unit price rather than pack price now that reduced and loyalty prices have had to carry one since 6 April 2026. Behind the shopfront, the supplier picture is poor and worth knowing: bottom of the Adjudicator's table on 68.6% and under investigation for late payment since June 2025.

faqs.q: Is Amazon grocery delivery free?
faqs.a: For Prime members it is free on same-day grocery orders over £20, on the figures Amazon published on 4 June 2026. Non-members pay £5.99 whatever the basket is worth. Amazon's Prime membership page, modified on 31 May 2026, separately offers Prime members free two-hour Amazon Fresh deliveries on orders above £60. The two apply to different services, and Amazon's help pages note that temporary promotions on delivery fees are not displayed, so check the figure at checkout.

faqs.q: Can I see the use-by date before I order?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, and there is no legal requirement that you can. Article 14 of assimilated Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 requires the mandatory food particulars to be available free of charge before the purchase is concluded, but it expressly excludes point (f) of Article 9(1), the date of minimum durability or the use-by date. That one has to be available at the moment of delivery, which is why checking the dates while the driver is still at the door is worth doing.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from on Amazon groceries?
faqs.a: It depends which shopfront you use. Amazon Fresh is Amazon's own. Morrisons orders are with WM Morrison Supermarkets PLC of Bradford, company number 358949; Iceland with Iceland Foods Ltd of Deeside, company number 01107406; Co-op with Co-operative Group Food Limited of 1 Angel Square, Manchester; and Gopuff with GoBrands UK Holdings Ltd, company number 12793914. Amazon publishes each entity with its VAT number and a customer service contact, and complaints go to the merchant rather than to Amazon.

faqs.q: What happens if frozen food arrives defrosted?
faqs.a: Report it through Your Orders within seven days of delivery and Amazon states it will refund without asking for the item back. Amazon Fresh purchases are refundable within 30 days, although most Fresh food is not returnable. Separately, food needing temperature control must not be kept above 8°C under paragraph 2 of Schedule 4 to the Food Safety and Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013, and persistent failures are a matter for the local authority's environmental health team.

faqs.q: Is there an Amazon Fresh shop I can visit?
faqs.a: No. On 23 September 2025 Amazon proposed closing all 14 of its Amazon Fresh stores in the UK, with five converting to Whole Foods Market by the end of 2026. Amazon's grocery business in Britain is delivery only, in eligible postcodes, with the company targeting access to at least one grocery partner for more than 80% of UK Prime members by the end of 2026.

faqs.q: Does Amazon show a price per 100g?
faqs.a: Unit pricing is a legal requirement for most groceries under the Price Marking Order, and since 6 April 2026 the rules have been tighter: the Price Marking (Amendment) Order 2024, as commenced by SI 2025/592, requires a product offered at more than one price to display each selling price and each unit price, and a price reduction to display the reduced unit price as well as the reduced price. Where pack sizes differ between sellers, the unit price is the only figure that compares them.

title: Amazon Health and Beauty: Fees, Returns and Who Is Answerable for What Is in the Bottle
meta_title: Amazon Beauty: 30-Day Returns, Fees and the Seal Rule
meta_description: Amazon allows 30 days on beauty returns where the law requires 14, charges sellers 8-15%, and stops at the hygiene seal. Rules checked 27 September 2026.
intro:
Amazon gives you 30 days to change your mind on a beauty order, against the 14 days the law actually requires, and repeat deliveries on a Subscribe & Save order carry free standard delivery to the UK and Ireland whether or not you pay for Prime. Both figures come from Amazon's own customer help pages, read on 27 September 2026. The next site-wide discount window is already dated: Prime Big Deal Days runs from 12:01am BST on 6 October 2026 to 11:59pm on 7 October, 48 hours, with beauty named as one of the six categories in it.

The range behind that is enormous and it is cheap to stock, which is the reason it is enormous. Amazon takes 8% of a beauty, health or personal care sale priced at or below £10 and 15% above it, with a 25p floor per item. That is the second-lowest band the company publishes for any consumer category, so a £5.99 shampoo is worth a seller's attention in a way it would not be at a flat 15%.

One mechanic decides more beauty arguments than any other and it is worth knowing before you order rather than after. Amazon's returns policy excludes "products which are not suitable for return due to health protection or hygienic reasons if unsealed by you after delivery". A sealed serum can go back inside 30 days. The same serum, opened, cannot go back at all, and that is the law rather than a shop rule.

headline.label: Returning an opened beauty product
headline.value: Not at all once the hygiene seal is broken — 30 days on sealed items against a statutory 14, with return postage from £1.99 (checked 27 September 2026)

key_facts.label: Amazon's cut on a beauty sale
key_facts.value: 8% on items priced up to £10, 15% above, minimum 25p per item

key_facts.label: Return window
key_facts.value: 30 days as a voluntary policy; 14 days is the statutory cancellation right

key_facts.label: Opened cosmetics
key_facts.value: Excluded from return once the hygiene seal is broken

key_facts.label: Return postage
key_facts.value: From £1.99 within the UK where free returns do not apply

key_facts.label: Seller costs
key_facts.value: £25 a month on the Professional plan, or 75p an item on the Individual plan, both excluding VAT

key_facts.label: Cosmetic safety reports on the register
key_facts.value: 182 cosmetic entries on the OPSS product safety register, 51 of them involving hydroquinone

key_facts.label: Complaints scheme membership
key_facts.value: No Amazon entity among the retailers listed by RetailADR, the CTSI-approved retail dispute scheme

key_facts.label: Next dated discount window
key_facts.value: Prime Big Deal Days, 6 to 7 October 2026, 48 hours

sections.heading: What a beauty seller pays, and why the shelf is so deep
sections.html:
Amazon publishes its referral fees openly, and the beauty band is unusually kind to cheap products. Beauty, Health and Personal Care attracts 8% on any item priced at or below £10 and 15% on anything above, with a 25p minimum referral fee per item sold. Sitting on top of that is either the Professional selling plan at £25 a month excluding VAT, or the Individual plan at 75p per item sold, also excluding VAT.

Work that through and the shape of the category explains itself. On a £7.99 hand cream the referral fee is 64p. On the same cream priced at £10.99 it is £1.65 — a jump of a pound in Amazon's favour for three pounds of extra price. The step at £10 is the reason so much of the beauty listing sits at £9.99 and below, and the reason multipacks appear at prices that cross the threshold in one go rather than creeping over it.

Subscribe & Save is the other lever, and it is worth being precise about what Amazon does and does not commit to. Every repeat delivery carries free standard delivery to the UK and Ireland, and a non-Prime customer may still pay on the first order if it sits below the free delivery threshold. The discount itself is not a published rate: Amazon says only that "the current discount for each item is posted on the product detail page when you sign up" and that it may rise or fall with daily pricing. Vouchers cannot be applied to an existing subscription, some items carry quantity limits, and Prime-Exclusive items need a Prime membership before the subscription will take at all. You can cancel at any time.

Prime itself is £8.99 a month or £95 a year, with a 30-day free trial, and £4.49 a month or £47.49 a year for students and 18 to 24 year olds on a six-month trial. For a beauty basket that is a delivery decision rather than a discount one, because the Subscribe & Save delivery benefit does not depend on it.

sections.heading: The name on the label that decides who is answerable
sections.html:
Every cosmetic sold in Great Britain has to have one identifiable company standing behind it, called the responsible person, and that company's name and address is required on the container or the packaging. It is the single most useful thing to look for on a delivered bottle, because it tells you which firm is legally on the hook for what is inside and which enforcement authority can knock on its door.

Behind that name sits a document most shoppers never hear of. Under Article 10 of the retained cosmetics regulation, a cosmetic product safety report must exist before the product goes on sale, and it has to be signed off by an assessor holding "a diploma or other evidence of formal qualifications awarded on completion of a university course of theoretical and practical study in pharmacy, toxicology, medicine or a similar discipline". Article 11 then requires the product information file — the safety report, the quantitative composition, the manufacturing method, the proof of any claimed effect and the animal testing record — to be kept for ten years after the last batch was placed on the market, in English, readily accessible at the address the responsible person notified to government. Article 13 requires that notification through the Submit Cosmetic Product Notifications service before a single unit is sold.

Two provisions matter especially on a marketplace. A distributor stops being merely a distributor and becomes the responsible person itself the moment it sells a product under its own name or trademark, or modifies one already on the market — so an own-label listing changes who is answerable, even where the factory is the same. And Article 23 puts the duty to report a serious undesirable effect on "the responsible person and distributors", without delay, naming the product and any corrective measure taken. The reporting address is a government mailbox, seriousundesirableeffects@businessandtrade.gov.uk, and enforcement itself sits with local authority Trading Standards, with the Office for Product Safety and Standards as the competent authority alongside the Secretary of State.

There is a deadline worth diarising if you buy imported brands. EU responsible person details may be used on GB labelling until 31 December 2027, after which UK responsible person details have to replace them. Until then a label naming a company in Warsaw or Milan is compliant; after that date it will not be, and the brands least likely to notice are the ones with no UK office to notice on their behalf.

sections.heading: What the safety register actually shows about beauty
sections.html:
There is no Defaqto for shampoo and no ombudsman for mascara, so the nearest thing to an independent scoreboard in this category is the government's own product safety register. Searched on 27 September 2026 it returns 182 entries for the keyword "cosmetic". A narrower search on a single banned ingredient, hydroquinone, returns 51 — and every one of the ten on the first page is classified as a serious risk.

Reading those titles in a row tells you where the danger concentrates. RODIS Creme Skin Light, Fair & White So White Skin Perfector Serum, Purec Egyptian Magic Whitening Face & Body Lotion, SWP+ Skin Whitening Body Lotion, Caro White Lightening Beauty Lotion, Cocopulp Skin Lightening Cream, Jaina Beauty Lightening Face Cream, Golden Pearl Beauty Cream, Angel Cosmetics Clairmen Lightening Program for Men. Skin-lightening preparations dominate the serious-risk end of the cosmetic register almost to the exclusion of everything else.

One entry shows what "serious" means in laboratory numbers. Parley Cosmetics Goldie Advanced Beauty Cream, reference 2508-0034a, recalled on 12 August 2025, was found to contain mercury at 16,680 mg/kg — 1.7% of the product — together with the corticosteroid clobetasol propionate at 1,470 mg/kg, or 0.15%. Mercury is prohibited in cosmetics outright. That consignment was rejected at the border and destroyed, which is the best possible outcome and also the one that depends entirely on the shipment being intercepted rather than posted.

The register also carries a very recent entry with Amazon's name on it. On 16 September 2026, eleven days before this page was written, Baylis & Harding PLC recalled the one-litre eco refill of its oud, cedar and amber hand wash, reference 2609-0060, batch codes 6210A and 6211A printed on the base of the pouch. Testing found Pluralibacter gergoviae, which "may lead to infection or adverse health effects, particularly in vulnerable users". The breach cited is of the cosmetics regulation itself. The product was made in the United Kingdom, the risk level is recorded as low, it was notified by local authority Trading Standards, and the retailers listed are Ocado, Sainsbury's, Waitrose and Amazon. Customers are told to stop using it immediately and return it to the place of purchase for redress.

That is worth reading carefully rather than as an accusation. A recall naming four large retailers is a recall of a British manufacturer's product that reached all four; it is evidence that the system found a contamination problem and published it, and Amazon appears there for the same reason three supermarkets do. What it does establish is that a brand being familiar, British and sold by household-name grocers is not on its own a safety argument, and that the batch code on the base of the bottle is the thing that decides whether yours is affected.

sections.heading: Peroxide, and the one percentage on a whitening kit that matters
sections.html:
Tooth whitening is the corner of health and beauty where the law draws a hard line at a number, and it is the corner where marketplace listings most often sit on the wrong side of it. A product sold to the public for home use may contain no more than 0.1% hydrogen peroxide. Between that and 6% the product may only be supplied through a dentist. Above 6% it has no lawful consumer route at all.

The scale of the gap between that rule and what is actually listed online was measured by Which?, whose findings the British Dental Association publicised. Of 36 whitening products bought from online marketplaces, 21 contained more hydrogen peroxide than the legal limit allows and 11 contained more than 6%. Two syringes bought through AliExpress came in at around 30% — described as roughly 300 times the amount that can lawfully be sold to a consumer. Paul Woodhouse of the BDA board put it as plainly as it can be put: "Hydrogen peroxide is a seriously strong chemical and not to be messed with."

Two caveats belong with those numbers. That testing was published in May 2021, so it is five years old and the sample was drawn across several marketplaces rather than from Amazon alone. No equivalent study of comparable size has been published since that a search will surface, which is itself worth saying. The 0.1% and 6% thresholds, on the other hand, have not moved, and they are printable on a box — which makes the concentration on the packaging a test any reader can apply in the time it takes to read a listing.

The same logic runs through the rest of the category. The retained regulation works by lists: Annex II names the substances a cosmetic may not contain at all, Annex III those allowed only within stated restrictions, Annex IV colourants, Annex V preservatives and Annex VI UV filters. A product outside those lists is not a matter of opinion or of house style. It is unlawful, and the ingredient panel is where it shows.

sections.heading: Sending it back, and the seal that ends the argument
sections.html:
Amazon's stated position is better than the legal minimum and then stops abruptly. The voluntary window is 30 days from receipt, where the statutory cancellation right is 14. Return postage, where free returns do not apply, starts at £1.99 within the UK and may be deducted from the refund — unless the item was defective, damaged, wrong or delivered late, in which case it should not be.

The exclusions are where beauty differs from everything else Amazon sells. The policy excludes "products which are not suitable for return due to health protection or hygienic reasons if unsealed by you after delivery, or which are, after delivery, inseparably mixed with other items", and separately excludes "goods which may deteriorate or expire rapidly". Together those two lines cover most of a beauty basket the moment it is opened. This mirrors the hygiene exception in consumer contracts law rather than inventing anything, and the practical consequence is worth stating flatly: the cellophane and the little sticker on the lid are not packaging, they are the boundary of your right to change your mind.

There is a narrower rule that catches fragrance and aerosols. On Luxury Stores listings, Amazon states that "beauty products made of hazardous materials, including flammable liquids or gases, are not returnable to Amazon". An eau de parfum is a flammable liquid. A shopper spending three figures on a scent should read that line before ordering rather than after deciding it does not suit them.

What Amazon does not publish anywhere reachable is a minimum shelf life on delivery. A cosmetic with a durability of less than 30 months has to carry a best-before date, and one above that carries the open-jar period-after-opening symbol instead; a distributor is separately forbidden from supplying a product whose minimum durability date has passed. None of that tells you how much of the life will be left when the parcel arrives, and no undertaking on that point could be found on the help pages, the product pages or the seller programme material.

sections.heading: Where a beauty complaint goes when the seller stops replying
sections.html:
Financial products have the Financial Ombudsman Service. Furniture has an ombudsman of its own. Beauty retail has an approved dispute scheme, and the interesting part is who has joined it.

RetailADR, run by Consumer Dispute Resolution Limited, is approved by government under the Alternative Dispute Resolution for Consumer Disputes (Competent Authorities and Information) Regulations 2015 and by the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. It is free to consumers, and between 1 January and 1 September 2026 it received 1,014 claims, accepted 905, published 793 determinations and turned cases round in an average of 21 days. Its published member list includes ALDI, ASOS, IKEA, Harrods, Poundland, Oliver Bonas, Richer Sounds, Topshop, Virgin Active and around forty others.

Checked on 27 September 2026, no Amazon entity appears on that list. Neither does Superdrug, Lookfantastic, Cult Beauty or The Body Shop; the only Boots name on it is Boots Kitchen Appliances, which is a different business from the chemist. Membership is voluntary, so this is not a rule anyone has broken — but it does mean that a beauty dispute Amazon declines to resolve has no independent adjudicator behind it, and that the A-to-z process and the card chargeback are the realistic routes rather than a first step towards one.

Two other doors are worth knowing. Product safety concerns — an unlabelled cream, a suspected banned ingredient, a reaction — go to Trading Standards and to OPSS, which is the body that publishes the register quoted above and which receives serious undesirable effect reports directly. And if the order includes a medicine rather than a cosmetic, the MHRA keeps a register of websites authorised to sell medicines online, searchable by name, company number or domain. The registration duty described in the government guidance is framed around selling medicines to the public in Northern Ireland, and an application can take up to 90 working days to process; how far that register covers a Great Britain shopper's purchase is a point this page could not settle from the published guidance and one to confirm with the MHRA directly.

sections.heading: The compliance paperwork Amazon asks its sellers for
sections.html:
Amazon runs a product compliance service for sellers and names "cosmetics and medicinal products" among the regulated areas it covers, alongside toys, electricals, chemicals, medical devices and food. The concrete mechanism it describes is narrower than the list implies: it collects responsible person details for non-EU brands and ASINs fulfilled through Fulfilment by Amazon, via a seller dashboard, on the basis that "since July 16 2021, it has been illegal to sell CE-marked products in the EU without a Responsible Person in the EU".

Note what that is and is not. It is an EU-facing requirement built around CE marking, gathered for products Amazon itself warehouses. Cosmetics are not CE-marked, the GB responsible person duty is a separate regime with its own register, and the pages carry Amazon's own disclaimer that they do "not constitute any legal or other compliance advice from Amazon". Whether a cosmetics seller is required to hold a signed safety report and a product information file before listing is therefore settled by the regulation, not by the marketplace — and no requirement to produce either before a beauty listing goes live could be found in Amazon's published seller material.

For a shopper that has one practical consequence. The document trail that makes a cosmetic lawful sits with the responsible person, and the responsible person is identified on the label rather than on the listing page. If the bottle that arrives carries no UK name and address at all, the problem is not the shop's returns policy. It is that nobody in this country has taken the legal responsibility for what is inside it, and Trading Standards is the right recipient for that rather than customer services.

pros: 30 days to return, where the statutory cancellation right is 14
Free standard delivery to the UK and Ireland on every Subscribe & Save repeat delivery, with or without Prime
Referral fees of 8% up to £10 keep genuinely cheap beauty products viable for sellers, which widens the range
Cancel a Subscribe & Save subscription at any time, with quantity limits shown before you confirm
Dated discount windows published in advance — Prime Big Deal Days on 6 and 7 October 2026
Return postage waived where the item was defective, damaged, wrong or delivered late
cons: An opened cosmetic cannot be returned at all: the hygiene-seal exclusion covers most of a beauty basket the moment it is used once

The Subscribe & Save discount is never published as a rate — Amazon says only that it appears on the product page and may rise or fall with daily pricing, so a repeat order carries no committed saving
No minimum shelf life on delivery is published anywhere reachable, so there is no undertaking about how much of a product's durability period will be left when it arrives
No Amazon entity appears on RetailADR's member list, so a beauty dispute has no independent adjudicator behind it
Fragrance and aerosols on Luxury Stores listings are non-returnable outright as flammable goods, which is easy to miss on a three-figure purchase

The seller compliance material collects responsible person details for CE-marked goods fulfilled by Amazon, and no requirement to hold a cosmetic product safety report before listing could be found in it
Return postage from £1.99 is deducted from the refund on any change-of-mind return outside free returns
Whether the MHRA's online medicine seller register covers a Great Britain purchase could not be established from the published guidance and needs confirming
verdict: Amazon's beauty proposition is a wide, cheap shelf with a returns policy that beats the legal minimum by a fortnight and then hits a wall at the hygiene seal. The 8% referral fee below £10 is why the range runs so deep at low prices, and Subscribe & Save's free repeat delivery is a real benefit even without Prime — though the discount attached to it is never committed to as a number. The part worth taking seriously is provenance rather than price. A cosmetic is lawful because one identifiable company has signed a safety report and keeps a product information file for ten years, and that company is named on the label, not on the listing. With 182 cosmetic entries on the OPSS register, 51 of them turning on a single banned ingredient, and one September 2026 recall that names Amazon alongside three supermarkets, the ten seconds it takes to look for a UK responsible person and a batch code on the bottle is the most useful thing a shopper can do here.

faqs.q: Can I return make-up or skincare to Amazon after opening it?
faqs.a: No. Amazon's returns policy excludes products that are not suitable for return for health protection or hygiene reasons once you have unsealed them after delivery, and separately excludes goods that may deteriorate or expire rapidly. Sealed items can go back inside the 30-day voluntary window, and the statutory cancellation right is 14 days. Return postage starts at £1.99 within the UK where free returns do not apply, though it should not be charged if the item was defective, damaged, wrong or delivered late.

faqs.q: How do I tell whether a cosmetic sold on Amazon is legal to sell here?
faqs.a: Look on the bottle or the box for the name and address of the UK responsible person. That company has to exist, has to have commissioned a cosmetic product safety report signed by a qualified assessor, and has to keep a product information file in English for ten years after the last batch was sold. EU responsible person details may still be used on GB labelling until 31 December 2027. A cosmetic arriving with no UK name and address at all is a matter for Trading Standards rather than for customer services.

faqs.q: How much hydrogen peroxide is a home teeth whitening kit allowed to contain?
faqs.a: 0.1%. Between 0.1% and 6% a whitening product may only be supplied through a dentist, and above 6% there is no lawful consumer route at all. When Which? tested 36 whitening products bought from online marketplaces, 21 exceeded the legal limit and 11 contained more than 6%, with two AliExpress syringes at around 30%. That testing was published in May 2021 and covered several marketplaces rather than Amazon alone, but the thresholds have not changed and the concentration is printed on the packaging.

faqs.q: What does Amazon charge a seller on a beauty product?
faqs.a: 8% of the total price on items at or below £10 and 15% above that, with a minimum referral fee of 25p per item. Sellers also pay either £25 a month on the Professional plan or 75p per item on the Individual plan, both excluding VAT. The step at £10 is sharp: the fee on a £7.99 item is 64p and on a £10.99 item £1.65.

faqs.q: Who can I complain to if Amazon will not resolve a beauty order?
faqs.a: There is no ombudsman for beauty retail, and no Amazon entity appears on the member list of RetailADR, the CTSI-approved retail dispute scheme, checked on 27 September 2026. That leaves Amazon's own A-to-z process and a card chargeback for the money side. For anything about the product itself — a missing label, a suspected banned ingredient, a reaction — the routes are local authority Trading Standards and the Office for Product Safety and Standards, which publishes the product safety register and receives serious undesirable effect reports.

title: Amazon Men's Fashion: Free Returns, Fibre Labels and Who You Are Buying From
meta_title: Amazon Men's Fashion: Free Returns and Label Rules
meta_description: Amazon pays return postage on men's clothes and shoes: 30 days, no minimum order. Fibre labels, the 80% shoe rule and leather limits, checked 27 Sept 2026.
intro:
Amazon pays the postage when men's clothes go back. Clothing, footwear, handbags, jewellery and watches flagged Free Return at checkout come with a prepaid label and 30 days from delivery, with no minimum order — checked on 27 September 2026 against Amazon's own returns pages. Anything else it sells starts at £1.99 for a UK return, taken out of the refund.

That is worth more in menswear than in most categories, because sizing is the thing nobody gets right first time. A jacket that turns up a size out costs nothing to send back here, against the £1.99 Amazon charges on a return that was not flagged as free. The condition is strict rather than hidden: new and unworn, with the original packaging, the tags and any certificate of authenticity still attached, and the free label has to have been offered on that listing when you bought it — on a site where a large share of the stock belongs to third-party sellers rather than to Amazon, it is not offered on everything.

The other thing worth knowing before you click is where the reliable information about a garment actually sits. It is not in the listing copy, which the seller writes. It is on the label stitched into the side seam, and what has to be printed there is set by statute — fibre content by percentage, in English, on something durable enough to survive a wash. The same is true of the pictograms inside a shoe. This page is about reading those, and about the points where Amazon's own rules pick the job up and the points where they put it down.

headline.label: What a return costs when it does not fit
headline.value: Nothing on clothes, shoes and accessories marked Free Return — against £1.99 upwards on anything else Amazon sells, deducted from the refund (checked 27 September 2026)

key_facts.label: What the law makes them print

key_facts.value: 30 days from delivery under Amazon's own policy, sitting on top of a statutory 14-day cancellation right

key_facts.label: Condition demanded
key_facts.value: New and unworn, with all original packaging, tags and certificates of authenticity; resized or altered items refused

key_facts.label: Cost if the listing was not flagged
key_facts.value: From £1.99 within the UK and from £8.09 from abroad, deducted from the refund unless the item was faulty, wrong or late

key_facts.value: None: sellers are barred from listing used or refurbished clothing, and the pre-owned designer storefront Amazon added on 6 February 2024 is womenswear

sections.heading: The label in the side seam is the one document that has to be true
sections.html:
Listing copy on a marketplace is written by whoever owns the stock. The composition label is written to a statute. The Textile Products (Labelling and Fibre Composition) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1102) bring the assimilated EU Regulation 1007/2011 into UK law, and they catch anything made of textile fibres plus anything that is at least 80% textile fibre by weight. A shirt, a suit, a knitted tie and the fabric part of an umbrella are all in. The duty falls on the manufacturer or the importer into the UK, which on Amazon usually means the seller rather than Amazon.

What the label has to say is more prescriptive than most shoppers realise. Where two or more fibres make up 85% of the finished garment, each is named with its percentage — cotton 80%, polyester 15%, nylon 5%. The word pure is reserved for a single-fibre garment, and a fibre name cannot be borrowed to flatter a texture, so silk acetate on an acetate shirt is unlawful rather than merely optimistic. Decorative matter accounting for 7% or less is left out of the calculation, which is why an embroidered motif does not appear in the numbers. Where a garment has components of different composition — a jacket and its lining being the obvious case — each component is declared separately, so a single figure on a lined coat is a sign the label is wrong.

Two more lines are worth hunting for. Only the fibre names in Annex I of the assimilated Regulation may be used, which is why you see elastane and not a brand name. And where any part of the item comes from an animal but is not a textile — a leather trim, a horn button, a fur collar — the wording contains non-textile parts of animal origin has to appear. That phrase is the one a shopper buying a wool coat with a trimmed hood should look for, because mislabelling real fur as fake is an offence in itself, and selling, importing or exporting cat or dog fur is prohibited outright under separate 2008 regulations.

The label has to be durable, easily legible, visible and accessible, and it has to be in English. Around forty categories are exempt in Annex VI — buttons, artificial flowers, flags, travel goods, toys, make-up cases, disposable articles and protective sports requisites other than gloves — and multipacks of identical items may be labelled once on the packaging rather than individually. Enforcement is a Trading Standards matter: regulation 11 puts the duty on local weights and measures authorities, regulation 5 creates the offence of making a non-compliant product available on the UK market, and regulation 6 sets the punishment at a fine up to the statutory maximum on summary conviction or an unlimited fine on indictment. There is no prison sentence attached. Home workers and self-employed tailors making customised garments sit outside the offence, which is a sensible carve-out and also a gap on a marketplace.

sections.heading: Shoes are labelled in three parts, and 80% is the number that decides
sections.html:
Footwear has its own rulebook and it is older: the Footwear (Indication of Composition) Labelling Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2489), covering England, Scotland and Wales. Every pair sold new has to declare the material of three separate parts — the upper, the lining and sock, and the outer sole — and the test is coverage rather than weight. The label names whichever material accounts for 80% of the surface area of that part. Where nothing reaches 80%, the two main materials have to be given instead, which is the honest answer on most modern trainers.

There are four material categories, each with its own pictogram: leather, coated leather, textile and the catch-all other materials. The distinction between the first two is the one that costs money. A shoe carrying the coated-leather symbol is not the same product as one carrying the leather symbol, and the pictogram says so where the listing photograph will not. The label may be printed, stuck, embossed or attached, it only has to appear on one shoe of the pair, and English or the pictograms are both acceptable. In a shop there must be a notice explaining what the symbols mean; for a distance sale the consumer has to be clearly informed of the same thing, which is a requirement an online listing meets far less often than a shop window does.

Four things fall outside the regulations altogether: second-hand footwear, protective footwear, anything containing asbestos, and children's play footwear for under-14s. Manufacturers and importers carry the labelling duty, and a retailer is expected to check compliance before selling and keep a record of having checked. Trading Standards enforces, and a misleading indication can also be attacked under the unfair trading provisions now sitting in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.

sections.heading: Leather has a chemical ceiling, and two pairs of gloves went past it
sections.html:
The least-known rule in menswear is a limit on a chemical. Chromium salts are what turn hide into leather, and the tanning process can leave behind chromium VI, a skin sensitiser. Entry 47 of Annex XVII to REACH caps it at under 3 mg/kg — three parts per million — in any leather article that comes into contact with the skin. Shoes, belts, gloves, watch straps and jacket trim are all inside that description. The industry test is EN ISO 17075, and part 2 of it, using high performance liquid chromatography, is the method recommended for dyed leather because the dye can otherwise mask the result.

It is not a theoretical limit. A search of the OPSS product safety register for chromium returned nine entries on 27 September 2026, and two of them are gloves. McCalifornia women's brown leather gloves were recalled on 5 February 2021 at serious risk. Ashwood fine leather gloves, style D8906, red with a faux fur lining and sold through TK Maxx, were recalled on 9 April 2021, also at serious risk, for chromium VI in the leather above the legal maximum; the entry was published on 25 March 2022, names the REACH Enforcement Regulations 2008 as the breach, records the country of origin as unknown and shows the recall as voluntary, notified by local authority Trading Standards.

Two points follow for anyone buying leather online. The country of origin being unrecorded on a formal recall tells you how thin the paper trail behind a leather good can be. And both of those recalls came from named businesses with a UK address to write to, which is exactly why they could be recalled at all.

sections.heading: What 248 entries on the recall register do and do not tell you
sections.html:
The Office for Product Safety and Standards runs a free, searchable register of alerts, reports and recalls at gov.uk, and almost nobody looking at a clothing listing thinks to use it. Searched on 27 September 2026, it returned 248 entries for clothing, 135 for textile and only 5 for footwear. Those totals cover several years and every retailer in the country, which is the first thing to hold on to: a clothing recall in Britain is rare.

The detail is more useful than the totals. Under textile the register carries an Ayan Textile hoodcord jacket recorded at serious risk on 12 February 2024, an Asda ladies' handbag range at serious risk on 2 September 2026, Primark purses and children's shorts, Mint Velvet slingback heels through Next in December 2024, and the La Redoute Alanis printed bathrobe on 15 September 2026. Under clothing, an AOOWU mermaid princess dress was reported at serious risk on 15 September 2026 with Amazon recorded as the seller.

Read that last one in both directions, because it deserves it. A serious-risk entry naming the shop you are about to buy from is not a reassuring sentence. It is also evidence that the system found the product, published it and can be searched by anyone in about thirty seconds — and Asda, Primark, Next and Morrisons are all on the same register for the same reason. What the register cannot show is the listing that was quietly pulled before anyone tested it, which on a marketplace of third-party sellers is the population that matters. Two searches by brand name before you order is a habit worth having.

sections.heading: Since March 2024 a 'responsible' range has to show its working
sections.html:
Menswear marketing leans hard on words like sustainable, conscious and responsible, and since 2024 those words have carried a regulatory cost. The Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation into environmental claims by ASOS, Boohoo and George at Asda on 29 July 2022 and closed it on 27 March 2024 by taking formal undertakings from all three. The undertakings are specific: green claims must be accurate with the key information clear and prominent, fabric claims such as organic or recycled must state the actual percentage, any named environmental range — ASOS's Responsible edit, Boohoo's Ready for the Future, Asda's George for Good — must publish the criteria a product has to meet to be in it, search filters must genuinely match what the garments are made of, natural imagery must not be used to overstate a benefit, target-based claims need a verifiable strategy behind them, and accreditation logos must make the scope of the certification clear. Each of the three reports to the CMA on compliance.

The CMA followed up on 18 September 2024 with guidance addressed to the whole fashion retail sector. It deliberately sets very few numeric thresholds — it does not say what percentage of recycled content earns the word recycled — and instead requires the figure itself to be shown, gives at least 50% recycled content as an example of a filter label that works, and warns that broad terms are far more likely to be inaccurate than specific ones. Amazon was not one of the three firms investigated, and it is fair to say so. The guidance applies to the sector rather than to those companies, the unfair trading rules behind it now sit in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, and the practical test for a shopper is the same either way: if the filter says recycled and the composition label does not carry a percentage, the claim has nothing under it.

sections.heading: Free returns are paid for twice, and only one of the prices is published
sections.html:
The free return is the best thing on this page and it is worth being precise about how it works. Amazon's voluntary policy gives 30 days from receipt to send most things back unused and undamaged, which sits on top of the 14-day statutory cancellation right rather than replacing it. Where the listing was marked eligible for a free return at the time of purchase, Amazon supplies a printable prepaid label and carries the cost on items it sold or dispatched; on a seller-fulfilled order the seller provides the label and pays. Where the listing was not marked eligible, the cost of the label comes off the refund, starting at £1.99 within the UK and £8.09 internationally — unless the item was defective, damaged, wrong or delivered late, in which case nothing is deducted. Hand-delivered returns are refused, and returning an eligible and an ineligible item in one parcel can still cost you postage on the ineligible one.

Somebody is paying for all of that, and on Amazon it is the seller. Amazon charges a returns processing fee on customer-returned goods in precisely the categories where it offers free return shipping — Clothing, Shoes and Handbags — and explicitly not on jewellery, watches or luggage, which get the free return without the fee attached. Amazon does not publish the amount of that fee anywhere a shopper can read it, which makes the true cost of a generous returns policy invisible in the price of the shirt.

The seller side has one more asymmetry a menswear shopper can use. Amazon's published referral fees put footwear on a flat 15% with a 25p minimum and no low-price band at all, while clothing and accessories are tiered so that cheap items are charged least, with the schedule last changed on 15 December 2025. Run the arithmetic on two £60 purchases fulfilled by Amazon and they are not taxed alike: a £60 jacket is charged 15% on the first £40 and 7% on the rest, coming to £7.40, while a £60 pair of shoes is charged 15% flat, or £9.00. That £1.60 gap is one reason the cheap end of Amazon's clothing is so deep and its footwear is comparatively thin. Sellers also pay £25 a month excluding VAT on the Professional plan or 75p per item as an Individual, and £0.62 to £1.51 per cubic foot a month to store stock, which is what a bulky winter coat costs to sit unsold through a warm November.

sections.heading: Who stitched it, and what Amazon says it checks
sections.html:
Garment supply chains are the reason the Modern Slavery Act 2015 exists, so the section 54 statement is a fair document to hold Amazon to. Its statement for the year to 31 December 2025, approved and signed in 2026 by UK country manager John Boumphrey, is made on behalf of 13 UK subsidiaries. On training it is detailed: 68,000 Amazon employees reached by e-learning during 2025, 2,500 suppliers trained through the same platforms, 24 in-person workshops across 13 countries engaging 253 suppliers, and 38 third-party courses made available.

On remediation it puts real money on the page, which is rarer. It records $340,632 returned to workers during the 2025 phase of a recruitment-fee repayment programme, 146 further workers reimbursed in a second phase, and 847 workers repaid a combined total of more than $2.2 million. Its audit findings are given as rates rather than counts: incomplete employment information under 1%, ineffectively communicated employment information 1.77%, mandatory overtime under 1%, worker-paid recruitment fees under 1% and document retention failures under 1%.

The limitation is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up. Every one of those figures is group-wide, covering a business that sells servers and groceries as well as shirts, and nothing in the statement is broken out for apparel or textiles specifically. A reader trying to find out about the factory that made a particular £12 polo shirt will not get there from this document. It is more than most marketplaces publish and it is still not an answer about clothes.

sections.heading: No used menswear, and one storefront that skips men entirely
sections.html:
Two absences are worth knowing about before you go looking. The first is second-hand. Amazon's own guidance to clothing sellers states that used or refurbished clothing cannot be sold on the site, and that only authentic apparel may be listed, with permission obtained from the retailer, wholesaler, manufacturer or designer first. That rule is why the counterfeit problem in clothing is smaller here than on some rivals, and it is also why the resale market that has taken over menswear elsewhere has no presence at all on Amazon.

The second is more specific. Amazon does run a pre-owned designer storefront in Europe: on 6 February 2024 it added Hardly Ever Worn It, a family-run resale business founded in 2012 and shipping to more than 40 countries, to Luxury Stores for customers in the UK, Germany, Spain and Italy, with a pre-screening process for authenticity. Its range is women's ready-to-wear, shoes, accessories, jewellery and watches. There is no equivalent for men.

Amazon's seller guidance is prescriptive in one way that does help menswear shoppers: it requires professionally shot, high-resolution photographs of the actual garment from multiple angles, on a model or a mannequin rather than on a hanger, with close-ups of details such as buttons and cuffs, and it requires a size chart giving the dimensions of the item in several international standards. Where a listing has none of those, it is not meeting the standard Amazon sets for it, and that is a reasonable reason to move on to the next one.

pros: Return postage is paid on clothing, footwear, handbags, jewellery and watches marked Free Return, with no minimum order and 30 days to decide
30-day return window is more than twice the 14-day statutory cancellation right, and nothing is deducted when an item arrives faulty, wrong or late
Third-party sellers are barred from listing used or refurbished clothing, and need permission from the brand or wholesaler to list at all
Seller rules require photographs of the actual garment on a model or mannequin from several angles, plus a size chart in multiple international standards
Tiered referral fees on clothing charge the least on the cheapest items, which is why the sub-£15 end of the range is unusually deep
Amazon's section 54 modern slavery statement puts figures on remediation rather than intentions, including more than $2.2 million of recruitment fees repaid to 847 workers
cons: Amazon charges sellers a returns processing fee in exactly the Clothing, Shoes and Handbags categories where it gives shoppers free returns, and publishes the amount nowhere a buyer can see it
Free returns only apply where the listing was flagged eligible at the moment of purchase; on everything else the label costs from £1.99 and comes out of the refund
Mixing an eligible and an ineligible item in one return parcel can still cost postage on the ineligible one, and hand-delivered returns are refused outright
There is no route to second-hand menswear: sellers cannot list used clothing, and the pre-owned designer storefront added in February 2024 covers womenswear only
The modern slavery statement's audit, training and remediation figures are all group-wide, with nothing broken out for apparel or textiles
Which? publishes rated shop surveys for baby products, technology and home goods but none for clothing, so there is no independent customer score for menswear retailers to measure Amazon against
A serious-risk product safety report published on 15 September 2026 records Amazon as the seller of the item concerned
Whether Prime Try Before You Buy still operates for UK customers could not be established from Amazon's own UK pages and needs confirming
verdict: For men's clothing Amazon's strongest feature is the one it charges nothing for: a prepaid return label on clothes, shoes and accessories, 30 days to use it and no minimum order, which takes the risk out of the sizing problem that makes buying menswear online awkward in the first place. The rules around it are strict rather than concealed — tags on, packaging kept, eligibility flagged at checkout — and the £1.99 charge on everything else is published plainly. Where the site is weakest is in what it tells you about the garment itself, because on a marketplace the listing copy belongs to the seller. The information that is reliable comes from the label rather than the page: fibre percentages under the 2012 Regulations, the three-part 80% pictogram on a shoe, the wording about non-textile parts of animal origin, and the 3 mg/kg chromium VI ceiling on leather that touches skin. Check those, run a brand name through the OPSS register before a larger order, and treat any environmental claim without a percentage next to it as decoration.

faqs.q: Does Amazon charge for returning clothes that do not fit?
faqs.a: Not on items marked Free Return at the time of purchase, which covers clothing, footwear, handbags, jewellery and watches. Amazon supplies a prepaid label and pays the postage on goods it sold or dispatched, and there is no minimum order. On a listing that was not marked eligible, the return label costs from £1.99 within the UK and from £8.09 from overseas, and the amount is deducted from the refund unless the item was faulty, damaged, wrong or late.

faqs.q: How long do I actually have to send something back?
faqs.a: Two periods run at once. The statutory cancellation right gives 14 days from the day the item is received, for any reason. Amazon's own voluntary policy gives 30 days from receipt on most products provided they are unused and undamaged, and that is the one most shoppers use. Amazon Haul orders are different again at 15 days. Fashion returns must go back new and unworn with all original packaging, tags and certificates of authenticity; anything resized or altered will be refused.

faqs.q: What has to be on the label of a shirt or a jacket sold in the UK?
faqs.a: Fibre content by percentage, in English, on a label that is durable, easily legible, visible and accessible. Where two or more fibres make up 85% of the garment, each is named with its share. The word pure may only be used for a single-fibre item. Decorative matter of 7% or less is excluded from the figures, and a garment with components of different composition, such as a lined jacket, must declare each component. Any part of animal origin that is not a textile triggers the wording contains non-textile parts of animal origin.

faqs.q: How do I tell real leather shoes from coated leather on a listing?
faqs.a: By the label rather than the photograph. Under the Footwear (Indication of Composition) Labelling Regulations 1995 every new pair must indicate the material of the upper, the lining and sock and the outer sole, using whichever material covers 80% of that part's surface area, or the two main materials where none reaches 80%. There are four categories, each with a pictogram: leather, coated leather, textile and other materials. The label need only appear on one shoe of the pair, and for a distance sale the seller is supposed to explain what the symbols mean.

faqs.q: Can I buy second-hand menswear on Amazon?
faqs.a: No. Amazon's guidance to clothing sellers states that used and refurbished clothing may not be sold on the site, and that only authentic apparel may be listed with the brand's or wholesaler's permission. Amazon does operate a pre-owned designer storefront in Europe — Hardly Ever Worn It joined Luxury Stores on 6 February 2024 for the UK, Germany, Spain and Italy — but its range is women's ready-to-wear, shoes, accessories, jewellery and watches, with no men's equivalent.

faqs.q: Is there a way to check whether a clothing brand has been recalled?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is free. The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes a searchable register of alerts, reports and recalls on gov.uk. Searching it on 27 September 2026 returned 248 entries for clothing, 135 for textile, 9 for chromium and 5 for footwear. Those numbers span several years and the whole UK market, so a clothing recall is genuinely uncommon; what the register cannot show is a marketplace listing withdrawn before anyone tested it.

title: Amazon Smart Home: Four Years of Security Updates, and the Dates They End
meta_title: Amazon Smart Home: 4 Years of Updates on Echo and Ring
meta_description: Amazon guarantees four years of security updates on Echo and Ring, with published end dates running to 2031. Prices, plans and the gaps, checked 27 Sept 2026.

headline.label: Guaranteed security-update period
headline.value: At least 4 years from the day you buy it new on Amazon.co.uk, and no Echo carries a published end date earlier than 31 December 2029 (checked 27 September 2026)

key_facts.value: 31 December 2029 on the Echo Dot 3rd to 5th generation, Echo Studio and Echo Sub; 31 December 2030 on the 2025 Echo Dot Max, 2025 Echo Studio, Echo Show 11 and Echo Hub
