meta_description: Avanti charges £0 booking fee and pays Delay Repay from 15 minutes late. The automatic claim, the £5 station refund fee and the 7 March 2027 handover.

headline.label: Booking fee per transaction
headline.value: £0 — no booking fee on any ticket bought on avantiwestcoast.co.uk or in the Avanti app

intro:
Avanti West Coast charges no booking fee at all — £0 on every ticket sold through its own website and app — and its Delay Repay starts at 15 minutes late, paying 25% of a single fare. Both numbers are the company's own, from its price promise page and the Passenger Charter dated April 2026, and both were checked on 3 October 2026.

The reason that matters more here than on a ticket-selling website is that Avanti is the railway as well as the shop. British rail fares are set by the industry, not by whoever sells them, so a London to Manchester ticket costs the same whether you buy it from the operator, an independent retailer or a machine at the station. What changes is the fee on top and who you are dealing with at 18:40 when the train has not moved. Buy direct from Avanti and those are the same company: the 23-train Evero fleet it ordered for £350m, the 34.9 million journeys it carried between April 2024 and March 2025, and the Delay Repay account that pays you, all sit inside First Trenitalia West Coast Rail Limited. Advance tickets bought direct can be set to claim compensation on their own, usually within 24 hours of travel, which is something a third-party retailer is not permitted to offer at all.

Advertised walk-up prices start at £12 one way from London to Birmingham and £35 to Manchester, e-tickets cost nothing to deliver, and the website promises to refund the difference if the same ticket turns up cheaper elsewhere. One thing to know before you book a journey months out: the Transport Secretary announced on 28 September 2026 that these services transfer to public ownership on 7 March 2027. Tickets, fares and compensation are unaffected — the Department for Transport already carries the revenue — but the name on the website will change.

sections.heading: The fare is fixed, so the fee is the whole contest
sections.html:
Rail fares in Britain are industry products. The operator does not price its own Anytime single any more than a newsagent prices a stamp, which is why comparing fares between sellers compares nothing at all. The only figure that genuinely differs from one seller to the next is what they add for selling it, and Avanti adds nothing: its price promise page says the website and app "will always have the lowest priced tickets for journeys on our trains" with "no booking fees". Digital tickets are delivered free. Against the 59p-to-£2.79 transaction fee charged by the largest independent retailer, buying direct saves the fee and nothing else — the ticket in your phone is identical.

What the operator does control is the shape of its own cheap fares. Advance tickets are the usual route to the £12 London to Birmingham and £35 London to Manchester prices advertised on the home page, with £26 quoted to Liverpool and £48 to Glasgow. Standard Premium sits between Standard and First Class on the Pendolino and Evero fleets, and Family Advance tickets, Off-Peak, Super Off-Peak, Anytime and Season tickets all appear in the same booking engine, with a seat picker rather than an automatic allocation.

Then there is Superfare, which is Avanti's own invention and is not sold on Avanti's website. Launched on 25 July 2023 for travel from 1 August with 100,000 tickets, it sells a time of day rather than a train: you book between seven and 21 days ahead, choose a morning, afternoon or evening slot, and are told which service you are on with roughly 24 hours' notice. Prices published when the trial widened ran from £12 to Birmingham and £15 to Liverpool up to £25 to Lancaster and £30 to Glasgow. More than 6,000 people bought one in the first phase. The booking is handled by Seatfrog on a separate site, avantisuperfare.co.uk, and Seatfrog's own help pages are blunt about the trade: "Superfare tickets are non-refundable unless the train was cancelled", and a Delay Repay claim has to go to Avanti rather than to the seller.

sections.heading: The company behind the brand, and the contract it runs on
sections.html:
Avanti West Coast is a trading name of First Trenitalia West Coast Rail Limited, company number 10349442, incorporated on 27 August 2016 as First West Coast Rail Limited and renamed on 23 January 2017. It is registered at 8th Floor The Point, 37 North Wharf Road, London W2 1AF under SIC 49100, passenger rail transport, interurban. Accounts were last made up to 31 March 2025 with the next set due by 31 December 2026, and the confirmation statement is next due on 17 January 2027. FirstGroup holds 70% of the West Coast Partnership and Trenitalia UK the other 30%.

The commercial arrangement is worth understanding, because it explains why the operator competes on service rather than on price. Under the National Rail Contract that began on 15 October 2023, the Department for Transport "retains all revenue risk and substantially all cost risk". Avanti is paid a fixed management fee of £5.1m a year plus a variable performance fee of up to £15.8m, assessed across five categories including operational performance and customer satisfaction, with an "acceptable" rating paying out roughly 65% of the variable element. Nobody at Avanti keeps your fare; the fare goes to the government, and the operator is paid to run the trains.

The scale behind that is substantial. ORR's own statistics sheet records 34.9 million passenger journeys and 6,609 million passenger kilometres between April 2024 and March 2025, 30.5 million passenger train kilometres, 1,310 kilometres of route operated and 16 stations managed as at 31 March 2025. The Hitachi-built Evero fleet runs to 23 units — ten seven-carriage Class 807 electrics and 13 five-carriage Class 805 bi-modes, the latter carrying 299 seats, 16% more than the Voyagers they replaced — at a cost of £350m, alongside a Pendolino fleet given a £117m refurbishment. Passenger Assist supported 76,633 customers in the year the company's own fact sheet covers.

sections.heading: What you are owed when the train is late
sections.html:
This is the part of the purchase where buying from the operator rather than a retailer changes something concrete, so the detail is worth having. The April 2026 Passenger Charter sets Delay Repay at 25% of a single fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes, 100% from an hour to just under two, and 100% at two hours or more. On a return the same bands pay 12.5%, 25%, 50% and 100%. Season tickets are compensated as a fraction of the whole price: a tenth of a weekly, a sixteenth of a Flexi, a fortieth of a monthly, a hundred-and-twentieth of a quarterly and a four-hundred-and-sixty-fourth of an annual, scaled by the same percentages. Every claim has to be in within 28 days of the journey, and Avanti says it aims to settle within five working days.

Automated Delay Repay is the feature that an independent retailer cannot match. Where the ticket is an Advance bought directly from Avanti, and the passenger has set up a Delay Repay account on the same email address and opted in before the travel day, a 15-minute delay generates a claim without anyone filling anything in, "usually within 24 hours of travel". The conditions are narrow and they are the point: walk-up Anytime and Off-Peak fares are outside it, and so is anything bought elsewhere.

If the answer is wrong, the escalation route is specific and it is not the Financial Ombudsman. Complaints go to Avanti first, with a target of five working days for a reply, and then to the Rail Ombudsman — either once 40 working days have passed without resolution, or within 12 months of a final response. Its decisions are binding on the operator and free to the passenger.

sections.heading: Refunds got harder on 1 April 2026
sections.html:
A change that applies across the industry, and that Avanti's refund page confirms in passing, landed on 1 April 2026: for flexible tickets bought on or after that date, the refund has to be requested before the ticket becomes valid rather than within the old 28-day window afterwards. Avanti's own instruction for a ticket bought at a station is to "head back to the station you bought it from by 23:59 the day before your ticket becomes valid for travel". Miss that and an unused flexible ticket is worth nothing, which is a real change in how a cautiously bought Anytime single behaves.

The fee schedule around it is simple enough to check. Refunding a station-bought ticket carries a £5 admin fee a ticket. Anytime and Off-Peak e-tickets bought online can be refunded through the website or app provided they are worth more than £5. Advance tickets and Season tickets cannot be refunded online at all, and neither can anything delivered by smartcard, by post or by station collection — those go through the contact centre or the ticket office. Where the train was delayed or cancelled and you chose not to travel, the refund is full and the admin fee does not apply, and the deadline for that claim is 28 days after the ticket expires.

sections.heading: The performance record, in the operator's own numbers
sections.html:
Avanti publishes a performance report every four weeks, which is more disclosure than most retailers of anything offer, and the numbers in it are hard going. For the period 26 July to 22 August 2026, across all services: 32.1% of trains arrived exactly on time, 50.3% within three minutes, 82.7% within 15 minutes, and 9.91% of planned services were cancelled, of which 7.13 percentage points were Avanti's own responsibility. The twelve-month moving averages in the same document are 36.8% on time, 56.1% within three minutes, 86.3% within 15 minutes and 7.4% cancelled. In that four-week period 541 trains arrived between 30 and 59 minutes late, 97 arrived between one and two hours late, and eight arrived more than two hours late.

Set against the industry, ORR's statistics for 1 January to 31 March 2026 put the national average at 86.4% of station stops reached within three minutes and 3.2% of trains cancelled. The windows are not the same and neither are the measures exactly, so this is not a like-for-like subtraction — but a 56.1% annual average against an 86.4% national quarter is not a rounding difference either. Avanti's own route breakdown shows where it concentrates: North Wales services were best on the three-minute measure at 49.3%, and London to Scotland direct services worst at 30.3%.

Responsibility for all that is contested in a way worth seeing from both sides. Avanti's fact sheet attributes 61% of delays in the twelve months from September 2023 to Network Rail, 28.9% to itself and 10.1% to other operators. The Department for Transport's September 2026 announcement describes infrastructure problems as accounting for about a third of delays on the West Coast Main Line. Those two statements cover different periods and almost certainly count differently, and neither party reconciles them, so the honest position is that the track takes a large share of the blame and the operator and its client disagree about how large.

Passenger opinion sits in between. Transport Focus's rail user survey scorecard for periods 11 to 13 of 2025–26 gives Avanti 87% overall journey satisfaction against a Great Britain average of 88%, and 81% satisfaction with punctuality. Value for money is where it parts company with the field: 52%, against a 59% national figure. No ratings agency scores train operators the way Defaqto scores insurance, so the satisfaction survey and the ORR data are the only independent measures available.

sections.heading: The price promise has a 24-hour clock, and a hole the regulator has already found
sections.html:
The guarantee is real but narrow, and the narrowness has been adjudicated. On 15 June 2022 the Advertising Standards Authority upheld a complaint against First Trenitalia West Coast Rail Limited over claims including "a price that can't be beaten" and "Unbeatable prices" on the Best Fare Finder and price promise pages. Two complainants had found cheaper fares for the same journeys using split-ticketing services. The ASA found the advertising breached CAP Code rules 3.1, 3.3 and 3.9 — misleading, omitting material information, and failing to state significant limitations — concluding that the advertisement "implied cheaper Avanti West Coast tickets could never be found… when that was not the case", and told the company not to repeat it in that form.

The terms as they stand in October 2026 still carry the exclusion the ruling turned on. The promise applies to "like for like tickets. That's the same journey at the same time, with one ticket taking you all the way", and says in terms that Avanti "can't guarantee to refund the difference if you split the tickets for your journey". Promotional prices and non-public negotiated fares are also outside it, and the original ticket must have been bought on Avanti's own website or app. The claim window is the tight part: a refund claim email has to reach Avanti "no later than 24 hours after you purchased your train ticket(s)", after which a verified difference is credited within 28 days. A promise you have to invoke the same day is a promise most buyers will never use, and split-ticket savings on long West Coast journeys are exactly the case it does not cover.

sections.heading: Public ownership arrives on 7 March 2027
sections.html:
On 28 September 2026 the Transport Secretary announced that Avanti West Coast services will be brought into public ownership on 7 March 2027, taken over by DfT Operator Limited, with the decision framed as calling time on performance that "remains behind the industry average". The contract would have allowed the private arrangement to continue: the National Rail Contract that started on 15 October 2023 ran a core term to 18 October 2026 with an extension available to 17 October 2032, and the government has chosen the first opportunity after the core term instead of the full nine years. Announced alongside it were £10m for power and signalling maintenance on the West Coast Main Line by the end of 2027, £50m for Euston station over three years, a further £10m for other route stations, and £840m of infrastructure investment already in train.

For a ticket buyer this changes administration rather than product. Fares are industry-set and government-owned already, Delay Repay is a national scheme, and the Rail Ombudsman covers publicly owned operators exactly as it covers private ones. The longer-term change is in retailing: the government's own Railways Bill material says the websites of 14 Department-contracted operators fold into a single Great British Railways app and site, while independent retailers "will also be able to retail to passengers, just as they do today", governed by a code of practice owned and administered by the ORR, with breach of it treated as a licence breach. Worth watching rather than worrying about — but if you hold an Advance ticket for travel after 7 March 2027, the website you bought it from will not be the one you go back to.

pros: No booking fee of any kind on the website or app, and e-tickets delivered free
Delay Repay begins at 15 minutes rather than 30, paying 25% of a single fare
Automated Delay Repay claims for Advance tickets bought direct, usually within 24 hours of travel, which independent retailers cannot offer
Complaints end at the Rail Ombudsman, whose decisions bind the operator, after 40 working days or within 12 months of a final response
Performance published every four weeks in the operator's own numbers, broken down by route
Advertised fares from £12 one way London to Birmingham, £26 to Liverpool and £35 to Manchester, plus Superfare at £12 to £30 for flexible travellers
A price promise that refunds the difference on like-for-like fares bought direct
cons: Punctuality is poor by any measure: 32.1% of trains exactly on time and 9.91% cancelled in the four weeks to 22 August 2026, against a national average of 86.4% within three minutes and 3.2% cancelled in the quarter to 31 March 2026
Value for money is the weakest thing passengers say about it — 52% satisfied against 59% nationally in Transport Focus's periods 11 to 13 scorecard
The ASA upheld a complaint on 15 June 2022 about "unbeatable prices" claims, and the price promise still excludes the split-ticket savings the ruling was about
A price promise claim must be emailed within 24 hours of buying the ticket, which rules out anyone who spots a cheaper fare later
Automated Delay Repay is limited to Advance tickets bought direct and needs an opt-in before the travel day, so walk-up fares still mean filling in a form within 28 days
Advance and Season tickets cannot be refunded through the website or app at all, and a station-bought refund costs £5 a ticket
Flexible tickets bought on or after 1 April 2026 must be refunded before the day they become valid, so an unused Anytime single bought as insurance is now worth nothing the next morning
Superfare is non-refundable unless the train is cancelled, confirms your actual train only about 24 hours ahead, and is sold on a separate site by a third party
verdict: If you are travelling on the West Coast Main Line, buying from Avanti rather than a retailer is the straightforward choice: the fare is identical because the industry sets it, the booking fee is £0, and compensation comes from the company that caused the delay — with the Advance-ticket automatic claim being something no third-party seller is allowed to provide. That is a genuine advantage, and on a railway cancelling 7.4% of its trains over twelve months it is one you may well use. The reservations are about the promises rather than the plumbing: a price guarantee with a 24-hour claim window and a split-ticketing exclusion the ASA has already ruled on, a refund route that excludes Advance and Season tickets online, and a 1 April 2026 rule that quietly made flexible tickets riskier to buy speculatively. Book direct, opt into Delay Repay before you travel, and if your journey is long enough to split, check that separately — the price promise will not.

faqs.q: Does Avanti West Coast charge a booking fee?
faqs.a: No. Its price promise page states the website and app have the lowest priced tickets for its trains with "no booking fees", and e-tickets are delivered free. The comparison worth making is with independent retailers, where a transaction fee of up to £2.79 is normal — the ticket itself costs the same either way, because rail fares are set by the industry rather than by the seller.

faqs.q: How late does the train have to be before Avanti pays compensation?
faqs.a: Fifteen minutes. The April 2026 Passenger Charter pays 25% of a single fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes and 100% from 60 minutes, with 100% on all ticket types at two hours or more. A return pays half those percentages up to the two-hour band. Claims must be submitted within 28 days of the journey and Avanti aims to conclude them within five working days.

faqs.q: Can Delay Repay be paid automatically?
faqs.a: Yes, within limits. Automated Delay Repay processes a claim for you, usually within 24 hours of travel, if your ticket was an Advance bought directly from Avanti, you have created a Delay Repay account on the email address used for the purchase, and you opted in before your travel day. It does not cover Anytime or Off-Peak walk-up fares, or tickets bought from anyone else.

faqs.q: What does it cost to refund an Avanti ticket?
faqs.a: Refunding a ticket bought at a station carries a £5 admin fee per ticket. Anytime and Off-Peak e-tickets worth more than £5 can be refunded through the website or app; Advance and Season tickets cannot, and nor can tickets delivered by post, smartcard or station collection. No admin fee applies where the train was delayed or cancelled and you did not travel, and that claim has 28 days from the ticket's expiry.

faqs.q: What changed about train refunds on 1 April 2026?
faqs.a: Flexible tickets bought on or after that date have to be refunded before they become valid rather than afterwards. Avanti's own guidance for a station purchase is to return to the ticket office by 23:59 the day before the ticket is valid for travel. Delay Repay and cancellation refunds are untouched — the change affects unused Anytime, Off-Peak and similar tickets bought in advance as a precaution.

faqs.q: What happens to my ticket when Avanti is nationalised in March 2027?
faqs.a: Nothing to the ticket. Services transfer to DfT Operator Limited on 7 March 2027, announced on 28 September 2026. Fares are industry-set and the Department for Transport already takes the revenue under the current contract, Delay Repay is a national scheme, and the Rail Ombudsman covers publicly owned operators in the same way. In time the operator's own website is expected to fold into a single Great British Railways site alongside 13 others.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if Avanti will not settle?
faqs.a: Avanti first — it aims to reply within five working days. If the complaint is unresolved after 40 working days, or within 12 months of a final response, it can go to the Rail Ombudsman, which is free to passengers and whose decisions bind the operator. The Financial Ombudsman Service has no role here; rail is outside its remit.

faqs.q: Is Avanti West Coast cheaper than buying the same journey elsewhere?
faqs.a: For an identical single ticket, yes, by the amount of the retailer's booking fee. For a journey that can be split into two or more cheaper tickets, not necessarily — the ASA upheld a complaint about Avanti's "unbeatable prices" claim on 15 June 2022 precisely because split-ticketing services were producing cheaper fares, and the price promise still says it cannot guarantee to refund the difference where tickets are split.

title: Avis Holiday Car Hire Review: Excess, Cover and What the Desk Charges
meta_title: Avis Car Hire Review 2026: Excess, Fees, Free Extra Driver
meta_description: Avis UK's damage excess runs £1,600 to £2,500 by car group, or £0 with Vehicle Cover. Age rules, the £300 hold and Which?'s 64% score, checked October 2026.

headline.label: Standard damage and theft excess
headline.value: £1,600–£2,500 by car group before extra cover — £0 with Vehicle Cover

intro:
Avis hires a car in the UK with a standard damage and theft excess of between £1,600 and £2,500 depending on which group you book, and its own Vehicle Cover package takes that figure to £0. Both numbers are published on Avis's additional cover page and were checked there on 3 October 2026. The excess is the number that decides what a holiday hire really costs you, and Avis is unusually direct about printing it.

The company behind the UK counter is Avis Budget UK Limited, company 00802486, incorporated on 24 April 1964 and trading as Avis Rent A Car Limited until 3 December 2012. It works from Avis Budget House, Park Road, Bracknell RG12 2EW, and its parent runs 4,695 Avis-branded rental locations worldwide — 2,745 of them company-operated and 1,950 run by licensees — inside a group of roughly 10,000 locations across about 180 countries. Avis began in 1946 when Warren Avis opened a desk at Willow Run Airport in Detroit with three cars.

Three things are worth knowing before you click. Booking direct includes the first additional driver free of charge, which is the single largest saving on the page for couples. Prepaying takes 15% off the rate. And Avis advertises no cancellation fees and full cash refunds, which matters on a holiday booked months out.

sections.heading: Who takes your money, and who owns the car
sections.html:
Two companies appear in the small print. The rental contract is with Avis Budget UK Limited (00802486), a private limited company that has been active since 24 April 1964 and sits under SIC code 77110, renting and leasing cars and light motor vehicles. Its most recent full accounts cover the year ended 31 December 2024 and were filed on 19 December 2025, with the 2025 set due by 30 September 2026. The website itself is operated by a different entity, Avis Budget Services Limited (01972749), from the same Bracknell address.

Above both sits Avis Budget Group, listed in New York, which reported full-year 2025 revenue of $11.7bn on 18 February 2026 against $11.8bn the year before, a net loss of $889m and adjusted EBITDA of $748m. Its International segment — the one the UK sits inside — turned over $2.8bn, up 3%, on 45.7 million rental days from an average fleet of 177,124 vehicles at 70.6% utilisation and $58.57 revenue per day. Group-wide the average fleet was about 684,000 vehicles and roughly 25,000 people work for it, about 7,500 of them in International.

One number explains the pricing of a holiday hire better than any other: 68% of group revenue is taken at airports, against 32% off-airport. Airport desks carry a premium location surcharge that Avis describes as covering the extra cost of operating there, and it is applied as a percentage to counter products as well as the rate. Picking up in town rather than in the terminal is the one structural saving available to a holiday renter.

sections.heading: The excess, group by group
sections.html:
Avis publishes its UK excess as a four-band table, which is more than most of its competitors manage. Basic cover — included in the rate — gives you theft cover and damage cover with an excess attached, and the excess depends on the group:

  • Groups SA, SC: £1,600
  • Groups SJ, SG, SD, SK: £2,000
  • Groups EE, MA, LI, MC: £2,200
  • Groups LG, MN, SP, LL, EI: £2,500

Vehicle Cover reduces that to £0 for every group listed, including MJ. Vehicle Cover Plus adds Roadside Assistance Plus on top. Windscreen cover is folded into the UK packages but is carved out of bookings in France, Italy and Iberia, which is worth checking if the holiday involves a one-way run into Europe.

Sold separately at the desk, the same protections appear under their trade names: CDW cuts the excess for new, non-negligent outer body damage, SCDW cuts it to zero, TP does the theft equivalent, WDW zeroes the windscreen excess, and RSN covers non-mechanical breakdown callouts such as a jump start or a tow. All of them are charged to your card at the end of the rental rather than up front. Personal Accident Insurance is a separate purchase again, paying £175,000 for accidental death, £2,500 of medical expenses and £250 of ambulance costs.

Theft cover has one hard exclusion worth memorising: Avis states plainly that you are not covered if you leave the vehicle with the keys in it.

sections.heading: What happens at the desk before you get the keys
sections.html:
The card hold is formulaic and Avis publishes the formula: the vehicle rental price plus £300, minus anything already paid. The £300 is there to cover fuel, late return, mileage overage and traffic charges, and it shrinks by the amount of any Fuel Up Front purchase. It is not a charge, but it reduces your available balance, and Avis says the release can take up to 28 days to show in your account — the card issuer controls that, not the rental station.

Paperwork is stricter than many renters expect. You need the plastic licence plus a DVLA licence check code, which is valid for up to 21 days and obtained from gov.uk or on 0300 083 0013. You need separate proof of address — a recent utility bill or bank statement — and Avis states that your driving licence will not be accepted for that. For higher-value vehicles two credit cards are required at the counter, and prepaid cards are accepted online but not at the desk. The name on the card has to match the main driver's licence.

On age, the UK minimum is 23 with a full licence held for at least a year, and drivers under 25 pay a surcharge of about £40 a day, capped at 10 days, with some car groups closed to them entirely. The cap is a genuine piece of consumer protection — on a fortnight's holiday it saves four days of surcharge — and it is quoted inside the booking price rather than sprung at the counter.

sections.heading: Discounts Avis actually publishes
sections.html:
Unusually for the sector, Avis names its discounts and their size rather than leaving them to a promo code hunt. Prepaying saves 15%. Avis Preferred is free to join and carries 10% off European bookings. Avis Drive, the subscription aimed at frequent renters, advertises up to 20% off UK rentals and 15% in Europe. New email subscribers get 5% off the base rental charge for 90 days. There is a cashback deal paying 10% back as an Amazon.co.uk gift card on rentals anywhere in the world, subject to restrictions.

Preferred membership also switches invoices to email; otherwise they arrive by post, and either way they appear online about 36 hours after the rental ends at abg-billing.com, retrieved with the agreement number and a surname. Deposits and pre-authorisations are both quoted as releasing within a maximum of 28 days from check-in.

Stacked sensibly — prepay plus Preferred plus the free second driver — those are real savings rather than the usual rounding. The catch is that the cheapest combinations are prepaid and online-only, and the all-inclusive cover package cannot be bought at the counter or bolted onto an existing booking.

sections.heading: How damage gets measured, and how the bill arrives
sections.html:
Avis publishes fair wear and tear in millimetres, which is rarer than it sounds and makes a counter argument winnable. Not charged: panel abrasions and scratches under 25mm, panel dents under 25mm, paint stone chips without a dent under 3mm, glass chips under 3mm, wheel scratches under 25mm, and interior tears or burns under 3mm, rising to 10mm on carpet. Anything beyond that is costed "in line with industry standards using estimating tools such as Audatex", up to the excess agreed at the start.

Reporting is on a clock. Any accident or damage has to go to the police immediately and to Avis within 48 hours, even where no third party was involved. Normal dirt is not chargeable; a car needing professional valeting beyond standard cleaning is.

Return timing is forgiving up to a point. There is no penalty for being up to 29 minutes late; past that you pay a full extra 24-hour day at the current rate plus a late return processing fee of £15.00 in the UK (CHF 20.00 in Switzerland, between €15 and €18.60 in the eurozone). Fuel works full-to-full, and if Avis refuels for you it charges a premium rate against the discounted Fuel Up Front price — but Fuel Up Front is not refunded if you bring the car back with fuel still in it.

Tolls and fines land later. Avis says toll charges come through "a few weeks following the end of your rental" once the authority supplies the detail, and possibly as several separate charges. The Blackwall and Silvertown tunnels are chargeable from 06:00 to 22:00 seven days a week in both directions, with until midnight on the third day after the journey to pay before a Penalty Charge Notice follows. Where a traffic fine can be transferred to the driver, Avis passes it on and adds an administration fee for doing so; where it cannot, it pays the lowest available fine and bills you.

sections.heading: What the independent evidence says
sections.html:
There is no Defaqto rating, no Fairer Finance ribbon and no Financial Ombudsman jurisdiction in car hire — none of those bodies reach the sector. The nearest thing to an independent assessment is the Which? survey of 3,637 adults carried out in February and March 2026, covering people who had hired a car in the UK or abroad in the previous two years.

Avis scored 64%, placing it third from bottom of the firms surveyed. The category detail is split: four stars for vehicle condition and four for speed of return, three for customer service and three for value for money, and two stars each for clarity of terms and speed of collection. Which? did not make Avis a recommended provider, singling out poorly displayed one-way fees and deposit information buried in long terms.

For context, the survey's top three were Autoreisen at 93%, Arnold Clark at 82% and Alamo at 76%, with Goldcar last at 48%. Across the whole sample, one in eight renters — 13% — paid more than the quote they were given, rising to 28% of Goldcar customers. The charges most often responsible were surcharges for drivers over 70, insurance left out of the headline price, and additional driver fees, where Which? cited a Hertz example at £144 a week. Against that last one, Avis's free first additional driver on direct bookings reads rather well.

sections.heading: The promises made in 2015, and the scoreboard in 2026
sections.html:
Car hire pricing has been under formal pressure for a decade, and Avis was named in it. In October 2015 the Competition and Markets Authority led a Europe-wide action in which five companies — Avis-Budget, Enterprise Rent-a-Car, Europcar, Hertz and Sixt, between them about two-thirds of EU private car rentals — gave commitments to be delivered over six months. They covered showing more price information up front so quotes could be compared, better pre-booking detail on optional waivers and insurance including prices and exclusions, more transparency about how vehicles are inspected before and after a rental, and giving customers a reasonable chance to dispute a damage charge before being billed for it. The British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association revised its own rental Code of Conduct alongside it.

The European Commission reported completion in March 2019. Enterprise and Sixt had finished by then; Avis committed to May 2019, Europcar including Goldcar to June 2019, and Hertz to the first quarter of 2020. The Commission's line at the time was that there would be "no more unpleasant surprises at the check-out desk when you're renting your car".

Seven years on, Which? still finds 13% of renters paying more than they were quoted and gives Avis two stars for clarity of terms. The commitments plainly changed the sector — every one of the five now shows an inclusive total — but the gap between a total price and a transparent one has not closed, and Avis's own documents are part of the evidence for that, as the next section shows.

sections.heading: Three places Avis's own numbers do not agree
sections.html:
These are not accusations, they are discrepancies anyone can check, and they are the reason to read the quote rather than the marketing.

The excess table lists one group twice. On the additional cover page, group EE appears in the £2,200 band and again in the £2,500 band. A renter in an EE car cannot tell from the page which excess applies, and the difference is £300.

Two Avis-run pages give different excess figures entirely. The group's own protection help page for the UK states that standard CDW reduces liability to £1,000 for most groups and £1,500 for groups K, M and N, with Super CDW priced at £9.58 a day for groups A and B, £12.50 for C, E, G, I and P and £15.00 for everything else. None of those group letters or amounts appears on avis.co.uk, which uses the SA-to-EI lettering and the £1,600–£2,500 bands. One of the two is out of date and neither carries a date.

The all-inclusive package has two different discounts. Avis's own product page describes Avis Inclusive as "up to 15% discounted coverage" against buying the elements separately; its own billing FAQ describes the same package as combining them "at 25% discount". The honest reading is that the saving varies by booking — but the page a customer lands on decides which number they believe.

Worth adding: Avis shows no price at all for Vehicle Cover or Vehicle Cover Plus, saying only that the cost "will depend upon the vehicle and length of rental". Since the whole point of the excess table is to let a renter weigh £2,500 of exposure against the cost of removing it, the half of that sum you need is the half Avis withholds until you are inside a quote.

sections.heading: Complaining, and the route that is not signposted
sections.html:
Car hire has no financial regulator and no ombudsman, but it does have an approved dispute scheme. The BVRLA is approved by government as a consumer ADR body under the Alternative Dispute Resolution for Consumer Disputes (Competent Authorities and Information) Regulations 2015 and holds Chartered Trading Standards Institute approval. Its rental Code of Conduct commits members to acknowledging a complaint within five working days and aiming to resolve it within 15 working days. If that fails, stage one of conciliation targets a resolution within 30 days on the papers; where either side disagrees, the Conciliation Committee must notify its decision within 30 working days of referral. A customer can refer a dispute; a member cannot refer one against a customer.

The code also obliges members to state, before the rental starts, exactly what the quoted price includes, the basis of any deposit "including any mandatory damage excess", the fuel or battery return policy, and "the fixed sum they will be liable for, when this will become due for payment and all exceptions which are not covered".

Avis's sister brand Budget publishes its BVRLA commitment on its own site and lists the eight standards it signs up to, and a copy of the BVRLA rental code sits on Avis Budget's own asset domain. No page on avis.co.uk reachable on 3 October 2026 states that Avis is a member or points a dissatisfied customer at conciliation, and the BVRLA's public member directory — 936 entries — could not be read in full to confirm the listing. Treat Avis's membership as likely but unconfirmed, and if a damage charge is disputed, ask the UK customer service team on 0808 284 0014 whether conciliation is open to you before escalating to your card provider. One renter quoted by Which? got nowhere with Avis's own dispute procedure and recovered an unexpected €167 additional driver charge only through a credit card chargeback.

pros: Publishes a four-band excess table by car group rather than hiding the figure behind a quote
Vehicle Cover takes the excess to £0 across every listed UK group
First additional driver free of charge on direct bookings, against £144 a week quoted elsewhere in the sector
Fair wear and tear defined in millimetres — 25mm scratches and dents, 3mm chips — which makes a counter dispute arguable
29 minutes' grace on a late return before any extra day is charged
Under-25 surcharge capped at 10 days, so a long holiday is not charged throughout
Four stars from Which? for vehicle condition and for speed of return
No cancellation fees and full cash refunds on flexible bookings
Named, sized discounts — 15% prepay, 10% Preferred in Europe, up to 20% on Avis Drive in the UK
4,695 Avis-branded locations in a group spanning roughly 180 countries, so a one-way or a replacement is usually possible
cons: Avis's excess table lists group EE in both the £2,200 band and the £2,500 band, a £300 difference a renter cannot resolve from the page
The group's own UK protection help page gives a completely different excess — £1,000 and £1,500 for groups K, M and N — and neither that page nor avis.co.uk carries a date, so one of them is stale
Avis Inclusive is described as "up to 15%" cheaper than buying cover separately on one Avis page and a "25% discount" on another
No price is published for Vehicle Cover or Vehicle Cover Plus, so the cost of removing a £2,500 excess is only visible inside a quote
Which? scored Avis 64%, third from bottom, with two stars for clarity of terms and two for speed of collection, and did not recommend it
Nothing on avis.co.uk that could be reached signposts the BVRLA conciliation scheme, the only consumer dispute route the sector has
The card hold is the rental price plus £300 and can take up to 28 days to clear back
Minimum age 23 and roughly £40 a day for drivers under 25, with some car groups closed to them altogether
Fuel Up Front is not refunded if the car comes back with fuel still in the tank
Two credit cards are required at the counter for higher-value vehicles, and a driving licence is not accepted as proof of address
verdict: Avis is a competent, well-stocked hire company that prints more of its numbers than most of the sector and then undermines itself with paperwork that does not agree. The excess table, the millimetre wear-and-tear thresholds, the £300 hold formula and the free second driver are all genuinely better disclosure than the category norm, and the Which? four stars for vehicle condition and return speed suggest the operational half works. The weak half is clarity: one car group sits in two excess bands, a second Avis-run page quotes excesses from a different scheme entirely, the all-inclusive package has two published discount figures, and the price of the cover that removes a £2,500 liability is the one number withheld. For a holiday hire, book direct, prepay, take the free additional driver, photograph the car against the published millimetre limits, and settle the cover question in the quote before you reach the desk.

faqs.q: What is the excess on an Avis hire car in the UK?
faqs.a: Between £1,600 and £2,500 depending on the car group — £1,600 for groups SA and SC, £2,000 for SJ, SG, SD and SK, £2,200 for EE, MA, LI and MC, and £2,500 for LG, MN, SP, LL and EI. Buying Vehicle Cover or Vehicle Cover Plus reduces it to £0. Note that Avis's own table lists group EE in two different bands, so confirm the figure on your quote.

faqs.q: How much does Avis hold on your card?
faqs.a: The rental price plus £300, less anything you have already paid on a prepaid booking. The £300 covers fuel, late return, excess mileage and traffic charges, and it is reduced by the amount of any Fuel Up Front purchase. It is a hold rather than a charge, but Avis says it can take up to 28 days for your card issuer to reflect the release.

faqs.q: Can you hire from Avis at 21 in the UK?
faqs.a: No. The UK minimum age is 23 and you must have held a full licence for at least a year. Drivers aged 23 and 24 pay a young driver surcharge of about £40 a day, capped at 10 days, and some car groups are not available to anyone under 25. The surcharge is quoted inside the booking price when you enter your date of birth.

faqs.q: Does Avis charge for a second driver?
faqs.a: Booking direct with Avis includes the first additional driver free of charge, which is worth having: Which? found additional driver fees among the most common unexpected charges in car hire and cited one competitor charging £144 a week. Any additional driver still has to hold a full valid licence and meet the age and identification rules, and a young driver surcharge can apply to them.

faqs.q: What happens if you return an Avis car late or not full of fuel?
faqs.a: You get 29 minutes' grace. Beyond that you pay a full extra 24-hour day at the current rate plus a late return processing fee of £15.00 in the UK. Fuel is full-to-full; if Avis refuels for you it charges a premium rate rather than the discounted Fuel Up Front price. Fuel Up Front itself is not refunded if you bring the car back with fuel left in it.

faqs.q: Who do you complain to about a car hire damage charge?
faqs.a: Start with Avis's UK customer service team on 0808 284 0014. If that fails, the BVRLA runs a conciliation service that is government-approved as a consumer ADR body under the 2015 ADR Regulations; its code gives members five working days to acknowledge a complaint and 15 working days to resolve one, with a Conciliation Committee decision within 30 working days of referral. Avis's UK site does not signpost this route, so ask whether it is open to you. A credit card chargeback remains the fallback.

title: Aviva Car Insurance
meta_title: Aviva Car Insurance Review: Limits, Excesses and Extras
meta_description: Aviva’s comprehensive limits, the £10 and £115 glass excesses, EV charging cover and its own complaints figures. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Aviva writes its motor policies through Aviva Insurance Limited, a company registered in Scotland at Pitheavlis in Perth under number SC002116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 202153. That reference is worth keeping: it lets you confirm on the Financial Services Register that the company taking your premium is the company carrying the risk, which is not always the case with motor brands sold online.

Scale is the first thing a driver is buying here. Aviva served almost 22 million UK customers at its 2025 full-year results, published on 5 March 2026, with group general insurance premiums up 18% to £14,145m and the UK and Ireland general insurance book up 27% to £9,787m at an undiscounted combined operating ratio of 94.1%. Its own repair network put more than 73,000 vehicles back on the road during 2025, and work done through that network is guaranteed for as long as you keep the car rather than for a fixed number of years.

The comprehensive wording is generous where it matters day to day. Personal belongings are covered to £500, tools to £500, non-manufacturer accessories to £1,000 a claim, and a child car seat is replaced after an impact even where nothing looks broken. Lost or stolen keys are met up to the market value of the car with no excess to pay, and being hit by an uninsured driver costs you neither your excess nor your claim-free years provided you can hand over the other registration. Aviva holds a 5 star Defaqto rating on its car product and says it was named a Which? recommended provider for car insurance in both 2025 and 2026.

key_facts.label: Insurer
key_facts.value: Aviva Insurance Limited — FCA/PRA firm reference 202153

key_facts.label: Registered
key_facts.value: Scotland, no. SC002116, Pitheavlis, Perth PH2 0NH

key_facts.label: Group scale
key_facts.value: Almost 22 million UK customers at the 2025 results

key_facts.label: Cover tiers
key_facts.value: Signature, Aviva, Gold and Platinum, plus the separate Aviva Zero brand

key_facts.label: Personal belongings
key_facts.value: £500 per incident on comprehensive

key_facts.label: Glass excess
key_facts.value: £10 to repair, £115 to replace through an approved fitter

key_facts.label: New car replacement
key_facts.value: Damage above 60% of list price within the first 12 months

key_facts.value: 14 days, with a £38 charge plus tax once cover has started

sections.heading: What the published limits actually say
sections.html:
Aviva prints most of the numbers that matter in its product information document rather than burying them in a schedule you only see after buying, which makes the cover unusually easy to price against a rival before you commit. Motor injury protection pays £5,000 per person per period of insurance as standard; the optional Plus version lifts that to £120,000 and adds up to £500 each per claim towards physiotherapy. Recovery of a damaged car is met to £500, and motor legal services, if you add them, run to £100,000.

A car written off or stolen in its first 12 months is replaced with a new one where the damage comes to more than 60% of the UK list price, provided you were the first registered keeper and bought it new rather than as an ex-demonstrator. A courtesy car comes with comprehensive cover only and stays with you for the whole repair, or for up to 28 days if the car is stolen or declared a total loss. On the Aviva, Gold and Platinum tiers the loan car is a three-door hatchback, or a five-door on Platinum.

Trips into Europe are where the tiers diverge. The Signature wording allows any one trip of up to 90 days with a total across the year of six months, while the base Aviva tier allows 60 days a trip and Gold and Platinum allow 90 days. A car loaned to you while yours is off the road is covered for up to 7 days. Driving someone else's car on your own certificate is limited to policyholders aged 25 and over and gives third party cover only.

sections.heading: Electric and hybrid drivers get more than a footnote
sections.html:
Aviva treats the charging equipment as part of the car rather than as household kit, which is still not universal. Charging cables are covered in the vehicle, while in use, and while stored in a private garage. A wall box fitted in the garage is insured, and comprehensive policies extend to breakdown of a home charging point including the electrical wiring between the fuse box and the unit itself, up to £2,000 a claim.

Batteries held on a lease rather than owned outright are covered as standard. If the car is stolen or written off, Aviva settles the vehicle's value minus the battery and deals with the battery separately with the manufacturer, which avoids the settlement stalling while the two sides argue over who owns what. Run flat on charge and, on comprehensive cover, an RAC mechanic will either put in enough charge to reach a working point or move the car and up to seven passengers to a working charger or your home, whichever is nearer. Hybrids are excluded from that last one.

sections.heading: The regulator's own reading of why motor claims cost more
sections.html:
Any quote makes more sense against what the market is paying out, and the sharpest free source is the FCA's multi-firm review of motor claims costs, published in July 2025 and drawn from 12 insurers covering more than half the private motor market. Between 2019 and 2023 total claims costs rose 34%, an increase of £2.3bn. The average claim went from £2,410 to £3,293, and cost per policy from £309 to £391.

The detail explains the delays drivers notice. The average insured vehicle rose in value by 42%, from £9,319 to £13,223; the wait to get a car into a body shop more than doubled from 15 days to 31 days; and bodyshop labour rates climbed 28%, from £35 to £45 an hour. Theft claims grew 14% more frequent and 49% more expensive. Claims made against untraced and uninsured drivers cost the Motor Insurers' Bureau £452m in 2024 against £329m in 2019, roughly 2.78% of what an average driver pays.

The FCA's general insurance value measures, published on 21 July 2026 for calendar year 2025, show the other side of that. Motor premiums fell 7% across the market during 2025 while claims costs as a share of premium rose from 54% to 59%. A renewal quote that has not moved much is doing so against a market where insurers kept less of every pound.

sections.heading: The excesses that stack behind the headline price
sections.html:
Aviva's excess structure rewards using its own suppliers and charges you for going elsewhere, and the amounts are set out plainly enough that there is no excuse for being caught out. Glass repaired through the approved fitter costs a £10 excess and a replacement costs £115. Use a fitter of your own choosing and the payout is capped at £185 in total, which will not cover a modern windscreen carrying the cameras for lane assist and automatic braking, all of which need recalibrating once the glass is fitted.

The same principle applies to body repairs, where taking the car to your own garage rather than an approved one adds a specific £200 excess on top of whatever excess your schedule already carries. On third party, fire and theft the accessories limit drops from £1,000 to £100. Cancel inside the 14 day cooling-off period after cover has begun and there is a £38 charge plus insurance premium tax as well as the pro-rata deduction; cancel later and the same £38 applies.

Several headline figures are not published at all. Personal accident benefit, medical expenses and the compulsory excess itself all appear only as the amount "shown in your schedule", which means they depend on the tier and the quote and cannot be compared across insurers until you have gone through a full application. Aviva also sells motor cover under Signature, Aviva, Gold, Platinum and the separate Aviva Zero brand, so two quotes carrying the same logo are not necessarily the same contract.

sections.heading: What Aviva's own complaints figures show
sections.html:
Firms of this size have to publish their complaints data, and Aviva's is on its own website rather than buried elsewhere. For the half year from 1 July to 31 December 2025, Aviva Insurance Limited opened 49,795 general insurance complaints, a rate of 2.72 per 1,000 policies. It closed 43.5% within three working days and a further 54.2% between three days and eight weeks. The uphold rate was 52.6%, meaning slightly more than half of everyone who complained was found to have had a point. The most common subject was general administration and customer service rather than a declined claim.

A complaint that cannot be settled goes to the Financial Ombudsman Service free of charge, at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR, and Aviva is bound by its decisions while you are not. Ombudsman figures for the first half of 2025 record 1,463 new complaints about Aviva Insurance Limited across general insurance and protection, against an overall uphold rate of 32% in the consumer's favour, down from 35% a year earlier. Aviva's motor complaints line is 0345 030 6984, with claims complaints on 0345 030 6925. Should the insurer be unable to meet its obligations, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may cover the shortfall.

pros: Personal belongings to £500, tools to £500 and accessories to £1,000 as standard on comprehensive
Repairs through Aviva's approved network are guaranteed for as long as you own the car
Charging cables, garage wall boxes and home charging point breakdown covered to £2,000 for EV drivers
Key replacement up to the car's market value with no excess
Uninsured driver promise refunds the excess and protects claim-free years
Most limits published in the product information document rather than hidden in a schedule
5 star Defaqto rating on the car product
cons: More than half of complaints go the customer's way: Aviva Insurance Limited upheld 52.6% of the 49,795 general insurance complaints it opened in the second half of 2025
Using your own body shop instead of an approved repairer adds a £200 excess, and glass fitted outside the network is capped at £185 against an industry average windscreen repair well above that
Personal accident benefit, medical expenses and the compulsory excess are only ever quoted as the amount shown in your schedule, so they cannot be compared before you apply
A £38 charge plus tax applies even inside the 14 day cooling-off period once cover has started
Driving other cars is restricted to policyholders aged 25 and over and gives third party cover only
European use on the base Aviva tier is limited to 60 days a trip against 90 on Gold and Platinum
Standard motor injury protection is only £5,000 per person unless you pay for the Plus version
verdict: Aviva sells a well-documented comprehensive policy from a balance sheet that few UK insurers can match, and it publishes more of its limits up front than most. The value sits in the repair network, the lifetime guarantee on its own workmanship and the electric vehicle cover, all of which are worth real money on a claim. The catch is that the price you see depends on which Aviva door you walked through, and that several of the numbers you would want for a like-for-like comparison only appear on your schedule. Get the quote, then read the schedule against the excesses set out above before you agree to it.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites an Aviva car insurance policy?
faqs.a: Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland under number SC002116 with its registered office at Pitheavlis, Perth PH2 0NH. It is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202153, which you can check yourself on the Financial Services Register. Policies sold through Aviva's online arm are arranged by Aviva UK Digital Limited, firm reference 728985.

faqs.q: What does Aviva charge to replace a windscreen?
faqs.a: A repair carries a £10 excess and a full replacement a £115 excess when the work goes through Aviva's approved glass supplier. If you use a fitter of your own, the most Aviva will pay towards the job is £185 in total, so on any modern screen with driver assistance cameras behind it you would be covering the balance yourself.

faqs.q: Am I covered driving in Europe?
faqs.a: Yes, at least to the minimum required by law in the listed countries, but the length of stay depends on the tier. The Signature wording allows a single trip of up to 90 days with six months in total across the year. The base Aviva tier allows 60 days per trip, and Gold and Platinum allow 90 days. Trips beyond the minimum legal cover need the separate motoring in Europe extension.

faqs.q: Will Aviva give me a new car if mine is written off?
faqs.a: Only in the first 12 months from new, and only if the repair cost or damage exceeds 60% of the vehicle's UK list price, or if the car is stolen and not recovered. You must have been the first registered keeper. Ex-demonstrators and nearly new cars are excluded from the replacement clause.

faqs.q: How do I complain about Aviva, and does it get me anywhere?
faqs.a: Motor complaints go to 0345 030 6984, or claims complaints to 0345 030 6925, or in writing to Building 8, Maxim Business Park, Eurocentral ML1 4WR. If eight weeks pass or you are unhappy with the answer, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will look at it free of charge on 0800 023 4567. Aviva's published figures for the second half of 2025 show 52.6% of complaints upheld in the customer's favour, so it is worth pursuing.

title: Aviva Landlord Insurance Review
meta_title: Aviva Landlord Insurance: Unlimited Cover, Three Properties
meta_description: Aviva covers up to three rental homes with no cap on the buildings sum insured. What the wording promises, what the schedule decides, and where it stops.
intro:
Aviva is the largest general insurer in the country and its landlord policy is one of the few that will not put a ceiling on the building. Cover is sold under the AvivaPlus name direct from aviva.co.uk, and the headline is an unlimited buildings and contents sum insured — no rebuild figure to guess at, no under-insurance argument after a fire. Three conditions come with it: the property must have five bedrooms or fewer, be built of brick, stone, slate or tile, and not be listed. Most terraced and semi-detached lets clear all three without trying.

The policy is written by Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland number 2116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 202153 — a number printed on the product documents themselves and checkable on the FCA Register. Subsidence and flood are in the standard cover rather than sold on. So is loss of rent or the cost of rehousing a tenant when insured damage makes the house unlivable, cover for contents in garages and outbuildings inside the boundary, replacement locks after keys are lost or stolen, and matching-set replacement when a damaged item in a suite cannot be paired. Employers' liability is included for anyone you employ around the property, which catches the cleaner and the gardener that landlords routinely forget.

Scale is the other half of the case. Aviva's half-year results on 14 August 2026 showed general insurance premiums of £8,093 million, up 29% year on year, an operating profit of £1,326 million and a UK and Ireland combined operating ratio of 93.4% — a company taking in comfortably more than it pays out, which is what you want from the firm holding your building. It serves 21.8 million customers in the UK. A landlord claim here is not going to a business that might not be there in five years.

sections.heading: Aviva now owns both sides of your shortlist
sections.html:
Something changed in this market on 1 July 2025 that has not filtered through to most landlord advice: Aviva completed its purchase of Direct Line Group. Direct Line, Churchill, Privilege and the rest of that stable now sit inside the same parent as Aviva. By the August 2026 results Aviva had banked £100 million of run-rate cost savings against a £225 million ambition, with over £350 million of capital synergies targeted by the end of 2026.

For a landlord ringing round for quotes, that is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon on it. Getting a price from Aviva and a price from Direct Line no longer samples two independent balance sheets; it samples two brands and two pricing models under one owner. The quotes will still differ, sometimes by a lot, because the underwriting engines and distribution costs behind them have not merged. But the diversification a cautious landlord thinks they are buying by splitting a portfolio across those two names is thinner than it looks, and a genuine third opinion now has to come from outside that group.

sections.heading: Unlimited buildings cover, with three conditions attached
sections.html:
The unlimited sum insured is the strongest single feature of this policy and it solves a real problem. Rebuild costs have run well ahead of house prices; the Association of British Insurers recorded an average household claim of £6,340 in the first quarter of 2026, up 20% in a year, with weather damage averaging £6,040 and theft £4,350. A landlord who set a buildings figure five years ago and let it index along is quite likely under-insured now, and the usual consequence is a proportionate reduction in the payout rather than a refusal. Removing the figure removes the argument.

The conditions are where it bites. Five bedrooms or fewer rules out the larger house in multiple occupation. Brick, stone, slate or tile rules out timber-frame, thatch and a good deal of 1960s system-built stock. Unlisted rules out period property in conservation areas, which is a substantial slice of the private rented sector in older towns. If a let fails any of the three, this is not the policy for it and the quote engine will say so rather than pricing it up.

Cover excludes wet and dry rot, frost damage, gradual deterioration, manufacturing defects and storm damage to fences, gates and hedges. None of those is unusual, but the fence exclusion catches people out after every winter gale, and on a let property the tenant tends to report it as though it were covered.

sections.heading: The boiler cover carries the numbers the main policy doesn't
sections.html:
Aviva's Landlord Combined home emergency add-on is unusually well documented, and for a landlord it may be the more useful purchase of the two. It pays up to £4,000 per claim with no cap on the number of claims in a year, above a £50 excess. Gas central heating breakdown is unlimited per claim as long as the boiler is not beyond economical repair. It covers water supply pipes, plumbing and drainage, internal gas pipes, electrical wiring emergencies, and emergency security work such as boarding up, lock replacement and tarpaulin on a roof. The annual CP12 gas safety inspection and a boiler service are included, which is a legal obligation on every landlord in England and Wales turned into a covered cost.

Two numbers to hold on to. There is a 14-day exclusion period at the start, so a new policy bought the week a boiler starts making noises will not answer — first-year cover is roughly 11 and a half months. And if the boiler is seven years old or over and beyond economical repair, the payment is a flat £200 towards a replacement rather than the replacement itself. Under seven years, it replaces. The boiler must be natural gas and rated under 60 kW.

Guttering, soakaways, showers, household appliances, chimneys, pests and unvented cylinders are all outside it, as is a boiler that works but is noisy.

sections.heading: What changes when you buy the fourth flat
sections.html:
Aviva will put up to three rental properties on the direct policy. Its own page sends anyone with more than three to a broker, and the product waiting there is not a bigger version of the same thing — it is the commercial Property Owners wording, and the terms are meaningfully different.

On the version Aviva's brokers circulate, loss of rent is written as 30% of the buildings sum insured with a maximum indemnity period of 36 months, trace and access is capped at £50,000, replacement locks at £50,000, glass at £2,000 in aggregate, recycling costs within debris removal at £10,000 and gardening equipment at £10,000. Employers' liability appears at £5,000,000. A building counts as unoccupied after 90 consecutive days, and once it is long-term unoccupied the wording demands documented inspections at least every 7 days, external openings locked and sealed, services off at the mains or heating held above 4°C, and combustible material cleared. Dishonesty by an employee has to be discovered within seven working days of the act to be claimable.

The quieter change is regulatory. The FCA's pricing rules in PS21/5 — the ones that stopped renewal quotes being priced above what a new customer pays — apply to insurance sold to consumers. A commercial property owners' policy sits outside them, so the renewal discipline you get on the direct product is not automatic on the broker one. Ombudsman access mostly survives the move: the Financial Ombudsman Service takes complaints from businesses turning over less than £6.5 million with a balance sheet under £5 million or fewer than 50 staff, which covers almost every private landlord, and its award limit rose to £455,000 on 1 April 2026 for acts on or after 1 April 2019. Worth checking rather than assuming, because the protection changes shape at exactly the point most people stop reading.

One landlord-specific clause survives in both: liability under the Defective Premises Act follows you for up to seven years after you sell the property. Selling a let does not close the file.

sections.heading: A wording that tells you almost nothing until the schedule arrives
sections.html:
Read the AvivaPlus landlord policy booklet cover to cover and you will not find a single pound figure. Public liability is "up to the limit shown on your schedule". The legal services section is "up to the amount shown on your schedule". Excesses are "the excess(es) shown on your schedule". The unoccupancy limit — the number that decides more landlord claims than any other — is "more than the period shown on your schedule". The product information document does the same. Compared with insurers who publish a £2 million or £5 million liability limit and a 45- or 60-day void period on the face of the document, Aviva makes it impossible to compare this policy against another one until you have run a full quote and read the schedule that comes back.

That is defensible underwriting — the limits genuinely are set risk by risk — and it is poor disclosure. It also means the comparison tables that quote an Aviva landlord liability limit are inferring it. Get the schedule, read the four numbers above, and only then put it next to a rival quote. There is no published starting price for the landlord product either, which is the one place AXA and Admiral are more forthcoming.

Aviva's own Defaqto five-star rating is quoted against its home insurance on the landlord page rather than against the landlord product itself. A separate landlord star rating could not be confirmed from Aviva's own material and should be treated as unverified.

sections.heading: The gap between what tenants do and what the policy pays
sections.html:
Three exclusions sit uncomfortably close to the risks that actually define letting. Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your tenants are excluded — not capped, excluded. Insurers that do cover it tend to cap it around £5,000; Aviva's direct wording does not reach it at all. A stripped property at the end of a bad tenancy is a cost you carry.

Accidental damage is an optional extra, covering things like a cracked bath, sink, toilet or window. Aviva's own claims analysis, published in April 2026 and covering January 2022 to March 2026, found accidental damage to be the single largest category at 32% of home claims, with the average payout up 63% from £1,148 in 2022 to £1,869. The most common cause was a television. Leaving off the cheapest add-on to the most frequent claim type is a false economy on a property somebody else lives in.

And there is no rent guarantee at any price. The loss of rent in the policy answers after insured damage, not after a tenant stops paying — a distinction that matters more since Section 21 possession ended on 1 May 2026 under the Renters' Rights Act 2025 and arrears cases began taking longer. Arrears cover has to be bought elsewhere.

On complaints, Aviva Insurance Limited published 2.72 complaints per 1,000 policies for the six months to 31 December 2025, closing 43.5% within three days and upholding 52.6%. The leading cause was general administration and customer service rather than claims decisions. A high uphold rate cuts both ways: it says a lot of complaints were justified, and it says complaining to Aviva is better than even odds of getting somewhere without going further. If it does go further, the Ombudsman is free.

One thing nobody can tell you: the regulator's general insurance value measures release of 21 July 2026 reports claims acceptance by product line, and landlord and property owners' cover is not one of the lines. Buildings insurance for owner-occupiers came in at a 62% acceptance rate against motor's 99%, but that is a different product. Any acceptance rate quoted for landlord cover, for Aviva or anyone else, has been inferred rather than published.

pros: Unlimited buildings and contents sum insured on standard-construction homes of five bedrooms or fewer, which removes the under-insurance risk entirely
Subsidence, flood, loss of rent and tenant rehousing are all in the standard cover rather than sold as extras
Employers' liability included for cleaners, gardeners and anyone else you employ at the property
Home emergency add-on pays £4,000 a claim with unlimited claims, a £50 excess, and includes the annual CP12 gas safety check
Backed by the UK's largest general insurer: £8,093m of GI premiums in the first half of 2026 and a 93.4% UK combined operating ratio
No charge for updating personal details or making changes to the policy
cons: Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your own tenants are excluded outright, not merely capped

The policy wording publishes no limits at all — liability, excesses, legal cover and the unoccupancy period are all "as shown on your schedule", so the policy cannot be compared with a rival until you have a full quote
Accidental damage is an optional extra even though it is 32% of Aviva's home claims at an average of £1,869
No rent guarantee is sold at any price, and loss of rent only responds after insured damage
Only three rental properties per policy; a fourth pushes you to a broker and the commercial Property Owners wording, where the FCA's consumer pricing rules no longer apply
Aviva Insurance Limited upheld 52.6% of complaints in the six months to 31 December 2025, and no starting price is published for the landlord product
Five-bedroom limit, standard construction and unlisted status rule out HMOs, timber-frame and period property in conservation areas
verdict: The right policy for a landlord with one to three ordinary brick-built houses who wants the rebuild risk taken off the table completely — the unlimited sum insured is genuinely valuable and few rivals match it. Add the accidental damage extra and the £4,000 home emergency cover, because between them they answer most of what actually goes wrong in a let. Read the schedule properly before you compare the price with anything, since the booklet will not tell you the limits. Buy rent guarantee somewhere else, and expect a different contract entirely the day you buy a fourth property.

faqs.q: How many rental properties can I put on one Aviva landlord policy?
faqs.a: Three. Aviva's own landlord page says you can cover up to three rental properties, and directs anyone with more to buy commercial cover through a broker. That broker product is the Property Owners wording, which carries different limits — loss of rent at 30% of the buildings sum insured over a 36-month indemnity period, a 90-day unoccupancy threshold and 7-day inspection requirements once a property is long-term empty.

faqs.q: Does Aviva really offer an unlimited buildings sum insured?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to three eligibility conditions: the property must have five bedrooms or fewer, be of standard construction in brick or stone with a slate or tile roof, and not be listed. Meet all three and there is no rebuild figure to estimate and no proportionate reduction for under-insurance. Fail any one and the property is not eligible for this policy.

faqs.q: Am I covered if my tenant damages or strips the property?
faqs.a: No. Theft, attempted theft, malicious damage and vandalism by your tenants are excluded from the AvivaPlus landlord policy. This is the exclusion most likely to cost a landlord real money, and it is worth pricing against insurers who cover it — usually with a cap in the region of £5,000 — before deciding on price alone. A deposit and a thorough inventory are doing that job here.

faqs.q: What does the Aviva home emergency add-on actually pay?
faqs.a: Up to £4,000 per claim with no limit on the number of claims in a year, above a £50 excess, covering plumbing and drainage, water and internal gas supply pipes, electrical emergencies, emergency security work and gas central heating breakdown, plus the annual CP12 inspection and boiler service. There is a 14-day wait before cover starts. If the boiler is seven years or older and beyond economical repair, you get £200 towards a new one rather than a replacement.

faqs.q: How long can the property stand empty between tenants?
faqs.a: On the direct policy the wording will not say — the limit is whatever appears on your schedule, and certain losses such as burst pipes and malicious damage fall away past it. On the broker Property Owners wording a building is unoccupied after 90 consecutive days, and long-term unoccupied property must be inspected at least every 7 days with a log kept, secured, cleared of combustibles and either drained at the mains or kept above 4°C. Find your own number and diary it the day the keys come back.

faqs.q: Who regulates Aviva and how do I complain?
faqs.a: Aviva Insurance Limited is registered in Scotland number 2116, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and PRA, firm reference 202153, verifiable on the FCA Register. Complain to Aviva first — 0800 158 4091 for claims, 0800 656 9717 otherwise. If you are unhappy with the answer, or eight weeks pass without one, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will review it free of charge. Its maximum award rose to £455,000 on 1 April 2026 for acts or omissions on or after 1 April 2019.

title: Aviva Life Insurance Review: Cover, Cost and the Documents Behind It
meta_title: Aviva Life Insurance: What £5 a Month Really Buys
meta_description: Aviva life insurance from £5 a month, ages 18 to 77, terms to 50 years. Premiums, terminal illness cover, the 8% mortgage assumption and claims, October 2026.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised premium
headline.value: £5 a month — Aviva Life Insurance Plan, level cover, amount and term chosen by the customer

intro:
Aviva's Life Insurance Plan is advertised from £5 a month, takes applicants aged 18 to 77, runs for terms of 1 to 50 years, and includes terminal illness cover at no extra charge. Those figures were checked on 3 October 2026 against Aviva's own policy summary, document DA03008 05/2023, and its consumer product pages.

The company behind them is the largest life insurer in the United Kingdom, with roughly a 25% share of the market, 21.8 million UK customers and more than 325 years of trading. In 2025 it paid £1.99bn across 61,632 individual and group protection claims, and it accepted 98.7% of individual life and terminal illness claims — 40,277 of them, worth £860.67m. The plan carries a Defaqto 5 Star rating, although Aviva's page does not date it.

One thing worth knowing before you start a quote: the sale is a direct, non-advised one. You buy from Aviva UK Digital Limited, and the policy itself is written by Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, the group's life company. There is no fee for the sale and no broker in the chain, so the firm answering the phone and the firm paying the claim are parts of the same business.
