sections.heading: £5 a month, £229 a year, and the distance between them
sections.html:
The £5 figure on Aviva's page is a floor, not a forecast, and the gap between it and what people actually pay is now a published number. The Financial Conduct Authority collected policy-level data from 11 insurers covering between 75% and 95% of all pure protection policies sold, and found that the median term assurance policy sold in 2024 carried an annual premium of £229 — about £19.08 a month, almost four times the advertised entry price.

The spread around that median is wide. Half of term assurance policies sold fell between £132 and £378 a year, and 80% between £82 and £630. At the bottom of that range you are close to Aviva's £5; at the top you are paying £52.50 a month for the same category of product. Price on a life policy is driven by age, health, smoking status, the sum assured and the term, and none of those is knowable until the questions have been answered.

Aviva does not publish a minimum or a maximum cover amount for this plan on either its product page or its policy summary. That is not unusual for the market, but it does mean the only way to find out what £5 buys at your age is to take the quote. The arithmetic that follows in the rest of this page uses Aviva's own published rules rather than a quoted price, because the rules apply to everybody and the price does not.

sections.heading: What the plan pays, and the three dates that decide whether it pays at all
sections.html:
This is a protection contract and nothing else. It pays a lump sum if the life covered dies during the term, or on an earlier diagnosis of terminal illness. Aviva's terms define that as "a definite diagnosis by the attending consultant of an illness that satisfies both of the following: the illness either has no known cure or has progressed to the point where it cannot be cured, and in the opinion of the attending consultant, the illness is expected to lead to death within 12 months". The judgement belongs to the treating consultant, not to Aviva's own doctor, which is the more generous of the two common constructions.

Three dates matter. The first is 12 months from the start, because Aviva will not pay if the life covered dies by suicide or intentional self-inflicted injury inside that window. The second is 60 days, the grace period on a missed premium; miss the whole 60 and the policy is cancelled, and because the plan has no cash-in value at any time there is nothing to show for the premiums already paid. The third is the 91st birthday of the oldest life covered, which every policy term has to end before.

The cooling-off period runs for 30 days from the later of the policy start and the arrival of the documents, with premiums refunded in full. After that, cancelling simply ends the cover on the day before the next premium is due and returns nothing.

sections.heading: Two Aviva companies, one phone call
sections.html:
The services document for this plan, reference GN14004 04/2024, is unusually plain about the structure. Aviva UK Digital Limited — company 09766150, firm reference 728985, registered at 8 Surrey Street in Norwich — sells the product. Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited — company 3253947, firm reference 185896, registered at Wellington Row in York — provides and underwrites it.

That document also states, in terms, that "you will not receive advice or a personal recommendation from us for life insurance, critical illness cover and income protection". The sale is information-only. You choose the sum assured, the term and the shape of the cover, and nobody at Aviva is on the hook for whether those choices suit you. For a reader who knows what they want that is a cost saved; for one who does not, it is the single most important sentence in the pack.

The same document says there is no fee, and then explains how the sale is paid for: "Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited pays commission to Aviva UK Digital Limited for selling this product." Commission moving between two companies in the same group is not a cost the customer sees as a line item, and it is a long way from the indemnity commission that drives the intermediated market. It is still worth knowing that a direct sale is not a commission-free one.

The policy is long-term insurance business, so the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers up to 100% of a successful claim with no upper limit, and complaints go to Aviva Customer Relations at PO Box 3182, Norwich NR1 3XE before the Financial Ombudsman Service.

sections.heading: What Aviva actually paid out in 2025
sections.html:
Aviva published its 2025 protection claims figures on 25 March 2026, and they are the best available answer to the question everybody asks about life insurance. Across individual and group protection the group paid £1.99bn on 61,632 claims. The individual book — the one this plan sits in — accounted for 51,222 claims worth £1.315bn.

Within that, life and terminal illness claims numbered 40,277 and came to £860.67m, an average of £21,368 a claim, and Aviva accepted 98.7% of them. Critical illness, children's cover and total permanent disability claims ran at a 90.7% acceptance rate across 5,586 claims worth £388.56m, and income protection at 90% across 4,154 claims worth £63.56m. The lower acceptance rates on the latter two are a feature of how those products are defined rather than a sign of a harder claims line: a death is a fact, a listed critical illness is a definition that has to be met.

Two caveats on reading those numbers. They are group-wide across every distribution channel, not specific to policies bought direct through this plan, and the 98.7% figure covers the whole individual life book, including policies written through advisers and through workplace schemes.

sections.heading: The inflation option costs more than it adds
sections.html:
Aviva offers an increasing cover option so that the sum assured keeps pace with prices. The terms set out both halves of the deal. The cover amount rises each year in line with the Consumer Prices Index, and "the maximum annual increase applied will be 10%". The premium rises too: Aviva will "multiply your current premium by 1.5 and the percentage increase in CPI", capped so that "your premium won't increase by more than 15% each year". If CPI does not rise, neither the cover nor the premium moves.

Multiplying the premium increase by 1.5 while the cover increase is left at 1.0 means the price of each £1,000 of cover rises every year the option is in force. At 3% CPI, after 10 years the cover has grown 34.4% and the premium 55.3%, so each £1,000 of cover costs 15.6% more than it did at the start. After 25 years the cover has grown 109.4% and the premium 200.5%, and the same £1,000 of cover costs 43.5% more.

Put in money: start at £20 a month for £100,000 of cover and run 25 years at 3% CPI. The cover ends at £209,378 and the premium at £60.11 a month. Total premiums over the 25 years come to roughly £10,696, against £6,000 if the cover had been left level. The option is not a trick — Aviva publishes both multipliers in the terms, and index-linked cover genuinely is worth more than fixed cover — but it is priced at a premium to the indexation it delivers, and the gap compounds. Anyone taking it should ask themselves whether they would rather buy more level cover now for the same money.

sections.heading: Decreasing cover assumes 8%, and your mortgage probably does not
sections.html:
Decreasing cover is sold to track a repayment mortgage down to zero, and Aviva is more candid than most about the mechanism: the terms say the cover amount "decreases every month, broadly in line with a repayment loan, for example a mortgage, using a fixed interest rate of 8%". Publishing that figure is to Aviva's credit. The problem is the figure itself.

Eight per cent is well above anything on offer. The Bank of England put the effective interest rate on new fixed-rate mortgages at 4.20% in May 2026, and Moneyfacts had the average two-year fix at 5.68% in June 2026. Because a higher assumed rate means more of each early payment goes on interest, Aviva's cover falls more slowly than a real mortgage balance does — so the mismatch leaves you over-covered rather than short.

On a £200,000 repayment mortgage over 25 years at 4.20%, the debt stands at £143,766 after ten years while the Aviva cover is still £161,527: £17,761 more cover than mortgage, or 12.4%. By year 20 the gap is £17,887 on a debt of £58,242 — 30.7%. At 5.68% the gaps narrow to £10,345 and £10,984. Nobody is left exposed by this, and that is the right way round for a safety net to fail. But you are paying for cover you cannot use, and on a long policy the overlap runs into tens of thousands of pounds. A reader with a cheap fix and a long term should price level cover at the real outstanding balance against decreasing cover at Aviva's 8% before assuming the decreasing option is the economical one.

sections.heading: What the regulator concluded about this market in September
sections.html:
The Financial Conduct Authority closed its pure protection market study on 21 September 2026 with final report MS24/1.5, and the headline conclusion is favourable to insurers. The regulator found that "competition generally delivers good outcomes for people who hold these products, with a wide range of products available and high claims acceptance rates", and chose to act through existing rules rather than new regulation, with industry work starting by the end of 2026 and a TechSprint planned for the third quarter of 2027.

The problem it identified is not the product but the absence of it. Some 58% of UK adults hold no pure protection product at all, and 59% of those have never considered whether they need one. Unnecessary switching affects roughly 19,000 customers a year, about 0.1% of policyholders.

The commission findings are where a direct buyer has something to compare against. On term assurance the FCA found a median commission rate in 2024 of 220% of the first year's premium, equivalent to about 20% of the lifetime projected premiums on the policy, with the median clawback period having moved from two years to four. Around 80% of term assurance policies are sold through intermediaries, 88.9% of those on indemnity commission paid up front; 68% of intermediated sales ran through restricted panels, 27% through whole-of-market panels and 4% through single-tie arrangements. Buying direct from an insurer does not escape commission — Aviva's own services document says so — but it does take the four-year clawback and the panel question off the table.

sections.heading: Aviva's own complaints figures, and the gaps in the paperwork
sections.html:
Aviva UK Digital Limited publishes its complaints return, and for the half-year from 1 January to 30 June 2026 the selling entity opened 164 insurance and pure protection complaints and closed 151. The rate was 0.04 complaints per 1,000 sales, which is low. Of those closed, 37.1% were resolved within three days and 60.9% between three days and eight weeks, and 34.4% were upheld. The largest single cause was "advising, selling and arranging" — which, on a sale Aviva's own paperwork describes as carrying no advice, is worth noting.

The Financial Ombudsman Service's annual figures for 2025/26, published on 21 May 2026, put term assurance at 884 new cases with 17% upheld, against 214,600 complaints across all products and a 30% average. Critical illness cover ran at 647 cases and 12% upheld. Life cover generates very few complaints relative to its size, and the ones it does generate are upheld at around half the rate of the market as a whole.

Three things in the documents are harder to defend. The policy summary and terms and conditions both carry 05/2023 version dates and the services document 04/2024, so the consumer pack has not been refreshed in over two years while the product pages have. Neither document states a minimum or a maximum cover amount, so the sum you can actually buy is invisible until you start a quote. And the Defaqto 5 Star rating on the product page carries no year, no product name and no link to the assessment, which makes it impossible to check what was rated or when.

pros: Terminal illness cover included at no extra cost, on a definition judged by the treating consultant rather than by an insurer's doctor
98.7% of individual life and terminal illness claims accepted in 2025, across 40,277 claims worth £860.67m
Premiums are guaranteed for the whole term on level and decreasing cover, so the price cannot be reviewed upwards
Underwritten by the largest life insurer in the UK — roughly 25% of the market, 21.8 million UK customers and £479bn under management
Aviva publishes the 8% interest assumption behind its decreasing cover, which many insurers do not
FSCS protection covers 100% of a successful claim with no upper limit, and the complaints rate at the selling company is 0.04 per 1,000 sales
DigiCare+ adds digital GP appointments, mental health support, nutrition guidance and a second medical opinion service
A 30-day cooling-off period with premiums refunded in full
cons: The inflation protection option raises the premium at 1.5 times CPI while raising the cover at 1.0 times it, so each £1,000 of cover costs 15.6% more after ten years at 3% CPI and 43.5% more after 25

Decreasing cover is calculated at a fixed 8% interest rate, far above the 4.20% effective rate on new fixed mortgages in May 2026, leaving a £17,761 overlap at year ten on a £200,000 loan that the customer pays for and cannot use
No minimum or maximum cover amount is published on the product page or in the policy summary, so the only way to find out what is available is to take a quote

The sale carries no advice and no personal recommendation, yet "advising, selling and arranging" was the largest single cause of complaints to Aviva UK Digital in the first half of 2026, with 34.4% of closed complaints upheld
The £5 a month headline sits a long way below the £229 median annual premium the FCA recorded for term assurance in 2024
The policy summary and terms and conditions both still carry 05/2023 version dates, over two years old, while the marketing pages are current
The Defaqto 5 Star rating is shown without a date, a product name or a link to the underlying assessment
Miss 60 days of premiums and the policy is cancelled with nothing returned, because the plan has no cash-in value at any time
verdict: Aviva's Life Insurance Plan is a straightforward guaranteed-premium term policy from the insurer with the largest share of the UK life market, and its claims record — 98.7% of individual life and terminal illness claims accepted in 2025 — is the number that matters most on a product like this. The direct route is clean: two Aviva companies, no broker, no fee, guaranteed premiums on level and decreasing cover, and a terminal illness definition that leaves the judgement with the treating consultant. The two options bolted onto the base plan deserve more scepticism than the plan itself. Inflation protection is priced at 1.5 times CPI for cover that rises at 1.0 times it, and decreasing cover is calculated at a fixed 8% when real mortgage rates are nearer 4.2%; both are published in Aviva's own terms, and both are worth doing the arithmetic on before you tick the box. Buy the level cover, read the 05/2023 policy summary before you sign, and treat the £5 a month as the floor it is.

faqs.q: How much does Aviva life insurance cost?
faqs.a: Aviva advertises its Life Insurance Plan from £5 a month. That is an entry price rather than a typical one: the FCA's 2024 policy-level data put the median term assurance premium across the market at £229 a year, roughly £19.08 a month, with half of policies between £132 and £378 a year. Your own price depends on age, health, smoking status, the cover amount and the term, and Aviva does not publish a rate table.

faqs.q: Who underwrites Aviva's life insurance, and who am I buying from?
faqs.a: Two companies in the same group. Aviva UK Digital Limited (company 09766150, firm reference 728985, Norwich) sells the plan; Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited (company 3253947, firm reference 185896, York) writes and underwrites it. Aviva Life & Pensions pays commission to Aviva UK Digital for the sale, and there is no separate fee charged to the customer.

faqs.q: Does Aviva's life insurance include terminal illness cover?
faqs.a: Yes, at no extra cost. It pays the full sum assured on a definite diagnosis by the attending consultant of an illness that either has no known cure or has progressed past the point of cure, and which that consultant expects to lead to death within 12 months.

faqs.q: Can Aviva put the premium up?
faqs.a: Not on level or decreasing cover — those premiums are guaranteed for the whole term. If you choose increasing cover, the premium changes every year: Aviva multiplies it by 1.5 times the CPI increase, capped at 15% a year, while the cover itself rises by CPI capped at 10%.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a payment?
faqs.a: You have 60 days from each due date to pay. Miss the whole 60 days and Aviva cancels the policy. The plan has no cash-in value at any time, so nothing is returned, and cover stops.

faqs.q: Is Aviva life insurance protected if the company fails?
faqs.a: Yes. Long-term insurance is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme at up to 100% of a successful claim, with no upper cash limit. Complaints go first to Aviva Customer Relations, PO Box 3182, Norwich NR1 3XE, and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which received 884 term assurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 17% of them.

title: Aviva Over 50s Life Insurance Review
meta_title: Aviva Over 50s Life Insurance: What £5 to £100 a Month Buys
meta_description: Aviva's over 50s cover is guaranteed acceptance for ages 50 to 80, from £5 a month, with premiums stopping at 30 years or age 90. Figures, limits and gaps.
intro:
Aviva has been selling guaranteed acceptance life cover to older customers for decades, and the current version is about as straightforward as this kind of policy gets. Anyone aged between 50 and 80 who lives in the UK can take it out. There is no medical, no health questionnaire and no way to be turned down. You pick either the monthly premium you want to pay or the lump sum you want paid out, anywhere between £5 and £100 a month, and the figure you agree on the day you buy is the figure that comes out of your bank account for as long as you pay it. Aviva rates the cover 5 Stars with Defaqto on its own product page.

The structure is worth understanding before you get a quote, because it is unusual. Premiums are not for life. They stop after 30 years, or on the policy anniversary after your 90th birthday, whichever arrives first — and the cover carries on until you die regardless. Buy at 50 and you pay for thirty years; buy at 80 and you pay for ten. The cover amount itself is fixed on day one and never moves. Aviva throws in access to DigiCare+, its health app, which covers digital GP appointments, mental health support, nutrition advice and bereavement support at no extra charge, and there is currently an Amazon.co.uk gift card of up to £200 once you have paid six monthly premiums.

Behind it sits Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, company number 3253947, firm reference number 185896 on the Financial Conduct Authority register. The parent, Aviva plc, reported over 25 million customers and operating profit of £2,203 million for 2025 in results published on 5 March 2026, up 25% on the £1,767 million it made in 2024.

sections.heading: What £5 to £100 a month actually buys
sections.html:
You approach the quote from one of two directions. Either you name the monthly premium you can afford and Aviva tells you the lump sum that buys, or you name the lump sum you want your family to receive and Aviva tells you the premium. The price depends on three things and three things only: your age when you apply, the amount of cover, and whether you smoke. No condition you have, or develop later, changes it.

The ceiling is firm. The policy summary states that the minimum is £5 a month and that "the total monthly premium can't be more than £100 per month" — and that £100 is a limit across every Aviva over 50s policy you hold, not per policy. So the most this product will ever be asked to do is whatever £100 a month buys at your age.

The premium term is the part most people miss. Aviva's own wording: "You'll stop paying your premiums after 30 years or the policy anniversary after your 90th birthday, whichever comes first, but your cover will continue until you die." A 55-year-old therefore pays 360 monthly premiums and then stops at 85 with the cover still running. A 69-year-old pays for 21 years, because turning 90 arrives before the thirtieth anniversary does. That cap matters more than any other single feature, and it is the reason the arithmetic further down this page has an end point rather than running forever.

What you cannot do is take money out. "The policy has no cash-in value at any time" appears in both the policy summary and the plan conditions. It pays on death and on nothing else. Aviva is blunt about this on its own site: "Our Over 50s Life Insurance is not a savings or investment plan."

sections.heading: The first twelve months work differently
sections.html:
Guaranteed acceptance has to be paid for somehow, and this is where. For the first year, Aviva only pays the full cover amount if the death is accidental. Die of anything else in that window and, in Aviva's words, "we'll pay a cash amount equal to the premiums already paid, but not the cover amount" — so a policy taken out in January that pays £40 a month returns roughly £360 if the worst happens in October, rather than the several thousand pounds on the schedule.

The definition of an accident is narrow and worth reading twice: "death resulting from bodily injury caused directly by accidental, external violent and visible means and not as a direct result of the life covered's sickness, disease or physical disorder." A fall caused by a stroke is unlikely to qualify. A fall caused by a loose stair rod is.

Five categories are carved out of even that. The published policy summary lists intentional self-inflicted injury including suicide, alcohol or drug misuse, taking part in a criminal act, flying other than as a fare-paying passenger on a commercial airline, and hazardous pursuits. There is a geographic limit as well — the accidental death benefit applies while you are in the UK, Europe, the USA, Canada, Australia or New Zealand. A fatal accident on a trekking holiday outside that list, in the first year, would fall outside it on two counts.

After twelve months and a day, all of that falls away. The guarantee becomes unconditional: any cause, anywhere, full amount.

sections.heading: Working out when you have paid in more than it pays out
sections.html:
Aviva says this itself, twice, in plain terms: "Depending on how long you live, you may end up paying more in premiums than the amount we pay out when you die," and in the policy summary, "the lump sum paid out could be less than the total amount you've paid in premiums." It is a real possibility rather than a legal formality, and it is arithmetic anyone can do at the kitchen table.

The Financial Conduct Authority did the sums for the market as a whole in its pure protection market study, published on 29 January 2026. Its worked example: a guaranteed acceptance over 50s customer paying £30 a month for £5,000 of cover would be expected to pass what the FCA calls the tipping point after 13 years and 11 months. Live longer than that and the estate receives less than the household paid in.

Set that against how long people actually live. The Office for National Statistics national life tables for 2022 to 2024, published on 10 December 2025, put period life expectancy at age 65 at 18.7 years for men and 21.2 years for women. A 65-year-old woman on those terms would, on average, pass the tipping point with roughly seven years to spare.

Aviva's premium cap changes the shape of that, and in the customer's favour. Because payments stop at 30 years or age 90, the total is bounded. Thirty years at £30 a month comes to £10,800; at the £100 ceiling it comes to £36,000; at the £5 floor, £1,800. An 80-year-old buying today pays for ten years at most, so £100 a month tops out at £12,000. Whether the policy is good value in your case turns on where your cover amount sits against those totals, and the only way to find out is to run a quote and multiply.

sections.heading: What the regulator found about this corner of the market
sections.html:
The FCA's interim report is the most useful document published about over 50s cover in years, and almost nothing written about these policies quotes it. Its findings are about the product type rather than about Aviva specifically, but they are the context every buyer should have.

Around 0.2 million guaranteed acceptance over 50s policies were sold in 2024, at an average monthly premium of £51. Roughly 79% went through single-tie or exclusive distribution arrangements rather than open comparison. The claims ratio — the share of premium that comes back out as claims — sat at about 52%, low against the rest of the protection market. Commission was the highest of any pure protection product, running at over 34% of lifetime projected premiums, with individual rates typically 170% to 250% of the first year's premium.

The sharpest figure is the comparison the FCA drew in its value annex: guaranteed acceptance over 50s customers pay an average of £71.73 in premiums per £1,000 of cover, against £8.10 for medically underwritten whole of life. That is close to nine times the price for each pound of protection, and it is the price of never being asked a health question. If you are in good health at 55, that trade is a poor one and an underwritten policy will almost certainly beat it. If a heart condition or a cancer history means underwriting would price you out or decline you outright, the same trade is the only one on the table.

The regulator also found that almost three-quarters of people who had bought one thought it offered value for money, and that 58% of UK adults hold no pure protection product at all, of whom 59% have never considered whether they need one. The FCA expects to publish its final report in the third quarter of 2026.

sections.heading: Aviva's claims record, and who is on the hook
sections.html:
Aviva publishes its claims figures in more detail than most, and they are good. Across 2025 the group paid £1.99 billion on 61,632 individual and group protection claims, announced on 25 March 2026. Life and terminal illness claims alone accounted for £860,665,410 across 40,277 claims, an average of £21,368, with 98.7% of them paid. Of the small remainder, misrepresentation accounted for 1% and a definition not being met 0.3%.

One caveat on those numbers: Aviva's book of claims excludes over 50s cover from its breakdown of causes, so the 98.7% figure is drawn from a wider pool than the product on this page. That said, a guaranteed acceptance policy has no health questions to misrepresent after the first twelve months, which removes the single largest ground on which life claims get declined anywhere.

For market context, the Association of British Insurers reported £7.84 billion of individual and group protection claims paid across the industry in 2025 — £21.5 million a day — with 97.9% of claims paid and 258,000 new individual claims at an average of £19,300.

The contract is with Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, registered in England number 3253947, firm reference number 185896, verifiable on the FCA register. The policy is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, which the summary says "may cover you for up to 100% of any successful claim" for long-term insurance. Complaints go to Aviva first and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, free of charge. The Ombudsman's annual data published on 21 May 2026 gives some sense of how often these disputes arise: against 214,600 new complaints across all products and a 30% average uphold rate, non-reviewable whole of life assurance drew 414 cases at 26% upheld, reviewable whole of life 434 at 38%, and term assurance 884 at 17%. Small numbers for a product held by millions.

sections.heading: Set against what a funeral now costs
sections.html:
Most people buy this cover with a funeral in mind, so the two numbers belong side by side. SunLife's Cost of Dying report for 2026 puts the average simple attended funeral at £3,828, up 5.3% in a year and the steepest rise since 2016. Add the send-off — wake, flowers, notices, averaging £1,312 — and the total cost of dying reaches £5,140. A direct cremation, now the choice in a growing share of cases, averages £1,628. Cremations outnumber burials by roughly 74% to 26%. The figures come from interviews with 100 funeral directors and 1,500 people who had organised a funeral, conducted between May and July 2025.

The problem is that Aviva's payout does not move. "The amount we'll pay on a successful claim is set when you buy our Over 50s Life Insurance — it won't go up as prices rise." A sum chosen today to cover a £3,828 funeral will be worth considerably less against the same funeral in twenty years' time, and on the last decade's trajectory that gap widens every year. Aviva does not sell a funeral plan and does not offer an index-linked version of this product, so there is no mechanism inside the policy to close it. Buying more cover than you currently need is the only lever available, and it costs more every month to pull.

One thing the policy does allow is writing it in trust, which Aviva supports. Done properly, that keeps the payout outside the estate for inheritance tax and gets money to the family without waiting for probate — which is the point, since funeral directors want paying long before probate finishes.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork falls short
sections.html:
Aviva publishes more than most providers in this market, and the documents are free to read before you buy, which is not universal. But two of them are old. The publicly served policy summary carries the reference DA03015 and the date 08/2020; the plan conditions for the Guaranteed Lifelong Protection version are dated 11/2016. A newer summary exists at reference SD11001, dated 09/2025, on Aviva's document library. The terms in the two summaries agree on everything checked here, but a shopper landing on the older one is reading a six-year-old document, and Aviva could tidy that up cheaply.

More awkwardly, no minimum or maximum cover amount appears anywhere in the pre-sale documents. The premium range is stated plainly in three places; the sum assured range is stated in none of them. That means you cannot work out what £5 a month buys at your age, or whether the cover you want is even available, without going through the quote journey and handing over your details. For a product sold on its simplicity, that is a strange gap.

The Defaqto 5 Star rating displayed on the product page carries no year against it. Defaqto ratings are reissued annually and providers usually date them; this one is presented as a current fact with nothing to anchor it. Worth asking about if the rating is part of why you are buying.

Two smaller points. The gift card is presented prominently but sits outside the contract — Aviva states it "isn't part of the policy terms and benefits" and that the offer "may be withdrawn or changed at any time," with one card per person and per policy. And there is a mismatch in how quickly a missed payment kills the policy: the plan conditions allow "thirty days grace" after which "the Plan will be cancelled and no cash in value will be paid," while Aviva's own frequently asked questions say cover is cancelled "60 days after the last premium was due." Both cannot be right for the same contract. If money is tight, ask which figure applies to your policy before you assume you have the longer window.

Nothing but a refund of premiums is paid if you die of natural causes in the first 12 months, and the accidental death cover that does apply excludes self-inflicted injury, alcohol or drug misuse, criminal acts, non-commercial flying, hazardous pursuits, and any death outside the UK, Europe, the USA, Canada, Australia or New Zealand

verdict: Aviva's over 50s cover is a well-run version of a product that only makes sense for some people. If you are 60-something with a health history that would make underwriting expensive or impossible, this pays a guaranteed lump sum, the price never changes, the payments stop at 90, and the claims record behind it is genuinely strong at 98.7% paid. If you are in decent health and could pass underwriting, the FCA's £71.73 against £8.10 per £1,000 of cover is the number that should stop you — an underwritten policy will almost certainly give your family far more for the same money. Work out your own tipping point before you buy: multiply the monthly premium by twelve, divide the cover amount by the answer, and see how that number compares with the 18.7 years a 65-year-old man and 21.2 years a 65-year-old woman can expect on ONS figures. That single calculation tells you more than any review can.

faqs.q: Can Aviva turn me down for this policy?
faqs.a: No. Acceptance is guaranteed for anyone aged 50 to 80 who is a UK resident with the legal right to live here. There is no medical examination and no health questionnaire, and nothing you disclose or fail to disclose about your health affects the price or the outcome of a claim. Your premium depends on your age, the amount of cover and whether you smoke.

faqs.q: What happens if I die in the first year?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. If the death is accidental, Aviva pays the full cover amount from day one. If it is from any other cause, Aviva refunds the premiums you have paid and nothing more. After twelve months the full amount is paid whatever the cause. Aviva defines an accident narrowly — "bodily injury caused directly by accidental, external violent and visible means" and not resulting from illness — and excludes several categories including alcohol or drug misuse, criminal acts and hazardous pursuits during that first year.

faqs.q: How long do I have to keep paying?
faqs.a: Until whichever comes first: 30 years from the start date, or the policy anniversary after your 90th birthday. Cover continues until you die either way. Someone starting at 55 pays for 30 years and stops at 85. Someone starting at 69 pays for 21 years, because their 90th birthday arrives before the thirtieth anniversary. The FCA notes that most insurers set this cap at 90, though a few use 95.

faqs.q: Could I pay in more than the policy pays out?
faqs.a: Yes, and Aviva says so on its own pages. The FCA's worked example puts the crossover for a typical guaranteed acceptance policy — £30 a month for £5,000 of cover — at 13 years and 11 months. Aviva's premium cap limits the damage, because payments stop at 30 years or age 90: thirty years at £30 a month totals £10,800, and at the £100 monthly ceiling, £36,000. Do the multiplication against your own quote before you sign.

faqs.q: Can I cash the policy in if I need the money?
faqs.a: No. Both the policy summary and the plan conditions state the policy has no cash-in value at any time. If you stop paying, cover ends and you get nothing back — the only exception is the 30-day cooling-off period at the start, during which Aviva refunds every premium paid. The plan conditions allow thirty days grace on a missed payment before cancellation, though Aviva's FAQs quote 60 days, so confirm which applies to your policy.

faqs.q: Is this the same thing as a funeral plan?
faqs.a: No. Aviva states plainly that it does not offer funeral plans. This policy pays a cash lump sum to your estate or your beneficiaries, who can then spend it on a funeral or on anything else. A funeral plan buys the funeral itself at today's prices; this buys a fixed sum of money that will not rise. With the average attended funeral at £3,828 in 2026 and rising 5.3% a year, that difference compounds. Writing the policy in trust helps the money reach the family faster.

faqs.q: How do I claim, and who regulates the policy?
faqs.a: Claims are made to Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, company number 3253947, authorised and regulated under firm reference number 185896, which can be checked on the FCA register. The policy is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme for up to 100% of a successful claim. If a complaint is not resolved to your satisfaction you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service free of charge; its 2025/26 data records 414 non-reviewable whole of life complaints at a 26% uphold rate, against a 30% average across all financial products.

title: Aviva Pension Review: Charges, Transfers and the Cash Margin
meta_title: Aviva Pension Review: 0.35% a Year and What Sits On Top
meta_description: Aviva Pension: 0.35% a year to £500,000 and nothing above, £25 a month to start, 5,000+ funds. Charges, transfer rules and complaints, checked October 2026.

headline.label: Annual charge
headline.value: 0.35% a year — the Aviva Charge on the first £500,000 held in the Aviva Pension (SIPP), nothing above that, fund charges on top

intro:
The Aviva Pension charges 0.35% a year on the first £500,000 you hold in it and nothing at all above that line, takes £25 a month or a £5,000 lump sum to open, and gives access to more than 5,000 funds plus UK shares, exchange-traded funds and investment trusts at £4.99 a trade. Those figures were read on 4 October 2026 from Aviva's own charges page and its key features document, reference RD01002 07/2026.

Behind the product is the biggest wealth business in British retail finance. Aviva reported £233bn of Wealth assets under management at 31 March 2026 across 5.8 million customers, took £2bn of workplace pension net flows in the first quarter of 2026 alone — up 71% on the £1.2bn a year earlier — and now looks after more than 4.8 million workplace pension members. Defaqto's half-year analysis of adviser recommendations, published on 12 August 2026, put Aviva top of the self-invested personal pension market.

One thing to settle before you start. Three different things get called an Aviva pension, and they do not cost the same. The 0.35% above belongs to the Aviva Pension you can open yourself online. If your pension came through an employer, your charge was negotiated by that employer and is not published anywhere; if it came through an adviser, it sits on a different Aviva platform with a different fee scale. The section below sets out how to tell which one you have.

sections.heading: Three products share the name, and only one has a published price
sections.html:
Search for an Aviva pension and you can land on any of three products. Sorting out which one you are looking at is the first useful thing you can do, because the charge is the main thing that differs and only one of the three publishes it.

The Aviva Pension, sometimes badged as a SIPP. This is the one you can open yourself in an afternoon. It sits on Aviva's consumer platform alongside its stocks and shares ISA and investment account, and the Aviva Charge is 0.35% a year on the first £500,000 of what you hold across all three, with nothing charged above that. Aviva's own worked example: 0.35% of £100,000 is £350 a year.

The workplace pension. Aviva's group personal pension carries more than 4.8 million members and is sold to employers with 10 staff upwards, with Aviva taking direct applications up to 100 employees. The annual management charge is quoted scheme by scheme and depends on how many members there are and how much they pay in, so there is no figure to look up — only the one on your own annual statement. The default investment is the My Future Focus Long Term Growth Fund, which holds everything until 15 years before your chosen retirement date, moves into My Future Focus Growth at that point and into My Future Focus Consolidation from 10 years out.

Pension Portfolio. The adviser-sold version, on Aviva's advised platform. It has its own charge scale and, as the cash section below shows, its own arrangement on interest. If a financial adviser set your pension up, this is almost certainly the one you hold.

The simplest test is who you pay. A charge appearing on a statement you receive at home, with no employer and no adviser in the picture, is the 0.35%. Anything else and the number you need is on your scheme documentation rather than on Aviva's website.

sections.heading: What 0.35% buys, and the four charges that sit on top
sections.html:
The Aviva Charge is worked out daily on the average value of the pension and taken monthly out of the cash account. If there is not enough cash sitting there, the terms (RD01003 06/2025) say Aviva sells across your investments proportionately to raise it, adding a 10% buffer so it does not have to come back for more a month later. That is tidier than it sounds: it means a pension fully invested with no cash float will be nibbled at twelve times a year by small forced sales.

Four things are charged separately from the 0.35%, and all four are easy to miss.

The first is the fund's own cost, shown as an ongoing charges figure. Aviva's example is blunt enough to be useful: £1,000 in a ready-made fund with an OCF of 0.35% costs £3.50 a year, and a fund with an OCF of 1% on £10,000 costs £100. On a portfolio of active funds this is routinely larger than the platform charge itself, which makes the 0.35% a floor rather than a total.

The second is dealing. Funds are free to buy and sell. Anything traded on an exchange — a UK share, an ETF, an investment trust — costs £4.99 a go, so a four-holding rebalance is £19.96. The third is tax and levies: 0.5% stamp duty reserve tax on UK share purchases, and the £1.50 Takeover Panel levy on trades over £10,000.

The fourth is the one nobody looks for, and it is covered in its own section at the end of this page, because it is money Aviva keeps rather than money it charges.

sections.heading: Getting money in: £25 a month, 30 days to change your mind, and the transfers Aviva will not take
sections.html:
The entry points are low. £25 a month opens the pension; so does a single £5,000 payment, or £1,000 if you also set up £25 a month. You can open one from 18, keep paying in to 75, and transfer in at any age. Tax relief works the usual way at source — £80 of your money becomes £100 in the pension — with higher and additional rate taxpayers claiming the rest back, up to 45%, or 48% in Scotland.

The allowances are set by HMRC rather than Aviva, and Aviva's own pages print the current ones: £60,000 a year, tapering towards £10,000 once income passes £200,000 or once you have flexibly accessed a pension, a lump sum allowance of £268,275 for 2026/27 and a lump sum and death benefit allowance of £1,073,100.

Transfers in are free from Aviva's side, take three to six weeks in its own estimate, and currently come with cashback of between £100 and £2,500 for new Aviva Pension customers transferring at least £20,000, applied for by 23 November 2026 and completed by 22 May 2027. Existing Aviva pensions do not qualify.

There are hard limits on what can come across. Aviva will not take a defined benefit or final salary pension, a pension you have already started drawing, or one carrying a guaranteed annuity rate or other safeguarded benefit. Its own transfer page also lists what you might be giving up elsewhere: a tax-free lump sum above 25%, loyalty bonuses, enhanced life cover, or the right to take the money before 55. Transfers of safeguarded benefits worth more than £30,000 require regulated advice before they can proceed.

The cooling-off period is 30 days from Aviva receiving your first payment. Cancel inside it and the single payment comes back, less any fall in the value of the investments in the meantime — so the refund is not guaranteed to be pound for pound.

sections.heading: Two Aviva companies, two reference numbers, and one that appears twice
sections.html:
The Aviva Pension is assembled from two regulated entities. Aviva Wrap UK Limited, registered in England and Wales as company 4470008, runs the platform. Aviva Pension Trustees UK Limited, firm reference 465132, provides the pension itself and acts as trustee of the scheme the money sits in. Both are part of Aviva plc, so there is no third-party administrator between you and the brand on the statement — which is not true of every pension sold under a household name.

One detail needs confirming with Aviva rather than asserting here. Firm reference number 231530 appears on the product page against the platform operator, and the key features document prints the same number against a different Aviva company in connection with the MyAviva service. One of the two is a documentation error. It makes no practical difference to a customer, since both firms are Aviva, but anyone checking the chain on the Financial Conduct Authority register should expect the mismatch and ask which entity holds which permission.

Compensation cover is where a pension platform differs from an insured pension fund, and the distinction is worth more than it looks. The key features document puts Financial Services Compensation Scheme protection at £85,000 per person for the collective investments, not the unlimited 100% cover that applies to insured long-term funds. Cash held in the pension's cash account is protected to £120,000 per bank, the higher limit the Prudential Regulation Authority confirmed on 18 November 2025 and which took effect on 1 December 2025.

For a workplace pension there is a second layer that the direct product does not have. Default funds in automatic enrolment schemes are capped by law at 0.75% a year under regulation 7 of the Occupational Pension Schemes (Charges and Governance) Regulations 2015, and Aviva's workplace book is overseen by an Independent Governance Committee that reports publicly every year. Mark Thompson was announced as its incoming chair in October 2026.

sections.heading: What Aviva's own governance committee found
sections.html:
That committee's 2026 report, covering the year to 31 December 2025, is the most useful document on Aviva's pensions anywhere, and it is unusual in being written by people whose job is to criticise the firm paying them. Its conclusion is favourable: Aviva "continues to provide good value for money for members of its workplace pension schemes". The detail is more mixed.

On price, 65% of Aviva policyholders pay 0.5% a year or less. The full distribution is 22.3% under 0.3%, 23.4% between 0.3% and 0.4%, 19.1% between 0.4% and 0.5%, 10.1% between 0.5% and 0.6%, 24.8% between 0.6% and 0.75%, and 0.3% above 0.75%. Read the other way round, a quarter of Aviva's workplace members pay between 0.6% and 0.75% — up to twice what the direct Aviva Pension charges — and a small group sit above the statutory cap, which is possible because the cap applies to default arrangements rather than to every fund a member can choose.

Performance to 31 December 2025 was strong in the growth funds: My Future Growth returned 14.3% over the year, My Future Focus Long Term Growth 14.2% and My Future Focus Growth 13.1%, against inflation of 3.3%. The committee was blunter about the Stewardship range, saying the fund "has not performed well against its benchmark over recent time periods", and it has gone on pressing Aviva to rename it so the label reflects what it actually invests in. It also criticised the pace of Aviva's own fund migration: a "significant cohort of members have not yet benefited from the new My Future Strategy because of the extended delay in their transition", and asked for that to be accelerated. On investment pathways, used by roughly 250,000 policyholders holding around £20bn, it judged asset allocation changes planned for late 2026 or early 2027 as possibly not going far enough.

Two service figures from the same report are worth having. Aviva traced about 41,000 lost members during 2025 and re-established contact with 44% of them, leaving its "gone away" population at 7% — in line with the industry average, which is another way of saying roughly one member in fourteen cannot be contacted. And 71,218 members attended one of 1,348 seminars during the year.

sections.heading: 20,143 complaints in six months, and what they were about
sections.html:
Aviva publishes its own complaints returns, which most providers bury. The numbers for 1 January to 30 June 2026 are the strongest argument against the product on this page.

In the decumulation and pensions category Aviva opened 20,143 complaints and closed 20,070 in those six months, a rate of 2.4 per 1,000 policies in force. It resolved 25.5% within three days and 63.2% within eight weeks, which leaves better than a third of complainants waiting longer than the regulatory window. And it upheld 72.4% of them. The single largest cause is recorded as "delays / timescales".

An uphold rate that high is not evidence of a firm being hard on customers — upholding a complaint means agreeing with it. It is evidence of a firm generating a very large number of complaints it then agrees were justified, overwhelmingly about taking too long. For a product whose worst-case failure is a transfer or a drawdown payment arriving late, that is the risk worth pricing in. The investments category on the same return is worse on uphold rate, at 83.8% of 4,005 closed cases, at 4.8 complaints per 1,000 client accounts.

For context from outside Aviva, the Financial Ombudsman Service published its 2025/26 annual data on 21 May 2026: 214,600 new complaints across all financial products and an average uphold rate of 30%. Personal pensions accounted for 3,777 cases with a 49% uphold rate. Aviva's own first-stage figure is well above both, though the two are not directly comparable — the Ombudsman sees only cases a firm has already refused.

sections.heading: The cash in your pension earns 2.08% while the bank pays 3.05%
sections.html:
Aviva does not charge for holding cash in the pension. It makes money on it instead, and it publishes exactly how in document RD06102, dated April 2026.

Interest earned on the pension's cash account is split in bands. Aviva passes on 60% of the first 1.5 percentage points, 75% of the next 1.5, and 90% of anything above 3%. The worked example in its own factsheet: at an underlying rate of 3.05%, the customer receives 2.08% and Aviva retains 0.97%. If the rate from the bank is zero or negative, Aviva keeps nothing.

Measured as a charge, 0.97% on cash is almost three times the 0.35% Aviva charges on invested money. On £5,000 of cash that is £48.50 a year that does not reach you. The practical lesson is that the cash account should hold what the monthly charge needs and little more, because money parked there is the most expensive money in the pension.

The split is also not the same across Aviva's platforms. Its separate note on charge changes for the advised platform — Pension Portfolio and its siblings, with the change applying no earlier than 17 August 2026 — sets the first band at 50% to the customer rather than 60%. Two Aviva documents, two first-band splits, so check which applies to your own plan rather than assuming the better of the two.

pros: Nothing is charged by Aviva above £500,000, which is rare — most platforms tier downwards but keep charging
Buying and selling funds costs nothing, and exchange trades are £4.99
£25 a month, or £1,000 with a monthly payment, is a genuinely low entry point
Over 5,000 funds plus UK shares, ETFs and investment trusts, with ready-made options for people who do not want to choose
Defaqto put Aviva top of the SIPP market for adviser recommendations in the first half of 2026
No charge to transfer in, three to six weeks typical, and £100 to £2,500 cashback on £20,000-plus transfers applied for by 23 November 2026
The workplace book is independently reviewed every year and the report is published in full, criticisms included
30 days to cancel, and both companies involved are Aviva rather than an outsourced administrator
cons: Aviva opened 20,143 decumulation and pensions complaints in the six months to 30 June 2026 and upheld 72.4% of them, with "delays / timescales" the main cause
Only 63.2% of those complaints were closed within eight weeks, so more than a third of complainants waited longer than the regulatory window
On cash, Aviva retains 0.97 percentage points of a 3.05% rate — nearly three times what it charges on invested money
The first-band cash split differs between Aviva's own documents, 60% on the consumer platform and 50% on the advised one
The 0.35% is effectively flat for almost everybody, since the only break is at £500,000, and cheaper platforms exist below that
Badged a SIPP, but the published asset list is funds, UK shares, ETFs and investment trusts — not the commercial property and unlisted holdings a full SIPP allows
FSCS cover on the investments is £85,000 per person, not the unlimited protection that applies to an insured pension fund
The workplace charge is quoted scheme by scheme and published nowhere; 24.8% of policyholders pay between 0.6% and 0.75% and 0.3% pay more
Aviva's own governance committee says the Stewardship fund has underperformed its benchmark and that a significant cohort of members are still waiting for the My Future transition
No defined benefit pension, no pension already in payment and nothing with a guaranteed annuity rate can be transferred in
Monthly charge collection sells across your holdings with a 10% buffer if the cash account is short, so a fully invested pot gets twelve small forced sales a year
verdict: As a place to hold a pension you manage yourself, the Aviva Pension is priced in the middle of the market and built better than its price suggests: 0.35% to £500,000 with nothing above, free fund dealing, £4.99 exchange trades, 5,000-plus funds and a £25 monthly minimum. The free transfer in and the cashback offer running to 23 November 2026 make consolidating old pots into it cheap to do, provided none of them carries a guarantee worth keeping. Two things should temper the decision. The first is service: Aviva's own published return shows 20,143 pensions complaints in six months with 72.4% upheld and delay the leading cause, which is the thing most likely to go wrong and the thing a glossy charges page will never tell you. The second is cash, where Aviva keeps 0.97 of 3.05 percentage points — fine if you hold a float for charges, expensive if you drift into cash and leave it there. If you already have an Aviva workplace pension, none of the 0.35% applies to you; find your own annual management charge on your scheme statement and compare that instead, because a quarter of Aviva's workplace members are paying between 0.6% and 0.75%.

faqs.q: What does the Aviva Pension actually cost a year?
faqs.a: The Aviva Charge is 0.35% a year on the first £500,000 you hold across your Aviva pension, ISA and investment account combined, and nothing above £500,000. On £100,000 that is £350, which is Aviva's own worked example. On top sit each fund's ongoing charges figure, £4.99 per trade on shares, ETFs and investment trusts, 0.5% stamp duty on UK share purchases and a £1.50 levy on trades over £10,000. The charge is calculated daily and taken monthly from the cash account.

faqs.q: How do I find out what my Aviva workplace pension charges?
faqs.a: Your annual statement, or your scheme documentation from your employer. Aviva quotes the annual management charge on its group personal pension scheme by scheme, based on member numbers and contribution levels, so there is no published figure. For scale, its governance committee reported that 65% of policyholders pay 0.5% a year or less, 24.8% pay between 0.6% and 0.75%, and 0.3% pay more than 0.75%. The 0.75% statutory cap applies to default arrangements, not to every fund you can pick.

faqs.q: Can I move an old pension into the Aviva Pension?
faqs.a: In most cases yes, and Aviva does not charge for it — three to six weeks is its own estimate. It will not accept a defined benefit or final salary pension, one you have already begun taking money from, or one with a guaranteed annuity rate or other safeguarded benefit. Check what you would lose before moving anything: a tax-free lump sum above 25%, a loyalty bonus, enhanced death benefits or an early access right can all be worth more than a charge saving. Transferring safeguarded benefits over £30,000 requires regulated advice.

faqs.q: When can I take the money out?
faqs.a: From 55 at present, rising to 57 on 6 April 2028 unless you hold a protected pension age. Normally 25% comes out tax free, up to the lump sum allowance of £268,275 for 2026/27, and the rest is taxed as income. On the consumer platform the income route is drawdown; buying a guaranteed income for life means moving the money to an annuity provider, which can be Aviva or anyone else. Anyone over 50 can get a free appointment with Pension Wise through MoneyHelper before deciding.

faqs.q: Is my money safe if Aviva fails?
faqs.a: The pension's assets are held separately from Aviva's own, and the scheme's trustee is Aviva Pension Trustees UK Limited, firm reference 465132. The key features document puts Financial Services Compensation Scheme cover at £85,000 per person on the collective investments — not the unlimited protection that applies to an insured pension fund, which is a real difference between a platform pension and an older-style insured one. Cash in the pension's cash account is covered to £120,000 per bank, the limit that took effect on 1 December 2025.

title: Avonline Broadband Satellite Internet
meta_title: Avonline Broadband: What Happened and Where It Went
meta_description: Avonline sold satellite broadband from 2002 and hit 30Mbps in 2016. The brand was renamed Bigblu in 2018. Here is the record and where the service is now.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised monthly price
headline.value: No longer sold — the last package advertised under the Avonline name was 30Mbps down and 2Mbps up, and the satellite business was renamed Bigblu on 31 August 2018

intro:
Avonline began installing television and telecommunications equipment in 1981, started putting satellite broadband into British homes in 2002, built fibre networks past more than 2 million UK premises and installed digital services in over 4 million homes and businesses. By 31 October 2016 it was advertising a 30Mbps satellite connection to anyone in England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, two years before the government's own universal service floor of 10Mbps came into force.

The brand is no longer sold. Avonline Satellite Services Limited (company 10201939) became Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018; Avonline Network Services Limited (company 10201726) became M Group Telecom Limited on 1 April 2025; and Avonline Limited, registered as Avonline plc until 2019, was dissolved on 16 March 2026. Nothing can be bought under the name today. Every figure on this page was checked on 4 October 2026 against Companies House, Ofcom, the London Gazette and the companies' own websites.

The service itself did not disappear with the name. It is sold today as Bigblu, run out of the same Oxfordshire town on a phone number one digit group away from the old one, at £24.99 a month for an average of 21Mb/s with no data cap. The complication is that avonlinebroadband.com is still live, still advertises the 2016 product in the present tense, and has had cryptocurrency link-spam injected into its home page. That is the gap this page is here to close.
