sections.heading: What Barclaycard actually puts on the shelf
sections.html:
There are nine personal cards, and they do four separate jobs. Four of them are Platinum balance transfer variants, all at 24.9% APR representative and a 24.9% p.a. variable purchase rate, separated only by how long the 0% runs and what the transfer costs: up to 29 months for a 3.45% fee, up to 21 months on purchases and transfers together for 3.45%, up to 20 months for 1.99%, and up to 12 months for no fee at all. The Amazon Barclaycard sits at 28.9% APR representative with six months at 0% on purchases and pays 1% back on Amazon spending and 0.5% everywhere else. Barclaycard Rewards is also 28.9% and pays 0.25% cashback. Barclaycard Forward, the credit-building card, is listed at 33.9%.

The two Avios cards are where the ladder breaks. Barclaycard Avios charges nothing and earns 1 Avios per £1 of eligible spending at 29.9% APR representative. Barclaycard Avios Plus charges £20 a month, earns 1.5 Avios per £1 at the same 29.9% purchase rate, and carries an 80.1% APR representative. The 50 percentage points between the two cards are not a difference in borrowing cost at all — both charge 29.9% on purchases. They are the £240 of annual fees expressed as an interest rate, because the representative APR has to include compulsory charges. It is a useful piece of arithmetic to have published rather than hidden, and it also means the 80.1% figure tells a borrower almost nothing about what interest they would pay.

Every one of the nine representative examples is calculated on an assumed £1,200 credit limit. The published minimums are a long way below that: £500 on the Amazon Barclaycard and, in the Barclaycard Rewards summary box, £50. An applicant approved at £500 on the Amazon card pays the same 28.9% but has a quarter of the headroom the example assumes, and on a card with a £50 floor the £1,200 example describes a customer the applicant may not turn out to be.

sections.heading: The 0% clock starts before the balance arrives
sections.html:
On all four Platinum variants the promotional period is counted "From the date you open your account", and the balance has to be moved "within 60 days" of that date to qualify for the offer at all. Those two conditions pull in opposite directions, and nothing in the advertising reconciles them. An applicant who opens the account and transfers the same week gets very nearly the full 29 months of 0% on the transferred balance. An applicant who waits until day 59 — still inside the rules, still entitled to the offer — gets about 27 months, because two of them have already been spent on an account with nothing on it.

Put that in money. On a £3,000 balance, Barclaycard's 24.9% standard rate costs roughly £747 over a year, or about £62 a month. Two months of the promotional period lost to a slow transfer is therefore worth about £124 of borrowing — more than the £103.50 the 3.45% fee cost in the first place. The offer is not misdescribed; the word "up to" is on the front of every one of these cards. But the thing that decides whether "up to 29 months" means 29 or 27 is how fast the customer acts after approval, and that is the opposite of the advice an applicant usually gets, which is to take time over a transfer.

The transfer rules themselves are set out in the terms for the mid-length Platinum offer: a minimum of £250 across up to five separate transfers for a new customer, £100 for an existing one, and balances accepted only from "cards issued by other banks". The offer is described there as available to new customers only, and the promotional term in that document is 24 months — a fourth number for a card family the main grid presents as four fixed options.

sections.heading: £103.50, £59.70, or nothing at all
sections.html:
The four Platinum variants invite a sum that Barclaycard does not print, which is the fee expressed as a monthly cost of the interest-free months it buys. On a £3,000 transfer the 3.45% fee is £103.50 for up to 29 months, which is £3.57 a month. The 1.99% fee is £59.70 for up to 20 months, which is £2.99 a month. The no-fee card gives 12 months for nothing, which is unbeatable per month but runs out first.

So the shorter paid card is the cheaper one per month of 0%, by about 16%, and the longer one is only worth its extra £43.80 to someone who genuinely needs the extra nine months. A borrower who can clear £3,000 in twenty months pays £59.70 on the 1.99% card and £103.50 on the 29-month card for a benefit they never use. A borrower who can clear it in twelve pays nothing at all. The fee is a one-off percentage added to the balance, so it also becomes part of the debt being repaid, which on the 3.45% card means repaying £3,103.50 rather than £3,000.

Against the alternative, all three are cheap. Carrying £3,000 on a 24.9% card for a single year costs in the region of £747 in interest; £103.50 buys more than two years without it. That is the case for the product, and it survives the arithmetic above intact — the arithmetic only decides which of the four to pick.

sections.heading: The transfer Barclaycard will not take
sections.html:
Barclaycard's help pages are blunt about the limit of the offer: "we can't accept transfers from other credit card or loan accounts held with Barclays Bank UK PLC or any other Barclays Group company. This includes our Partnership card – Hilton Honors." The balance transfer terms put the same rule from the other direction — "you can't make a transfer to any other Barclaycard or our partner cards" — and the mid-length Platinum terms restrict incoming balances to "cards issued by other banks".

Two things make this wider than the group exclusions other issuers publish. The first is that it covers loan accounts, not just cards, so a Barclayloan cannot be moved onto a 0% card inside the same group. The second is that it reaches a co-branded card most customers would not think of as a Barclays product at all: the Hilton Honors partnership card is named in the exclusion by Barclaycard itself. For anyone already banking with Barclays and carrying a balance there — and Barclays UK had 14.1 million digitally active customers at 30 June 2026 — this is the first question to settle, because it decides whether the whole range is available or none of it is.

sections.heading: Both ends of the same transaction
sections.html:
Barclaycard is unusual among UK card brands in sitting on both sides of a card payment: it issues cards to shoppers and it also acquires card transactions for merchants, which is where a large share of the brand's revenue comes from. The Payment Systems Regulator measured that side of the business in its card-acquiring market review, MR18/1.8, published in November 2021. Over 2014 to 2018, it found, Barclaycard and Worldpay together "accounted for [70-80]% of card transactions by volume and [60-70]% by value", and the two of them supplied card-acquiring services to 50 to 60% of large merchants. Mastercard and Visa transactions, which is what the review covered, were about 98% of all UK card payments in 2018.

The precise splits between the two firms are redacted in the public report, so the honest reading is that Barclaycard is one of two dominant acquirers rather than that it holds any particular share on its own. It matters to a cardholder for one reason: the interchange a merchant's acquirer collects is part of what funds the 0% offers, the cashback and the Avios on the issuing side. A card paying 0.25% back on everyday spending is not a gift; it is a share of the fee the shop pays, returned to the customer to keep the card in the wallet.

sections.heading: Where £20 a month earns its keep, and where it does not
sections.html:
The two Avios cards are the clearest case on the range of a fee-paying and a free version of the same product, and Barclaycard publishes enough to settle the comparison without guessing at what an Avios is worth. The free card earns 1 Avios per £1, pays 5,000 Avios for £1,000 of spending in the first three months, and gives a British Airways cabin upgrade voucher — or 7,000 bonus Avios instead — at £20,000 of spending in twelve months. Avios Plus costs £20 a month, earns 1.5 Avios per £1, pays 25,000 Avios for £3,000 in the first three months, and reaches the same voucher at £10,000.

Because both cards price the voucher's alternative at 7,000 Avios, Barclaycard has effectively published its own exchange rate, and the comparison can be done in Avios rather than in pounds. At £10,000 of annual spending, Avios Plus returns 15,000 Avios plus the voucher; the free card returns 10,000 and no voucher. The £240 fee therefore buys 12,000 Avios, or 2p each. At £20,000 of spending the free card earns its own voucher, so Plus returns 30,000 plus a voucher against the free card's 20,000 plus a voucher — 10,000 extra Avios for the same £240, which is 2.4p each. Below £10,000 neither card earns a voucher and the difference is only the extra half an Avios per pound: at £5,000 of spending that is 2,500 Avios for £240, or about 9.6p each.

The fee card is therefore at its best in a fairly narrow band, roughly £10,000 to £20,000 of annual spending, and gets slightly worse rather than better above it. The first year is a separate calculation: the extra 20,000 Avios in the welcome bonus is worth considerably more than £240 on any sensible valuation, which makes Avios Plus a good first-year card and a questionable second-year one. Barclaycard publishes no redemption value for an Avios anywhere on its own site, so the 2p and 9.6p figures above are costs per Avios, not statements about whether that is good value — that depends on what the holder redeems them for, and only they can decide it.

sections.heading: Cash is priced on a different system
sections.html:
The interest-free period on purchases does not exist on cash. Barclaycard charges 27.9% compound equivalent on cash borrowing "daily, from the date we add the transaction to your account, until you've repaid your cash balance in full" — and its own fee page spells out that this applies "even if you pay your total outstanding balance in full by your payment due date". On top of the interest there is a transaction fee of £2.99 on withdrawals under £100 and 2.99% above it, with gambling transactions treated as cash at the same typical 2.99%.

The rest of the charge list is short. The default fee is £12 for each late payment, missed payment or payment below the minimum, and Barclaycard caps it: "we won't charge this fee more than four times in a year." A default fee carries no interest for 28 days from the date the customer is told about it, and the standard rate after that. Non-sterling transactions cost 2.99%, with the Barclaycard Rewards card the exception — its summary box records no non-sterling fee on purchases, a 0.00% cash transaction fee, no over-limit fee and no returned payment fee.

The minimum repayment, as published in the Amazon Barclaycard summary box dated July 2024, is the highest of £5, 1.00% of the balance, or 100% of the interest plus 100% of any default fees plus 1.00% of the rest. Payments are applied to the highest-rate balance first. The same document shows how the interest rate is actually quoted: a simple rate of 25.65% against a compound equivalent of 28.9%, with 2.1375% as the monthly figure — the number that decides what lands on a statement.

sections.heading: Four rules the regulator wrote for cards and nothing else
sections.html:
Credit cards have their own chapter of post-contract rules in the FCA's Consumer Credit sourcebook, and they are worth knowing because they are entitlements rather than features. CONC 6.7.4R, in its current form from 1 October 2021, requires that a firm "must first allocate a repayment to the debt subject to the highest rate of interest" — which is why a Platinum cardholder who spends on a 0% transfer card still sees overpayments attack the 24.9% purchase balance first rather than the 0% one.

CONC 6.7.8R, from 19 March 2019, requires firms to let a customer "reduce or decline offers to increase the credit limit" at any time, and to decline receiving such offers altogether. CONC 6.7.7R, from 19 December 2018, goes further and stops a firm raising a limit at all where the customer has asked for no increases or is at risk of financial difficulties. Both are opt-outs a cardholder has to exercise; neither happens by default.

The fourth is the persistent debt regime. CONC 6.7.27R, also from 19 December 2018, requires a monthly assessment of whether a customer has paid more in interest and charges than principal over the preceding 18 months, and CONC 6.7.30R and 6.7.31R set out what the firm must then do to help the balance come down without causing financial harm. On a card taken out for a 29-month transfer, the 18-month mark falls while the 0% is still running, which is exactly when the rule is most useful and least likely to be noticed.

sections.heading: Three Barclaycard pages, three different Platinum offers
sections.html:
Reading Barclaycard's own site on 5 October 2026 produced three incompatible descriptions of the same card family, and none of them is marked as superseded. The main card grid and the balance transfer landing page both listed four Platinum variants at 24.9% APR representative — up to 29 months at 3.45%, up to 21 months on purchases and transfers at 3.45%, up to 20 months at 1.99% and up to 12 months at 0%. A separate Platinum purchase-and-transfer page on the same domain gave 20.9% APR representative, 18 months at 0% on both purchases and transfers, and a 2.9% transfer fee. The Barclays-branded version of the range, on barclays.co.uk, offered a 30-month transfer card and two 22-month variants. The terms document for the mid-length offer refers to a 24-month promotional period.

The Rewards card has the same problem in a sharper form. The card grid listed it at 28.9% APR representative and the Barclaycard Rewards summary box agreed, at a 25.65% simple rate and a 28.9% compound equivalent. The dedicated Rewards product page, fetched twice on 5 October 2026, gave 22.9% APR representative and a 22.9% purchase rate, and still carried the line "Get an additional £25 cashback when you spend in the first month of receiving your card. Offer ends 6 March 2020." A page advertising a promotion that closed six and a half years ago is not a second set of terms; it is a page nobody has refreshed. The Forward card shows a milder version: 33.9% on the grid against 34.9% on the eligibility checker page.

The diagnosis matters more than the discrepancy. Where a summary box and a product page disagree, one of them is the regulated disclosure and the other is marketing. Here the summary boxes are current and internally consistent, and it is the product pages that have drifted. The practical consequence is that the eligibility checker — which returns a personalised result without touching the applicant's credit rating, and which on Barclaycard Forward gives a yes or no rather than a score — is the only statement of what any individual has actually been offered. On this range that is the step to take before believing a headline, not after.

sections.heading: The numbers Barclaycard keeps to itself
sections.html:
Three gaps are worth naming. Barclaycard's own UK complaints return could not be read on 5 October 2026: the pages holding it on home.barclays returned a 403 error on every attempt, as did the equivalent page on barclays.co.uk, so the January to June 2026 figures could not be quoted or checked. The complaints route itself is published clearly enough — 0800 151 0900 or 0333 200 9090, or PO Box 10200, LE18 9ER, with an update promised at four weeks, a final response after eight, and the Financial Ombudsman Service after that — but the volumes and uphold rates behind it were not readable from here.

Second, the acquiring figures above are the newest public ones and they are old: a report published in November 2021 on data from 2014 to 2018, with the firm-level splits redacted. Barclaycard publishes no current figure for merchants served or transactions processed anywhere a search reaches. Third, no ratings agency scores a credit card. Defaqto rates insurance rather than credit, and nothing independent publishes a star rating for a Barclaycard product, so the absence here is a gap in the market rather than a poor result for Barclaycard.

For context on the market the range sits in, UK Finance's Household Finance Review for the second quarter of 2026, published in September 2026, recorded that 47.3% of total card debt was interest-bearing in April 2026 — "the lowest figure on record" — rising slightly to 47.6% by June but remaining effectively at a record low. Slightly more than half of all card balances in the country are now carried by people who clear them every month and pay no interest at all. That is the figure that decides which half of this range makes sense for a given reader: the Platinum cards are built for the interest-bearing half, and the Rewards, Amazon and Avios cards only work for the other one.

pros: The longest 0% balance transfer on the range runs for up to 29 months, which is close to two and a half years of interest-free borrowing for a one-off 3.45% fee
Four Platinum variants let the borrower pick where the cost sits: 3.45% for up to 29 months, 1.99% for up to 20, or no fee at all for up to 12
The eligibility checker returns a result without affecting the applicant's credit rating, and on Barclaycard Forward a yes means approval subject to status rather than a score

A full summary box per card, published in HTML rather than buried in a PDF, giving the simple monthly rate, the compound equivalent, the minimum credit limit, the minimum repayment formula and the payment allocation order
Barclaycard Rewards charges no annual fee, no over-limit fee, no returned payment fee, a 0.00% cash transaction fee and nothing on non-sterling purchases, with 0.25% cashback on everyday spending
Payments are applied to the highest-rate balance first, which is a regulatory requirement under CONC 6.7.4R but is still set out plainly in each summary box
Barclaycard Avios Plus pays 25,000 Avios for £3,000 of spending in the first three months, which is five times the free Avios card's welcome bonus for three times the spend
cons: The 0% period is counted from the date the account is opened rather than the date the balance arrives, and transfers are allowed up to 60 days later — so an applicant who transfers late can lose two of the advertised 29 months before the balance has moved

Barclaycard's own pages disagree about its own rates. On 5 October 2026 the card grid listed Barclaycard Rewards at 28.9% APR representative while the dedicated Rewards page showed 22.9% and still advertised a £25 cashback offer that closed on 6 March 2020

The Platinum purchase-and-transfer page showed 20.9% APR representative with 18 months at 0% and a 2.9% fee, against 24.9% and 21 months at 3.45% for the equivalent card on the main grid, and 22 months on the Barclays-branded version of the same range
The group exclusion is wider than most issuers': it rules out transfers from any Barclays Group credit card or loan, and specifically names the Hilton Honors partnership card
Cash interest runs daily from the transaction date and is not cleared by paying the statement balance in full, which is the opposite of how the interest-free period works on purchases
The £20 monthly fee on Barclaycard Avios Plus only beats the free Avios card between about £10,000 and £20,000 of annual spending, because above £20,000 the free card earns its own upgrade voucher
Every representative APR on the range is quoted on an assumed £1,200 credit limit while the published minimum limits are far lower — £500 on the Amazon Barclaycard and £50 on Barclaycard Rewards

The newest public figure for Barclaycard's scale as a card acquirer comes from a 2021 regulatory report built on 2014 to 2018 data, and Barclaycard's own UK complaints return could not be read at all on 5 October 2026
verdict: Barclaycard is the strongest balance transfer shelf of the five big card issuers covered here, and the four Platinum variants are the reason: 3.45% for up to 29 months, 1.99% for up to 20, or nothing at all for up to 12 is a genuine choice rather than a single offer with a single price. The 1.99% card costs £59.70 on a £3,000 balance against £103.50 for the longer one, which works out cheaper per month of interest-free borrowing, and either beats the roughly £747 a year that 24.9% would cost on the same balance. Two things decide whether the headline applies to you. The 0% clock starts when the account opens, not when the balance lands, so the transfer wants doing in the first week rather than the sixtieth day; and nothing already inside Barclays Group can be moved across, loans included. The rewards end of the range is thinner. Avios Plus at £240 a year is only worth its fee in a narrow band of spending, the Rewards card's own product page has not been updated since an offer expired in March 2020, and the three different Platinum offers live on Barclaycard's site at once mean the eligibility checker, not the advertising, is the only reliable statement of what you have been offered.

faqs.q: How long do I have to make a balance transfer on a Barclaycard Platinum card?
faqs.a: Sixty days from the date the account is opened. Barclaycard's balance transfer pages state that transfers "must be made within 60 days" to get the 0% offer. The promotional period itself is counted "From the date you open your account", not from the date of the transfer, so a late transfer shortens the interest-free run. On an "up to 29 months" offer, transferring on day 59 leaves roughly 27 months.

faqs.q: Can I move a balance from a Barclays credit card or loan to a Barclaycard?
faqs.a: No. Barclaycard states that it "can't accept transfers from other credit card or loan accounts held with Barclays Bank UK PLC or any other Barclays Group company. This includes our Partnership card – Hilton Honors." The exclusion covers loans as well as cards, and the balance transfer terms add that "you can't make a transfer to any other Barclaycard or our partner cards" either.

faqs.q: What does a 3.45% transfer fee cost in money?
faqs.a: On a £3,000 balance, £103.50, added to the balance so the amount repaid becomes £3,103.50. The 1.99% fee on the shorter card is £59.70 and the 12-month card has no fee. For comparison, carrying £3,000 at Barclaycard's 24.9% standard rate for a year costs in the region of £747, so £103.50 for up to 29 months at 0% is cheap borrowing even allowing for the fee.

faqs.q: Why is the representative APR on Barclaycard Avios Plus 80.1% when the purchase rate is 29.9%?
faqs.a: Because a representative APR has to include compulsory charges, and Avios Plus carries a £20 monthly fee — £240 a year on an assumed £1,200 credit limit. The free Barclaycard Avios card has the same 29.9% purchase rate and a 29.9% APR representative. The 50-point gap between the two cards is the fee, not the interest, so 80.1% is not what a borrower would pay on a balance.

faqs.q: Is Barclaycard's eligibility checker a full credit application?
faqs.a: No. Barclaycard states that using it "won't have any affect on your credit rating". On most cards it returns a score indicating the likelihood of approval; on Barclaycard Forward, "get a yes and you'll be approved (subject to status)". Given that Barclaycard's own product pages currently show conflicting rates and promotional lengths for the Platinum and Rewards cards, the checker is the more reliable statement of what an individual has been offered.

faqs.q: Does the interest-free period apply to cash withdrawals on a Barclaycard?
faqs.a: No. Cash interest is charged at 27.9% compound equivalent "daily, from the date we add the transaction to your account, until you've repaid your cash balance in full", and Barclaycard confirms this applies "even if you pay your total outstanding balance in full by your payment due date". There is also a transaction fee of £2.99 under £100 or 2.99% above it, and gambling transactions are charged as cash.

title: Barclays Mortgage Deals: 5.03% After Two Rate Rises in One Week
meta_title: Barclays Mortgages: 5.03% Fixed and £270k on Two Incomes
meta_description: Barclays repriced twice in the week to 2 October 2026. The rates, the £899 and £999 fees, and how Mortgage Boost turns £168,375 into £270,000.

headline.label: Lowest advertised fixed rate
headline.value: 5.03% — 5-year fixed, Barclays' repriced range effective 29 September 2026, replacing a 4.93% deal; the announcement did not state the LTV or product fee, and 62 further products were repriced upward on 2 October 2026

intro:
Barclays advanced £17.7bn of new mortgages in the first half of 2026, up from £15.4bn a year earlier, and its UK mortgage balances stood at £176.7bn on 30 June 2026 against £166.8bn twelve months before. Those are the bank's own interim figures, and everything on this page was checked on 5 October 2026.

The pricing has moved recently and in one direction. Barclays withdrew a market-leading 4.75% two-year fix and a 4.93% five-year fix on 29 September 2026, raising the two-year range by 30 basis points to 5.05% and the five-year to 5.03%, then repriced 62 further products upward on 2 October — its second increase inside a week. Across the ten biggest lenders, the average cheapest two-year remortgage fix moved from 4.68% at the start of September to 5.11% by the end of it. A rate anyone noted in August is no longer on sale.

What Barclays does better than most of the high street is lend against somebody else's money. Mortgage Boost puts a relative's income on the application without putting their name on the title deeds. Family Springboard was priced at 4.99% for 95% of a purchase price and 5.19% for the whole 100% in the June 2026 range. And since 8 April 2025 a council or housing association tenant exercising the Right to Buy can borrow the entire discounted price with no deposit of their own.

sections.heading: A year of repricing, rung by rung
sections.html:
Barclays reprices often, and the direction reversed in the autumn. Taking the bank's own announcements in order through 2026, the two-year fix at 60% loan to value with an £899 fee went from 3.57% to 3.65% on 5 February, to 4.25% on 19 March in a round that touched 62 residential products at once, down again to 4.30% on 19 June and to 4.25% on 10 July, before the September rises took the whole ladder past 5%.

The 9 July round was the deepest cut of the year: reductions of up to 0.66%, which took the fee-free two-year fix at 90% loan to value from 5.45% to 4.79%, the Green Home version of the same product from 5.35% to 4.69%, and the fee-free two-year fix at 95% loan to value to 5.11%. The 7 August round cut the ten-year fix at 60% loan to value with a £999 fee by a full 50 basis points, from 5.62% to 5.12%, and introduced a Great Escape three-year remortgage fix at 4.88% with a £50,000 minimum and a £2m maximum loan.

Then it turned. On 7 September the two-year fix at 90% loan to value with an £899 fee rose from 4.96% to 5.14%, the fee-free equivalent from 5.11% to 5.29%, the two-year at 95% from 5.35% to 5.53%, the three-year at 90% from 5.04% to 5.22%, the five-year at 90% from 4.85% to 5.03% and the five-year at 95% from 5.30% to 5.48%. Three weeks later the 4.75% and 4.93% headline deals went, and the 2 October round followed. David Hollingworth of L&C Mortgages put it down to rising funding costs and warned of more to come.

Bank Rate itself has not moved. The Monetary Policy Committee held at 3.75% on 17 September 2026 on a 6–3 vote, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill all preferring 4%, against August CPI of 3.1%. The next decision is 5 November 2026. Fixed rates are priced off swaps rather than Bank Rate, which is why Barclays could raise its range twice in a week with the base rate unchanged.

sections.heading: £37,500 of income, £270,000 of mortgage: the Mortgage Boost sum
sections.html:
Mortgage Boost is a joint borrower sole proprietor arrangement, and Barclays publishes the arithmetic rather than describing it. A buyer earning £37,500 with a £30,000 deposit could borrow a maximum of £168,375, enough for a £198,375 home. Add a parent earning the same £37,500 to the application and the maximum becomes £270,000, enough for a £300,000 home. That is £101,625 of extra borrowing, a rise of 60%, from a person who will not own a square foot of the property.

Run the two sums against income and something useful falls out. On one income Barclays stretched to 4.49 times earnings. On two it lent 3.6 times the combined £75,000 — a lower multiple, not a higher one, because the deposit stayed at £30,000 and the purchase price rose, pushing the loan to 90% of value. The booster's income buys a bigger loan; it does not buy a better income multiple. Anyone modelling a boost on the assumption that two incomes attract the same 4.49 times will be £68,000 out.

The obligations are real and worth reading before the call. Boosters are jointly and severally liable from completion, which means Barclays can pursue either party for the whole debt. Every booster is credit checked, the mortgage appears on their credit file, and each one has to take independent legal advice. Boosters are named on the mortgage and not on the deeds, so they carry the liability without the asset. Mortgage Boost also cannot be combined with Family Springboard, Right to Buy, the First Home Fund, Help to Buy Equity or the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme — it is one route or the other. Sian McIntyre, managing director of life moments at Barclays, framed the product around how much harder a first purchase has become; the mechanism is older than the framing, and the figures are the part to check.

sections.heading: The deposit somebody else puts up
sections.html:
Family Springboard is the other side of the same idea: instead of a relative's income, their savings. In the range Barclays announced on 19 June 2026 the five-year Springboard fix was 4.99% fee-free for 95% of the purchase price and 5.19% fee-free for the full 100%, cut from 5.32% and 5.54%. A 100% advance at 5.19% against a standard 95% five-year fix at 5.09% that same month is a 10 basis point premium for needing no deposit at all, which is a narrow gap by the standards of high loan-to-value lending.

The Right to Buy product, launched on 8 April 2025, is the most generous thing on the shelf and the least advertised. Barclays will lend up to 100% of the discounted price, provided that figure does not exceed 90% of the open market valuation, so the statutory discount does the work of a deposit. A tenant with a 40% discount is treated as having a 40% deposit and priced at 60% loan to value — the cheapest rung of the ladder rather than the dearest. Higher-value homes are capped more tightly, at 100% of the discounted price but no more than 80% of open market value, and the thresholds are published: houses valued at £640,000 or above and flats at £310,000 or above. Above those lines a deposit is still needed. Lee Chiswell, head of mortgages, described the point as removing the deposit barrier entirely, and on the published terms that is what it does for a tenant under the value caps.

Barclays is also lending at the top of the range far more than it was. Loans above 90% loan to value were 4.4% of new UK home lending in the first half of 2026, against 1.6% in the same period of 2025 — roughly £780m against £250m. Balances above 90% are now 2.1% of the book, up from 1.7% at December 2025.

sections.heading: What Premier status is worth, measured on one day
sections.html:
Barclays runs a Premier range alongside the core one, and the gap between them is measurable because both move in the same announcement. On 7 September 2026 the Premier five-year fix at 90% loan to value rose from 4.65% to 4.83% while the standard five-year at the same loan to value rose from 4.85% to 5.03%. That is a flat 20 basis point discount for Premier customers on identical terms. On a £250,000 loan over 25 years, 20 basis points is in the region of £27 a month.

Premier pricing shows up elsewhere in the range too. The two-year tracker Barclays introduced on 19 June 2026 at 3.99% with a £999 fee up to 60% loan to value was a Premier product, and in the 18 June round the Premier two-year fix at 75% loan to value was 4.47% against 4.50% for the standard product with an £899 fee. Existing borrowers have a third range again, the Existing Mortgage Customer Reward: on 7 August its two-year fix at 60% loan to value was 4.66% with a £999 fee, and its ten-year fix at 75% was 5.12% with a £749 fee — the lowest product fee in any Barclays range this year.

Barclays does not publish the Premier qualifying test on any page this review could read, so the income or balance needed to reach that 20 basis points could not be confirmed and is worth asking about before an application is built around it.

sections.heading: £177.8bn falls due by Christmas, and most of it will never be shopped
sections.html:
Barclays publishes an analysis of the CACI Mortgage Market Database, and the June 2026 edition, using data to March 2026, found £177.8bn of UK mortgages maturing in the second half of 2026 — £154.5bn residential, up 5.1% on 2025, and £23.3bn buy-to-let. December alone carries £38bn of residential maturities against £16.2bn in November. By region the residential total splits £33.6bn in London, £31.1bn in the South East, £18.5bn in the East of England, £9bn in Scotland and £2bn in Northern Ireland.

What happens to maturing loans is the single most revealing statistic in this market. UK Finance's half-year figures for 2026 show £143bn of internal product transfers against £41bn of external remortgaging — three and a half times as much money staying put as moving. Its December 2025 forecast put the full year at £261bn of product transfers against £77bn of remortgaging, and 2027 at £272bn against £80bn. Total gross lending was £145bn in the first half against a £300bn full-year forecast, of which £82bn was house purchase and £5bn buy-to-let.

A product transfer is also the one route where nobody has to look at the wider market. Under MCOB 4.8A.10R a lender can vary a rate on an execution-only basis provided there is no additional borrowing beyond fees and it shows the customer every product they are eligible for. MCOB 4.8A.14R then requires the firm to say plainly that it is not assessing suitability and that the customer loses the protections an advised sale carries. Those rules are a floor, not a recommendation: a borrower clicking through a switcher screen has been told, in terms, that nobody checked whether the deal suits them. Execution-only is barred outright for a statutory Right to Buy, for debt consolidation and for shared equity agreements under MCOB 4.8A.7R, and high net worth customers are exempted from parts of it under MCOB 4.8A.9R.

For scale, the Office for National Statistics put the average UK house price at £272,000 in June 2026, with annual growth of 2.0%, down from 3.0% in May: £293,000 in England, £213,000 in Wales, £195,000 in Scotland and £202,000 in Northern Ireland in the second quarter. A 10% deposit on the English average is £29,300, which is almost exactly the £30,000 in Barclays' own Mortgage Boost illustration.

sections.heading: Who is actually lending, and what the complaints record shows
sections.html:
The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676, company number 09740322, incorporated on 19 August 2015 and registered at 1 Churchill Place, London E14 5HP, with accounts to 31 December 2025 and SIC code 64191. That entity is the ring-fenced UK bank created out of the old Barclays Bank PLC, and it is the counterparty on a residential mortgage. The FCA's register is a JavaScript application that does not return firm data to an automated request, so the firm reference above was taken from a published FCA final notice rather than from the register; it is worth two minutes to check it yourself.

That final notice, dated 14 July 2025, fined Barclays Bank UK PLC £3,093,600 for breaches of Principle 3 and SYSC 6.1.1R over account opening checks for WealthTek. It concerns client money controls in another part of the bank, not mortgage lending, and it should not be read as evidence about either.

On complaints, the independent numbers are thinner than they look. The Financial Ombudsman Service received 53,600 new complaints in the quarter to 30 June 2026, upholding 26% of them — 30% once motor finance commission cases are stripped out. First charge residential mortgages accounted for 1,291 of those complaints with 26% upheld, buy-to-let 153 at 21% and lifetime mortgages 71 at 13%. Mortgages are a quiet product at the Ombudsman compared with credit and motor finance, and that is worth saying plainly. The FCA's own aggregate data for the second half of 2025, published on 15 May 2026, recorded 1.74m complaints across financial services, with home finance falling 3.8% from 78,616 to 75,658.

Barclays publishes its own UK complaints return every six months, broken down by product group. The January to June 2026 page refuses automated access, so the home finance complaint count, the rate per 1,000 accounts, the eight-week closure rate and the uphold rate could not be read for this review. Those are the figures that would place Barclays against its peers, and they need confirming directly.

sections.heading: Four documents that would not open, and one rating that does not exist
sections.html:
A review is only as good as the paperwork behind it, so here is what could not be read. Barclays' own customer rate sheet, its intermediary residential and buy-to-let rate sheet dated 2 October 2026, its criteria and packaging guide and its complaints data pages all return a 403 to an automated request, and repeated attempts over the course of this review did not change that. Every Barclays rate quoted above therefore comes from the bank's own dated repricing announcements as carried by the mortgage trade press, not from a rate table and not from a comparison site. The live sheet may have moved again since 2 October.

Three specific gaps follow from that, and they matter more than the rates do. First, the follow-on rate: no Barclays page reachable for this review states what a fixed deal reverts to, or whether that rate is capped against Bank Rate. A lender whose reversion rate is capped at a stated margin and a lender whose reversion rate is uncapped are selling different products, and Barclays' answer could not be established. Second, the early repayment charge ladder: the percentage payable in each year of a two, five or ten-year fix was not readable, and on a ten-year product at 5.12% that is a material unknown. Third, the tariff of charges — telegraphic transfer, arrears visits, redemption administration — could not be verified either. Ask for all three in writing before you sign, and treat any figure you are quoted verbally as provisional.

On independent ratings, be clear which kind of absence this is. Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges at all, and Fairer Finance's mortgages customer-experience table returned "Sorry, there are no ratings to show here just yet" when checked on 5 October 2026. No rating exists to report, which is different from a poor one.

The credit signals in Barclays' own half-year numbers are mixed and belong here rather than higher up. Average loan to value on new lending held at 70%, but the whole book rose from 54% to 57%, lending above 90% loan to value nearly tripled as a share of new business, and the credit impairment charge rose from £237m to £338m year on year. None of that is alarming for a book of this size; all of it is the shape of a lender reaching further up the loan-to-value ladder, and a borrower at 95% should know they are part of that shift.

pros: Mortgage Boost adds a relative's income without putting them on the deeds, and Barclays publishes the worked figures: £168,375 becomes £270,000 on a second £37,500 income
Right to Buy tenants can borrow 100% of the discounted price with no deposit, and a 40% discount is priced as though it were a 40% deposit
Family Springboard was 4.99% at 95% loan to value and 5.19% at 100%, both fee-free, in the June 2026 range
Premier customers got a flat 20 basis point discount on the five-year 90% loan to value product in the 7 September 2026 repricing — 4.83% against 5.03%
Existing borrowers have their own range with the cheapest product fee seen all year, £749 on the ten-year fix at 75% loan to value
Barclays reprices frequently and publishes each change with the product, the loan to value and the fee, so the direction of travel is checkable
A ten-year fix at 60% loan to value was cut 50 basis points to 5.12% on 7 August 2026, which is a genuine long-term option few lenders price keenly
Green Home versions of the core products carried a visible discount, 4.69% against 4.79% on the two-year 90% loan to value fix in July 2026
cons: No Barclays page reachable for this review states the follow-on rate a fixed deal reverts to, or whether it is capped against Bank Rate — this needs confirming in writing before you commit
The early repayment charge ladder and the tariff of charges could not be verified, because the criteria guide and rate sheets refuse automated access; on a ten-year fix that is a large unknown
Rates moved at least eight times in 2026 and twice in the week to 2 October, when 62 products were repriced upward; the 4.75% and 4.93% market-leading deals lasted weeks, not months
Mortgage Boost makes a booster jointly and severally liable for the whole debt, puts the mortgage on their credit file and gives them no share of the property
Two incomes did not attract a better income multiple in Barclays' own illustration: 4.49 times on one income fell to 3.6 times on the combined £75,000
Mortgage Boost cannot be combined with Family Springboard, Right to Buy, the First Home Fund, Help to Buy Equity or the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme
Barclays' own half-yearly complaints return, which would show the home finance uphold rate, could not be read, so there is no provider-published complaints figure on this page
No independent rating exists to cite: Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges and Fairer Finance's mortgage table was empty on 5 October 2026
verdict: Barclays is at its most useful when a borrower needs somebody else's income or somebody else's deposit. The Mortgage Boost figures are published rather than hinted at, the Right to Buy product prices a statutory discount as a deposit, and Family Springboard will lend the full purchase price for 20 basis points over its own 95% product. Against that, the rate position is unstable — two increases in the week to 2 October 2026, with the 4.75% two-year and 4.93% five-year headline deals withdrawn on 29 September — and the documents that would let a borrower price the whole deal rather than the first few years, the reversion rate and the early repayment charge ladder, are not readable from outside. Go to Barclays for what it will lend and on whose income; get the follow-on rate and the charge schedule in writing before you sign anything.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest Barclays mortgage rate right now?
faqs.a: The most recent figure that can be verified from Barclays' own announcement is 5.03% on the five-year fix, effective 29 September 2026, replacing a 4.93% deal; the two-year equivalent went to 5.05%. Barclays then repriced 62 further products upward on 2 October 2026 without publishing the individual rates, and its own rate sheet refuses automated access, so treat 5.03% as a floor rather than today's number and ask for the current sheet.

faqs.q: How much more can Mortgage Boost let me borrow?
faqs.a: On Barclays' own illustration, a buyer earning £37,500 with a £30,000 deposit could borrow £168,375. Adding one person earning another £37,500 took that to £270,000 — £101,625 more, a rise of 60%. The booster is named on the mortgage, not on the title deeds, is jointly and severally liable for the whole balance, is credit checked, has the mortgage recorded on their credit file and must take independent legal advice.

faqs.q: Can I get a Barclays mortgage with no deposit?
faqs.a: In two situations. Family Springboard was priced at 5.19% fee-free for 100% of the purchase price in the June 2026 range, with a helper's savings standing behind it. And since 8 April 2025 a Right to Buy tenant can borrow 100% of the discounted price, capped at 90% of open market value, with the statutory discount doing the work of a deposit — though homes valued at £640,000 or more, or flats at £310,000 or more, are capped at 80% of open market value and still need a deposit.

faqs.q: Is it worth switching to a new Barclays deal or remortgaging elsewhere?
faqs.a: UK Finance recorded £143bn of internal product transfers against £41bn of external remortgaging in the first half of 2026, so most borrowers stay. An internal switch is quick and, under MCOB 4.8A.10R, can be done execution-only with no additional borrowing — but MCOB 4.8A.14R means the lender has told you it is not assessing whether the deal suits you. With £177.8bn of UK mortgages maturing in the second half of 2026 and £38bn of it in December alone, it is worth at least pricing the external market before accepting the switcher screen.

faqs.q: Who regulates Barclays mortgages and where do I complain?
faqs.a: The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676, authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority. Complain to Barclays first; if you are not satisfied, or eight weeks pass, you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which upheld 26% of the 1,291 first charge residential mortgage complaints it received in the quarter to 30 June 2026.

title: Barclays Personal Loan: the Rate You Only See Once You Bank There
meta_title: Barclays Personal Loan: 6.5% APR and the Account It Needs
meta_description: Barclays lends up to £50,000, shows a personal rate with no credit-score hit, and charges 30 days' interest to settle early. Rates, rules and the catch.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 6.5% APR representative — Greener Home Loan, £7,500 to £15,000 over 2 to 5 years, up to £250 cashback

key_facts.label: Lender
key_facts.value: Barclays Bank UK PLC, FCA firm reference 759676

key_facts.label: Maximum advance
key_facts.value: £50,000, over terms up to 5 years — or up to 10 years for “selected existing customers”

key_facts.label: Who can get a rate
key_facts.value: Holders of a Barclays current account or Barclaycard, with Online Banking or the app

key_facts.label: Early settlement charge
key_facts.value: A fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount repaid; the 2004 regulations allow up to 58

key_facts.label: Price guarantee
key_facts.value: Beat a like-for-like APR within 30 days of signing and Barclays drops the rate to match

key_facts.label: Scale
key_facts.value: Barclays UK held £220.8bn of loans and advances to customers at 30 June 2026

intro:
A Barclays personal loan is one of the few you can price before you commit to anything: the bank shows most of its own current account holders a personal rate inside the app, and the one headline it publishes on its open pages is 6.5% APR representative on £7,500 to £15,000 over two to five years for the Greener Home Loan, which also pays up to £250 cashback. Figures checked on 13 September 2026 against barclays.co.uk.

Barclays lends up to £50,000, normally over terms of one to five years and “up to 10 years for selected existing customers”. The quote is the selling point and the bank says so in its own words: “With some lenders, you won't know your actual rate until you've applied. And if you're not happy with the APR you're offered, your credit rating could still be affected even if you don't take out the loan. We're different – in many cases we can give you a personalised price quote up front, with no impact on your credit score.” Settle the loan early and the charge is “a fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying”, which is a good deal less than the law lets a lender take. There is also a price guarantee: find a like-for-like unsecured loan at a lower APR within 30 days of signing and Barclays will “reduce the interest rate to produce an APR equal to the competing offer”.

The condition is that you already bank there. The provisional offer and the personal rate are for people who hold “a current account with us” — the car loan page also accepts a Barclaycard — together with Online Banking or Barclays Mobile Banking. Somebody arriving from a comparison page with neither cannot obtain a Barclays rate at all, and on five separate Barclays loan pages read on 13 September 2026 the representative example was served with its numbers missing, so there is no published rate to fall back on either. That is worth knowing before you spend a click on it.

sections.heading: What the 6.5% covers, and what the open pages leave blank
sections.html:
The Greener Home Loan rate is tied to a narrow slice of the product. Barclays sets it out as “6.5% APR Representative on loans of £7,500 - £15,000 over 2-5 years, (your rate may differ*)”, and you only reach it by selecting “Greener home” as the purpose in the application. Borrow £2,000, or borrow £40,000, or spread it over a single year, and that figure tells you nothing.

For the ordinary Barclayloan the picture is thinner still. On barclays.co.uk/loans, /loans/personal, /loans/calculator, /loans/home-improvement-loan and the Premier Barclayloan page, the representative APR was served as “0 APR Representative on loans of 0 over 2-5 years” and the example beneath it read “APR Representative based on a loan of repayable over months at an interest rate of pa (fixed). Monthly repayment of. Total amount payable.” The figures are plainly injected by the page's own scripts rather than absent from the product, and a shopper using an ordinary browser may well see them fill in — but they are not in the page as delivered, and no Barclays page that could be opened on 13 September 2026 stated the standard representative APR, the minimum advance or the maximum rate. Treat that as unestablished rather than as a gap in the product, and ask for the number before you apply.

One line on the loan calculator is worth keeping whichever rate you are shown: “The representative APRs shown are based on all loan applications made by Barclays customers.” A representative APR has to be available to at least 51% of the people who take the advertised product under CONC 3.5, so the other 49% can be charged more. Barclays repeats the point itself — “A representative APR is the rate that most people will get, but yours could be different” — and adds that the rate offered “will be based on your personal circumstances, the loan amount and the repayment term”.

sections.heading: The document the law promises you, and the moment it arrives
sections.html:
Every regulated loan in Britain comes with a standard disclosure form, and most borrowers have never heard of it. The Consumer Credit (Disclosure of Information) Regulations 2010 were made on 28 March 2010 and came into force on 30 April 2010. Regulation 3(2) says that “In good time before the agreement is made, the creditor must disclose to the debtor, in the manner set out in regulation 8, the pre-contract credit information”, and regulation 8(1) says that information “must be disclosed by means of the form contained in Schedule 1”. Schedule 1 is headed Pre-contract credit information (Standard European Consumer Credit Information), and it is the one place a borrower sees the rate, the total amount payable, the duration, the charges and the early settlement terms set out to a fixed pattern that can be laid alongside another lender's.

The timing matters as much as the content. “In good time before the agreement is made” is not the same as before you apply: it lands inside the application journey, once Barclays has decided what to charge you. So the comparison the form was designed to make possible happens at the point you are most committed, and on a product where the public pages carry no rate table it is the first document with real numbers on it. Barclays publishes no specimen version of it for a personal loan that could be found on 13 September 2026, and the full terms of its price guarantee, linked from the loan page as “See our full price guarantee terms and conditions”, would not open from here either. Neither absence is proof that the documents are hard to get once you are in the application; both mean you cannot read them first.

sections.heading: A soft search now, a hard one later
sections.html:
The no-impact quote is real, and it is worth understanding what it does and does not settle. A quotation search leaves a footprint only you can see; the full application leaves one every other lender can. Between the two sits the assessment the FCA requires, and the rules are more demanding than most people expect.

CONC 5.2A.4R obliges a firm to carry out a creditworthiness assessment before entering into a regulated credit agreement or significantly increasing the credit provided. CONC 5.2A.10R makes the firm weigh two different things: “the risk that the customer will not make repayments under the agreement by their due dates (credit risk)” and the risk to the customer of not being able to make them at all. CONC 5.2A.12R(5) puts it in the borrower's terms — the question is whether repayments can be made “without the repayments having a significant adverse impact on the customer's financial situation”. CONC 5.2A.14R stops the lender counting any guarantee, indemnity or security when it judges that second risk. All four have carried the date 1 November 2018 since the affordability rules were rewritten.

The practical effect on this particular loan is that Barclays is assessing you partly from data it already holds. Your salary credits, your standing orders and your overdraft behaviour are all in the same bank, which is one honest explanation for why the personalised quote can be produced without a credit search, and why the product is closed to people who do not bank there. Barclays states the residual risk plainly: “All loans are subject to status” and “Not everyone can apply for a Barclayloan...certain restrictions apply.”

sections.heading: Clearing it early, and the price of borrowing more
sections.html:
“You have the right to repay your loan early, in part or full, at any time,” says the loan page, and that right comes from section 94 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 rather than from Barclays. What varies between lenders is the compensation they take for it. Barclays charges “a fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying”. Under the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004, regulation 5 puts the settlement date 28 days after the borrower's notice and regulation 6 lets the creditor push it back by a further 30 on an agreement running more than a year, and most mainstream lenders take the whole 58. Barclays taking 30 is roughly half the industry maximum, and on a £10,000 balance at a mid-single-digit rate that is a difference of tens of pounds rather than hundreds — small, but in the borrower's favour and rarely mentioned.

The same fee is where a top-up quietly costs money. Borrow more from Barclays and it does not add a second agreement: “we set up a new loan for the remaining balance plus the extra amount you want to borrow” and pay off the first one, which means the 30 days' interest falls due on the loan being settled. The bank also warns that “the new loan may have a different interest rate from your initial loan”, so a top-up can reprice the original borrowing at whatever the bank is charging on the day. The combined ceiling is £50,000. Anyone with a cheap existing loan and a small extra need should price a separate borrowing route before rolling the two together.

sections.heading: Who the money actually comes from
sections.html:
The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676 — the ring-fenced retail bank, a different authorised entity from Barclays Bank PLC (122702), which houses the investment bank. Barclays UK reported £220.8bn of loans and advances to customers at amortised cost and £245.6bn of customer deposits at 30 June 2026, with £1,767m of profit before tax for the half year, a net interest margin of 3.70%, a return on average allocated tangible equity of 20.1% and 14.1 million digitally active customers excluding Tesco Bank.

The regulator has been in the file twice in recent years. On 16 July 2025 the FCA fined the group £42m over financial crime risk management, split as £3,093,600 against Barclays Bank UK PLC — reduced from £4,419,500 — and £39,314,700 against Barclays Bank PLC, reduced from £56,163,900; Barclays also agreed a voluntary payment of £6.3m to WealthTek clients facing a shortfall. The older penalty is the one that bears directly on a loan, and it is in the next section.

A borrower's protections are worth stating precisely, because one of them does not exist here. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers deposits, not borrowing; being a Barclays depositor changes nothing about a Barclays loan. What you do get is the Financial Ombudsman Service, free to use, whose decisions bind the bank if you accept them — and which has already been asked about this product.

sections.heading: If the payments stop
sections.html:
This is the part of a loan page most lenders would rather nobody read, and it is where Barclays has history. On 15 December 2020 the FCA fined Barclays Bank UK PLC, Barclays Bank PLC and Clydesdale Financial Services Limited £26,000,000 for failures in the treatment of customers in financial difficulty between April 2014 and December 2018, affecting at least 1,530,000 customer accounts. The penalty carried a 30% settlement discount from £37,223,500, breached Principles 3 and 6, and followed more than £273m of redress paid since 2017. Mark Steward, then the FCA's Executive Director of Enforcement and Market Oversight, said that “[c]onsumers should feel reassured that their lender will work with them to help resolve any financial difficulties”.

The rules he was enforcing are in CONC 7 and they are short enough to quote. CONC 7.3.4R: “A firm must treat customers in or approaching arrears or in default with forbearance and due consideration.” CONC 7.3.5BR requires a firm to “take all reasonable steps to ensure that any repayment arrangements agreed with customers are sustainable”. CONC 7.3.9R forbids a policy of refusing to negotiate with a customer developing a repayment plan; CONC 7.3.10R forbids pressing a customer to clear the debt in one or very few payments, within an unreasonably short time, or by selling property or borrowing more; CONC 7.3.11R requires the lender to suspend active pursuit of the debt for a reasonable period while a plan is being worked out. Those are entitlements, not favours, and they are worth naming on the phone.

Barclays' own support pages are a mixed picture. The dedicated page for a customer struggling with a Barclayloan or overdraft would not open on 13 September 2026, which may be a fetching problem rather than a broken link. The general money-worries page did open, and it still points readers at “The Money Advice Service” — a brand that stopped existing on 30 June 2021, when the Money and Pensions Service folded it together with The Pensions Advisory Service and Pension Wise into MoneyHelper. The same page still carries the line “Check the government site for the latest advice and support on the coronavirus.” StepChange, the other organisation it names, is very much still there and still free.

sections.heading: The price guarantee, as an ombudsman read it
sections.html:
Matching a rival's APR is an unusual promise and it deserves testing rather than repeating. The Financial Ombudsman Service has published a decision on exactly this, reference DRN8017479, decided by ombudsman Rebecca Connelley against Barclays Bank Plc. A customer had applied for a loan elsewhere at a lower rate and expected Barclays to match it. The ombudsman found the bank had been entitled to insist on an actual loan agreement from the other lender rather than a completed application form, and declined to order the lower rate; the bank was told to pay £50 for distress and inconvenience because there was “enough evidence to conclude that the bank misrepresented the price match promotion”.

Read alongside the promise itself, that decision is the instruction manual. The claim window is 30 days from the date the Barclayloan agreement was signed, the comparison has to be like-for-like and unsecured, and the evidence has to be a real agreement rather than an indicative quote or a submitted application. Which means anyone intending to rely on the guarantee has to take out a second loan agreement, with a second lender, inside a month of taking the first — a sequence with real consequences for a credit file. The remedy if it works is a rate cut and recalculated monthly repayments, not a refund.

sections.heading: Where unsecured lending sits this year
sections.html:
The Bank of England's Credit Conditions Survey for 2026 Q2, published on 2 July 2026 and covering the three months to end-May, found that lenders reported the availability of unsecured credit to households increased in the quarter and expected it to decrease in Q3. Demand for unsecured lending other than credit cards rose and was expected to fall back. Lenders also reported that default rates for total unsecured lending increased in Q2 and were expected to increase again in Q3, while overall unsecured lending spreads narrowed and were expected to narrow further. A market where spreads are tightening and defaults are rising is one where a lender with a captive, well-understood customer base can price more finely than one buying applications from a comparison table — which is the commercial logic behind Barclays keeping this product inside its own banking app.

Independent scoring is thin on credit products. Defaqto rates insurance, not lending, so there is no star rating or ribbon to point at on any personal loan. Smart Money People, which does cover credit, lists the Barclays personal loan at 4.51 out of 5 from 108 individual reviews — against 4.31 from 4,963 for the current account, 3.44 from 95 for the fixed rate mortgage and 4.06 from 12 for car finance. No “last reviewed” date is shown for any of them, so treat the loan score as a modest sample of unknown vintage rather than a verdict.

pros: A personal rate before you apply, with no credit search and no mark on your file
Early settlement costs 30 days' interest, against a statutory maximum of 58
Up to £50,000, and terms of up to 10 years for selected existing customers
A price guarantee that cuts your rate to match a cheaper like-for-like loan within 30 days of signing
6.5% APR representative with up to £250 cashback on the Greener Home Loan, at £7,500 to £15,000 over two to five years
A large, well-capitalised ring-fenced lender: £220.8bn of loans and £245.6bn of deposits at 30 June 2026
cons: No rate for anyone who does not already hold a Barclays current account or Barclaycard, so most people arriving from a comparison page cannot be quoted at all

On five Barclays loan pages read on 13 September 2026 the representative example was served with its figures missing, and no standard representative APR, minimum advance or maximum rate could be established from any page that opened

The Standard European Consumer Credit Information required by the 2010 Regulations arrives inside the application, so the one document built for comparing lenders reaches you after Barclays has priced you
The full price guarantee terms would not open, and a published ombudsman decision shows the bar is a signed agreement from another lender within 30 days, not a quote
A £26m FCA penalty in December 2020 for the treatment of customers in financial difficulty, covering at least 1,530,000 accounts between April 2014 and December 2018
A top-up settles the existing loan, triggering the 30 days' interest charge and repricing the original balance at the current rate
The money-worries page still signposts the Money Advice Service, retired on 30 June 2021, and still carries coronavirus guidance
verdict: For somebody who already banks with Barclays, this is one of the least stressful ways to borrow: a real rate on screen before any credit search, up to £50,000, a 30-day price guarantee and an early settlement charge at roughly half what the regulations permit. For everybody else it is close to unquotable, because the personal rate lives behind the app and the published pages carry a representative example with no numbers in it. Open the pre-contract credit information the moment it appears in the application, check the APR and the total amount payable against a rate you have been offered elsewhere, and remember that the guarantee needs a rival's signed agreement rather than a screenshot.

faqs.q: Can I get a Barclays loan without banking with Barclays?
faqs.a: Not on the same terms. The provisional offer and the personalised quote are described as being for people who hold “a current account with us” plus Online Banking or Barclays Mobile Banking, and the car loan page also accepts a Barclaycard account. Barclays states that “[n]ot everyone can apply for a Barclayloan” and that all loans are subject to status. If you hold neither account, expect to open one first or to borrow elsewhere.

faqs.q: What does it cost to pay a Barclays loan off early?
faqs.a: “A fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying”, on top of the interest already due. Section 94 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 gives you the right to settle at any time, in part or in full, and the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004 let a lender charge for up to 58 days. Barclays taking 30 is at the cheaper end of the market.

faqs.q: How much can I borrow and for how long?
faqs.a: Up to £50,000 in total, including any existing Barclays loan you are topping up. Terms run to five years for most borrowers, and Barclays refers to terms “up to 10 years for selected existing customers” without publishing what makes a customer selected. The representative APR quoted on its pages is stated for loans over two to five years.

faqs.q: Will checking my rate hurt my credit score?
faqs.a: Barclays says it can give “a personalised price quote up front, with no impact on your credit score” in many cases. The full application is different and will leave a search other lenders can see. The assessment behind both is governed by CONC 5.2A, which requires the bank to weigh the risk of you not repaying against the risk that repaying would have “a significant adverse impact on the customer's financial situation”.

faqs.q: What happens if I cannot keep up the repayments?
faqs.a: CONC 7.3.4R requires Barclays to treat you “with forbearance and due consideration”, CONC 7.3.5BR requires any arrangement agreed to be sustainable, and CONC 7.3.11R requires the bank to suspend active pursuit of the debt for a reasonable period while you put a plan together. Missed payments will still reach your credit file. Free help is available from StepChange and from MoneyHelper, the service that replaced the Money Advice Service on 30 June 2021.

title: Branded Beauty Review: Clearance Prices on High Street Makeup Brands
meta_title: Branded Beauty Review: 99p Lipsticks, Free Post Over £25
meta_description: Branded Beauty sells L'Oréal, Maybelline and MAC as clearance stock from 49p. Prices, delivery, the 14-day returns rule and what to check on the box.

headline.label: Deepest verified discount
headline.value: 90% off — L'Oréal Color Riche lipstick at £0.99 against a £9.99 comparison price, checked 17 September 2026

intro:
Branded Beauty was selling a L'Oréal Color Riche lipstick at £0.99 against a £9.99 comparison price when we read its sale pages on 17 September 2026, and a Maybelline Baby Lips crayon at 49p against £2.99. Delivery is £2.99 by Royal Mail 48, free once a basket passes £25.

The shop is run by Branded Beauty Limited, a company registered at Companies House on 30 April 2013 under number 08509792 and trading from Unit 8 Trafalgar Business Centre on River Road in Barking. It stocks makeup, skincare, haircare, fragrance, nails, sun care and bath and body from names most people already own something by — L'Oréal, Maybelline, MAC, NYX, Revolution, Benefit, Clarins and Essie among them.

The prices come from what the stock is. Branded Beauty's own terms tell buyers that products "may have superficial and cosmetic markings" and that they accept "slight visual defects and/or clearance stickering" when they order. That is a clearance operation, stated plainly by the shop rather than discovered by a reviewer, and it is the whole explanation for a 99p L'Oréal lipstick. A reader expecting the boxed, shrink-wrapped item from a department store counter should know that before they click; a reader who only wants the contents of the tube has just found the cheapest route to it.
