sections.heading: What £4.52 a month buys, and what caps it
sections.html:
The smallest policy on sale is £1,000 of cover and the price British Seniors advertises against it is £4.52 a month for a non-smoker taking the plan out at 50. That is £54.24 over a year. The ceiling is set by age at the start date rather than by health: £10,000 is the most anyone aged 50 to 69 can take, dropping to £9,000 between 70 and 74 and £6,000 from 75 to 80. Nothing in the plan asks a single question about your health, your weight, your prescriptions or your family history, and nothing in it allows Aviva to decline you on those grounds.

What the plan does instead is postpone. For the first 12 months — the deferred period — Aviva will not pay the benefit amount for a death from natural causes. What it pays in that window is the premiums already collected, returned. From the first anniversary onwards the benefit is payable whatever the cause. That structure is standard for guaranteed acceptance cover and it is the price of not being asked anything, but it means the first year of a policy is not, in the ordinary sense, life cover at all unless the death is accidental.

Cover then continues for the rest of the policyholder's life. Premiums do not: they are payable only up to the policy anniversary on or following the life insured's 95th birthday, after which the cover stands with nothing further to pay. For somebody who buys at 50, that is a payment run of up to 45 years.

sections.heading: The name on the policy changed in January, and the reason goes back to 2024
sections.html:
The key facts document British Seniors served a year ago — version 4, dated November 2023 — named the insurer as AIG Life Limited, company 6367921, reference 473752. The current version, 4.2 and dated January 2026, names Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, company 3253947, reference 185896. That is the same book of business under a different insurer, and the chain behind it is public.

Aviva agreed to buy AIG's UK protection arm in September 2023 and completed the purchase on 9 April 2024 for £453 million, acquiring AIG Life Limited outright from Corebridge Financial. The company was renamed Aviva Protection UK Limited in February 2025. The policies then moved to their final home by a transfer under Part VII of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 — the court process that shifts insurance business from one authorised firm to another — covering roughly 2.5 million policies, sanctioned through the High Court of Justice in England and Wales with parallel proceedings in Jersey and Guernsey, with a transfer date of 31 December 2025.

Aviva's own customer material on the transfer records the Independent Expert's conclusion that it would have no adverse effect on the security of policyholder benefits or on service standards, that policy conditions, benefits and payments were unchanged, that access to the Financial Ombudsman Service and the FSCS continued, and that policyholders paid none of the cost. For a reader comparing plans in 2026 the practical upshot is short: the entity behind a British Seniors policy is now a mainstream UK life insurer with a very large protection book, and anyone holding an older British Seniors plan issued under the AIG name is in the same place.

sections.heading: Double for an accident, on a 90-day clock
sections.html:
Accidental death is the one benefit that pays from day one, and it pays twice the benefit amount — so £2,000 on the smallest policy and up to £20,000 on a £10,000 one. Most guaranteed acceptance plans pay the face amount for an accident in the first year and nothing more thereafter; paying a multiple, for the whole life of the policy, is the most commercially generous thing in this product.

The definition is tight and worth reading before relying on it. The document defines accidental death as death occurring as a direct result of an accident that took place while the life insured was covered, where death occurs within 90 days of the accident. An accident, in turn, means bodily injury caused directly and solely by accidental, violent and external means, and not self-inflicted. Two things follow. A fall in February that leads to a death in June is outside the clock even though the fall caused it. And a death from an illness that an accident triggered, rather than from the injury itself, will turn on that phrase "directly and solely".

After the first 12 months this matters much less, because the benefit amount is payable for any cause by then — the question becomes whether the estate receives the benefit or double it. Inside the first year it is the whole of the cover.

sections.heading: Paying until 95 for a sum fixed at 50
sections.html:
Take the advertised entry price and run it forward. At £4.52 a month a 50-year-old pays £54.24 a year for £1,000 of cover. Premiums equal the benefit after 18 years and 5 months — at roughly age 68 and a half. From that point the policy is paying out less than it has taken in, and it keeps taking in. Run the payments to the last one due, at the anniversary on or after 95, and the total is £2,440.80 paid for a £1,000 benefit.

That arithmetic is not a scandal and British Seniors does not hide the inputs — the premium is on the product page and the age-95 rule is in the key facts document, both in plain sight. It is simply the shape of the product. Guaranteed acceptance cover prices in the fact that nobody is screened, so the people who most want it are the people the price assumes. What the sum does establish is who the plan suits: someone who wants a fixed, modest, certain sum released quickly to an estate and who is not in a position to be medically underwritten, rather than someone in reasonable health buying the cheapest £1,000 of protection available to them.

The accidental death multiple changes the sum considerably. Against the doubled payout of £2,000, the same premium takes 36 years and 11 months to catch up — which is to say, on the cheapest policy, an accidental death at any point before about age 87 pays out more than has been paid in.

sections.heading: The increase option costs more than it adds
sections.html:
Cover of £1,000 agreed in 2026 is still £1,000 in 2046. British Seniors offers an Increasing Benefit Option against that, and the two rates inside it are not the same. The benefit rises by a fixed 3% of the initial benefit amount each year. The premium rises by a fixed 4.5% of the initial premium amount each year. The price of the cover therefore climbs half as fast again as the cover does, every year, for as long as the option runs.

On the advertised entry policy that looks like this. After 20 years of increases the benefit is £1,600 and the monthly premium is £8.59. At the outset, £1 of monthly premium was buying £221 of cover; after 20 years of increases the same £1 buys £186. Total premiums paid across those 20 years come to about £1,549, against £1,085 with the option declined throughout and a benefit still at £1,000.

Whether that is worth having depends on what the alternative is, and there is a real argument for it: a fixed sum does lose purchasing power, and no other mechanism inside this plan addresses that. The option can be declined in any given year, which is the sensible way to treat it — but three consecutive refusals remove the option from the policy permanently, so declining it twice and then a third time is a decision that cannot be revisited.

sections.heading: Reading the £135 gift card against the £4.52 premium
sections.html:
New policyholders are offered a £135 gift card, or £270 on a joint policy, redeemable with M&S, Tesco or Amazon. The qualifying rule is published, in the offer's own terms and on the product page: the card becomes available following the sixth successful monthly premium and once the total premiums paid exceeds the value of the card. Those are two conditions, not one, and on the cheapest advertised premium they fall a long way apart.

At £4.52 a month, six payments come to £27.12. Premiums paid do not exceed £135 until the 30th payment — £135.60, two and a half years in. For the £135 card to arrive at the six-month mark the premium has to be more than £22.50 a month; for the £270 joint card, more than £45 a month. The offer and the entry price are both true and they are not true of the same customer.

The rest of the terms are conventional and worth knowing. The policy must still be active when the card is issued, delivery is within 28 days of selection, the card must be selected within six months of becoming eligible, the offer is for new customers buying direct rather than through a comparison site, and it is administered by the Marketing Lounge Partnership. The terms carry the reference BSI-54 and a last-updated date of 1 September 2024.

sections.heading: What the regulator found about who gets paid on a plan like this
sections.html:
The Financial Conduct Authority published the interim report of its market study into how pure protection is sold — reference MS24/1.4 — in January 2026, and it is the most current independent reading of this corner of the market. It is not about British Seniors specifically, and none of the figures below are the firm's own, but they describe the product class this plan sits in.

Around 0.2 million whole of life policies were sold in 2024, mostly guaranteed acceptance over 50s plans, with about 36,000 of them medically underwritten. The claims ratio the regulator calculated for guaranteed acceptance over 50s cover was 52%, the second lowest of the six product types it measured and below whole of life at 66%, term assurance at 60% and accelerated critical illness at 59%. On distribution, guaranteed acceptance over 50s products pay the highest commission of any protection product as a proportion of premiums: lifetime commission runs from roughly 20% of projected premiums on critical illness up to 34% on guaranteed acceptance over 50s, with first-year commission generally between 170% and 250% of the premium. About 96% of commission is paid up front on the sale, with clawback periods that the report says have been moving from two years to four.

One structural point from the same report bears directly on how to use this page. 79% of guaranteed acceptance over 50s policies sold in 2024 went through single-tie arrangements — a seller offering one insurer's product and no other. British Seniors is exactly that: Aviva's plan, sold under British Seniors' name, with no panel behind it. There is nothing improper in the arrangement, and it is why the paperwork is simple and the price is quotable in seconds. It does mean that a British Seniors quote is a quote from one insurer, and comparing it is a job the reader has to do themselves.

sections.heading: Where the documents stop short
sections.html:
Three gaps are worth flagging. First, the key facts document publishes the benefit amounts but no minimum or maximum monthly premium — so a shopper can see that £1,000 to £10,000 of cover is available, and can see one advertised price of £4.52, but cannot work out what any other premium buys without going through the quote. Second, the pre-sale documents say nothing at all about what British Seniors earns for the sale, which is common across the market and is one of the things the FCA's market study is examining.

Third, on independent ratings: nothing on British Seniors' own pages gives this plan a Defaqto star rating, and the recognition the firm does put forward — a Platinum service award for a sixth consecutive year, and a ten-year service award dated 2024 — measures customer service rather than the policy's features. Fairer Finance maintains a page for the brand, but its ratings load by script and could not be read directly; anyone who wants that verdict should check it themselves rather than take it second-hand.

The exit terms deserve the same attention as the entry price. There is no cash-in value at any time, so a policy stopped in year 19 returns nothing at all. Two consecutive missed monthly premiums end the policy with no value — a harder rule than several competitors, some of which allow a longer grace period. Aviva may also cancel where it believes a claim to be false or fraudulent, where an incorrect date of birth was given at application, or where two consecutive premiums went unpaid. The 30-day cooling-off period from receipt of the documents is the only point at which money comes back in full.

Complaints go to British Seniors first, on 0800 542 7618 or service@britishseniors.co.uk, with an acknowledgement promised inside five working days. If it is unresolved after eight weeks, or the answer is unsatisfactory, the Financial Ombudsman Service takes it on 0800 023 4567 or 0300 123 9123, at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR. Both British Seniors and Aviva are covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme; in this class of business the FSCS would first look to move the policy to another insurer, preserving 100% of the benefits, rather than pay cash. And because the benefit is normally paid to the estate, it can fall inside inheritance tax — the key facts document says so, and points to writing the policy in trust as the way around it.

pros: Guaranteed acceptance between 50 and 80 with no medical and no health questions, so a condition that would price you out of underwritten cover is irrelevant here
Accidental death pays two times the benefit amount from the first day, up to £20,000 — more generous than the single payout most guaranteed acceptance plans offer
Cover advertised from £4.52 a month for £1,000 at age 50, and the premium is fixed unless you choose the Increasing Benefit Option
The policy is written by Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, firm reference 185896, one of the largest life insurers in the UK, with FSCS protection at 100% of the benefits
Premiums stop at the policy anniversary on or following age 95 while the cover itself continues for life
British Seniors says Aviva approved and paid 100% of British Seniors claims received in 2025 under the policy terms, and more than 200,000 people have held cover since 2012
The key facts document is current — version 4.2, January 2026 — and names both companies, both registration numbers and both firm references on its face
A 30-day cooling-off period from receipt of the documents, with all premiums refunded
A £135 gift card, or £270 on a joint policy, for new customers who buy direct
The Increasing Benefit Option can be declined in any year rather than being locked in at the outset
cons: The cheapest advertised premium and the headline gift card do not belong to the same customer: at £4.52 a month, six premiums total £27.12 and it takes 30 payments — £135.60, two and a half years — before premiums paid exceed the £135 card. The card arrives at the sixth premium only if the premium is above £22.50 a month, or £45 for the £270 joint version

Premiums run to the anniversary on or following age 95, which is 26 years past the point where a 50-year-old on the cheapest premium has paid in more than the benefit — £2,440.80 in total for a £1,000 payout if the policy runs its full course

The Increasing Benefit Option raises the premium by 4.5% of the initial amount a year against 3% for the benefit, so the cover bought by £1 of monthly premium falls from £221 to £186 over 20 years, and three consecutive refusals strip the option out permanently
Two consecutive missed monthly premiums end the policy with no value, there is no cash-in value at any point, and Aviva may cancel where an incorrect date of birth was given at application
The maximum benefit falls with age at entry — £10,000 at 50 to 69, £9,000 at 70 to 74 and £6,000 at 75 to 80 — so the applicants closest to claiming can buy the least cover
No minimum or maximum monthly premium is published anywhere in the key facts document, so beyond the single advertised £4.52 figure you cannot tell what a premium buys without completing a quote

No Defaqto rating for this plan appears on British Seniors' own pages; the awards it names measure service rather than the policy, and the Fairer Finance brand rating could not be read from a primary source and needs confirming

Nothing in the pre-sale documents states what British Seniors earns on the sale, while the FCA's January 2026 interim report puts lifetime commission on this product type at up to 34% of projected premiums, first-year commission at 170% to 250%, and the class claims ratio at 52%
For the first 12 months only accidental death pays the benefit, and it must follow within 90 days of an accident caused directly and solely by accidental, violent and external means
verdict: British Seniors does the thing it sells well: one product, one insurer, a price you can get in a couple of minutes, and a genuinely unusual accidental death benefit that pays double for the life of the policy rather than only in the first year. The move of the book to Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, completed by Part VII transfer on 31 December 2025, leaves a mainstream UK life insurer behind the promise. It suits someone who wants a modest, certain sum released to an estate and who cannot realistically be medically underwritten. It suits almost nobody else, because the sums are unforgiving at the bottom of the range — £2,440.80 of premiums for £1,000 of cover if a 50-year-old pays to 95 — and the increase option that is meant to answer that costs half as much again as it adds. Anyone in reasonable health should price underwritten cover first. Anyone taking this plan should read the gift card conditions before treating the £135 as part of the deal, and should be clear that a quote here is a quote from one insurer.

faqs.q: Who actually insures a British Seniors policy?
faqs.a: Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited, company 3253947, firm reference 185896, registered at Wellington Row, York YO90 1WR. British Seniors Insurance Agency is the seller — a trading name of Neilson Financial Services Limited, company 07986483, firm reference 594926, of 2 Windsor Dials, Arthur Road, Windsor SL4 1RS. Older documents named AIG Life Limited, which Aviva bought on 9 April 2024 and whose policies transferred to Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited on 31 December 2025.

faqs.q: What happens if I die in the first year?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. During the 12-month deferred period Aviva will not pay the benefit amount for a non-accidental death; it returns the premiums paid. An accidental death pays two times the benefit amount, provided the death follows within 90 days of the accident and the injury was caused directly and solely by accidental, violent and external means and was not self-inflicted.

faqs.q: How much cover can I buy?
faqs.a: A minimum of £1,000 and a maximum that depends on your age when the policy starts: £10,000 between 50 and 69, £9,000 between 70 and 74, and £6,000 between 75 and 80. British Seniors advertises £4.52 a month for £1,000 of cover for a 50-year-old non-smoker, but publishes no premium range for anything above that, so the only way to price a larger policy is to take a quote.

faqs.q: When do the premiums stop?
faqs.a: At the policy anniversary on or following the life insured's 95th birthday. The cover continues after that with nothing further to pay. Miss two consecutive monthly premiums before then and the policy ends with no value, and there is no cash-in value at any stage, so stopping payments means losing what has been paid in.

faqs.q: Is the £135 gift card automatic after six months?
faqs.a: No. Two conditions have to be met: six successful monthly premiums, and total premiums paid exceeding the value of the card. On the advertised £4.52 premium, six payments come to £27.12 and premiums do not pass £135 until the 30th payment. The premium needs to be above £22.50 a month for the £135 card to arrive at the sixth payment, or above £45 a month for the £270 joint card. The card must also be selected within six months of becoming eligible and arrives within 28 days of selection.

faqs.q: Can I complain if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: Yes. Take it to British Seniors first on 0800 542 7618 or service@britishseniors.co.uk; it undertakes to acknowledge inside five working days. If it is still unresolved after eight weeks, or you are unhappy with the answer, the Financial Ombudsman Service will look at it on 0800 023 4567 or 0300 123 9123, at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR. Both firms are covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

title: Brittany Ferries Ferry Tickets: Routes, Fares and the Rules Behind Them
meta_title: Brittany Ferries Review: Fares, Fees and Refund Rights
meta_description: Routes, fare types and small print for Brittany Ferries: what a crossing costs, what changing a booking costs, and the delay compensation you can claim.
intro:
Brittany Ferries runs the long Channel crossings — the overnight ones, the ones with a cabin and a restaurant, the ones that put you in Normandy or Brittany or northern Spain instead of at the wrong end of France with six hours of motorway still to drive. It was founded in 1972 by the Breton farmer Alexis Gourvennec and a group of his neighbours who wanted to get cauliflowers and artichokes to British supermarkets. Their first ship was a freighter named Kerisnel, after the village the cauliflowers came from, and the company describes itself as "officially born on a bleak New Year's Day in 1973". The unusual part is that the arrangement held: the operator's own history page states that "the Breton farming groups who founded the company remain its main shareholders to this day". Fifty-three years on it is a farmers' co-operative that happens to own a fleet of cruise ferries.

The scale is real. At its last full published results the company was running 12 ships on 14 maritime routes through 12 ports — Roscoff, Saint-Malo, Cherbourg, Caen, Le Havre, Plymouth, Portsmouth, Poole, Cork, Rosslare, Santander and Bilbao — with around 2,500 employees including 1,600 seafarers on a full-time equivalent basis. Five new vessels joined the fleet between 2019 and 2025, four of them LNG-powered. Fares are not the budget-airline sort, but they are lower than most people assume: on the Portsmouth to Santander route, a 24 to 32 hour crossing sailing three times a week aboard the flagship Pont-Aven, the operator's own October price guide starts at £265 for a car and passengers on the Saturday 08:45 Économie sailing, or £314 on a Cruise sailing with an inside four-berth cabin included. Portsmouth to Caen, which the company calls its most popular route, takes six to eight hours.

One thing to know before you plan a 2027 trip: the map is being redrawn. On 30 June 2026 the company announced that Portsmouth to Le Havre closes in October 2026 and Poole to Cherbourg in November 2026, with the 1992-built Barfleur and the 2007-built Cotentin both to be sold. A new daily Portsmouth to Cherbourg service replaces part of that, and from 1 November 2026 the Islander takes a triangular Portsmouth–Guernsey–Cherbourg rotation while the high-speed catamaran Voyager works Poole to Guernsey with an onward St Malo option. Bookings for that one opened on 6 August 2026 and run to 7 November 2027: the Voyager does up to 42 knots, carries 850 passengers and 280 cars, and reaches St Malo from Poole in six hours. If your usual sailing is one of the two being withdrawn, check the timetable before you book anything else.

key_facts.value: BAI SA (Roscoff), selling through B.A.I. (U.K.) Limited, company 01080495, Millbay, Plymouth PL1 3EW

key_facts.value: 12 ships, 14 routes, 12 ports across the UK, France, Spain and Ireland

key_facts.value: Early Bird (60+ days ahead), Standard, Flexi (free changes to four hours before sailing)

key_facts.label: Change fee
key_facts.value: £10/€10 extra to amend by phone what could be amended online; £25 on promotional fares

key_facts.value: Non-refundable on amendment as well as cancellation; balance due 60 days before sailing

key_facts.value: 25% or 50% of the ticket price under assimilated Regulation (EU) 1177/2010

sections.heading: The company on the ticket is not the company on the funnel
sections.html:
Two legal entities sit behind a British booking and the terms say so plainly. The carrier is BAI SA, registered at Port du Bloscon, CS 60 072, 29688 Roscoff Cedex in France. It sells here through "BAI UK Limited, a company registered in England and Wales under company number 01080495, and whose registered office is at Millbay, Plymouth, PL1 3EW", described in the booking conditions as its appointed sales agent. Companies House shows that firm as B.A.I. (U.K.), Limited, incorporated on 7 November 1972 — five weeks before the first ship sailed — active, private limited, filed under SIC codes 50100 for sea and coastal passenger water transport and 50200 for freight, with accounts last made up to 31 October 2025 and a confirmation statement dated 7 July 2026.

That split matters for one practical reason and it is a reassuring one. Although the carrier is French and the package holiday terms are issued by BAI SA in Roscoff, the ferry booking conditions state that they "and any dispute or claim in connection with your booking will be governed by the law of England". A British passenger arguing about a refund is arguing under English law with a Plymouth address to write to, which is not something every continental operator offers.

sections.heading: Three fare names, three quite different contracts
sections.html:
The ferry-only booking uses three ticket types and the differences are larger than the price gap suggests. Early Bird is "the cheapest fare, ideal if you're confident your travel plans will not change", and is only sold 60 or more days before departure. Standard is the middle option and allows amendment or cancellation "within certain conditions". Flexi carries the useful promise: "the freedom to make free amendments up until four hours before your outbound sailing". Four hours before a Portsmouth sailing is a genuinely late cut-off, and on a route where a sick child or a broken-down car is the usual reason for changing plans, it is the feature worth paying for.

Two rules cut across all three. Where the booking is made inside 60 days of the outward journey, "the full price will have to be paid at the time of booking for all ticket types" — so the deposit structure only exists for people booking well ahead. And the deposit itself, in the conditions' own words, "is always non-refundable in case of amendment and/or cancellation". Read that twice: not only cancelling but changing the booking forfeits the deposit, whatever the cancellation table says about the fee on top. There is a 24-hour cooling-off period in which you can decide you no longer want to continue, with a full refund, and a separate facility to hold a quoted price for 24 hours pending payment.

Promotional fares are a fourth category and they are the strict one. The promotional terms state flatly "This fare is non-refundable", set "an amendment fee on this promotional fare of £25" for any change plus any fare difference, require full card payment at booking, and add a trap that catches people every summer: "if the outward portion of any return itinerary is not used, we will cancel the return and no refunds will be paid". Miss the boat out and the boat back disappears with it.

sections.heading: What a late ship actually owes you
sections.html:
Ferry passengers have statutory rights that almost nobody claims, because almost nobody knows the numbers. They come from Regulation (EU) No 1177/2010 on the rights of passengers travelling by sea, which remains part of UK law after Brexit and is enforced here under the Merchant Shipping (Passengers' Rights) Regulations 2013. The trigger throughout is 90 minutes.

Article 17 says that once departure is delayed beyond that, the carrier must supply "snacks, meals or refreshments in reasonable relation to the waiting time" free of charge, and where an overnight stay becomes necessary must provide "adequate accommodation on board, or ashore" — with the cost of shore accommodation capped at €80 per night, for a maximum of three nights, transport to and from the port excluded. Article 18 gives the passenger a choice at the same 90-minute mark: re-routing "under comparable conditions, as set out in the transport contract, at the earliest opportunity and at no additional cost", or reimbursement of the ticket price, payable within seven days.

Article 19 is the money. Compensation of 25% of the ticket price becomes payable for an arrival delay of one hour on a scheduled journey of up to four hours, or two hours on a journey of more than four but not more than eight hours. Double those delays and the figure becomes 50%. On a six-hour Portsmouth to Caen sailing that means two hours late pays a quarter of the fare and four hours late pays half of it; on the 24-hour-plus Santander run the bands are longer again. The regulation does not reach the very short hops — Article 2 excludes services where "the distance of the overall passenger service is less than 500 metres, one way" or where the crew numbers no more than three — but every route on this network is comfortably inside it.

sections.heading: Injury, luggage and the unit nobody explains
sections.html:
Liability at sea runs on the 2002 Athens Convention, given effect through Regulation (EC) No 392/2009, and the operator publishes the limits on its own passengers' rights page. For death or personal injury caused by a shipping incident the carrier is liable up to 250,000 SDR without proof of fault and up to 400,000 SDR where fault or neglect is shown; for a non-shipping incident the ceiling is 400,000 SDR on proof of fault. Cabin luggage is covered to 2,250 SDR, vehicles to 12,700 SDR, and other luggage and valuables to 3,375 SDR. Mobility equipment sits outside the caps: under Article 4 the measure is replacement value or the cost of repair.

Two provisions in the same regulation are worth knowing because they work in the passenger's favour quickly. Article 6 requires an advance payment "within 15 days of the identification of the person entitled to damages" to cover immediate economic needs, with a floor in the UK version of £18,500 in the event of death — paid without any admission of liability and set off against whatever is eventually agreed. Article 7 obliges the carrier to give passengers comprehensible information about these rights at the point of sale and before departure, which is why the summary sits on the website at all rather than being buried in a claims file.

The SDR is the International Monetary Fund's Special Drawing Right, a basket unit whose sterling value moves daily. The operator's page prints the SDR figures and does not convert them, so a passenger reading it cannot tell from that page alone whether a suitcase is insured for four figures or five. As a rough guide the unit has traded well above £1 for years, which puts vehicle cover in the tens of thousands and the injury ceiling in the hundreds of thousands — but check the current rate rather than relying on that sentence.

sections.heading: Dogs, cabins and the €400 muzzle rule
sections.html:
The pet offer is the reason a large number of people choose this operator over flying at all. Animals travel in one of three ways — in your own car on the vehicle deck, in an onboard kennel, or in a pet-friendly cabin — and pet-friendly cabins are fitted on the cruise ferries including Pont-Aven, Armorique, Galicia, Normandie and Saint-Malo, in two-berth and four-berth, inside and outside, and in Commodore grade. A dog that would spend a flight in a cargo hold instead spends the night on the floor of your cabin.

The conditions attach a penalty to the one rule people forget. Non-compliance with the obligation to muzzle a dog "will incur a fine of €200 for the first offence", rising to €400 for repeated breaches. That is the operator's own charge rather than a French customs penalty, and it is easily the largest single number a pet owner is likely to meet on the crossing. Carry a muzzle even if your dog has never worn one.

Cabins are where the fare structure gets easier to compare than it looks. On the Spanish routes the cabin is bundled: the £314 October Cruise fare quoted above includes an inside four-berth with an occupancy discount, and a September sailing at £470 includes an inside two-berth. On the high-speed services the trade-off runs the other way — no cabins, and "luggage sizes in public areas on high-speed services are limited to 45cm", which is a cabin-bag rule rather than a ferry one and catches people who have packed for a car deck.

sections.heading: The border step that did not exist two years ago
sections.html:
Anyone who last took this crossing before autumn 2025 will meet something new. The European Union's Entry/Exit System started on 12 October 2025 and applies to British passport holders entering the Schengen area. Travellers are asked to give fingerprints and have a photograph taken at dedicated booths; the resulting digital record is valid for three years, so the slow version happens once and subsequent crossings are quicker.

Where it happens depends on the port, and the government's guidance — last updated on 10 April 2026 — is specific. At the Port of Dover and Eurotunnel, "any EES checks will be completed at the border, before you leave the UK", because French officers are stationed on this side. Passengers using other ferry ports complete the checks on arrival in the destination country instead. For a Portsmouth or Plymouth sailing that means the queue is at the far end, after a night at sea, rather than on the quayside at home. The system also counts your days: the total stay in the Schengen area must be no more than 90 days in every 180, which is the rule second-home owners in France and Spain have to watch.

The Irish routes are unaffected. The Republic of Ireland and Cyprus are outside the Schengen area, so EES does not apply to Cork or Rosslare sailings at all — a small but real advantage of the western network that nothing on the booking page tells you.

sections.heading: A ferry ticket carries far less protection than a holiday
sections.html:
This is the part that deserves reading before you decide how to book, because the difference between two purchases on the same website is substantial. Book a package — crossing plus hotel or gîte — and the organiser is BAI SA, which provides "full financial protection for our package holidays through a bond held with the Association of British Travel Agents" under ABTA membership Y6117, including refunds and repatriation if the company were to fail, as required by the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018. The package terms take a 10% deposit, want the balance at least 30 days before travel, and charge £25 for each change.

Book the ferry on its own and none of that attaches. A crossing is a single travel service, so it is not a package, so there is no insolvency protection, no bond and no repatriation promise; there is no ATOL cover either, because ATOL is the Civil Aviation Authority's flight-based scheme and no flight is involved. The ferry-only conditions say as much by omission — they state that if you have booked a ticket together with accommodation other than onboard accommodation, "these Booking Conditions will not apply", because you have bought the protected product instead.

There is no ombudsman either. Financial services have the Financial Ombudsman Service, telecoms have two Ofcom-approved adjudicators, and sea travel has neither. What it has instead is prosecution: the Merchant Shipping (Passengers' Rights) Regulations 2013 name the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as the designated enforcement body, and breaches of the assistance, re-routing and compensation articles carry "a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale" on summary conviction, with the more serious categories exposed to an unlimited fine on indictment. A fine paid to the court does nothing for the passenger. Your own route is the county court, and the deadline is tight: proceedings must be instituted "before the end of the period of six months beginning when the infringement complained of occurred", extendable by three months if conciliation is started inside that window. Six months is short. Diary it the day the crossing goes wrong.

sections.heading: Where the small print thins out
sections.html:
Three gaps are worth naming. The first is the weather exemption, and on the western Channel it is not theoretical. Article 20 disapplies both the assistance duty and the compensation entitlement where "the cancellation or delay is caused by weather conditions endangering the safe operation of the ship". A February gale in the Bay of Biscay is exactly the scenario in which a passenger most wants the 50% and exactly the scenario in which it is least likely to be paid. That is the law rather than the operator's choice, but it means the compensation right is worth less on this network than the percentages suggest.

The second is the £10 charge. The conditions provide that "an extra £10/€10 service charge will apply if you choose to make the amendment through our Contact Centre, where the amendment could have been made on our website". It is a small sum and a common policy, but it lands hardest on the customers least able to use the website, and nothing in the wording carves out a passenger who cannot manage the online journey.

The third is that no independent body rates ferry operators. Defaqto rates insurance products; Ofcom measures telecoms complaints; the national tourist boards assess accommodation. None of them reaches a shipping line, and there is no published acceptance rate, uphold rate or star band for any carrier on this network. The nearest thing to independent oversight is the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's safety role and the enforcement powers above, neither of which produces a score. Anyone comparing operators is comparing timetables, fares and documents — which is a reason to read the documents rather than the marketing.

pros: Long crossings that land you in Brittany, Normandy or northern Spain rather than at the Calais end of France
Still majority-owned by the Breton farming co-operatives that founded it in 1972
Flexi fares allow free changes up to four hours before the outbound sailing
Pet-friendly cabins across the cruise fleet, so a dog need not travel in a hold or a car
Cabin included in the headline fare on the Spanish routes, from £314 in October
Ferry booking conditions governed by English law with a Plymouth address to write to
Package holidays bonded with ABTA under membership Y6117
Irish routes fall outside the Schengen Entry/Exit System entirely
cons: The deposit is non-refundable when you amend a booking, not only when you cancel it — a date change costs money before any fee is added
Promotional fares cannot be refunded at all, cost £25 to change, and the return leg is cancelled outright with no refund if the outward leg goes unused
Two routes are being withdrawn: Portsmouth to Le Havre in October 2026 and Poole to Cherbourg in November 2026
Statutory delay compensation of 25% or 50% falls away where the delay is caused by weather endangering safe operation, which is the commonest cause of disruption on these routes
There is no ombudsman or ADR scheme for ferry travel: enforcement is by prosecution through the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, and a passenger's own claim must reach court within six months
A ferry-only ticket carries no ABTA bond, no insolvency protection and no ATOL cover, unlike the same company's package holidays
The Athens Convention limits are published in Special Drawing Rights with no sterling conversion anywhere on the page
Amending by telephone costs £10 more than doing the same thing online, with no exception for customers who cannot use the website
No ratings agency covers ferry operators, so there is no independent score for this carrier or any of its competitors
verdict: For a car, a dog and a fortnight in France or Spain, this is the operator whose product genuinely differs from the short-hop alternatives: a cabin, a restaurant, a night at sea and a landfall that saves several hundred miles of driving. Fares from £265 with a car are competitive once the fuel and the overnight stop you no longer need are counted. Buy the Flexi fare if there is any chance your plans move, because the four-hour amendment window is the best term on offer and the deposit on the cheaper fares does not come back even when you are only changing the date. Book the crossing and the accommodation together if you want ABTA protection, and check the 2027 timetable before assuming your usual sailing still exists.

faqs.q: What happens if my Brittany Ferries sailing is delayed or cancelled?
faqs.a: Past 90 minutes the carrier must provide refreshments and, where an overnight stay becomes necessary, accommodation costing up to €80 a night for up to three nights. You may choose re-routing at no extra cost or a refund of the fare within seven days. Arrival delays attract 25% of the ticket price at one hour on journeys up to four hours or two hours on journeys of four to eight hours, and 50% at double those figures — unless the delay was caused by weather endangering safe operation, in which case nothing is payable.

faqs.q: Is a Brittany Ferries ticket financially protected if the company fails?
faqs.a: A package holiday is: BAI SA holds an ABTA bond under membership Y6117 covering refunds and repatriation under the Package Travel Regulations 2018. A ferry-only crossing is a single travel service and therefore not a package, so it carries no bond, no insolvency protection and no ATOL cover. Paying by credit card gives separate protection on purchases above £100 under section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974; confirm the position with your own card issuer.

faqs.q: Can I change or cancel a Brittany Ferries booking?
faqs.a: It depends which fare you bought. Flexi allows free amendments up to four hours before the outbound sailing. Standard permits changes and cancellation within set conditions and a fee scale by notice period. Early Bird is the cheapest and the least forgiving, and promotional fares cannot be refunded at all and cost £25 to amend. In every case the deposit is stated to be non-refundable on amendment as well as cancellation, and amending by phone rather than online adds £10.

faqs.q: Do I need to register for the EU Entry/Exit System before sailing?
faqs.a: Registration happens at the border rather than in advance. The system began on 12 October 2025 and takes fingerprints and a photograph, creating a digital record valid for three years. At Dover and Eurotunnel the checks are done before you leave the UK; from other ferry ports, including Portsmouth and Plymouth, they are done on arrival in the destination country. Sailings to Cork and Rosslare are exempt because Ireland is outside the Schengen area.

faqs.q: How much can I claim if my luggage or car is damaged on the crossing?
faqs.a: The 2002 Athens Convention limits apply: 2,250 SDR for cabin luggage, 12,700 SDR for a vehicle and 3,375 SDR for other luggage and valuables, with personal injury covered to 250,000 SDR without proof of fault and 400,000 SDR where fault is shown. Mobility equipment is compensated at replacement or repair cost rather than under a cap. SDR is an IMF unit, so check the current sterling rate before assuming a figure.

faqs.q: Can my dog travel in the cabin with me?
faqs.a: Yes on the cruise ferries, which carry pet-friendly cabins in two-berth and four-berth, inside and outside, and in Commodore grade on ships including Pont-Aven, Armorique, Galicia, Normandie and Saint-Malo. Kennels and the option of leaving the animal in your vehicle are the alternatives. Bring a muzzle: the booking conditions impose a fine of €200 for a first breach of the muzzling obligation and €400 for repeat breaches.

title: BusinessMobiles.com Review: Business Contracts Across EE, O2, Vodafone and Three
meta_title: BusinessMobiles.com Review: All Four Networks, One Dealer
meta_description: An independent West London dealer selling EE, O2, Vodafone and Three business contracts since 1999. Prices, price rises, contract terms and the catches.
intro:
BusinessMobiles.com is a West London dealer that has been selling mobile contracts to UK companies since 1999 and now says it manages more than 20,000 business mobile lines. What makes it worth a look is the range: it sells EE, O2, Vodafone and Three from one order desk, which very few independents do, and it will quote a sole trader on a single line as readily as a company with fifty. Headline prices at the time of writing start at £1 a month for a business SIM, £16 a month for a Samsung handset deal, £14 a month for mobile broadband and £22 a month for a business laptop, with free next-working-day delivery to most of the UK and a sales line on 0800 999 2999 open 8.30am to 5.30pm on weekdays.

One number needs reading carefully before you compare anything. Every price on the site excludes VAT, and the site says so plainly: "Our prices always exclude VAT." A £16 business tariff is £19.20 leaving the bank account, so setting it against a £19 consumer deal is not the like-for-like comparison it looks like. If the business is VAT registered it reclaims the difference and the ex-VAT figure is the real one; if it is not, the inclusive price is what it pays.

The company is an official partner of all four networks rather than a reseller of one, it won EE's 2025 Business Growth Award for Partners, and it offers an early upgrade from six months into a contract on selected networks — a good deal earlier than most dealers will touch a handset. Contracts run 12, 24 or 36 months.

sections.heading: The name took three goes to arrive at
sections.html:
The trading story on the About page and the registry record agree on the year and differ on the detail, which is worth knowing if you are checking who you are dealing with. Companies House holds the firm as BUSINESSMOBILES.COM LTD, company number 03772025, incorporated on 17 May 1999 and active, at Suite 301, Boundary House, Boston Road, Hanwell, London W7 2QE, under SIC code 61200 — wireless telecommunications activities. Its last accounts were made up to 31 December 2024, the next are due by 30 September 2026, and the most recent confirmation statement was dated 16 May 2026.

The name changed three times before it settled. The company was incorporated as FAST FONES DIRECT LTD, became 31E CELLULAR OPERATIONS LIMITED on 24 May 2000, then 31E CELLULAR LIMITED on 13 July 2000, and finally took its present name on 17 January 2007. The About page tells the same story a year early — "In 2006, we became BusinessMobiles.com" — which is the sort of small drift that creeps into copy nobody has re-read for a while. The 1999 founding date, which is the part that matters, checks out exactly.

sections.heading: Buying as a business moves you outside the consumer rulebook
sections.html:
This is the fact that separates a business mobile purchase from the one a shopper makes, and almost nothing on any dealer's site explains it. The 14-day cancellation right people associate with buying online is a consumer right under the distance selling rules, and it does not follow a company that buys in its own name. Neither does the Consumer Rights Act 2015, whose 30-day short-term right to reject faulty goods is written for an individual acting for purposes wholly or mainly outside a trade or business. A limited company or a partnership buying handsets sits outside both.

Read that way, the return window in BusinessMobiles.com's own terms is a commercial concession rather than a legal minimum. The terms give "a 7-day right of return. The 7 days commencing on the date your order is activated or despatched, whichever is earlier". Seven days is half the consumer period and the clock can start at despatch rather than delivery, so a handset that spends two days in transit has five days left on arrival. That is still seven days more than the law obliges a business seller to give, and it is worth setting against dealers who give none.

Two charges sit alongside it. The customer pays the cost of return carriage, and an Incomplete Restocking Charge of £250 applies where a handset comes back without all of its parts. Keep the box, the cable and the paperwork.

sections.heading: Twelve, 24 or 36 months — and the longest one has a rule attached
sections.html:
The FAQ page puts contract length at "12, 24 or 36 months". The 12-month option is not a courtesy: Ofcom requires providers to offer at least one 12-month contract for each service, and that requirement covers business customers of any size. The 36-month option is the one that needs a question asked, because Ofcom's General Conditions cap the length of most small-business contracts at two years.

Condition C1.11 is explicit: "Regulated Providers shall not include a term in any contract, other than an Instalment Contract for a Physical Connection, with a Relevant Customer, that stipulates a Commitment Period of more than 24 months in duration." A Relevant Customer for that purpose covers consumers, microenterprise and small enterprise customers and not-for-profit organisations, unless the business has expressly agreed otherwise. So a 36-month term is available to larger companies, and to a small one only where it has knowingly signed away the cap. Nothing on the site says which of those applies to a given quote, and it is a fair thing to ask on the phone before you sign.

The same conditions give small business customers end-of-contract notifications and annual best-tariff information, so a company that stays put after its minimum term should be told, in writing, what it is paying and what it could pay instead.

sections.heading: The annual rise is pounds and pence on some tariffs and a percentage on others
sections.html:
Ofcom's statement of 19 July 2024 banned inflation-linked mid-contract increases, and from 17 January 2025 any rise written into a new contract has to be expressed in pounds and pence. The scope is wider than most coverage suggests. The statement applies the rules to services "purchased by residential customers, Microenterprise or Small Enterprise Customers and Not-For-Profit Customers" — small businesses are inside the protection, not outside it.

The catch is that a business tariff is not automatically a small-business tariff, and the networks this dealer sells are running several regimes at once. EE Business raises prices from 31 March each year: contracts taken between 2 September and 18 November 2024 go up by £3.00 a month across every plan type, while contracts from 19 November 2024 onwards go up by £3.00 on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM-only, tablet, laptop, watch and router plans. Anything signed before 2 September 2024 is still on the old CPI plus 3.9% formula.

Three Business steps its increase by tariff size each April — "Plans with an original Monthly Charge of £9.99 or less will increase by £0.50 per month. Plans from £10 to £20 will increase by £0.75 per month. Plans from £20.01 will increase by £1.50 per month" — but its Adapt and Dynamic plans are the exception and rise by 4.5% each April instead. Business broadband goes up £1.60 a month excluding VAT.

Vodafone Business is the clearest illustration that the pounds-and-pence rule has not reached every business bill. Contracts entered on or after 9 December 2020 are rising from 1 April 2026 by CPI of 3.4% plus 3.9%, a combined 7.3% — £1.61 a month on a £22 plan and £2.92 on a £40 one. Older contracts move with RPI at 4.2%, published on 21 January 2026. Vodafone's SOHO customers on contracts from 2 July 2024 get a fixed £1.50 excluding VAT instead, and contracts from 12 November 2025 rise by between £2.08 and £3.00. O2's business price page is built around RPI adjustments and offers a calculator rather than a published schedule; its figures load through JavaScript and could not be read directly, so the amount on an O2 business tariff needs confirming with the dealer.

The arithmetic is worth doing before you sign rather than after. Take the EE Business iPhone 17 deal the site lists at £33.00 a month excluding VAT on a 24-month term, bought in September. It runs seven months at £33.00, twelve at £36.00 and five at £39.00 — £858 across the term, against £792 if you simply multiply the headline by 24. That is £66 the advertised figure does not show, and £1,029.60 once VAT is added to what actually leaves the account.

sections.heading: One phone per employee, and the contract has to be in the company's name
sections.html:
The FAQ says a business contract "is also tax deductible", which is true and slightly undersells the mechanism. HMRC's guidance exempts a mobile phone provided to an employee from tax and from reporting entirely, but on conditions. The exemption applies where "you provide your employee with only one mobile phone or SIM card" and "the phone contract is between you and the supplier". A second handset for the same employee falls outside it, and so does a phone bought on the employee's own account and reimbursed. The exemption also does not apply where the phone comes through a salary sacrifice arrangement, which has to be reported.

That is the practical reason a company buys through a business channel rather than picking up a consumer deal in a shop. The contract has to be in the company's name for the exemption to work, and a dealer selling business tariffs puts it there as a matter of course. It is a genuine advantage of the route, and neither the FAQ nor any network page spells it out.

sections.heading: Who adjudicates a dispute depends on how many people you employ
sections.html:
Ofcom approves exactly two dispute schemes for telecoms: CISAS, the Communication and Internet Services Adjudication Scheme, and the Communications Ombudsman. Of the four networks on this site, O2, Vodafone and Three belong to CISAS while EE belongs to the Communications Ombudsman. Two companies buying the same kind of contract from the same dealer on the same day can end up in front of different adjudicators, depending only on which network they chose.

Eligibility is narrower than most buyers expect. Ofcom's own wording admits a residential customer, "a small business (up to 10 employees)" or a not-for-profit with up to ten working individuals, volunteers excluded. An eleven-person firm has no free adjudicator at all and is left with the courts. A complaint can be taken to the scheme once "it has been at least six weeks since you made the initial complaint", or straight away on a deadlock letter, which stays usable for 12 months.

None of that reaches the dealer itself. BusinessMobiles.com's terms route a dispute through negotiation, then mediation with LawBite, then arbitration if it is unresolved within 60 days. That is a private contractual ladder rather than an Ofcom-approved scheme, so a disagreement about what was promised at the point of sale — rather than about the network service — sits outside both CISAS and the Ombudsman. The terms also exclude liability for "loss of income, profit, business, data, contracts, goodwill or savings", while keeping responsibility for death or personal injury caused by negligence and for fraud.

sections.heading: Where the site's own numbers stop agreeing with each other
sections.html:
The savings claims are the weakest part of the site. The EE page leads on "Save 37% on Phone/SIM" and "over 30% off"; the Three page offers "Save over 20% on network prices". Neither page shows what the 37% or the 20% is measured against, over what term, or on which tariff. The CAP Code sets a clear standard for this: rule 3.34 requires that comparisons with identifiable competitors "objectively compare one or more material, relevant, verifiable and representative feature of those products", and CAP's guidance asks advertisers to signpost how a reader can check. The ASA has upheld against telecoms comparison claims on exactly that ground before, including Vodafone's "The UK's Best Network" in 2021, where the verification detail was there but out of reach. A dealer buying at trade prices very probably can beat a network's list price; publishing the comparison would make the claim worth more, not less.

Two of the company's own figures also disagree. The home page says 27 years of experience; the EE and Three pages both say 26 Years in Business. Counting from May 1999, 27 is right and the network pages are a year behind. The network awards quoted are also ageing: Three's Ookla "Fastest 5G Network" run is cited as five awards ending H1 2023, which is three years old, and predates the merger of Vodafone UK and Three UK.

There is no independent rating for a mobile dealer to fall back on. Ofcom's quarterly complaints data measures networks rather than the shops that sell them, there is no Defaqto equivalent for this trade, and the review score shown on the site is collected on the company's own behalf. The honest position is that the networks behind the contract are measured and the dealer in front of it is not.

pros: Sells all four UK networks — EE, O2, Vodafone and Three — from one order desk, which few independents do
No minimum number of lines: sole traders are quoted as readily as larger companies
Trading since 17 May 1999 under company 03772025, with a registry record that matches the founding date claimed
Early upgrade available from six months into a contract on selected networks, well ahead of the 10 to 40 day end-of-contract notification Ofcom requires
A 7-day right of return offered where the law gives a business buyer none
Prices start at £1 a month for a business SIM and £16 for a handset deal, with free next-working-day delivery to most of the UK
Named an EE Business Growth Award for Partners winner in 2025
cons: Savings claims of 37% on EE and over 20% on Three are published with nothing showing the comparison basis, which is the standard CAP Code rule 3.34 sets
The 7-day return window runs from activation or despatch rather than delivery, and a £250 Incomplete Restocking Charge applies if a handset comes back without all its parts
Disputes with the dealer go to LawBite mediation and then arbitration after 60 days, not to an Ofcom-approved scheme — and no free adjudicator exists at all for a business with more than 10 employees
A 36-month contract is offered without explaining that Ofcom's Condition C1.11 caps most small-business commitments at 24 months unless the customer expressly agrees otherwise
Annual price rises are not shown on the deal pages, and they vary sharply by network: £3.00 a month on an EE handset plan against 7.3% on many Vodafone business contracts from 1 April 2026
The company's own pages give its age as both 26 and 27 years, and the Three awards quoted were last won in H1 2023
verdict: A long-established West London dealer with a real advantage: it quotes all four networks, it takes single-line customers, and it puts the contract in the company's name, which is what HMRC's one-phone-per-employee exemption actually requires. The prices are ex-VAT and the advertised monthly figure is not the whole term — an EE Business plan at £33 a month costs £858 over 24 months once the 31 March increases land, not £792. Ring 0800 999 2999 and ask three things before signing: what the annual increase is in pounds for the tariff you are being quoted, whether the term offered is 12, 24 or 36 months and why, and which network's dispute scheme you would be using. The answers are all knowable and none of them are on the website.

faqs.q: Do the prices include VAT?
faqs.a: No. The site states that its prices always exclude VAT, so a £16 tariff is £19.20 including VAT at 20%. A VAT-registered business reclaims that; one below the registration threshold pays it. Comparing a business price against a consumer price without adding VAT first is not a like-for-like comparison.

faqs.q: Can a sole trader buy from BusinessMobiles.com?
faqs.a: Yes. Asked whether there is a minimum number of lines, the FAQ answers: "No. We are as passionate about serving our sole traders as we are about serving our corporates." Contracts run 12, 24 or 36 months.

faqs.q: What happens if the handset is faulty or I change my mind?
faqs.a: The terms give a 7-day right of return running from activation or despatch, whichever is earlier, with the customer paying return carriage and a £250 Incomplete Restocking Charge if parts are missing. The 14-day distance selling right and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 both apply to consumers rather than to a company buying in its own name, so this window is a commercial concession and not a statutory minimum.

faqs.q: Will my monthly price go up during the contract?
faqs.a: Almost certainly, and by an amount that depends on the network. EE Business raises prices each 31 March by £3.00 on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM-only and device plans taken from 19 November 2024. Three steps its April increase from £0.50 to £1.50 by tariff size, except Adapt and Dynamic plans which rise 4.5%. Many Vodafone business contracts rise by CPI plus 3.9% — 7.3% from 1 April 2026. Ask for the figure in pounds before signing.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: For a problem with the mobile service, the route runs through the network: EE is a member of the Communications Ombudsman, while O2, Vodafone and Three all belong to CISAS. You can escalate after six weeks, or immediately with a deadlock letter, if you are a business with up to 10 employees. For a dispute with the dealer itself, its terms use negotiation, then LawBite mediation, then arbitration after 60 days.

title: Carmoola Car Finance Review: Rates, Limits and What It Won't Fund
meta_title: Carmoola Car Finance: What 14.9% APR Really Buys You
meta_description: Carmoola lends direct with no dealer arranging the deal. Representative 14.9% APR, £2,000 to £40,000, used cars only. The rates, rules and gaps, checked.
intro:
Carmoola is a London car finance lender that does something almost nobody else in the market does: it lends its own money straight to the buyer, and the dealership plays no part in arranging the loan. You get a budget on your phone before you go shopping, pay the dealer with a Carmoola card, and the garage never touches the credit application. Carmoola Limited is company 12992987, incorporated on 3 November 2020 at 1 Whittlebury Mews West, Primrose Hill, London NW1 8HS, and is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference number 958057.

The headline is a representative 14.9% APR on hire purchase and PCP, borrowing from £2,000, with no deposit required and a £1 option-to-purchase fee at the end. On the site's own worked example, £12,500 over 60 months at 14.9% fixed costs £290 a month, £4,901 in interest and £17,401 in total. Approval takes 60 seconds for an indicative budget, most applicants are fully approved within one to two working days, and that budget then stays open for 30 days while you look.

One rule decides whether any of this is relevant to you. Carmoola funds used cars only, bought from one of the dealerships on its network — no vans, no motorbikes, no brand-new cars, and no private sales. Diesels must be registered from September 2015 onwards. If the car you have in mind is a van, a bike, a nearly-new registration or a Facebook Marketplace find, this is not the lender for it.
