sections.heading: What the panel's medical limits actually run to
sections.html:
A comparison page is only as good as the numbers it puts side by side, so here are two panel members' published tables rather than a summary of them. Post Office sells three levels: Economy carries £5 million of emergency medical cover with a £125 excess, £1,000 of cancellation and £1,500 of baggage; Standard lifts medical to £10 million, drops the excess to £99 and raises cancellation to £3,000; Premier reaches £15 million on a £50 excess, with £5,000 of cancellation, £3,000 of baggage and £500 of money, rising to £750 if the currency came from a Post Office branch. Missed departure is absent from Economy, worth £750 on Standard and £1,500 on Premier.

Admiral, underwritten by EUI Limited (company 02686904, firm reference 309378), starts where Post Office finishes. Its base policy pays £10 million of emergency medical on a £100 excess, Gold pays £15 million on £75, and Platinum pays £20 million on £50, with cancellation climbing £1,500, £3,000, £5,000 and baggage £1,000, £2,000, £3,000 alongside it.

So the range this one form reaches across is roughly £5 million to £20 million of medical cover and £125 down to £50 of excess — a fourfold spread on the limit and a two-and-a-half-fold spread on what you pay before the insurer does. Two quotes eleven pence apart can sit either side of that. The form asks your destination early because it is the one answer that moves the medical limit you should be aiming for: a broken hip in Spain and the same break in Florida are not the same bill.

The Association of British Insurers puts a floor under how often this matters. UK travel insurers paid £472 million across more than 500,000 claims in 2024. Medical expenses were the single most common reason to claim at 34% of the total, worth £262 million between them, and one insurer alone settled a claim of over £1 million for emergency hospital treatment in the United States and a flight home.

sections.heading: A Gibraltar licence, a Surrey postbox and the question in between
sections.html:
The insurers on the panel must be FCA-authorised. The company running the panel is licensed somewhere else. Aequotech Limited holds permission from the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission under Gibraltar's own Financial Services Act 2019 for “taking up or pursuing insurance distribution – general”, and the firm's terms say it works into Britain “on a freedom of services basis” — selling from Gibraltar rather than from a UK office.

The FCA publishes a consumer page on exactly this arrangement, last updated 2 September 2026. It distinguishes a branch passport, meaning a physical UK presence, from a services passport, meaning none; and it says plainly that such firms “won't have been assessed or authorised by us or the Prudential Regulation Authority”. On complaints it is narrower still: where there is no UK branch, “you'll generally only be able to complain to the Financial Ombudsman if the firm has joined its voluntary jurisdiction.”

Compare Your Travel Insurance's own complaints page offers the Ombudsman without qualification — Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR, 0800 023 4567, available “if we do not provide a final response within 8 weeks” — and mentions no Gibraltar scheme at all. Complaints are posted to a UK address, PO Box 125, Hindhead, GU27 9HQ. Whether that adds up to a UK branch for Ombudsman purposes, or to voluntary-jurisdiction membership, is not something either the firm's pages or the FCA's answer for you, and it is a fair thing to ask by email before you buy. In practice it bites rarely: a complaint about the policy goes to the insurer, who is FCA-authorised and firmly inside the Ombudsman's compulsory jurisdiction. It is a complaint about the comparison itself — a price that changed between quote and checkout, a filter that hid a policy — where the answer matters.

There is a clock on the arrangement, too. Gibraltar firms reach the UK market through transitional provisions kept alive year by year while the permanent Gibraltar Authorisation Regime in the Financial Services Act 2021 is brought into operation. The most recent extension, the Financial Services (Gibraltar) (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2025, was made on 11 November 2025, came into force on 16 December 2025 and runs the current arrangements to 31 December 2026. Nothing about that threatens a policy you bought through the site — your contract is with the insurer — but it is why the regulatory wording on this site will probably be different a year from now.

sections.heading: One licence, five shopfronts, and the one you may actually want
sections.html:
The Gibraltar register lists five trading names against licence 20376: Compare Your Travel Insurance, Compare Your Cruise Insurance, Medical Travel Compared, Juxtify and Signposter Plus. It also records two former company names, CYTI (Gibraltar) Limited and Medical Travel Compared Limited, which is a useful clue about where the business started: the quote journey at quote.compareyourtravelinsurance.co.uk still identifies itself internally as CYTI.

The practical point is the sister site. Medical Travel Compared runs the same commission model from the same licence, and works with “over 30 specialist providers”, naming 33 of them — several of which, including Free Spirit, Good to Go and Travel Insurance 4 Medical, exist mainly to quote on conditions a mainstream insurer prices out of reach. If you are shopping with a heart condition, a cancer history or anything recently investigated, that is the panel to be on, and it belongs to the same company. Neither the medical-conditions page nor the FAQ on this site tells you it exists.

Two UK companies carrying the CYTI name also sat on the Companies House register until this year. CYTI Limited (number 07368288), incorporated on 7 September 2010 at 1 Dean Street, London, registered under the codes for non-life insurance and information technology services, and CYTI (Holdings) Limited (11080164, incorporated 23 November 2017, filing as dormant) were both dissolved on 24 March 2026. Public records do not state that either belonged to this group, and the site names no UK company anywhere, so treat the connection as unconfirmed — but it is the reason the only British address left in the chain is a postbox in Surrey.

sections.heading: The medical questions are the ones that decide a claim
sections.html:
The site is straight about declaration, and the wording deserves quoting because it is the sentence most travellers skim: “If you need to make a claim and your insurer discovers you did not disclose your medical history fully, they may deem your policy invalid.” Its FAQ adds two conditions people miss — cover applies only to conditions “you've declared and the insurer has accepted in writing”, and a condition that has not been diagnosed yet is not covered at all, however plainly it was brewing.

The Ombudsman's caseload says the same thing from the other end. Travel insurance complaints reached 4,466 in the year to 31 March 2024, up 19% on 3,745 the year before and well clear of the 2,510 recorded in 2019/20. Declined claims lead the list, and undisclosed or under-disclosed medical history leads the declines. The Ombudsman's own advice is blunter than any insurer's: you may have to declare a condition “even if you have fully recovered”.

Where this site falls short is the step the regulator built for precisely this reader. Since 26 April 2021, under policy statement PS20/3, firms selling retail travel insurance — intermediaries and comparison sites included — must point customers with serious pre-existing conditions towards a directory of specialist firms, of which two qualify: MoneyHelper's and BIBA's. The rules were tightened again from 1 January 2026: the premium level that triggers signposting rose from £100 to £200, it will be revised against the Consumer Prices Index every 5 years, and each firm may now hold only one entry per directory. The FCA's own review of the regime estimated it had produced about 21,000 additional policy sales.

Compare Your Travel Insurance's page on pre-existing medical conditions carries no link to either directory, and no directory link appears in its FAQ. The page instead describes medical screening as “a friendly chat about your health history”. That is a fair description of the questionnaire, and a thin substitute for a signpost — particularly from a firm that already owns a specialist panel it could send you to.

sections.heading: Where the website stops short of finishing itself
sections.html:
Small things, individually forgivable, and worth knowing before you judge the brand by its polish.

The Meet the Team page carries six profiles. One, Tommy Lloyd, has a photograph and a line of biography claiming 15 years in insurance. The other five have no photographs and placeholder Latin where the biography should be, under the names Daryl Dixon, Maggie Greene, Morgan Jones, Eugene Porter and Alicia Clark — a cast list borrowed from a television drama and never replaced.

Two different registered addresses are in circulation for the same company. The site's terms and privacy policy give PO Box 475, Suite 23 Portland House, Glacis Road, Gibraltar GX11 1AA; the Gibraltar regulator's register gives Unit 104, Royal Ocean Plaza, Ocean Village, at the same postcode. The about page dates the business to 2013 while the register dates the company to 18 July 2014. A /providers/ page returns a 404, so the panel list survives only on the about page. And the privacy policy names 18 firms that receive your data against the 26 shown as panel members, without explaining the gap.

None of that changes a quote. It does tell you how much of the site is maintained, which is worth a moment's thought before you hand over a date of birth and a medical history.

sections.heading: Money, timing and the two things to check at checkout
sections.html:
The service is free to use and paid by the insurer: “that provider gives us a small percentage of the policy cost. This is our commission.” The size of the percentage is not published, and the firm says it does not affect the order results appear in. Prices are described as live and set by the provider, so the same search an hour later can return a different number, and there are no site-only discounts to hunt for.

Every policy bought through the panel carries a 14-day right to cancel. Two checks are worth making inside those 14 days rather than at an airport. First, buy cancellation cover the day you book the trip, not the week you fly — cancellation is the one section that is working from the moment the policy starts, and a policy bought late covers nothing that has already gone wrong. Second, read the medical acceptance in writing: the quote screen shows a price, and the acceptance shows which of your declared conditions the insurer has actually agreed to carry.

Finally, the form is the fastest part and the documents are not. The journey asks for cover type, destination, dates, trip length, group size and dates of birth before it shows a price, which takes a couple of minutes; the policy wording behind the cheapest result takes rather longer, and it is where the excess, the limits in the table above and the activity exclusions live. The site itself gives no advice and makes no recommendation — its terms say so twice — which means every one of those judgements is yours.

pros: 26 named providers, all required to be FCA-authorised, including medical specialists alongside high-street brands
No upper age limit on who can request a quote, and single trips run to 94 days
Quotes advertised from £8.23, with gadget, winter sports and cruise cover as switches on the same form
Commission model disclosed in plain words on the about page rather than buried in terms
A 14-day right to cancel on every policy bought through the panel
A sister panel of 30-plus specialist medical providers sits behind the same licence
Complaints acknowledged within 5 working days, with a named UK complaints address
cons: The comparison company is licensed in Gibraltar, not assessed or authorised by the FCA, and its own complaints page offers the Financial Ombudsman without explaining the branch or voluntary-jurisdiction condition the FCA attaches to that
Its pre-existing medical conditions page links to neither the MoneyHelper nor the BIBA directory, which the signposting rules in force since 26 April 2021 exist to require
It never mentions Medical Travel Compared, the specialist panel of 30-plus providers run from the same Gibraltar licence and better suited to a serious condition
No advice or recommendation is given, so a £5m limit with a £125 excess and a £20m limit with a £50 excess are left to the reader to tell apart
The Meet the Team page shows five profiles with placeholder Latin text under names taken from a television series

Two different Gibraltar registered addresses are published for the same company, the about page dates the business to 2013 against an incorporation date of 18 July 2014, and the /providers/ page returns a 404
The commission percentage is not published, and the privacy policy names 18 data recipients against a panel of 26
verdict: A tidy, quick panel with real names on it and an honest line about how it gets paid, worth a couple of minutes if you want mainstream travel cover and a spread of medical limits from £5m to £20m in one list. Two caveats decide whether it suits you. If you have a pre-existing condition of any weight, the same company's Medical Travel Compared panel is the one you want and this site will not tell you so. And the comparison itself is run from Gibraltar rather than Britain, which is worth a question by email if a complaint about the comparison — rather than about the policy — is something you would want an Ombudsman to hear.

faqs.q: Does Compare Your Travel Insurance sell the insurance itself?
faqs.a: No. It is a comparison service run by Aequotech Limited and paid a commission by whichever insurer you choose. Your contract, your claim and your policy documents all come from that insurer, and its terms state twice that no advice or recommendation is given.

faqs.q: How much medical cover will I be shown?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the policy. Across the named panel the published limits run from £5 million on Post Office's Economy level to £20 million on Admiral Platinum, with excesses between £125 and £50. Two results a few pence apart can sit at opposite ends of that range, so read the limit as well as the price.

faqs.q: Is the company regulated in the UK?
faqs.a: It is licensed by the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission under licence 20376 and appears on the UK register under firm reference 677661, working into Britain on a freedom of services basis. The FCA's own guidance notes that such firms have not been assessed or authorised by the FCA, and that access to the Financial Ombudsman generally depends on a UK branch or voluntary-jurisdiction membership. The insurers on the panel are separately FCA-authorised.

faqs.q: I have a pre-existing condition. Is this the right panel?
faqs.a: Possibly not. The same company runs Medical Travel Compared, which works with over 30 specialist providers including Free Spirit, Good to Go and Travel Insurance 4 Medical. For anything serious or recently investigated, start there, or with the MoneyHelper or BIBA directories. Declare everything either way: the site warns that an incomplete history can leave a policy invalid at claim stage.

faqs.q: What does it cost to use?
faqs.a: Nothing. The insurer pays the site a percentage of your premium after you buy, which the about page describes as commission and says does not influence how results are displayed. The percentage itself is not published, and prices are live, so the same search can return a different figure an hour later.

faqs.q: How long can a single trip be?
faqs.a: Up to 94 days on a single-trip policy, with the form offering duration bands of 35 days or under, 36 to 60 days, and 61 days or more. Longer stays are handled by a separate long-stay journey, and annual multi-trip cover has its own per-trip limit that is worth checking before you rely on it.

title: Coverwise Travel Insurance Review: Five Levels, One Medical Limit
meta_title: Coverwise Travel Insurance: £20m Medical, Cover From £3.60
meta_description: Coverwise sells five levels of travel cover from £3.60, and every one carries £20,000,000 of emergency medical. What changes is the excess, not the limit.

headline.label: Emergency medical cover
headline.value: £20,000,000 on all five levels — Standard Plus to Platinum. Excess £100, £50 or nil

intro:
Coverwise advertises single-trip cover from £3.60 and annual cover from £10.95, and every one of its five cover levels carries £20,000,000 of emergency medical expenses — the same limit on the cheapest policy as on the dearest. Limits read off Coverwise's own policy wordings on 18 September 2026.

That is unusual, and it is the most useful thing about the range. Most travel insurers sell the medical limit as the reason to trade up, so the cheap tier gets £5 million and the expensive one gets £15 million. Coverwise does not ration it. Standard Plus, Bronze, Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum all stop at the same £20,000,000, and the money you spend moving up the ladder buys a smaller excess and a bigger cancellation limit instead. Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum each hold a Defaqto 5 Star rating, and there are optional gadget, winter sports and business extensions from £19.95.

The licence on the paperwork is a Gibraltar one — Coverwise Limited, company 103717, registered at 2 Irish Town and holding Financial Services Commission registration FSC1107B. The telephone is not. Sales and complaints both run through 01903 255 650 in West Sussex, and the complaints address in the firm's own terms is a fourth-floor office in Worthing. That gap between where a brand is licensed and where it is actually answered is worth understanding before you buy, and it is set out further down.

sections.heading: The five levels, and the one number that never moves
sections.html:
Here is the ladder as the wordings print it, all five dated V.1.N 05/22 and all five underwritten by Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch.

Standard Plus pays £20,000,000 of emergency medical on a £100 excess, with £1,000 of cancellation, £1,000 of baggage, £200 of personal money, £50,000 of legal expenses and a £200 excess on the personal liability section. Bronze keeps the £100 excess and lifts cancellation to £1,500 and baggage to £1,750. Silver Plus halves the excess to £50 across almost every section, takes cancellation to £2,000, adds £1,000 of missed departure and drops the liability excess from £200 to £50. Gold holds the £50 excess and moves cancellation to £3,000 and baggage to £2,000. Platinum pays £6,000 of cancellation and £3,500 of baggage, lifts personal accident to £30,000 and delayed departure to £350, and charges no excess at all on most sections, including the medical one.

Read down that list and the medical column never changes. The gap between the cheapest policy and the dearest is £5,000 of extra cancellation cover, £2,500 of extra baggage and an excess falling from £100 to nothing. It is not more cover for a broken hip in Spain.

Which way that cuts depends on what you are protecting. If the trip cost £400 and your worry is a hospital bill, the £3.60 policy carries the identical limit to the expensive one and the upgrade buys you very little. If you have paid £4,000 up front for a fortnight and your real exposure is having to call it off, Standard Plus caps you at £1,000 and only Platinum's £6,000 covers the whole thing. Cancellation, not medical, is the section that should decide which row of this table you land on — which is the opposite of how the range is usually shopped.

One detail that is easy to miss on the cheaper levels: an excess normally applies per person and per section. Two travellers claiming on baggage and personal money on a Standard Plus policy meet £100 four times over, and on a £1,000 baggage limit that is a sizeable share of the claim.

sections.heading: Two insurers behind one brand, and the FAQ that is written twice
sections.html:
Coverwise is an intermediary, so it does not carry any of this risk itself, and the name on the certificate is not always the same one. The footer of the website says the insurance is underwritten by AWP P&C S.A. acting through its UK branch, authorised in France by L'Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel et de Résolution and regulated here under firm reference 534384, and administered by AWP Assistance UK Ltd, trading as Allianz, under firm reference 311909. Every current policy wording served from the site's /Documents/UK/5/ path instead names Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch, part of the AXA Group, firm reference 202664, with claims run by AXA Travel Insurance. An older Gold wording sitting one directory across, at /Documents/UK/6/, is the AWP one.

The frequently asked questions settle the matter: every answer is given twice, once for AWP P&C S.A. and once for Inter Partner Assistance S.A. Both sets of schemes are live, in other words, and the honest reading is that this is a brand with two panels of paper behind it rather than a site that has forgotten to update itself.

The reassuring part is that the two sets of numbers match. The AWP Gold wording and the AXA Gold wording both pay £20,000,000 of emergency medical on a £50 excess, £3,000 of cancellation and £2,000 of baggage. Whichever insurer you are given, the cover summary is the same document with a different crest on it, and both firms are large European travel insurers rather than anybody obscure.

The answers do diverge in one place worth knowing about. Under an AWP policy, legal expenses pay up to the limit for you but “not more than twice this amount in total for all people insured under this policy”. Under an Inter Partner Assistance policy, legal expenses carry “a limit per policy (single trip) or a limit per trip (annual multi trip) irrespective of the number of individuals insured”. On a family annual policy making one legal claim between four people, those are different sums of money. Nothing on the quote screen tells you which rule you are buying.

sections.heading: What the free card does, and the part it never touches
sections.html:
A £20,000,000 limit sounds like a number invented by a marketing department, and it is worth saying plainly why it is not. The expensive half of a travel medical claim is rarely the treatment. It is the aeroplane: an air ambulance, a stretcher across three rows of a scheduled flight, a doctor and a nurse travelling with you, and a second seat home for whoever you were travelling with.

That is also exactly the part the state does not cover. The NHS Business Services Authority is unambiguous about the free UK Global Health Insurance Card: “Your UK EHIC or UK GHIC is not a substitute for travel insurance. It may not cover all health costs and never covers repatriation costs. Make sure you have travel insurance as well as a UK EHIC or UK GHIC.” The card is free to apply for and covers emergency treatment and A&E visits on the same terms as a local resident. It will not fly you home, and outside its list of countries it does nothing at all.

So the sensible way to read Coverwise's cheapest policy is as the repatriation cover the card cannot give you, bought for the price of a sandwich. At £3.60 for four days in Europe, that is 90p a day against a limit of £20 million, and even the £100 excess only bites on claims small enough that you would probably have paid them yourself. Carry the card as well — it costs nothing and it can settle the local bill before the insurer is involved — but the insurer is the one with the aeroplane.

Where the same arithmetic stops flattering the cheap tier is the ski page. Winter sports cover starts at £19.95 and is capped at 17 days in a policy year on an annual multi-trip, which is a fortnight and a long weekend. A second week on the snow is not covered by simply paying the premium again.

sections.heading: Gibraltar on the licence, Worthing on the telephone
sections.html:
Coverwise Limited is a Gibraltar company, number 103717, with its head office at 2 Irish Town, Gibraltar GX11 1AA, licensed by the Financial Services Commission there under registration FSC1107B and trading into the UK on a freedom of services basis under firm reference 533101. Read that on its own and you might expect an offshore shell.

The documents say otherwise. The complaints route in Coverwise's own terms is “The Operations Manager, 4th Floor, Southfield House, Liverpool Gardens, Worthing, BN11 1RY”, with a duty manager reachable on 01903 255 650. Its older policy wordings give a different West Sussex address, 77-79 High Street, Steyning, BN44 3RE. Both belong to Southdowns Insurance Services Limited, a UK broker at Companies House under number 07285096, incorporated on 15 June 2010 as Southdowns Contact Services Limited and renamed on 12 March 2013, which publishes its terms of business from the Worthing address, answers a duty manager on 01903 255659 and files its accounts to 31 March. Its documents sit behind the same directory structure as Coverwise's. Neither firm's public paperwork states the relationship, so treat the link as what the addresses and the file paths show rather than as a stated fact — but the practical point stands, which is that a Gibraltar licence here does not mean a call centre you cannot reach.

Two things about that paperwork are less impressive. The terms and conditions say Coverwise is licensed “under the Financial Services Act 1989”. Gibraltar replaced that regime on 15 January 2020, when the Financial Services Act 2019 came into force and consolidated roughly 90 separate pieces of legislation into one framework. The citation has been out of date for more than six years. And the About Us page carries no trading history, no customer numbers and no scale figures of any kind, under a copyright line reading 2010 — so how big this business is, and how long it has been doing this, is not something the site will tell you.

Nor will it tell you what it earns. The terms are clear that no advice or recommendation is given, which is fair and normal for an online travel policy, but the commission taken from your premium is not stated anywhere, and the Southdowns terms of business separately allow “an administration fee of up to £25.00 for any mid-term change to the policy”.

sections.heading: The ages, the dates and the declarations that decide a claim
sections.html:
Three eligibility rules do more to determine whether Coverwise suits you than any benefit limit, and none of them is on the front page.

The first is age. An annual multi-trip policy is “not available to anyone aged 66 or over”, and a single trip policy is not available to anyone aged 76 or over. Those are hard doors rather than loadings: a 66th birthday ends the annual product outright, and a 76th ends the relationship. For an older traveller this is the wrong provider, and the range gives no route round it.

The second is trip length. Standard Plus and Bronze cover “any trip not exceeding 24 days” on an annual policy; Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum stretch that to 31 days. A five-week visit to family, or a month plus a few days either side, falls outside the two cheaper levels entirely, and the difference costs less to fix at the quote stage than at the airport.

The third is your medical history. The Select wordings require disclosure of “any medical condition for which you have taken or been prescribed medication…within the last 2 years”, and an undeclared condition is treated as deliberate or reckless misrepresentation, which lets the insurer cancel the policy with no refund and decline the claim. Coverwise's own medical page puts it more directly: an omission “could affect the validity of your policy or result in claims being declined, even if the claim is not related to the undeclared condition”. To its credit, the firm says it does not sell policies that simply exclude undeclared conditions, and it points travellers it cannot quote for towards MoneyHelper's travel insurance directory on 0800 138 7777. Medical-screened cover starts at £15.00.

One last date. You have 14 days from receiving the documents to cancel for a full refund, provided you have not travelled and have not claimed. After that the terms give no refund at all, whatever is left of the policy year — so an annual policy cancelled in month two is paid for in full.

sections.heading: What a five-star rating is actually measuring
sections.html:
Coverwise puts Defaqto 5 Star against Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum, and the rating is real. Defaqto describes its method plainly: its experts “choose between 30 and 100 features and benefits, against which every policy/product in the market is scored”. A five-star travel policy is a policy with a long and generous feature list, independently scored.

What that sentence also tells you is the limit of the badge. It is a count of what is in the wording, so it says nothing about the price, nothing about how quickly a claim is settled, and nothing about the telephone. A 5 Star policy with a £100 excess and a 5 Star policy with no excess score on the same scale.

The rating on the Coverwise site also carries no year against it, which matters because Defaqto refreshes these and a wording dated 05/22 has had four years to be overtaken. If the star rating is part of why you are buying, it is worth asking which cover level and which year the award belongs to before you rely on it. The same goes for the two lower levels, Standard Plus and Bronze, which are not claimed to hold the rating at all — on a range where the medical limit is identical throughout, the honest summary is that the badge is marking the cancellation and excess columns, not the headline one.

pros: £20,000,000 of emergency medical cover on every level, including the £3.60 one
Prices advertised from £3.60 single trip, £10.95 annual, £15.00 with medical screening and £19.95 with winter sports
Platinum carries no excess at all on most sections, including emergency medical
£50,000 of legal expenses from the cheapest level upwards
Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum each hold a Defaqto 5 Star rating
Travellers the firm cannot quote for are pointed to MoneyHelper's directory, with the phone number given
No policies sold that simply exclude undeclared medical conditions
Sales and complaints answered on a UK number in West Sussex despite the Gibraltar licence
cons: The terms and conditions still cite Gibraltar's Financial Services Act 1989, replaced on 15 January 2020 by the Financial Services Act 2019 — a citation more than six years out of date
Annual multi-trip cover closes at 66 and single trip cover at 76, with no route round either, which rules the range out for many older travellers
You cannot tell before buying whether your policy will be underwritten by AWP P&C or by Inter Partner Assistance, and the two differ on how the legal expenses limit is shared between travellers
Cancellation cover on Standard Plus stops at £1,000, which is below the cost of the holidays most people insure
Excesses of £100 on the two lower levels, and £200 on their personal liability section, apply per person and per section rather than once per claim
No refund of any kind after the 14-day cancellation window, however much of an annual policy is unused
The commission taken from the premium is not published, and the About Us page gives no trading history, customer numbers or scale figures under a copyright line reading 2010
The Defaqto 5 Star claim carries no year and no cover-level detail beyond the three tiers named
verdict: A cheap, plain travel policy that is better value at the bottom of the range than at the top, because the £20,000,000 emergency medical limit — the number most people are actually buying — is identical on all five levels. Pay for Silver Plus or above if your exposure is cancelling a costly trip or if you want the excess down to £50 or nothing; the extra money buys nothing medical. The two rules that decide whether Coverwise suits you at all are the age doors at 66 and 76, and the 24-day trip limit on the two cheapest levels. Read which of the two insurers your certificate names before you need to ring anyone.

faqs.q: How much medical cover does the cheapest Coverwise policy have?
faqs.a: The same as the dearest. All five levels — Standard Plus, Bronze, Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum — carry £20,000,000 of emergency medical expenses. What rises with the price is the cancellation limit, from £1,000 to £6,000, and what falls is the excess, from £100 to £50 to nil on Platinum.

faqs.q: Who actually insures a Coverwise policy?
faqs.a: One of two firms. The current wordings name Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch, part of the AXA Group, firm reference 202664. The website footer names AWP P&C S.A., part of Allianz, firm reference 534384, administered by AWP Assistance UK Ltd, firm reference 311909. Coverwise Limited itself is the intermediary and carries none of the risk. The cover limits are the same either way; check your certificate for the name.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is strict. Annual multi-trip cover is not available to anyone aged 66 or over, and single-trip cover is not available to anyone aged 76 or over. There is no loading or referral route past either point, so an older traveller needs a different provider.

faqs.q: Do I still need a GHIC if I buy this?
faqs.a: Carry both. The UK Global Health Insurance Card is free and covers emergency treatment abroad on local terms, but the NHS Business Services Authority states that it “never covers repatriation costs” and is “not a substitute for travel insurance”. Getting you home is the expensive part, and that is what the £20,000,000 limit is for.

faqs.q: How long can a single trip be?
faqs.a: On an annual multi-trip policy, 24 days per trip on Standard Plus and Bronze and 31 days on Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum, with winter sports limited to 17 days in total across the policy year. Single-trip durations are shown on the schedule you are quoted.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if I change my mind?
faqs.a: Within 14 days of receiving the documents, yes, provided you have not travelled and have not made a claim. After those 14 days the terms give no refund at all, so an annual policy cancelled part-way through the year is paid for in full.

title: Direct Line Car Insurance
meta_title: Direct Line Car Insurance: What the Policy Actually Pays
meta_description: Direct Line's comprehensive limits, the five-year repair guarantee, and why the version sold on Compare the Market is a different policy. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Direct Line opened for business in Croydon in 1985 as the first UK insurer to sell car cover straight down a telephone line, cutting the broker out of the transaction, and it has been one of the largest names in British motor insurance ever since. At the last set of published accounts it carried 3.831 million motor policies and took £2,700m in motor premium and associated fees, part of a book of 8.827 million in-force policies across the group.

Buy the comprehensive policy direct and the standard inclusions are unusually complete for a mainstream brand. A hire car is guaranteed for the whole time an approved repairer holds your vehicle rather than for a fixed number of days; repairs done through that network carry a five-year guarantee on parts, materials and workmanship; the uninsured driver promise refunds your excess and protects your claim-free years when someone without cover hits you and you can give them the other registration; and Direct Line charges no fee at all for mid-term changes on a policy bought from it directly.

Ownership changed hands last summer. Aviva's takeover of Direct Line Insurance Group completed on 1 July 2025, with the shares delisted two days later, creating a combined business Aviva describes as serving 20 million UK customers. The underwriter behind every Direct Line motor policy is unchanged: U K Insurance Limited, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202810, which you can look up yourself on the Financial Services Register.

sections.heading: The numbers inside the comprehensive booklet
sections.html:
The published motor policy booklet sets the limits out plainly, and they are worth knowing before a claim rather than during one. Personal belongings are covered to £250 on Comprehensive and £500 on Comprehensive Plus. Personal accident benefit runs to £5,000 and £10,000 respectively, with emergency medical expenses at £200 and £400. Lost, damaged or stolen car keys are covered to £1,000, and replacement child car seats after an impact carry no cash limit at all — a genuinely generous line, given a seat must be scrapped after any collision.

Glass is where the small print earns its keep. Use Direct Line's approved glass supplier and a repair or replacement is met in full. Go elsewhere and the payout is capped at £40 for a repair and £125 for a replacement. That cap has not kept pace with the vehicles it applies to: the trade body's own tracker puts the average windscreen repair at £283, up 7% in a single quarter, because a modern screen carries the cameras that drive lane assist and automatic braking and has to be recalibrated after fitting.

Two more worth carrying with you. A new car replacement applies if the vehicle is written off or stolen while under 1 year old on Comprehensive, or under 2 years old on Comprehensive Plus. And if a hire car cannot be supplied when it should have been, the policy pays £50 a day towards alternative travel up to £500 for the claim. Comprehensive Plus extends full cover in Europe for 90 days per period of insurance.

sections.heading: What the wider market is doing to your renewal
sections.html:
Judging a Direct Line quote needs a benchmark, and the most reliable one is the insurance trade body's premium tracker, which measures what drivers actually paid across more than 28 million policies a year rather than what was advertised. The average comprehensive premium paid was £566 in the second quarter of 2026, up £6 on the quarter before, and £560 in the first quarter, which was £20 below the same point in 2025. Adjusted for inflation the current figure sits £14 below where it was a year earlier.

Premiums are flat while claims are not. Insurers paid a record £3.2bn to motor customers in the second quarter of 2026, 7% more than a year earlier, with the average payout at £4,900 and the average accidental damage repair running at £3,699. The regulator's own value measures data, published on 21 July 2026, records motor premiums falling 7% across 2025 while claims costs rose to 59% of premium. Cover priced that tightly tends to be defended tightly at claim stage, which is an argument for reading limits rather than headline prices.

One rule works in your favour and is routinely forgotten. Since 1 January 2022 an insurer may not quote a renewing customer more than it would charge an equivalent new customer through the same channel. The regulator built that rule after finding that around 6 million loyal policyholders would have saved £1.2bn in a single year had they paid a price matched to their risk, and it estimated the change would return £4.2bn to consumers over 10 years. If a Direct Line renewal arrives above the price its own new-business quote returns for identical details, that is a question to put to them.

sections.heading: Buying it on a comparison site gets you a different policy
sections.html:
For most of its history Direct Line sold only direct, and the absence from comparison sites was the brand's defining trait. That ended on 20 December 2024, when three Direct Line motor products appeared on Compare the Market. The important detail is in Direct Line's own wording: these were designed for comparison-site buyers, and they are not the policies sold on the company's own site.

The comparison-site range runs Essentials Online, Standard Online and Premium Online. Windscreen cover is absent from the entry tier and only appears at Standard Online. Motor legal and roadside breakdown arrive at Premium Online. Features Direct Line lists as standard on its direct policies — misfuelling cover, the vandalism promise that protects your no-claim discount, and the guaranteed hire car — are not part of the online range, which is self-service by design and comes without call centre support.

There is also a fee. Change a comparison-site policy mid-term and Direct Line charges up to £19.04 including Insurance Premium Tax. On a policy bought direct, its published position is that no fee applies to policy changes. If you find a Direct Line price on a comparison site and like it, the sensible move is to run the same details through directline.com before buying and compare the two on cover rather than on price alone.

sections.heading: Where the complaints actually land
sections.html:
U K Insurance Limited publishes its regulatory complaints return, and the split inside it is more revealing than the headline. For the six months to 31 December 2025 the insurance side recorded 567 complaints opened, a rate of 0.34 per 1,000 policies, with 54% closed inside three days and 47% upheld by the firm.

The consumer credit line tells a different story: 37,282 complaints opened in the same six months, 4.54 per 1,000 active credit agreements, and 67% upheld. That category covers paying for insurance by monthly instalments, which is a regulated credit agreement rather than a payment plan. Two thirds of those complaints going the customer's way is a strong signal that if you intend to pay monthly, you should read the credit agreement and the APR as carefully as the policy wording, and keep the paperwork.

Beyond the firm's own complaints team, the Financial Ombudsman Service handled 13,420 new car and motorcycle insurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 35% of them. The service is free, and the route to it opens once your insurer has issued a final response or 8 weeks have passed without one.

sections.heading: A ten-million-pound fine, and what it was actually for
sections.html:
On 11 March 2026 the Prudential Regulation Authority fined U K Insurance Limited £10,625,000 — reduced by 50% from £21.25m under a scheme that rewards early cooperation, and the first case ever concluded that way. The firm had miscalculated its Solvency II balance sheet, overstating its capital position by roughly £99.9m at the end of 2023, with the error running from 1 June 2022 to 23 August 2024 before it was found.

It is worth being precise about what this was and was not. It was a failure of prudential reporting and internal control — wrong numbers filed with the regulator and published to the market — not a finding that customers were mistreated or claims wrongly declined. No policyholder lost money because of it. The PRA's deputy governor framed it as being about the reliability of the data supervisors depend on.

It still belongs in a buying decision, because it is evidence about the control environment behind the brand rather than about the marketing. A finance function that could not spot a nine-figure double count for fifteen months is a fair thing to weigh, particularly during the integration of two large insurers into one.

pros: Hire car guaranteed for the full length of the repair when an approved garage does the work, not capped at a set number of days
Five-year guarantee on approved-repairer parts, materials and workmanship for as long as you keep the car
No fee for mid-term policy changes when you buy direct
Uninsured driver promise refunds the excess and protects claim-free years if you can supply the other registration
Unlimited cover for replacing child car seats after an impact
Underwritten in-house by U K Insurance Limited rather than placed with a third party, so the insurer and the brand are the same company
cons: The version sold on comparison sites is a separate self-service product: no misfuelling cover, no vandalism promise, no guaranteed hire car, no call centre, and no windscreen cover at all on the entry tier
Mid-term changes on a comparison-site policy carry a fee of up to £19.04 including tax, where the direct policy has none
Glass work outside the approved supplier is capped at £40 to repair and £125 to replace, well short of the £283 average repair cost once camera recalibration is involved
Paying monthly is a credit agreement, and the consumer credit complaints line ran to 37,282 in six months with 67% upheld
The policy booklet published on the website is dated 07/06/2022, so the wording that applies to a new 2026 policy should be confirmed against the documents issued with your own schedule
The PRA fined the underwriter £10,625,000 in March 2026 over years of inaccurate solvency reporting
verdict: Direct Line is a strong pick if you buy it the way it was designed to be bought — direct, at Comprehensive or above, with the repair going through an approved garage. That combination gets you the guaranteed hire car, the five-year repair warranty, the fee-free amendments and limits that are competitive rather than merely present. Buy the same brand through a comparison site and you are buying a thinner, self-service product that charges for changes, so check which one you are being quoted. Price it against the £566 market average, and if you plan to pay monthly, read the credit agreement first.

faqs.q: Is Direct Line on comparison sites now?
faqs.a: Yes. Three Direct Line motor products launched on Compare the Market on 20 December 2024, ending a long run of direct-only selling. They are separate products built for that channel — Essentials Online, Standard Online and Premium Online — and they carry less as standard than the policies on Direct Line's own site.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites a Direct Line car policy?
faqs.a: U K Insurance Limited, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202810. It has been part of Aviva plc since the takeover completed on 1 July 2025. The reference number is on Direct Line's own disclosure and can be checked on the Financial Services Register.

faqs.q: What does Direct Line pay for a windscreen?
faqs.a: Through its approved glass supplier, the full cost of repair or replacement, subject to the glass excess shown on your schedule. Through anyone else, the booklet caps the payout at £40 for a repair and £125 for a replacement. Given the average windscreen repair now runs at £283, using the approved supplier is close to essential.

faqs.q: How long do I have to cancel?
faqs.a: 14 days from the start of the policy or from the day you receive your documents, whichever is later. Cancelling within that window means paying only for the days on cover, unless you have already claimed. Any cancellation charge is set out in your schedule, so confirm it against the documents you were sent.

faqs.q: Can I complain to the Ombudsman about a Direct Line claim?
faqs.a: Yes, once Direct Line has issued a final response or 8 weeks have gone by without one. The Financial Ombudsman Service is free to use and its decisions bind the insurer if you accept them. It received 13,420 car and motorcycle insurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 35%.

title: Direct Line Landlord Insurance
meta_title: Direct Line Landlord Insurance: Limits, Voids and Rent Cover
meta_description: What the Direct Line landlord policy pays: £1,500 emergency cover, £250,000 rent guarantee, £2m liability, and the empty-property rules. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Direct Line's landlord cover is not sold beside its car and household policies. It sits with Direct Line for Business, the arm of the group that writes commercial and property risks, and it has grown into one of the larger books in the private rented sector — the company says more than 350,000 properties are insured with it, and it has taken Best Landlord Insurance Provider at the what MORTGAGE Awards 13 years running.

The standard policy is fuller than most landlords expect before they read the wording. Buildings cover runs to the usual perils — fire, storm, flood, subsidence, escape of water, malicious damage, impact — and carries £2 million of property owners' liability, which can be raised to £10 million. Boiler and heating breakdown is built in rather than bolted on: parts, labour and call-out are met on failures such as a cracked heat exchanger, a failed expansion vessel or a dead circuit board, subject to a £200 excess, and a portable heater is supplied to the tenant while the repair is arranged. Permanent internal fixtures and fittings are insured to £50,000, replacement locks to £25,000, and if an insured event leaves the property unfit to live in the policy funds tenants' temporary accommodation to £100,000.

Where a landlord supplies white goods and furniture, contents are settled new for old with no deduction for age or wear, and floor coverings are included to £5,000 as standard with the option to increase that. Several addresses go on one schedule — Direct Line quotes up to 15 properties on a single policy — with discounts for adding between two and five further residential addresses. The underwriter throughout is U K Insurance Limited, firm reference 202810 on the Financial Services Register.

sections.heading: The numbers behind a landlord quote
sections.html:
Most of what separates one landlord policy from another sits in the optional layers, and Direct Line prices them individually rather than bundling them into tiers. Landlord Emergency pays up to £1,500 including VAT per claim to get a tradesperson out to a failed boiler, a burst pipe, a broken lock or a roof letting water in — useful on a let where the tenant rings at nine on a Sunday evening. One condition is easy to miss: on an address added to an existing policy part-way through the year, emergency claims in the first 7 days are not covered.

The personal accident benefit that comes with the policy pays up to £50,000 on death and £250 a week during temporary disablement, and applies between the ages of 16 and 75. Legal expenses can be added to fund repossession proceedings, the eviction of squatters and tax investigation protection. Loss of rent, accidental damage, employers' liability, terrorism, theft by a tenant or employee and malicious damage by a tenant are each separate additions rather than inclusions.

Glass and sanitary ware are replaced under the buildings section, and locks and keys are covered to £15,000 per claim on the buildings cover in addition to the contents limit. Leasehold flats are handled properly: fixtures inside the demise that the freeholder's block policy does not touch are insured under the landlord's own cover, which is where a lot of flat owners find a gap after a kitchen fire.

sections.heading: Rent guarantee after the end of Section 21
sections.html:
The ground moved under every landlord policy on 1 May 2026, the date section 21 no-fault eviction was abolished in England. Assured shorthold tenancies converted to periodic assured tenancies, and possession now runs through section 8 grounds — rent arrears, antisocial behaviour, the landlord selling, or the landlord moving in. Notices served before that date can still be used, but only if proceedings begin within six months of service or by 31 July 2026, whichever comes first.

That makes rent protection a different purchase than it was a year ago. Direct Line's Rent Guarantee pays up to £250,000 per claim and up to 12 months of arrears, with no excess and no cap on the number of claims in a policy year. If the property is damaged and cannot be let, it pays 50% of the rent previously received for up to 3 months or until the property is re-let. Against an average English private rent of £1,398 a month as at July 2025, twelve months of arrears is real money, and the private rented sector it protects covers roughly 19% of UK households, about 5.4 million homes.

The conditions are strict and worth meeting before a tenancy starts rather than after. Direct Line requires a written reference from the previous landlord or managing agent, a written reference from an employer or other source of income, and a credit check covering county court judgments. Rent must be at least one month overdue before a claim, claims are excluded if made more than 90 days after the missed payment, and on tenants already in place when a property is bought, claims are restricted for the first 90 days.

sections.heading: Judging the price with no comparison table
sections.html:
Direct Line for Business does not appear on any price comparison site, and says so on its own landlord page. For a product bought once a year that is a genuine inconvenience: the quote has to be obtained direct, and there is no screen on which to line it up against ten rivals. The quote holds for 30 days, which at least gives time to gather others by hand.

The nearest public benchmark is the trade body's quarterly figures for what householders actually paid, though they describe owner-occupier cover rather than let property. In the first quarter of 2026 the average combined buildings and contents premium paid was £375, down £5 on the year; buildings-only averaged £306, down 6%; contents-only £117, down 12%. Treat those as a floor rather than a target. A landlord policy carries property owners' liability, tenant damage exposure and loss of rent that a residential policy does not, so it should and does cost more.

What is not falling is the cost of a claim. Home insurers paid £846 million in that quarter, on an average claim of £6,340 — the highest recorded and up 20% year on year. Weather-related claims averaged £6,040, up 38%. Subsidence, the peril that most often leaves a rental uninhabitable for months, averaged £17,820, up 9% from £16,295. Those numbers are the argument for reading the alternative accommodation and loss of rent limits closely rather than the premium.

sections.heading: Empty weeks are where the wording tightens
sections.html:
The obligations on an unoccupied property are the part of this policy most likely to cost somebody a claim. A property must be reported to Direct Line within 30 days of becoming vacant. Cover continues in defined circumstances — newly purchased, between tenants, being redecorated — but restrictions bite after 60 days. While it is empty the landlord must inspect inside and out every 7 days, turn services off at the mains, and, between 31 October and 31 March, keep the heating running at a minimum of 10°C.

A weekly internal inspection is a demanding condition for anyone who does not live near the property. Letting agents commonly inspect quarterly, and a monthly visit — which most landlords would consider diligent — breaches it. The condition is not unusual in the market, but it is the sort of clause that is read for the first time after a burst pipe rather than before, and it applies to exactly the period when a house is most likely to suffer one.

The 60-day clock has also become harder to beat. With possession now running through the courts on section 8 grounds rather than a section 21 notice, the gap between one tenant leaving and the next arriving is less predictable than it was. That collides with a specific exclusion in the Rent Guarantee wording: arrears accruing during court delays caused by legislation or government guidance are not covered. Delays of precisely that kind are the most plausible consequence of the transition now under way, and it is the single clause a landlord buying rent protection this year should read twice.

sections.heading: Tenants and properties Direct Line will not take
sections.html:
Eligibility is narrower than the marketing suggests, and it is worth checking before spending time on a quote. At least one tenant must be employed, retired, in full-time education or in receipt of disability benefits. A property where every tenant is unemployed and claiming benefits is not covered at all. Houses in multiple occupation are handled case by case: student lets are commonly accepted, bedsits are declined.

The exclusions on the policy itself follow the usual shape but deserve stating plainly. Tenants' own belongings are not insured — that is their contents policy, not the landlord's. Wear and tear and routine maintenance are excluded, as they are everywhere. Pest infestation is excluded. Deliberate damage by a tenant is only covered if the optional malicious damage extension has been bought, which on a product sold specifically to landlords is a curious thing to leave off the standard schedule, given that tenant damage is one of the two risks that distinguishes letting from living in a house.

One inconsistency could not be resolved from the public pages and needs confirming with Direct Line directly: its multi-property page states that up to 15 properties can go on one policy, while the page metadata for the same product refers to 25. Anyone building a portfolio policy around that figure should get it in writing at quotation.

sections.heading: The company standing behind the cover
sections.html:
Two developments at the underwriter matter to anyone buying a multi-year relationship. On 11 March 2026 the Prudential Regulation Authority fined U K Insurance Limited £10,625,000 for miscalculating its Solvency II balance sheet across 2023 and 2024, overstating its solvency position to the regulator and to the market. The PRA found inadequate preventative and detective controls and staffing gaps in the finance and actuarial functions, and cited breaches of Fundamental Rule 6 alongside its notification and reporting rules. The firm settled early under the Early Account Scheme and received a 50% reduction; the penalty would otherwise have been £21.25 million. This was a reporting and controls failure rather than a claims-handling one, but it is a large fine and it is public.

The second is a change of legal insurer. Around 8.2 million in-force policies written by U K Insurance Limited — Direct Line, Churchill, Privilege, Green Flag, Darwin and By Miles — are proposed to transfer to Aviva Insurance Limited under Part VII of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, High Court case CR-2026-001308. The final English hearing is listed for 15 December 2026, the Jersey hearing for 18 December, with a proposed effective date of 31 December 2026. Terms, premiums, renewal dates and policy numbers are not expected to change. A policyholder who believes they would be adversely affected can object, ideally before 8 December 2026, on 0800 158 2502.

If a claim goes wrong, the route is a complaint to Direct Line first and then the Financial Ombudsman Service. The Ombudsman's own figures for April to June 2026 show 53,600 new complaints across all financial products with 26% upheld. Buildings insurance generated 1,766 of them at a 33% uphold rate, contents 472 at 24%, and home emergency 550 at 32%. Property claims are disputed successfully more often than the average across financial services, which is a reason to document the condition of a let property before a claim rather than during one.

pros: Boiler and heating breakdown included as standard, not sold as an add-on, with a £200 excess
£2 million property owners' liability as standard, extendable to £10 million
Tenants' temporary accommodation funded to £100,000 after an insured event
Rent Guarantee carries no excess, pays 12 months of arrears and up to £250,000, with no cap on claims per year
Contents settled new for old with no deduction for age or wear, floor coverings to £5,000
Several addresses on one schedule with discounts for adding two to five further properties
cons: Sold direct only and absent from every comparison site, so the premium cannot be benchmarked against rivals in one place
Rent Guarantee excludes arrears building up during court delays caused by legislation or government guidance — the most likely source of delay during the Renters' Rights Act transition
Unoccupied-property conditions are demanding: inspections inside and out every 7 days, mains services off, and restrictions after 60 days
Whole categories of tenant are refused — a property where every tenant is unemployed and claiming benefits is not covered, and bedsit HMOs are declined
Malicious damage and theft by tenants are optional extras rather than standard cover on a policy sold specifically to landlords
The underwriter was fined £10,625,000 by the PRA in March 2026 for overstating its solvency position across 2023 and 2024
Direct Line's own pages disagree on how many properties one policy will hold — 15 on the product page, 25 in its metadata
verdict: A well-stocked standard policy with unusually good bones — boiler breakdown included, £2 million of liability, £100,000 of tenant accommodation and new-for-old contents — wrapped in eligibility and empty-property conditions that are stricter than the sales pages let on. It suits a landlord with employed or student tenants, a property that is rarely empty for long, and the discipline to inspect weekly when it is. It suits far less anyone letting to benefit-dependent tenants, running bedsits, or holding property at a distance. Because it is sold direct only, the honest advice is to get the Direct Line quote and then price two or three brokered alternatives by hand before deciding.

faqs.q: Is Direct Line landlord insurance available on comparison sites?
faqs.a: No. Direct Line for Business sells this product direct only and states as much on its own landlord page. A quote must be requested from Direct Line, and it stays valid for 30 days, which gives time to gather competing quotes separately.

faqs.q: How long can the property be empty before cover is affected?
faqs.a: Direct Line must be told within 30 days of the property becoming vacant, and restrictions apply after 60 days of unoccupancy. While it is empty the property must be inspected inside and out every 7 days, services turned off at the mains, and heating kept to at least 10°C between 31 October and 31 March.

faqs.q: Does the policy cover damage caused deliberately by a tenant?
faqs.a: Only if the optional malicious damage by tenants extension is added. It is not part of the standard schedule. Theft by a tenant, employee or other lawful occupant is likewise a separate addition, and tenants' own possessions are never covered by the landlord's policy.

faqs.q: Who underwrites the policy and is it regulated?
faqs.a: The underwriter is U K Insurance Limited, firm reference 202810, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA. That reference can be checked on the Financial Services Register. Around 8.2 million of its policies are proposed to transfer to Aviva Insurance Limited on 31 December 2026, subject to a High Court hearing on 15 December 2026.

faqs.q: What does Rent Guarantee actually pay, and what does it require?
faqs.a: Up to £250,000 per claim and up to 12 months of arrears, with no excess, plus 50% of previous rent for up to 3 months if damage makes the property unlettable. It requires a written reference from the previous landlord or agent, a written employment or income reference, and a credit check. Rent must be a month overdue before claiming, and a claim made more than 90 days after a missed payment is excluded.

title: Eversure Breakdown Cover Review

meta_description: Eversure breakdown cover reviewed: Silver, Gold and Platinum tiers, £17.47 starting price, the 15-year vehicle limit and who actually underwrites it.
intro:
Eversure sells UK and European breakdown cover starting at £17.47 a year, which is roughly what a month of patrol-branded membership costs. The Guildford firm has been arranging insurance since 2008 and says it has helped more than 250,000 people buy a policy, across a range that also takes in cycle, drone, camera, caravan and car hire excess cover. Breakdown is one line among ten rather than the whole business.

The breakdown product comes in three tiers — Silver, Gold and Platinum — and covers up to four people living at the same address rather than a single named driver. Eversure quotes an average response time of 46 minutes, says 85% of vehicles are fixed at the roadside and 76% of home callouts are fixed on the driveway. National recovery to your home address is included from the entry tier upward, which is not true of every budget policy.

Personal cover, which follows the person into any eligible vehicle they are travelling in, starts higher at £33.81. European cover is priced separately: £20.54 for a single trip, £50.28 for an annual policy covering trips of up to 90 days across 39 listed territories.
