sections.heading: Where the money goes when you press book
sections.html:
Two of Hostelworld's own documents describe the same payment in different terms, and reading them side by side is the quickest way to understand the business. The consumer booking terms call it "a deposit (being a part payment towards the total value of your booking)". The company's investor presentation is more direct about what it is for: Hostelworld says it will "charge hostels a commission when consumers book on our platform – we collect that commission directly from consumers in the form of a deposit". Both statements are true at once. The money you hand over at the point of booking is the platform's fee, taken from you rather than invoiced to the hostel, and the hostel is paid the rest when you turn up.

That makes the size of the deposit a published figure, because the commission rate is in the accounts. It ran at 15.3% in 2024, 16.2% across 2025, and 17.7% in the six months to 30 June 2026 against 15.8% a year earlier. Set that against a net average booking value of €13.43 in 2025 and €14.90 in the first half of 2026 and the arithmetic is undramatic: on a typical booking the platform keeps something in the region of €14 to €15, and the remainder of the bed price is settled at the hostel counter.

Sitting alongside the deposit is a booking fee. The terms mention it once, to say that "where We charge a booking fee, it is non-refundable in all circumstances", and no amount appears anywhere in the document. That matters more than it first looks, for a reason covered near the end of this page: the booking fee is also the number Hostelworld uses to cap what it can ever owe you.

sections.heading: The balance, the city tax and the costs the search page does not show
sections.html:
Because only the deposit passes through Hostelworld, everything else is a transaction between you and the hostel, and hostels charge for a longer list of things than most hotels do. Hostelworld's own guide to extra costs is unusually candid about it. City or tourist tax is collected "in cash, at check-in or check-out" and hostels are "required by law" to take it: roughly €0.20 to €2 per person per night in France, €1 to €4 in Italy, €0.50 to €4 in Spain, and in the Netherlands around 12.5% of the booking total, which on a week in Amsterdam is a real number rather than loose change.

The rest of the list is smaller but adds up. Bed linen is included almost everywhere; a bath towel is "often extra" at €1 to €3. Lockers can carry a daily fee of €1 to €3 or a refundable deposit on the padlock. Late check-in, where somebody has to stay awake to let you in, runs from €5 to €25. Breakfast is €3 to €6 for a basic spread and €10 or more for a buffet.

A live listing shows how this looks in practice. Castle Hostel 1004 in Bled, rated 9.4 from 2,932 reviews at the time of checking, states a city tax of €3.13 per person per night, luggage storage at €2 per guest and an early or late check-in charge of €5 per person — none of which is in the price you compare on the search results page. Two nights for two people there carries €12.52 of tax alone. Add the extras up before deciding that one hostel is cheaper than another.

sections.heading: Why there is no fourteen-day cooling off on a booked bed
sections.html:
Buy almost anything else online from a UK address and you get 14 days to change your mind. Accommodation is carved out of that right by regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, which excludes services tied to "a specific date or period of performance" — accommodation, transport of goods, vehicle rental, catering and leisure services. A bed booked for the night of the fourteenth is exactly that, so no statutory cancellation right ever attaches to it.

Everything you can cancel, then, you can cancel because a hostel chose to let you, not because the law says so. That is why the cancellation window varies property by property. Hostelworld's terms say deadlines are "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date, unless otherwise stated", and the Bled listing above sets its own at 72 hours. A non-refundable rate is a different animal again: book one and, in the platform's own words, "you will be charged the full amount of your booking" if you cancel. Simply not turning up is worse still, because the terms let the property charge your card "an amount not exceeding the charge for one night's stay" without asking you first.

The practical reading is that a free cancellation badge is a commercial concession worth checking the exact hours on, and that the discount on a non-refundable rate has to be big enough to be worth losing the whole booking over.

sections.heading: Tours, experiences and the package rule that changes in 2027
sections.html:
A bed on its own is a single travel service. Under regulation 2 of the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 a package needs a combination of at least two different types — carriage of passengers, accommodation, vehicle rental or another tourist service — so accommodation booked alone carries no organiser liability and no insolvency protection. There is no ATOL cover either, because no flight is involved. That is true of every accommodation platform rather than of this one in particular, but it is worth stating plainly: if a hostel closes between your booking and your arrival, nothing in the package travel regime stands behind your deposit.

Hostelworld is more exposed to the next change than a pure bed platform would be, because it also sells tours and experiences alongside accommodation. The Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements (Amendment) Regulations 2026 come into force on 6 April 2027. They delete the linked travel arrangement regime outright, they widen the definition of a package to catch travel services bought under separate contracts where one trader facilitated "the separate selection of and separate payment for each of the travel services" during a single visit to its point of sale, and they replace the old right of redress with a refund obligation running to 14 days. A traveller who books a bed and a walking tour in the same session on the same platform may well be buying a package from April 2027 who is not buying one today.

Nothing on the consumer site addresses this yet, which is unremarkable given the date. It is a reason to check the position again next spring rather than a criticism of the platform now.

sections.heading: What the accounts show about a business built on €15 bookings
sections.html:
The published numbers explain a good deal about how the site behaves. For the year to 31 December 2025, reported on 26 March 2026, net revenue was €93.8 million against €92.0 million, on 7.0 million net bookings. Adjusted EBITDA fell 9% to €19.9 million and the margin slipped from 24% to 21%. Operating profit was €8.4 million and profit for the year €7.0 million. Direct marketing cost €45.3 million, or 48% of generated revenue — close to half of every euro taken. The company still paid a total dividend of 2.40 cent a share and bought back 3.1 million shares for £3.9 million under a £5 million programme, ending the year with €12.2 million of cash and €1.6 million of net debt.

The half-year figures published on 29 July 2026 were stronger. Net revenue rose 12% to €52.2 million on 3.8 million transactions, up just 1%, with the average transaction value up 11% to €14.90. Adjusted EBITDA rose 11% to €8.2 million at a 16% margin, profit for the period was €0.5 million, cash reached €15.0 million and the group moved to €2.5 million of net cash. Marketing absorbed 49% of revenue. Europe produced €26.0 million of the revenue, Asia, Africa and Oceania €16.4 million and the Americas €9.8 million, from a headcount of about 275.

Read those two sets together and the strategy is obvious enough: bookings are barely growing, so revenue growth has to come from taking more per booking. Chief executive Gary Morrison said as much, attributing the half's growth to a tool that "lifted our effective commission rate to 17.7%, up from 15.8% a year earlier". Nobody is hiding it, and a traveller who understands it can shop accordingly.

sections.heading: Reviews written only by people who slept there
sections.html:
The review base is the strongest thing on the platform and it is worth being specific about why. Hostelworld's review guidelines state that "we only accept reviews from customers who have actually booked and stayed at a property booked through our website". A great many travel and retail sites accept reviews from anybody with an account; requiring a completed, verified stay is a meaningfully higher bar, and with 13.7 million reviews collected over more than two decades the sample sizes on individual hostels are large.

Scores are a weighted average across six categories — cleanliness, location, staff, atmosphere, facilities and security — with cleanliness, location and staff carrying more influence than the rest. Hostelworld's own advice on reading them is sensible: treat 50 to 200 reviews as showing "reliable trends emerging", 200 to 1,000 as "strong consistency" and 1,000 or more as "long-term trustworthiness", and "scan the last 10 reviews for the most accurate snapshot", because a hostel under new management can turn in either direction faster than an average will show.

The rules around all of this changed on 7 April 2025, when the consumer protection provisions of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 came into force. Posting or commissioning fake reviews is now explicitly banned, concealed incentivised reviews with it, and the Competition and Markets Authority's guidance of 4 April 2025 requires businesses that publish reviews to take "reasonable and proportionate" steps to detect and deal with them, with any incentive "made apparent". Penalties reach 10% of global turnover. In its first year under those powers the CMA opened investigations into 14 businesses, secured £760,000 of consumer refunds and £4.7 million of fines, issued 157 advisory and warning letters, wrote to 54 firms about reviews and opened five investigations off the back of it. A platform that only accepts reviews from verified stays starts that regime in a comfortable position.

sections.heading: Two guarantees, and the conditions under each
sections.html:
The Booking Guarantee covers the specific nightmare of arriving to find no reservation. If "the property reception agent has no record of your reservation", Hostelworld credits your account with the deposit you paid plus "US$50 extra for the inconvenience caused". Three conditions matter. You must contact the company within 48 hours of arrival through the guarantee form. The money arrives as account credit, not cash, and must be used within 6 months. And it does not apply where a listed property "ceases operation due to unforeseen circumstances" — a hostel that has shut down being, on the face of it, one of the commoner reasons a reception desk cannot find your name.

The best price promise says that "if you find a booking cheaper on any other website, we'll refund you the difference". You have 24 hours from making the booking to claim, and the rival deal must be an exact itinerary match on property, room type, dates and conditions. Blind bookings, membership and loyalty rates, rewards programmes, special promotions and offline group bookings are excluded. The timing is the part to note: the claim "will only be processed after you have checked out of the property and we have verified your stay", with payment by bank transfer within up to 14 days after checkout. You are being reimbursed weeks after the trip, not undercharged at the time.

Neither promise is unusual by the standards of online travel, and having both in writing is better than having neither. They are worth reading as insurance against specific failures rather than as a general assurance.

sections.heading: Elevate, third-party listings and how the results are ordered
sections.html:
The clearest gap between what the company tells investors and what it tells travellers concerns the ordering of search results. In its 2025 results Hostelworld described "the successful launch of ‘Elevate’, our marketplace monetisation tool, which increased our commission rate to 16.7% in H2", and the half-year statement credited Elevate with lifting the rate to 17.7%. What Elevate does mechanically is not explained in either document, and nothing on the consumer site sets out how hostels are ranked, whether a property that pays more appears higher, or how a traveller would tell.

That question has history in this sector. On 13 September 2019 the Competition and Markets Authority concluded action against the accommodation booking industry: 31 firms in total, six of them under formal enforcement — Booking.com, Expedia, Agoda, Hotels.com, ebookers and trivago — on practices including "pressure selling, misleading discount claims and the effect that commission has on how hotels are ordered", together with commitments to stop "giving a false impression of a room's popularity" and to "always display the full cost of a room upfront". Hostelworld was not among the 31 and those undertakings do not bind it. The 2024 Act does bind everybody, and drip pricing — showing one price and adding fees as the customer proceeds — is one of the practices it prohibits.

A second change is worth knowing about for a different reason. In December 2025 Hostelworld launched third-party inventory across 50 destinations and has since extended it to around 18,000, with engagement "strongest on searches with fewer direct Hostelworld results". Some of what a search now returns is accommodation sourced through another supplier rather than a hostel the company deals with directly. That is a reasonable answer to thin results in an unfamiliar city; it does mean the review base and the relationship behind a listing are not uniform across the page, and the site does not label which is which.

sections.heading: Booking from Britain, under Irish law
sections.html:
The corporate structure is more British than the Dublin address suggests, and it is worth a paragraph because it decides who you would be dealing with. The contracting party is Hostelworld.com Limited, registered at 8 Harcourt Street, Dublin 2, D02 AF58, VAT number 9689072B, and the terms are "governed by the laws of Ireland". Above it sits Hostelworld Group plc, company 09818705, incorporated on 9 October 2015 and registered at 1 Chamberlain Square Cs, Birmingham B3 3AX, under SIC code 64209, with accounts last made up to 31 December 2025. A third company in the group carries the history of a rival: Hostelworld Services Limited, company 02841908, was incorporated on 3 August 1993 as MBO MBI Limited, traded as HostelBookers.com Limited from 2 July 2003, and took its present name on 26 May 2015.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the liability cap. Hostelworld's terms limit its "maximum aggregate liability to you" to "the value of the booking fee that has been paid for that booking" — not the deposit, not the room price, the booking fee, which is the one number the terms never put an amount against. Second, there is no ombudsman. Accommodation booking is not a regulated financial service, so the Financial Ombudsman Service has no jurisdiction over it, and no equivalent scheme exists for travel platforms.

If a booking goes badly, the realistic routes are the hostel itself, the Booking Guarantee where it applies, and your card provider. Note one detail before assuming the last of those covers you: section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 bites where the cash price of the item is more than £100 and no more than £30,000, and a deposit of €14 or €15 on a cheap bed sits well below that floor. A chargeback through the card scheme is the more likely mechanism, and the terms on those vary by issuer, so confirm the position with your own bank rather than taking it as read.

pros: Around 17,000 hostels in more than 180 countries, with 13.7 million reviews behind the scores
Reviews come only from people who booked and stayed through the site, which is a stricter test than most travel platforms apply
A small deposit holds the bed; the bulk of the money stays in your pocket until you arrive
Free cancellation is widely available, and the deposit is returned in full inside the hostel's window
Audited, published accounts — you can read the company's revenue, margins and cash position for yourself
The Booking Guarantee pays your deposit back as credit plus US$50 if the hostel has no record of your reservation
Six rated categories per property, weighted towards cleanliness, location and staff
App handles 63% of bednights and shows traveller profiles and chat for the hostel you have booked
cons: The booking fee is never given an amount anywhere in the terms, yet it is non-refundable in every circumstance and is also the ceiling on Hostelworld's liability to you — “limited solely to the value of the booking fee that has been paid for that booking”.

The deposit percentage is not stated in the booking terms either. A company blog post says “about 12-15%” while the group reported an effective commission rate of 17.7% for the first half of 2026, and nothing reconciles the two figures.

Hostels can now pay to improve their position through Elevate, the company's marketplace monetisation tool, and nothing on the consumer site explains how properties are ordered in search results or whether paying more moves one up the page.

Your contract is with the hostel and the terms are governed by Irish law, so a dispute about the stay is not something Hostelworld resolves for you and there is no UK ombudsman scheme covering accommodation bookings.
The best price promise is only paid after you have checked out and the stay has been verified, by bank transfer up to 14 days later — and the claim itself must be made within 24 hours of booking.

The Booking Guarantee pays a site credit rather than cash, it expires after 6 months, and it does not apply where a property “ceases operation due to unforeseen circumstances”, which is one of the likelier ways a booking fails.
The HOSCAR awards are described only as “voted for by YOU”, with no published methodology, no minimum review count and no threshold a hostel must clear to be eligible.
Since December 2025 some results are third-party inventory rather than hostels Hostelworld deals with directly, and the search page does not flag which is which.
verdict: For finding a hostel bed in a city you do not know, Hostelworld is hard to beat: 17,000 properties, 13.7 million reviews written only by people who actually stayed, and a deposit small enough that a change of plan costs you very little. Read it as a directory with a payment system attached rather than as your counterparty, because that is exactly what the terms say it is. Take the free cancellation rate over the non-refundable one unless the discount is large, note the hostel's own deadline rather than assuming 24 hours, and carry enough cash for the balance and the city tax. The things worth grumbling about — an unnamed booking fee that also caps the company's liability, a commission rate climbing from 15.3% to 17.7% in eighteen months, and no published explanation of how the search results are ordered — are worth knowing before you book, not reasons to book somewhere else.

faqs.q: How much does Hostelworld take when I book?
faqs.a: You pay a deposit at the time of booking, which Hostelworld's own guide describes as "about 12-15% of the total cost". The group's accounts put its effective commission rate at 17.7% for the first half of 2026, up from 15.8% a year earlier, on an average booking of €14.90. The rest of the bed price is paid directly to the hostel when you arrive.

faqs.q: Can I cancel and get the deposit back?
faqs.a: Usually, if you are inside the hostel's window. Hostelworld says deadlines are "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date, unless otherwise stated", and individual properties set their own — 72 hours is common. Non-refundable rates charge the full booking value. There is no statutory 14-day cooling-off period, because regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 excludes accommodation booked for a specific date.

faqs.q: What happens if the hostel has no record of my booking?
faqs.a: The Booking Guarantee credits your account with the deposit plus US$50, provided you contact Hostelworld within 48 hours of arrival and the claim is verified. The credit expires 6 months after it is applied, and the guarantee does not cover a property that has ceased operating.

faqs.q: Are the reviews on Hostelworld reliable?
faqs.a: They are drawn from a narrower pool than most: only customers who booked and stayed through the site may leave one, and there are 13.7 million of them. Scores are a weighted average across cleanliness, location, staff, atmosphere, facilities and security. Read the most recent 10 alongside the headline number, and treat a property with fewer than 50 reviews as unproven.

faqs.q: Do I need anything besides the balance when I arrive?
faqs.a: Bring cash for city tax, which hostels must collect and which is not in the price you compared: roughly €1 to €4 per person per night in Italy, €0.50 to €4 in Spain and around 12.5% of the booking total in the Netherlands. Towels at €1 to €3, lockers at €1 to €3 a day and late check-in at €5 to €25 are common extras.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong with the stay?
faqs.a: The hostel, in the first instance — your contract for the accommodation is with the property, not with Hostelworld, and the platform's terms are governed by Irish law. There is no ombudsman for accommodation bookings, and Hostelworld caps its own liability at the value of the booking fee. A card chargeback is often the practical fallback; section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 will rarely help, because it applies only where the cash price exceeds £100.

title: HotelPlanner: Group Hotel Rates and How the Bidding Works
meta_title: HotelPlanner Review: How Group Hotel Bidding Cuts Rates
meta_description: HotelPlanner lists London rooms from $60 and puts its average three-star London group rate at $111.36. How the bidding works, and what the terms say.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised London room, per night
headline.value: $60 a night — HotelPlanner's own London lead-in price (Travelodge London Dagenham East), quoted in US dollars, checked 22 September 2026

intro:
HotelPlanner's London hotel list opens at $60 a night — a Travelodge out at Dagenham East — and the company puts the average three-star London group rate it booked over the past 365 days at $111.36. Both figures come from HotelPlanner's own city pages, read on 22 September 2026. The business has been selling rooms since 2003, says it works with 100,000 group-friendly hotels, and runs its European operation from Level 5a Maple House on Tottenham Court Road with a UK freephone line on 0800 808 5603.

One thing is worth knowing before you click, because it decides whether the site is any use to you. For a single room, HotelPlanner behaves like any other booking site: pick a hotel, pay, done. For a group it does not sell you anything at all — you fill in a form, a planner is assigned, hotels bid against each other for your block, and you compare and haggle online before choosing. The lowest-rate guarantee attaches at nine rooms a night or more, and on most group bookings you settle up with the hotel directly rather than with HotelPlanner. If you want an instant confirmation for a Friday night, that is a different product from the one this page is about.

The company you are dealing with is Reservations Group, LLC of 11780 U.S. Highway One, Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, trading as HotelPlanner.com. The UK arm, HotelPlanner Limited, is company 08235172, incorporated on 1 October 2012. One genuinely good thing sits in the small print for British readers: where most booking platforms cap what they will pay you at the amount you handed over, HotelPlanner's terms cap its liability to a UK or EU consumer at the greater of three times the value of the booking or €2,500. That is a more generous ceiling than its larger rivals publish.

sections.heading: Nine rooms is the line, and crossing it changes the price you are shown
sections.html:
Almost every hotel site sells you the rate the hotel has loaded that morning. HotelPlanner's group side runs the transaction backwards: your requirement goes out to matching properties, they quote against it, and the quotes land in one place where you can push back on them. The company describes the result plainly enough — "Our private rates provided to you are typically lower than online rates offered to the general public" — and the process costs nothing to start: "Pay the hotel separately. It's FREE with no obligations!"

The guarantee that sits behind the marketing is narrower than the headline, and reading it is worth a minute. HotelPlanner says it "will meet or beat any price on your group's travel needs when reserving 9 rooms per night or more at a hotel of equal or greater quality". Three conditions, all of them doing work: nine rooms, per night, and a like-for-like property. The free rooms offered to whoever is organising the trip carry their own qualifier — they apply "to participating hotels only and required group size may vary among hotels" — so the coordinator's free bed is a hotel-by-hotel matter, not a HotelPlanner policy.

The two averages the site publishes give you a sense of what actually clears. London three-star group rooms averaged $111.36 over the past year and Manchester $90.30, which puts the advertised "up to 70%" saving in proportion: it is a ceiling drawn from somebody's best week, not a number to budget on. Set those averages against the $60 London lead-in on the individual side of the site and the group route is not automatically cheaper per room — it is cheaper for a block of rooms that a hotel would rather fill in one go than one at a time.

sections.heading: The commission is printed, which is rarer than it sounds
sections.html:
Booking platforms tend to treat what they earn as a trade secret. HotelPlanner puts it in its terms: a 10% referral fee on business that actualises, dropping to 7% for hotels that take a preferred membership, and rising to 12% where a travel agent brings the group. Agents who register get "a flat rate equal to a 10% referral fee on hotel room revenue produced", paid once HotelPlanner has itself been paid by the hotel, and the hotel's own fee falls due within 21 days of the group's departure date.

That tells a group organiser something useful. The bids you receive already have a commission of up to a tenth built into them, and the hotel knows it — which is the honest explanation for why a direct call to the same property sometimes beats the platform, and why it often does not, since the hotel is paying for a sales channel it would otherwise have to staff itself. Publishing the rate is a point in the company's favour, and it is the sort of thing a reader can check against any quote they are given.

There is one charge pointed the other way. Cancel a non-refundable booking and HotelPlanner says it "will honor your request for a refund if full waiver is obtained, but reserves the right to charge you 3% transaction fee". Getting a hotel to waive a non-refundable rate is a favour, and a 3% fee for extracting it is not unreasonable — but it is money you will not see coming unless you have read that clause.

sections.heading: A Florida company with a London office, and a fair bit of history
sections.html:
Reservations Group has been at this for 23 years, and the scale it claims now is substantial: around 2,000 call centre staff, 36,000 destinations, more than 1 million groups booked and $2bn of projected gross hotel sales for 2025, on revenue growth the company puts at 351% since 2022. It placed 917th on the Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing American private companies announced on 18 August 2026.

It came close to being a public company and is not one. In August 2021 HotelPlanner and Reservations.com agreed a three-way merger with Astrea Acquisition Corp, a blank-cheque vehicle, at an enterprise value of $567.1m, with more than $120m of cash expected onto the balance sheet and 2022 revenue forecast at around $170m. The deal was called off on 14 February 2022, the three parties saying only that terminating it "is the best path forward for all parties". No reason was given then and none has been given since, so the projections in that filing are the last detailed financial picture anybody outside the company has had.

The UK entity is smaller than the London address suggests. HotelPlanner Limited files total exemption full accounts — the small-company regime, which means a balance sheet and no profit and loss account, so no turnover, no booking volume and no UK customer count is on the public record. Its registered office moved to Tottenham Court Road on 30 April 2025, and its SIC code, 82990, is the catch-all for business support services rather than anything travel-specific.

sections.heading: It quietly runs other people's group desks
sections.html:
Type a group request into Hotels.com and the page you land on is not run by Hotels.com. Its group travel terms name "Reservations Group Incorporated, operating under the name HotelPlanner" at the same Palm Beach Gardens address, and cap the hotel voucher rebate on offer at $250 per group stay. Expedia runs a separate group booking domain on the same pattern. The company also says more than 4,000 affiliates use its technology, and it has held the group hotel contract for sports and tourism bodies including the United Soccer League and the LPGA.

For a reader comparing group tools, that matters more than any marketing claim on this page: several of the "different" group booking forms on the internet are the same engine wearing different clothes. Going straight to HotelPlanner removes a layer, and the quotes you get back are drawn from the same pool either way.

sections.heading: The phones are answered by software now
sections.html:
HotelPlanner was an early and unusually committed adopter of voice AI. It announced an end-to-end AI voice reservationist in late 2024 handling around 10,000 calls a day in 15 languages, trained on 8 million recorded customer calls, and launched the product commercially as Reservations.ai on 22 October 2025. By that launch the company said the AI was driving 40% of HotelPlanner bookings, working alongside the human call centre rather than replacing it — co-founder John Prince's framing was that "our human call centre team can look after customers with the more complicated and higher value bookings".

The practical reading for a group organiser: a straightforward block of rooms will likely be quoted and confirmed by a machine, quickly, at any hour. Anything with a wrinkle in it — a split stay, a late rooming list, a contract the venue wants changing — is where you should ask for the human planner the site promises to assign you, and where you will find out how good that assignment is.

sections.heading: What a UK group booking is actually worth
sections.html:
Group hotel bookings in Britain are largely business events, and the sector is bigger than most people assume. The Culture, Media and Sport Committee's report of 6 July 2026 put UK business events at £33.6 billion a year, over half of the £61.7 billion generated by the wider events industry, and noted that 38% of business events take place outside London. Domestic conferences and meetings alone ran to 1.08 million events with 95.4 million delegates and £19.3 billion of value in 2024.

The inbound side is where the money per head sits. VisitBritain counts 6.8 million inbound business visits in 2024 worth £5.9 billion, of which the meetings and events segment accounts for 2.6 million visits and £2.8 billion. A delegate arriving from outside Europe spends an average of £1,824; one from within Europe £872; a UK delegate £328. The committee also flagged the uncomfortable backdrop — Britain ranked 113th of 119 countries on travel and tourism cost competitiveness in 2024 — which is the reason a hotel would rather discount a block of nine rooms than watch the conference go to Lisbon.

sections.heading: Where the small print sends a British customer
sections.html:
The terms you accept are Florida's. Disputes "shall be resolved exclusively through final and binding arbitration in Palm Beach County, Florida, rather than in court", with a class action waiver attached and a window of 30 days from first accessing the site in which to reject arbitration in writing. UK and EU consumers are treated better than most — they are "encouraged but not required" to arbitrate — but the alternative the terms point them at is the European Commission's Online Dispute Resolution platform, and that platform was switched off on 20 July 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/3228. It had not covered UK consumers since Brexit in any case. The signpost leads nowhere, and there is no named UK or EU alternative dispute resolution scheme in its place.

Nor is there a trade body standing behind the booking. A hotel booked on its own is not a package under the Package Travel Regulations, so there is no ATOL certificate and no ABTA bonding, and no ABTA membership number appears anywhere on HotelPlanner's site. On the group side the money usually goes to the hotel rather than the platform, which is convenient until something goes wrong: a company that never took your payment has very little it can refund, and the generous-looking liability cap is measured against a booking value it may never have handled.

One fee deserves reading twice. The terms describe "Packaged Bundled Costs" as "a mandatory charge retained by ResGroup as compensation for those services and benefits", included in the total price displayed. Including it in the displayed total is the right side of the law — showing a price that grows at the checkout has been prohibited since the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024's consumer provisions came into force on 7 April 2025, backed by fines of up to 10% of global turnover. But the clause never says how large the charge is or what it buys, so the one number a customer would want from it is absent. For the record, HotelPlanner was not among the firms the Competition and Markets Authority took action against over hotel booking displays in September 2019.

sections.heading: Three numbers on the same website that do not match
sections.html:
The group threshold changes depending on which page you are standing on. The home page asks "Need 5+ rooms per night?" and then promises "Guaranteed Lowest Group Rates" when "reserving 10 rooms per night or more"; the London, Manchester and Group Rate pages all say 9. Three minimums, one company, and no way for a reader to know which applies to them until a planner tells them.

The inventory count moves about too. The home page title offers "250K+ Hotels", the body of the same page says "100,000 group friendly hotels worldwide", the travel agent page says "over 100,000 hotels and meeting venues", and the partnership copy says "1M+ properties". Those may all be true of different things — directly contracted hotels, group-capable hotels, total bookable properties — but nothing on the site explains which is which.

Then there is the matter of the register. HotelPlanner Limited received a first Gazette notice for compulsory strike-off on 4 March 2025. It filed two years of overdue accounts — for 2023 and 2024 — on 28 March, and the strike-off action was discontinued on 29 March 2025. The company was never in any danger of vanishing, since the trading entity is American and the UK company is an office rather than the till. It is still a fair thing to know about the London address printed on the contact page, and the accounts filed to clear it tell a reader nothing, because the small-company regime does not require a profit and loss account.

pros: Group pricing is genuinely negotiated rather than listed — hotels bid for the block and you can push back on the quotes online, at no cost and with no obligation
The commission is published: 10% as standard, 7% for preferred hotels and 12% on travel agent bookings, which lets you judge any quote you are given
The liability cap for UK and EU consumers is the greater of three times the booking value or €2,500 — more generous than the 'what you paid us' cap most booking platforms use
Real UK contact points: a London office on Tottenham Court Road, a group freephone on 0800 808 5603 and a 24-hour line
23 years of trading, around 2,000 call centre staff and over 1 million groups booked — this is an established operator, not a shell
The AI booking line answers quickly at any hour and handles around 10,000 calls a day in 15 languages
cons: The dispute clause sends you to Florida: binding arbitration in Palm Beach County under Florida law, with a class action waiver and only 30 days from your first visit to opt out

The alternative dispute route offered to UK and EU consumers is the EU Online Dispute Resolution platform, which was shut down on 20 July 2025 and never covered UK consumers after Brexit — no replacement scheme is named
The group minimum is stated as 5, 9 and 10 rooms per night on different pages of the same website, and the inventory as 100,000, 250,000 and 1 million properties
'Packaged Bundled Costs' is described as a mandatory charge retained by the company, but the terms never say how much it is or what it pays for
On most group bookings you pay the hotel directly, so the platform has taken no money from you and has correspondingly little to give back if the booking fails
Prices on the UK city pages are quoted in US dollars, and no ABTA membership or ATOL cover applies to a hotel-only booking
The UK company files small-company accounts with no profit and loss account, and picked up a first Gazette strike-off notice on 4 March 2025 before clearing two years of late filings
verdict: HotelPlanner is a specialist doing something the big booking sites do badly: putting a block of nine or more rooms out to competitive bid and letting the organiser haggle. It has been at it since 2003, it publishes the commission it takes, and it quietly runs the group desks behind several household-name travel brands. The reservations are about paperwork rather than competence — Florida arbitration, a dead European dispute link, a mandatory charge of unstated size, and a group threshold the site states three different ways. For a wedding block, a conference or a team trip it is well worth putting a request through and seeing what comes back, since it costs nothing to ask. For one room on one night, a straightforward booking site will serve you better.

faqs.q: How many rooms do I need before HotelPlanner is worth using?
faqs.a: The lowest-rate guarantee attaches at nine rooms per night or more at a hotel of equal or greater quality, which is the figure given on the city and Group Rate pages. The home page separately invites enquiries from five rooms up and elsewhere quotes ten, so the safe reading is that five will get you a quote and nine is where the guarantee bites. Below that you are better off on the individual side of the site, where London rooms start at $60 a night.

faqs.q: Do I pay HotelPlanner or the hotel?
faqs.a: On group bookings the usual arrangement is that you settle with the hotel directly — the site's own words are "Pay the hotel separately". HotelPlanner is paid by the hotel afterwards, at 10% of the room revenue as standard, 7% for preferred-member properties and 12% where a travel agent is involved, due within 21 days of the group's departure. Individual reservations made through the site are paid for in the usual way at the time of booking.

faqs.q: What protection do I have if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: A hotel booked on its own is not a package, so there is no ATOL certificate and no ABTA bonding. HotelPlanner's terms cap its liability to a UK or EU consumer at the greater of three times the booking value or €2,500, which is better than most platforms offer, but they also route disputes to arbitration in Palm Beach County, Florida under Florida law. The alternative route the terms name for European consumers, the EU Online Dispute Resolution platform, closed on 20 July 2025. If you paid by credit card, the usual UK card protections still apply to your own payment.

faqs.q: Is the 'up to 70%' saving real?
faqs.a: Treat it as a ceiling rather than an expectation. The numbers HotelPlanner publishes itself are more useful: its average three-star London group rate over the 365 days to 22 September 2026 was $111.36, and Manchester was $90.30. The saving on any particular block depends on how badly the hotel wants to fill those nights, which is the whole point of putting the request out to bid.

faqs.q: Who actually runs HotelPlanner?
faqs.a: Reservations Group, LLC of Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, trading as HotelPlanner.com and operating since 2003. The UK arm is HotelPlanner Limited, company number 08235172, incorporated on 1 October 2012 and registered at Level 5a Maple House, 149 Tottenham Court Road, London W1T 7NF. The group also powers the group booking services of some larger travel brands, and it agreed and then abandoned a US stock market listing through a $567.1m merger with Astrea Acquisition Corp, terminated on 14 February 2022.

title: HPI Check Review: The Register Behind Everyone Else's Car Check
meta_title: HPI Check Review: What £19.99 Buys and the £30,000 Cover
meta_description: HPI Check costs £19.99 for 80+ data points, a £30,000 guarantee and the National Mileage Register. What it finds, what it misses and where it is cheaper.
intro:
HPI has been running the same register since 1938, when it produced what its own corporate timeline calls “Britain’s first ever vehicle provenance check”. That is 88 years of finance houses, insurers and the police filing entries against vehicle identities, and it is the reason “doing an HPI check” became the phrase people use for the whole exercise. The trading company is HPI Limited, registered in England under number 04068979 and incorporated on 6 September 2000, with its registered office at 8a Platform, New Station Street, Leeds LS1 4JB. It is owned by HPI Holding Limited (06765994) and has been part of Solera since 2008; Solera bought the valuation business cap in 2014 and merged the two into cap hpi in 2015, so the trade pricing book and the consumer provenance check now sit under one roof.

The consumer product comes in three sizes. The full hpi check® is £19.99 and covers what HPI describes as “80+ in-depth data points” — outstanding finance, stolen markers, insurance write-off category, previous keeper count, scrappage, logbook and VIN verification, mileage discrepancies, plate changes, import and export records, MOT history and a valuation. A Basic Check is £9.99 and a MultiCheck is £29.99 for three full checks. The full check carries a £30,000 guarantee that runs for two years from the date of the check.

The scale behind it is the part worth knowing before you spend anything. HPI says it holds “over 7 million current finance agreements”, that “each year 150,000 vehicle thefts are recorded by insurers”, and that its check “uncovers more than 2,000 insurance write-offs every day”. It also operates the National Mileage Register, and reckons 1 in 11 vehicles on its database carries a mileage discrepancy. Those are the four things a used car can be hiding, and one company has been collecting all four of them for longer than most of the cars on the road have existed.

sections.heading: Six registers, one report
sections.html:
An hpi check® is not one database. It is a query run across several, and knowing which is which tells you how much weight each answer deserves. HPI names the DVLA for registration and keeper data, the Police National Computer for stolen markers, finance houses for outstanding agreements, insurers through the Motor Insurance Anti-Fraud and Theft Register for write-offs, the SMMT for technical specification, and its own National Mileage Register for odometer readings.

The finance and write-off registers are the two you cannot get anywhere else, and they are also the two that depend entirely on somebody else choosing to file an entry. A lender that does not register an agreement leaves no trace for HPI to find; an insurer that has not yet notified a total loss leaves the category blank. HPI is candid enough about this in its own small print, saying that because the information “is aggregated from various sources, we cannot accept any liability for the accuracy of content” and that visitors “are strongly encouraged to independently verify the information before acting”. A clear report means nothing has been filed, which is a different statement from nothing having happened.

The mileage register is HPI’s own asset and the one it has built for longest. Its corporate timeline records the National Mileage Register passing 150 million readings in 2012. Readings come from MOT tests, service records, finance and insurance transactions, so a car that has spent years off the road or out of the country produces gaps rather than lies — the register can only show what somebody wrote down.

sections.heading: The £9.99 version leaves out the two things you were worried about
sections.html:
The Basic Check at £9.99 is half the price of the full report and, on HPI’s own description, it “won’t benefit from our guarantee and elements such as mileage discrepancies and write off details will not be included”. Read that against the company’s own headline figures — 2,000 write-offs uncovered a day, 1 in 11 vehicles carrying a mileage discrepancy — and the £10 saving removes the two checks the numbers say are most likely to catch something.

The gap between the two products is really about the guarantee. Only the full check is backed, so the Basic Check is a data lookup with no financial promise attached. If the point of paying is to have someone stand behind the answer, the Basic Check is not the product doing that job, and HPI does not pretend otherwise.

The MultiCheck at £29.99 works out at £10.00 a check and is the only sensible option if you are shortlisting more than one car, which most buyers are. Two full checks bought separately cost £39.98, so the third is effectively free plus £9.99 back in change.

sections.heading: What the £30,000 actually promises
sections.html:
The guarantee is the product, and it is worth reading rather than assuming. HPI’s terms set the maximum at “£30,000 where you have supplied us with the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), Vehicle Registration Mark (VRM)”, and it covers losses arising from inaccurate information about write-offs, insurance total loss, or a failure to acquire good title. Claims can be submitted for “two years from the date of your HPI Check”.

The write-off limb is capped separately and much lower: “50% of the market value of the vehicle, or £15,000, whichever is the lower”. On a £12,000 car that is £6,000, not £30,000. The headline figure applies to the title limb, where the whole purchase price can be at stake.

Then come the exclusions, and there are several. The guarantee does not cover the vehicle’s description, its value, its mileage or the accuracy of its documents. Vehicles with a recorded mileage discrepancy are excluded, as are vehicles bought more than 30% below retail market value, vehicles without a valid MOT certificate, and “Q” prefix or suffix registrations. Motor traders and anyone buying for profit are outside it entirely. You must also have supplied the VIN and the V5C details and completed the verification before you buy — a check run the morning after the money changed hands is not a covered check.

Taken together, the exclusions describe a careful private buyer paying a fair price for a roadworthy car with clean paperwork. That is exactly the buyer least likely to need the guarantee, which is how most indemnities work, but it means the bargain-hunter buying a cheap car at a keen price — the person with most to lose — has quietly stepped outside the cover.

sections.heading: A 1964 Act already protects private buyers, and nobody mentions it
sections.html:
HPI’s finance pages say that if you buy a vehicle with an outstanding agreement on it “you’re in danger of losing both the vehicle and the money you paid for it”. For a trade buyer that is accurate. For a private buyer it is not the whole story, because Part III of the Hire-Purchase Act 1964 has said otherwise for 62 years.

Section 27(2) provides that where a vehicle still subject to hire purchase or conditional sale is sold to a private purchaser, and “he is a purchaser of the motor vehicle in good faith without notice of the hire-purchase or conditional sale agreement”, that disposition “shall have effect as if the creditor’s title to the vehicle has been vested in the debtor immediately before that disposition”. In plain terms, you get good title and the finance company’s claim is against the person who sold the car, not against you. Section 27(3) extends the same protection to the first private purchaser where the car passed through a dealer first.

Two conditions carry all the weight. The buyer must be a private purchaser — a motor trader or finance company gets nothing from the section — and must be acting without notice. That second phrase is the one worth pausing over, because a check that reveals outstanding finance gives you notice of it. Run the check, see the marker, buy the car anyway, and you have argued yourself out of the statutory protection you would otherwise have had. The check is therefore most valuable as a reason to walk away, and least valuable as something to note and ignore.

None of that makes the finance check pointless. It saves you a fight you would rather not have, it protects you from a seller who cannot settle, and it matters enormously if you are buying through a business. It does mean the risk being described in the marketing is larger than the risk the law actually leaves sitting with an honest private buyer.

sections.heading: The logbook loan is the hole the law never filled
sections.html:
There is one form of secured lending where the 1964 Act gives no help at all, and the check earns its price. A logbook loan is a bill of sale under Victorian legislation, not a hire purchase agreement, so section 27 does not touch it. The Law Commission put the consequence bluntly in its work on the subject: “as the loan follows the vehicle, buyers may lose cars bought in good faith”, and it recorded a case of a van repossessed from a buyer who had done nothing wrong and lost both the van and the money.

The Commission also measured the growth of the practice — bills of sale rose from under 3,000 in 2001 to over 37,000 in 2015 — and published a full report in September 2016 with 34 recommendations, including repealing the bills of sale legislation, a new Goods Mortgages Act, and express protection for good-faith private buyers. That protection has not arrived. Until it does, the logbook loan marker on an hpi check® is the single line on the report with no legal safety net behind it, and HPI includes it in the full check.

sections.heading: Two government services answer part of the question for nothing
sections.html:
Before paying anyone, it is worth knowing exactly what the state gives away. GOV.UK’s MOT history service shows every test result for cars, motorcycles and vans since 2005 — pass or fail, the mileage recorded at each test, failure items, advisories and the test location — with HGV, trailer and bus records from 2018 and Northern Ireland from 2017. All you need is the registration.

The DVLA vehicle enquiry service adds, free, the current tax rate and expiry, SORN status, MOT expiry, date of first registration, the last V5C issue date, year of manufacture, type approval category, weight, engine size, fuel type and CO2 emissions. Keeper details are the one thing you cannot get online — DVLA requires a written request for information about a current or previous registered keeper.

Between them, those two free services cover the mileage story as far as the MOT record goes, and the identity and tax position of the car. HPI itself runs a free MOT history lookup and says of the wider product that a comprehensive check “isn’t something that can be offered for free”, warning that “some less reputable companies use our well-recognised name to attract customers to their own, often inferior, products”. On the four things only the paid check can see — finance, stolen markers, write-off category and mileage readings from outside the MOT record — that is a fair claim.

The write-off category is worth understanding before you read it. The ABI’s Code of Practice for the Categorisation of Motorised Vehicle Salvage sets the four letters: A is scrap, B is break for parts, S is structurally damaged but repairable, and N is non-structural damage. The ABI updated the code in May 2025, its first revision since 2019, adding guidance on electric and hybrid vehicles, megacasting and reusable components. It remains a voluntary framework, which is another reason a blank field is not the same as a clean history.

sections.heading: The identical report costs £14.99 with somebody else’s badge on it
sections.html:
This is the awkward part, and it is verifiable in about two minutes. The AA’s vehicle check site carries the line “Powered by HPI”, sells a single check at £14.99 and a MultiCheck at £29.99, describes the report as outstanding finance, stolen markers, insurance write-offs, V5C and VIN match plus “more than 72 other pieces of information”, and answers its phone on 0113 222 2012 — a Leeds number, which is where HPI sits.

The RAC does the same. Its car data check is also “Powered by HPI”, at £14.99 for the full check, £9.98 for a basic one and £29.97 for a multi-check, carrying the same “£30,000 data guarantee (on qualifying claims)” valid for two years, and throwing in up to £35 of RAC Shop vouchers on the full check and up to £55 on the multi. Parkers runs a fourth badge on the same engine, stating that it “is partnered with award winning vehicle history experts, HPI”.

So the same underlying report, with the same guarantee behind it, is £19.99 from the company that compiles it and £14.99 from two motoring organisations that license it — £5.00, or 25%, more expensive at source. The MultiCheck is the exception: £29.99 at HPI against £29.97 at the RAC is a two-pence difference and not worth crossing the road for. If you only need one check, buying direct from HPI is the dearest of the routes on offer, and that is not a small point on a £20 purchase.

sections.heading: Where HPI’s own pages disagree, and who you complain to
sections.html:
Two of HPI’s own consumer pages give different sizes for the same register. The sample report on hpicheck.com states that “HPI operates the National Mileage Register® (NMR), containing over 200 million recorded mileages”, while the mileage page on home.hpicheck.com says it “contains over 369 million readings”. Neither carries a date, so there is no way to tell which is current and which is stale copy. The same pair disagrees about the cost of clocking: £100 million a year on one page, “over £800 million annually” on the other, alongside a claim that clocking “can add up to £4,000 to the price of a used car”. The “1 in 3” fraction also does double duty — one page says one in three cars checked “is still on finance” and another says one in three has “some form of hidden history”, which cannot both be the same measurement.

The check terms are dated in a different way. They tell you that if HPI provides the information before the cancellation period ends “under The Consumer Protection Distance Selling Regulations 2000, then your right to cancel will end as soon as we provide the Information”. Those regulations were revoked and replaced by the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, in force since 13 June 2014. The practical outcome is much the same — you lose the cancellation right the moment the report appears on screen, which is a few seconds after you pay — but a live consumer contract citing an instrument repealed twelve years ago is not a good look for a company whose business is keeping records current.

Finally, there is no ombudsman here. A vehicle data check is not a regulated financial service, so the Financial Ombudsman Service has no jurisdiction over a dispute about a report, and there is no alternative dispute resolution scheme named in the terms. The site conditions disclaim liability for “any direct, indirect or consequential loss or damage arising from your reliance on any information contained on this website” and submit everything to the exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts. Outside the guarantee, a disputed report is a county court matter, and no independent ratings body publishes a verified score for vehicle data checks the way Defaqto does for insurance. HPI Limited last filed accounts to 31 March 2025, with the next set due by 31 December 2026.

pros: The longest-running vehicle provenance register in Britain, running since 1938
Over 7 million current finance agreements and the National Mileage Register behind one lookup
£30,000 guarantee on the full check, claimable for two years
80+ data points including logbook loans, which carry no statutory protection for buyers
MultiCheck at £29.99 works out at £10.00 a car if you are looking at more than one
Free MOT history lookup on the site with no purchase required
cons: At £19.99 the full check is £5.00 dearer bought direct than the identical HPI-powered report sold by the AA and the RAC at £14.99
The £30,000 headline is capped at 50% of market value or £15,000, whichever is lower, on a write-off claim
The guarantee excludes trade buyers, cars bought more than 30% below retail value, cars without a valid MOT, Q-registrations and any vehicle with a recorded mileage discrepancy
The £9.99 Basic Check drops write-off and mileage data and carries no guarantee at all
HPI's own pages give two sizes for the National Mileage Register (200 million and 369 million readings) and two costs for clocking (£100 million and over £800 million a year), none of them dated
The check terms still cite the Consumer Protection (Distance Selling) Regulations 2000, revoked on 13 June 2014
No ombudsman and no ADR scheme covers a disputed report, and no independent ratings body scores vehicle data checks
A clear report means nothing has been filed by a lender or insurer, which is not the same as nothing having happened
verdict: HPI compiles the register that almost every other vehicle check in Britain is querying, and on the four things a used car can hide — outstanding finance, a stolen marker, a write-off category and a mileage reading from outside the MOT record — there is no free substitute. The £30,000 guarantee is real but narrower than the number suggests, and the exclusions land hardest on the bargain buyer. Read section 27 of the Hire-Purchase Act 1964 before you assume the finance check is the only thing standing between you and losing a car, and check the logbook loan line carefully, because that is the one with no law behind it. If you are buying a single check, the same report carries a £14.99 price under the AA and RAC badges; if you are checking three cars, the £29.99 MultiCheck is the best value HPI sells.

faqs.q: How much does an HPI check cost?
faqs.a: The full hpi check® is £19.99 and covers 80+ data points with a £30,000 guarantee. The Basic Check is £9.99 but excludes write-off and mileage data and carries no guarantee. The MultiCheck is £29.99 for three full checks, or £10.00 each. The same HPI-powered report is sold at £14.99 by the AA and the RAC.

faqs.q: Can I lose a car I bought if it turns out to have finance on it?
faqs.a: Under section 27 of the Hire-Purchase Act 1964, a private purchaser who buys in good faith and without notice of a hire purchase or conditional sale agreement takes good title, and the lender’s claim lies against the seller. Motor traders get no such protection, and neither does anyone who knew about the agreement. A logbook loan is different: it is a bill of sale, section 27 does not apply, and the Law Commission has said buyers “may lose cars bought in good faith”.

faqs.q: What can I check for free?
faqs.a: GOV.UK shows every MOT result since 2005, including the mileage recorded at each test, failure items and advisories. The DVLA vehicle enquiry service gives tax status and rate, SORN, MOT expiry, date of first registration, last V5C issue date, year of manufacture, engine size, fuel type and CO2. Neither shows outstanding finance, stolen markers or write-off category, and keeper details require a written request to DVLA.

faqs.q: How long does the guarantee last and what does it not cover?
faqs.a: Claims can be made for two years from the date of the check. The guarantee does not cover the vehicle’s description, value, mileage or documentation, and excludes vehicles with a recorded mileage discrepancy, purchases more than 30% below retail market value, cars without a valid MOT, “Q” registrations, and anyone buying as a motor trader or for profit. Write-off claims are limited to 50% of market value or £15,000, whichever is lower.

faqs.q: Who owns HPI?
faqs.a: HPI Limited (company 04068979, registered at 8a Platform, New Station Street, Leeds LS1 4JB) is controlled by HPI Holding Limited (06765994) and has been part of Solera since 2008. Solera bought the valuation business cap in 2014 and merged the two operations into cap hpi in 2015. The consumer check dates back to 1938.

title: HSBC Credit Cards Review 2026: Seven Cards, 18.9% to 100.2% APR
meta_title: HSBC Credit Cards: 36 Months at 0% for a 3.09% Fee
meta_description: Seven HSBC credit cards, 18.9% to 100.2% APR, with up to 36 months at 0% on transfers for 3.09%. Rates checked against HSBC's own pages, 4 Oct 2026.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 18.9% to 100.2% variable across seven cards, all but the student card quoted on an assumed £1,200 credit limit

intro:
HSBC's Balance Transfer Credit Card advertises up to 36 months at 0% on a transferred balance for a 3.09% fee, which is £92.70 on a £3,000 debt. Those figures were taken on 4 October 2026 from HSBC's own product pages, and the 36-month window is at the long end of what any UK bank is publishing. There is no annual fee on it, and the minimum income is £6,800 of UK taxable income or pension before tax.

The wider range is seven cards and the rates run a long way: 18.9% on the student card, 24.9% on Purchase Plus, 25.9% on the balance transfer card, 26.9% on Rewards, 29.9% on both Classic and Premier, and 100.2% on the £290-a-year Premier World Elite Mastercard. Five of the seven carry no annual fee. Purchase Plus is the other side of the same coin as the transfer card: up to 24 months at 0% on spending, plus up to 17 months at 0% on transfers at a 3.49% fee. HSBC UK Bank plc is the ring-fenced bank that holds all of it, with 14.5 million retail and wealth customers and more than 23,000 staff.

One rule decides whether any of the 0% offers can help a given reader, and it is worth knowing before applying rather than after. A balance cannot be moved onto an HSBC card from another card issued inside the same group: HSBC's own second-card page states that "You can't transfer balances between two HSBC credit cards, including First Direct or M&S Bank." Transfers also have to be made within 60 days of the account being opened. An HSBC, first direct or M&S Bank balance is therefore the one debt this card cannot rescue, and HSBC counts over 15 million active UK customers.

key_facts.value: HSBC UK Bank plc, Financial Services Register firm reference number 765112, company number 09928412, registered at 1 Centenary Square, Birmingham B1 1HQ

key_facts.value: Seven, five of them with no annual fee

key_facts.value: Up to 36 months on the Balance Transfer Credit Card, 3.09% fee (minimum £5), transfers within 60 days of opening

key_facts.label: Longest 0% on spending
key_facts.value: Up to 24 months on Purchase Plus, which also offers up to 17 months at 0% on transfers at 3.49% (minimum £5)

key_facts.value: 18.9% to 100.2% variable; the top figure is a 29.9% purchase rate plus a £290 annual fee

key_facts.value: £6,800 of annual UK taxable income or pension before tax on the Balance Transfer, Purchase Plus and Rewards cards

key_facts.value: £500 on the balance transfer card and £250 on Classic, against the £1,200 limit assumed in the representative examples

key_facts.value: A maximum of two HSBC UK credit cards, with no new card or limit increase in the previous six months
