sections.heading: Who carries the risk, and who you deal with
sections.html:
Two firms stand behind a Row.co.uk policy. BIG Warranties Limited is the administrator: it takes your money, answers the phone and handles the claim, and it holds firm reference 798998 on the FCA register. The insurer that actually pays is Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (company 01708613, firm reference 202846), part of the Collinson group. Astrenska is not a minor name. Its 2025 solvency report shows gross written premium of £297.2 million, up from £221.4 million the year before, a profit after tax of £4.3 million, and a solvency coverage ratio of 176%, down from 205%. Its book expressly includes “Property Ancillary, Mobile, Gadget and Cycle Insurance products”, so phone cover is core to what it does rather than a sideline.

BIG Warranties itself is worth a moment. Companies House shows it was incorporated on 27 August 2009 as Elite Sky Repairs Limited and took its present name on 10 November 2010, a repair business that grew into a warranty and insurance administrator. Row.co.uk is now one shopfront on a wider range that runs to appliance cover, boiler and home-emergency plans, motor breakdown and even a novelty “Pokédex” gadget policy, all sold from the same Poole office.

sections.heading: Where the £1.49 earns its money back
sections.html:
The premium is genuinely low, so the excess is the figure to read before you buy. Row publishes it plainly, which many rivals do not: £40 where a gadget is covered for £200 or less, £75 where it is covered for more, and £80 for a laptop. On top of that the wording adds a further charge, and this is the part that repays close reading. It states that “an additional £30 excess will be applied for each of the following: loss or theft, international claims, claims within the first three months of the policy start date”. Because those add up, a phone insured for more than £200 that is lost while you are abroad in the second month of cover carries £75 plus three separate £30 charges, a £165 excess before the policy pays a penny; a laptop in the same situation reaches £170. The events that trigger the surcharges, theft, loss and travel, are the ones most people buy the cover for.

Two smaller limits are worth knowing. Accessories are capped at £100 a claim, whatever the phone is worth, and cover for unauthorised calls after a theft runs for only 48 hours from the theft, to a ceiling of £1,000 including VAT.

sections.heading: The rules on what you can insure
sections.html:
Row will only start cover on a device that is under 12 months old at the date of application. That is a narrower door than several phone specialists, which accept handsets up to two or three years old, and it shuts out precisely the ageing phones whose batteries and screens are most likely to fail. Once you are on cover, nothing is paid for a claim in the first 14 days, accidental-damage and breakdown claims are unlimited, but you may claim only once for theft or loss in a policy year.

The family clause is narrower than it first appears. A gadget is covered in an immediate family member’s hands for breakdown and accidental damage, but not for theft or loss, so a phone lent to a partner and then stolen would fall outside that extension. Replacements “may be new or reconditioned units”, so an approved claim will not always return a brand-new handset. Cancelling inside 14 days brings a refund, but an annual policy cancelled later is refunded pro rata less a £30 administration charge, and there is no refund at all once a claim has been made.

sections.heading: The gadget market in the regulator’s numbers
sections.html: There is useful context in the FCA’s general insurance value measures data for 2025, published on 21 July 2026. Across the whole market, the share of gadget premiums paid back out in claims fell from 42% to 36%, one of the steepest drops of any product line, with 7.5 million gadget policies in force after a 5% fall in the year. The figure is about the market, not about Row, and it cuts both ways: cover is getting cheaper to run, which is good for insurers’ margins and less obviously good for buyers. What the release does not give for gadget cover is a claims-acceptance rate, the way it does for motor and home, and the Financial Ombudsman Service does not break out a gadget or mobile-phone uphold rate either, so there is no published benchmark to hold Row’s claims record against. That absence is a fact about the whole product, and worth knowing before you assume any gadget policy is a safe bet.

sections.heading: How much independent evidence there is
sections.html: Row is not rated by Defaqto for gadget cover, and no Which? or Fairer Finance assessment of the product could be found, which is common for this corner of the market but leaves little to lean on. The one independent source that carries it, Smart Money People, scores Row.co.uk gadget insurance 4.51 out of 5, but from 247 reviews last refreshed on 31 March 2019, so the number reflects a policy sold more than seven years ago rather than the cover on offer today. A recent, dated rating would tell a buyer far more, and none exists.

pros: Among the cheapest headline prices on the market, from £1.49 a month, or £1.41 paid annually
One policy can cover several gadgets, with 5% off per extra device up to 15% (20% on an annual plan)
Backed by a sizeable insurer, Astrenska Insurance Limited, which wrote £297.2 million of premium in 2025
Unlimited accidental-damage and breakdown claims across a policy year
Up to 90 days of cover abroad and a replacement aimed within 24 hours of a claim being approved
The standard excess is published on the site, which is more than many phone insurers do
cons: The £30 additional excesses stack: a phone covered for over £200 that is lost abroad in the first three months carries a £165 excess (£170 for a laptop) before the policy pays anything
Cover can only start on a device under 12 months old, shutting out the older phones most likely to need it
No claim is paid in the first 14 days of the policy, and only one theft or loss claim is allowed per year
The family extension covers breakdown and accidental damage only, not theft or loss, and replacements may be reconditioned rather than new
An annual policy cancelled after 14 days is refunded less a £30 administration charge, with no refund at all once a claim has been made
The only independent rating, Smart Money People’s 4.51 from 247 reviews, was last reviewed on 31 March 2019, and there is no Defaqto or Which? assessment
verdict: Row.co.uk is a cheap, broad gadget policy from a small Poole administrator, sitting on the balance sheet of a real insurer in Astrenska. The headline of £1.49 a month is honest as far as it goes, and the multi-gadget discount makes it attractive if you want one policy over several devices. The catch is the excess: the £30 surcharges for theft, loss and travel stack, so the exact claims most people insure against can cost £165 or more before anything is paid, and the 12-month age limit rules the policy out for older handsets. Read the excess table and check your phone’s age before you judge it on price alone.

faqs.q: Who underwrites Row.co.uk phone insurance?
faqs.a: The policy is administered by BIG Warranties Limited (firm reference 798998) and underwritten by Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (company 01708613, firm reference 202846), part of the Collinson group. Astrenska wrote £297.2 million of premium in its 2025 financial year.

faqs.q: What would the excess be if my phone were lost abroad?
faqs.a: For a phone insured for more than £200, the standard excess is £75. The wording adds £30 for a loss or theft claim, £30 for an international claim, and £30 for a claim in the first three months, and these apply separately. A phone lost abroad in the first three months would therefore carry a £165 excess; a laptop, £170.

faqs.q: Can I insure an older phone with Row.co.uk?
faqs.a: No. Cover can only start on a device that is under 12 months old at the date of application. Several phone specialists accept handsets up to two or three years old, so if your phone is older you would need a different provider.

faqs.q: Is my family covered under my policy?
faqs.a: A gadget is covered while in the possession of an immediate family member, but only for breakdown and accidental damage. Theft or loss while the device is with a family member is not covered by that extension.

faqs.q: How quickly is a claim settled?
faqs.a: Row aims to get a replacement to your door within 24 hours of approving a claim, or to complete a repair within about three working days. Replacements may be new or reconditioned units, and there is a 14-day exclusion period at the start of the policy during which no claim is paid.

title: Saga Landlord Insurance Review
meta_title: Saga Landlord Insurance: £1m Cover, Arranged by Uinsure
meta_description: Saga landlord insurance gives £1m buildings and £2m liability cover, arranged through Uinsure since October 2024. Limits, fees and conditions checked.
intro:
Saga has been selling to people over 50 since 1951, and insurance has been the steady half of the business for most of that time. The group finished its financial year on 31 January 2026 with 1,294,000 insurance policies on the books, a customer database of 9.3 million people and underlying revenue of £654.6m, up 11% on the year before. Landlord cover is a small corner of that, but it is a well-built one: buildings protection up to £1,000,000, contents up to £35,000, property owners liability of £2,000,000, and a product that has held a Defaqto 5 Star rating every year since 2015.

The policy you buy from Saga today is arranged and run by Uinsure Limited, a Manchester firm Saga partnered with on 1 October 2024. Saga puts its name and its over-50s audience to the product; Uinsure sets the price, picks the insurer from its panel and handles the claim. That is worth knowing before you ring, because it decides which phone number you need and whose complaints department you would be writing to.

key_facts.label: Sold by

key_facts.value: 20% of the buildings claim limit

key_facts.label: Rent guarantee (optional)
key_facts.value: £2,500 a month for up to 12 months

key_facts.label: Home emergency (optional)

sections.heading: One date in October split this policy in two
sections.html:
Saga landlord policies sold on or before 30 September 2024 were underwritten by Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance plc, company number 93792, on a Saga-branded wording. Everything sold from 1 October 2024 comes through Uinsure Limited instead — company number 06046870, registered at the XYZ Building, Hardman Boulevard, Manchester M3 3AQ, and authorised by the FCA under firm reference 463689, a number you can check yourself on the Financial Services Register.

Saga keeps both routes open and staffs them separately. An older RSA-era policy is serviced on 0800 027 1355 from 9am to 5.30pm on weekdays, with a claims line on 0800 027 1357 that runs around the clock. A policy bought since the changeover goes to Uinsure on 0344 844 3844, weekdays 9am to 5pm, and the Saga-badged sales team at Uinsure answers 0161 524 3051 from 8.30am to 7pm on weekdays and 9am to 3pm on Saturdays. Ring the wrong one and you will be transferred rather than helped.

The split matters for a second reason. Saga sold its own underwriter, Acromas Insurance Company Limited, to Ageas for £65m plus £2.5m on completion, and signed a 20-year partnership worth £80m upfront and up to £30m in contingent payments. Motor went live under that arrangement in December 2025 and home followed on 23 April 2026. Landlord did not go to Ageas. It went to Uinsure seven months before the Ageas deal was even announced, and it sits outside the partnership that now defines the rest of Saga's insurance business.

sections.heading: What the £1m headline actually buys
sections.html:
The buildings limit is £1,000,000, or the rebuild cost if the property is a flat. Underneath it sit the sub-limits that decide most real claims. Trace and access — the cost of pulling up a floor to find a leak — is covered to £10,000, which is generous; a great many landlord policies stop at £5,000. Replacing locks after keys are lost or stolen is covered to £1,000. Metered water and oil lost through an escape is covered to £1,500. Theft from outbuildings, on the contents section, is limited to £1,000.

Liability is where the numbers get large. Property owners liability runs to £2,000,000 and liability to a domestic employee — a cleaner or a gardener you pay — to £5,000,000. Both are the market standard rather than a selling point, but a landlord without the second one is exposed in a way that is easy to overlook.

Loss of rent and the cost of rehousing a tenant are treated as one pot, capped at 20% of the buildings claim limit. On a £250,000 rebuild figure that is £50,000, which is ample. Buy contents cover on its own and the equivalent pot is £3,000 at the £15,000 contents level or £7,000 at £35,000 — a much tighter number, and the one that applies if you let a flat where the freeholder insures the structure.

Set those against what the market is actually paying out. The ABI's property tracker put £846m of home claims settled in the first quarter of 2026, an average claim of £6,340 against an average combined premium of £375, and by the second quarter the average subsidence claim had reached a record £20,000. A £10,000 trace and access limit stops looking like small print at that point.

sections.heading: The optional covers are where the conditions live
sections.html:
Legal expenses and rent guarantee are provided through Arc Legal Assistance Limited, FCA firm reference 305958, and they are the parts of the policy most likely to be bought and least likely to be read. Legal cover runs to £100,000 with unlimited access to the advice line, extends to £1,000,000 for a Defective Premises Act claim, and pays £20,000 if a tax liability falls due on accidental death. A tax dispute carries a £200 excess.

Rent guarantee pays £2,500 a month for a maximum of twelve months. The excess is one month's rent, arrears below £250 are outside the cover, and Arc will not run a case it rates at less than a 51% chance of winning. It also requires the tenant referencing paperwork to exist — a claim without it is declined on the file rather than on the merits.

That condition has become sharper since 1 May 2026, when the Renters' Rights Act 2025 converted most existing assured shorthold tenancies into assured periodic tenancies and removed Section 21 altogether. Possession now runs through Section 8 grounds, which takes longer, and a Section 8 notice served since commencement stays live for twelve months rather than the six a Section 21 notice used to give. Landlords also had to issue tenants an information sheet by 31 May 2026, with penalties reaching £7,000 for not doing it. Twelve months of rent guarantee is a different proposition when possession itself has slowed down.

Home emergency is the third add-on: £1,000 including VAT per claim, with no cap on the number of claims in a year. It carries a 48-hour waiting period from inception unless you held equivalent cover immediately before, and you must report a problem within 48 hours of noticing it.

sections.heading: Fees, excesses and the things the quote does not show you
sections.html:
Uinsure's own terms of business document, in its September 2025 version, sets an annual administration fee of £48 on landlord insurance and £36 on home insurance, on top of the premium and the insurer's commission. Instalment charges are levied separately by Close Brothers. None of that appears on Saga's landlord pages, so treat £48 as the figure to look for on the quote summary and confirm it before you pay.

Excesses are harder to pin down, because the wording defers all of them to the schedule you are shown at quote. There is no published standard excess, no published escape of water excess and no published subsidence excess anywhere in the customer-facing documents — and subsidence is the one that hurts, given the £20,000 average claim now being recorded. You cannot compare this policy on excess until you have run a quote, which is a real obstacle to shopping around and needs confirming case by case.

The security condition is published, and it has teeth. Uinsure's landlord wording requires the final exit door and any other external, sliding, patio or double-leaf french doors to carry a five-lever mortise deadlock conforming to BS3621, a rim automatic deadlock or a multi-point locking system. An older let with original door furniture may not meet that, and the time to find out is before a theft claim rather than after one.

One more piece of housekeeping. The FCA has a standing warning about a clone firm using the Saga Services name, first published on 17 August 2020 and last updated on 29 March 2021, which was operating on 0208 002 8791. The genuine firm is Saga Services Limited, FRN 311557, at 3 Pancras Square, London N1C 4AG. If a Saga landlord quote arrives from a number you did not dial, check it against the Register before sending money.

sections.heading: Sixty empty days, and the sixty-first
sections.html:
Cover under several sections falls away once the property has been unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days. That is a fairly standard allowance and slightly better than the 30 days some landlord wordings impose, but the count is of consecutive days with nobody living there, not days between tenancies on paper. A void running from a tenant leaving in early July to a new one moving in mid-September crosses it.

Optional malicious damage cover is the add-on landlords most often want, and it is also the one the unoccupancy rule bites hardest. Damage by a tenant, their staff or their guests is excluded from the standard policy unless the extension is bought, and drug cultivation damage sits behind the same extension. Neither responds while the property is over the 60-day line.

Saga's own home book gives some sense of how the market has moved. Home policies in force fell 19% over the year to 31 January 2026, from 506,000 to 412,000, while motor rose 12% to 675,000 — the shape of a business that has been repricing property risk hard. The Financial Ombudsman Service, in the annual figures it published on 21 May 2026, logged 6,399 new buildings insurance complaints against 214,600 across all products, with an average uphold rate of 30%. Property claims are argued about more than most, and the wording is where those arguments get settled.

pros: Buildings cover to £1,000,000, or full rebuild cost on a flat, with £2,000,000 property owners liability and £5,000,000 for domestic employees
Trace and access to £10,000, which is double the limit many landlord policies stop at
Loss of rent and rehousing pooled at 20% of the buildings claim limit rather than a flat cash cap
Defaqto 5 Star rated landlord product every year since 2015, and home since 2014
Two staffed service routes kept open, so pre-October 2024 RSA policies still have a 24-hour claims line
Rent guarantee at £2,500 a month for a full twelve months, with unlimited legal advice included
cons: The £48 annual administration fee in Uinsure's terms of business is not mentioned anywhere on Saga's landlord pages, so it only surfaces at quote
No excess figures are published at all — standard, escape of water and subsidence all defer to the schedule, which makes the policy impossible to compare before quoting
Cover under several sections stops after 60 consecutive days of the property being empty, and that includes the optional malicious damage extension landlords buy specifically for void periods
Malicious damage by a tenant and drug cultivation damage are both excluded unless you pay for the extension
Home emergency will not respond on a boiler over 15 years old or rated above 238,000 btu, or on a flat roof over 10 years old — common features of older let property
Rent guarantee needs tenant referencing on file and a 51% prospect of success before Arc Legal will act, and arrears under £250 are outside it entirely
The Saga brand is doing the marketing while Uinsure sets the price, holds the panel and answers the phone, so a Saga quote is a Uinsure quote in Saga livery
verdict: A capable landlord policy sold under a brand that no longer builds it. The limits are sound — £1,000,000 buildings, £2,000,000 liability, £10,000 trace and access, twelve months of rent guarantee at £2,500 — and the Defaqto rating has held since 2015. What you are buying is Uinsure's panel product with Saga's name on the front, priced by Uinsure and claimed against with Uinsure, and the two things to settle before you commit are the £48 administration fee and the excesses, neither of which is published. If your property sits empty between tenancies for long stretches, read the 60-day condition first.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites Saga landlord insurance?
faqs.a: Since 1 October 2024 the policy is arranged by Uinsure Limited (FRN 463689), which places the risk with an insurer from its own panel. The individual insurer is named on your policy schedule rather than on Saga's website. Policies bought on or before 30 September 2024 were underwritten by Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance plc.

faqs.q: Do I have to be over 50 to buy it?
faqs.a: Saga markets the product to the over-50s and none of its landlord pages states a hard minimum age. Because the quote is produced by Uinsure rather than Saga, eligibility is set on Uinsure's system, so confirm it on the quote if you are under 50 rather than assuming either way.

faqs.q: How long can the property be empty?
faqs.a: Sixty consecutive days. Past that, cover under several sections — including the optional malicious damage extension — stops until the property is lived in again. Tell Uinsure before a longer void starts rather than after it.

faqs.q: What does the rent guarantee cover pay?
faqs.a: Up to £2,500 a month for a maximum of twelve months, with an excess equal to one month's rent. Arrears below £250 are excluded, tenant referencing must be on file, and Arc Legal Assistance (FRN 305958) will only run a case it rates at 51% or better.

faqs.q: Is there a fee on top of the premium?
faqs.a: Uinsure's September 2025 terms of business set a £48 annual administration fee on landlord policies, with instalment charges applied separately by Close Brothers. Saga's own pages do not mention it, so check the quote summary before paying.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: For a policy bought since October 2024, Uinsure Customer Services at PO Box 1189, Doncaster DN1 9RP, or 0330 912 2502. If eight weeks pass without resolution you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which upheld 30% of the 214,600 complaints it closed in the year to 31 March 2026.

title: Saga Travel Insurance Review
meta_title: Saga Travel Insurance: No Age Cap, £20,000 Cancellation
meta_description: Over-50s only, but with no upper age limit at all: £20,000 cancellation and £20m medical on annual Plus, cruise cover as standard, Defaqto 5 star.
intro:
Saga writes travel insurance for people aged 50 and over, and nobody else. That restriction is the whole point of the product: rather than treating older travellers as an awkward edge case to be surcharged, the entire policy is built around them.

It shows in the limits. The Plus tier carries £20 million of emergency medical cover and £20,000 for cancellation — four times Aviva's top-tier cancellation limit. There is no upper age limit at all, and cruise cover is included as standard rather than sold as an add-on.

The trade is that you cannot buy it if you are 49, and premiums for a healthy 52-year-old on a short European break will often look expensive against a mainstream insurer.

sections.heading: The limits are in a different league
sections.html:
Set the Plus tier against a mainstream insurer's top tier and the gap is stark:

  • Cancellation: £20,000 against a typical £5,000
  • Baggage: £10,000 against a typical £2,500
  • Medical: £20 million against a typical £15 million

The cancellation figure is the one that earns its keep. A couple booking a three-week escorted tour or an ocean cruise can easily commit £12,000 or more in non-refundable payments. That sits comfortably inside Saga's limit and well outside most competitors'.

The £10,000 baggage limit is similarly aimed at a specific customer — someone travelling with camera equipment, jewellery or medical devices, where £2,500 does not cover the contents of the case.

sections.heading: No upper age limit, and why that is rarer than it sounds
sections.html:
Most mainstream travel insurers taper away as you age. Annual policies often close to new customers at 75 or 79, and single-trip premiums climb steeply from 80 onwards. Some decline outright past 85.

Saga has no upper age limit on any policy. An 88-year-old can buy the same Plus cover as a 52-year-old, subject to medical screening.

For anyone in their eighties who still travels, that is often the difference between insured and uninsured. It is worth knowing that the specialist market for very elderly travellers is thin, and prices there are frequently worse than Saga's.

sections.heading: Medical screening: what 'diagnosed only' actually excludes
sections.html:
Saga covers most pre-existing conditions after screening, but with a specific and important restriction: only diagnosed conditions are covered. Anything undiagnosed or still under investigation is excluded.

That distinction catches people out. If you are waiting on test results, or have symptoms your GP is still investigating, that condition is not covered — and neither, potentially, is anything that turns out to be connected to it. The policy will cover a diagnosed heart condition you have declared; it will not cover chest pain you are being investigated for.

The practical advice is to complete screening after your diagnosis rather than during investigation, and to re-screen if your health changes between buying the policy and travelling. Declaring more is always safer than declaring less.

sections.heading: Cruise cover included, and the 180-day allowance
sections.html:
Most insurers treat cruising as an add-on, charging extra for cabin confinement, missed port departures and itinerary changes. Saga includes it as standard, which reflects who the product is for.

Trip length is generous too: 180 days on a single trip, against Aviva's 120. The annual policy allows 180 days of travel a year with a 45-day per-trip maximum, extendable to 60 or 90 days for some regions.

That combination — long trips, cruise cover as standard, no age cap — is aimed squarely at retired travellers taking extended winter breaks, and it is a coherent product for exactly that person.

sections.heading: Who should not buy this
sections.html:
Anyone under 50 cannot, and that is a hard line.

Beyond that, a healthy 52-year-old taking a £600 long weekend in Spain is paying for limits they will never approach. Twenty thousand pounds of cancellation cover on a £600 trip is dead weight, and a mainstream insurer's mid tier will almost certainly cost less for equivalent practical protection.

The value appears when the trip is expensive, long, or when your age or medical history makes mainstream insurers expensive or unwilling. Below that threshold, you are paying for headroom you cannot use.

pros: £20m emergency medical and £20,000 cancellation on the Plus tier — far above mainstream limits
No upper age limit on any policy
Cruise cover included as standard rather than charged as an add-on
Single trips up to 180 days, and 180 days a year on annual cover
£10,000 baggage limit suits travellers carrying valuable equipment
5-star Defaqto rating
Most pre-existing conditions covered after screening
cons: Unavailable to anyone under 50
Expensive relative to mainstream insurers for short, cheap trips
Only diagnosed conditions are covered — anything under investigation is excluded
Annual policies cap individual trips at 45 days despite the 180-day annual allowance
High limits are wasted on travellers who will never approach them
verdict: The right choice for expensive trips, long trips, cruises, and anyone whose age or medical history makes mainstream insurers awkward. The £20,000 cancellation limit and absent age cap are genuinely difficult to match elsewhere, and cruise cover as standard removes a common add-on cost. It is the wrong choice for a healthy person in their early fifties taking a cheap short break, where you are paying for headroom you will never use. If you are waiting on a diagnosis, complete medical screening once you have it — conditions under investigation are not covered.

faqs.q: Can I buy Saga travel insurance if I am under 50?
faqs.a: No. Fifty is the minimum age and there are no exceptions. Every Saga product is built around over-50s travellers.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: No. Saga has no upper age limit on any of its travel policies, which is unusual — many mainstream insurers close annual policies to new customers at 75 or 79.

faqs.q: Does it cover cruises?
faqs.a: Yes, as standard rather than as a paid add-on. Most insurers charge extra for cruise cover.

faqs.q: What does 'diagnosed conditions only' mean?
faqs.a: Saga covers pre-existing conditions that have been formally diagnosed and declared at screening. Conditions that are undiagnosed or still under investigation are excluded, along with anything that turns out to be related to them.

faqs.q: How long can I travel for?
faqs.a: Up to 180 days on a single trip. Annual policies allow 180 days of travel a year with a maximum of 45 days per trip, extendable to 60 or 90 days for some regions.

headline.label: Emergency medical cover
headline.value: Up to £20 million on Plus. Minimum age 50, no upper limit

title: SamBoat Review: 50,000 Boats, a French Contract and Who Carries the Risk
meta_title: SamBoat Review: What Hiring a Boat Really Costs
meta_description: SamBoat lists 50,000+ boats worldwide and 161 in the UK. What a week costs, the 20% commission, the deposit rules and who you deal with if it goes wrong.

headline.label: Typical price for a week's hire
headline.value: €2,400 for a monohull sailboat, €4,300 for a catamaran — SamBoat's own averages, boat only, before fuel and skipper

intro:
SamBoat lists more than 50,000 boats for hire and its own pricing guide puts a motorboat at about €300 a day before fuel, a week aboard a monohull sailboat at roughly €2,400 and a catamaran at €4,300, with a skipper adding around €200 a day. Search the United Kingdom and 161 boats come back, from two-berth narrowboats in Staffordshire to a skippered sailing day out on Windermere. Figures checked on 19 September 2026 against SamBoat's own pages.

The business was built in Bordeaux in 2014 by Laurent Calando and Nicolas Cargou, and it was already carrying 25,000 boats across 120 countries when Dream Yacht Charter bought it on 6 November 2018, backed by a €5 million fundraising to which the Next Stage fund contributed €2.9 million. The two founders and their twenty staff stayed on. Since then the platform has absorbed LateSail, Vents de Mer, Argos and CYC, and it now advertises more than 1,400 destinations and around 300,000 people sailing with it each year. Plenty of the English canal boats on it are marked "No licence", and on most listings a skipper is optional rather than compulsory.

One thing is worth knowing before you book rather than after: the hire contract is with the boat's owner, not with the platform. SamBoat's terms, last updated on 4 April 2026, say it "acts as a technical and commercial intermediary in putting Users in touch" and "is not a party to the Rental Agreements concluded between Users". The company behind the site is LACANI SAS of 223 Avenue Émile Counord, Bordeaux, registered at Bordeaux under RCS 799 758 412 with share capital of €2,030,000, and the whole arrangement runs under French law. That decides who you deal with when a boat is not where it should be, so it is better read now than at a pontoon.

sections.heading: Where the money goes when you press book
sections.html:
SamBoat takes its living from both sides of the transaction, and the owner's half is published plainly: a service fee of "20% (twenty percent)" of the rental, dropping to "10% (ten percent) for extras such as stand-up paddleboarding, masks and snorkels, fishing equipment". That is the number an owner weighs against listing the boat privately, and it is in the same range as the big accommodation platforms.

Your side is less tidy. The terms describe a separate Renter Protection Fee covering "payment security, assistance, customer support and Booking management services", and say both charges are "due upon confirmation of the Booking, regardless of the actual completion of the rental" — but nowhere in the document is that fee expressed as a percentage or a sum. You see it as a line on the checkout total rather than as a published rate, so compare the all-in price rather than the headline day rate when you are weighing two boats.

Payment is handled by Adyen N.V. in Amsterdam for ordinary bookings and by Stripe Payments Europe in Dublin where the boat comes from a broker or partner fleet. The owner is paid "within 24 (twenty-four) hours after the first day of rental", which is quick by charter standards and tells you the platform is holding your money only briefly.

sections.heading: The paperwork a canal boat needs before anyone may hire it out
sections.html:
This is the part a marketplace listing cannot show you, and on English and Welsh canals it is specific. The Canal & River Trust requires a hire operator to hold a business licence, to carry "third party and public liability insurance cover... which covers liabilities of at least two million pounds for each claim" from an insurer authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, and to hold a hire boat safety scheme certificate — a requirement that has applied to every hire boat regardless of age since 1 April 2018.

There is more. The operator must "prepare a detailed handover procedure which you must use each time you hire out the boat", covering navigation rules, locks and bridges, boat handling and equipment, and must run "a 24 hour emergency call out service", unless it holds British Marine's Quality Accredited Boatyard certificate instead. New operators pay a non-refundable £105 including VAT to have an operating proposal assessed, and the Trust aims to give an in-principle decision within six weeks.

SamBoat's own requirement of an owner is a single sentence: the boat must be "insured for the rental activity". The platform sets out no check on licences, safety certificates or handover training, so on an inland listing those are questions for the owner before you pay, not afterwards.

sections.heading: Skippered, bareboat, and the coding question at sea
sections.html:
Away from the canals the rules change again. The Royal Yachting Association's guidance is that a vessel needs to be commercially coded "to operate a boat for skippered or bareboat use usually for commercial gain" and "to take people afloat who pay more than a reasonable contribution towards the trip". Coding means a survey against the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's small commercial vessel code, published as MGN 280, and for a skippered boat it also means a commercially endorsed skipper.

Most of the UK listings on SamBoat are either professional operators, who will have been through that, or inland boats where the code does not apply. The grey area is a privately owned sea boat being let out by its owner for cash. Ask two questions before you book one: is the boat coded for the area you are going to, and does the owner's policy cover hire and reward? The platform's answer to both is that these are the owner's responsibility, so the checking falls to you.

On the water itself the terms put the practical duties on the renter: hold the required pleasure boat licence, see that "people on board wear a life jacket or buoyancy aid", return the boat clean, with the same fuel level, and never sublet it or charge the people aboard.

sections.heading: Four cancellation policies, and the one you get by default
sections.html:
Owners choose from four policies and the choice is theirs, not yours, so it is worth reading on the listing before the dates are set. FLEXIBLE refunds everything up to the day before departure. MODERATE puts half the cost on the owner if you give more than two weeks' notice. STRICT charges you the full rental "regardless of the notice period". And where the owner has picked nothing at all, ZEN applies: "70% (seventy percent)" back if you cancel five days or more ahead, and nothing at all inside five days.

Weather is the usual reason a boat holiday falls apart, and the terms are strict about it. Force majeure needs an "unforeseeable, irresistible event external to the parties", evidenced by a special weather statement from a competent authority or an administrative ban on navigation, and the document says in terms that "normal or foreseeable weather conditions... do not in themselves constitute force majeure". A grey, blowy week on the south coast is not a refund.

An owner who cancels on you owes SamBoat a penalty of "50% (fifty percent) of the rental amount, with a minimum of €200.00", which is a real deterrent. Note, though, that the penalty is payable to the platform rather than to you.

sections.heading: Deposits, damage and the tariff for bringing a boat back dirty
sections.html:
The security deposit is set by the owner and taken from your card "48 hours (forty-eight hours) before the start of the rental", so it lands before you have seen the boat. It covers "damage caused during the rental, namely the amount of repairs, fuel level defects, rental delays, expert fees, administrative fees", and if SamBoat has to activate it, "5% (five percent) of the amount of the Security Deposit will be debited with a minimum of 100 € (hundred) Euros" as a handling charge on top of whatever the damage costs.

Several charges are fixed rather than argued over, which cuts both ways: €175 for abnormal exterior dirt, €155 for abnormal interior dirt, "40 Euros + 2.50 Euros / liter" for returning with the tank down, a minimum of €200 for tears, burns, stains or breakages, and the hourly rate increased by 50% for bringing the boat back late. Knowing the tariff in advance is better than discovering it, and a photographic record at handover and return is the cheapest insurance there is.

Complaints have short fuses. A renter has "24 (twenty-four) hours from the date of taking possession" to raise a problem and an owner has 48 hours from the end of the rental, so a fault noticed on day three of a week is already outside the window.

sections.heading: The cover you can buy, and the cover nobody is selling you
sections.html:
SamBoat does not insure the boat. The terms are explicit that owners must arrange their own cover for the rental activity and that the platform excludes liability if something is damaged. What it does sell, as a registered intermediary under ORIAS number 16001576, are three add-ons arranged with insurance partners including MAIF, Gritchen, Mutuaide Assistance and NEAT.

Deposit insurance covers up to €5,000 and starts at €30, refunding the money taken from your card after an accident. Cancellation insurance covers up to €20,000 from €20, for named reasons including illness, accident, redundancy, theft of documents, natural disaster, terrorism and riot, and it has to be bought at the time of booking rather than later. Repatriation cover pays the cost of getting you home or to hospital with 24-hour assistance. On the owner's own policy arranged through the platform, the excess is "10% of the amount of damages with a minimum of €500 and a maximum of €1,000".

Set the deposit cover against the deposit being asked. On a boat wanting €2,000 held on your card, €30 is a sensible trade; on a small inland boat with no deposit at all — and several UK listings ask for none — it buys you nothing.

sections.heading: Two pages of the same group, two fleet sizes
sections.html:
SamBoat's own site says "+ 50 000 to rent worldwide". Dream Yacht's page about SamBoat, published by its parent, says the platform has "over 30,000 boats to search". Both were live on 19 September 2026 and they cannot both be current. The gap is large enough to matter if you are choosing a platform on breadth, and the honest reading is that one of the two figures has not been revised since the fleet moved — it was 25,000 boats in 120 countries at the 2018 acquisition, so the direction of travel is clear, the arithmetic is not.

A second mismatch sits in the small print. The guarantees page names Stripe and MangoPay as the payment processors; the terms of 4 April 2026 name Adyen N.V. and Stripe Payments Europe. Neither is alarming on its own, and the terms are the document that binds, but a marketing page that has drifted from the contract is a reminder to take figures from the contract wherever both exist.

The satisfaction score on the home page — 4.88 out of 5 from 215,700 users — is the platform's own count of its own customers, not an independent assessment. There is no Defaqto, Which? or Fairer Finance rating for boat rental marketplaces, so no external rating was found for this page.

sections.heading: Where a British customer stands if the boat is not there
sections.html:
There is no United Kingdom company behind any of this. Dream Yacht Charter UK Limited, company number 12143353, was incorporated on 7 August 2019 at 27 New Dover Road, Canterbury, and was dissolved on 26 December 2023; an earlier Dream Yacht Charter UK Ltd, 07501705, was dissolved on 11 November 2014. The contract, the complaint and the court are all French: the terms are "governed by and subject to French law", disputes may go to a consumer mediator free of charge under Article R616-1 of the French Consumer Code, and proceedings may be brought where the defendant is based, where the boat was hired, or where the claimant is.

Nor is a boat hire an ATOL-protected flight or an ABTA-bonded package, so those familiar acronyms do nothing here. The protection a British customer does have runs through the card. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes a credit card provider "jointly and severally liable" with the supplier for misrepresentation or breach of contract, on any single item with a cash price above £100 and not more than £30,000 — which covers most weeks afloat and few day hires. Below that, or on a debit card, chargeback is the route, and it is a scheme rule rather than a legal right.

Paying by credit card for anything over £100 therefore does more for you here than any of the optional add-ons, and it costs nothing.

sections.heading: What 161 UK listings actually look like
sections.html:
The UK is not where this platform is strongest, and the search results say so. England's bareboat canal boats come almost entirely from one Staffordshire fleet — boats of 47 to 70 feet sleeping two to eight, every one marked "No licence" — plus a 60-foot narrowboat at Adlington. Ullswater returns a single boat. Windermere has a 1985 Jeanneau Tonic 23 that is skippered only, with the skipper included free, fuel included and no deposit required, offered by the day or in two- and four-hour blocks.

That is a thin national choice next to the hundreds of boats the same platform lists around the Mediterranean, and it means the UK boater is often comparing one boat against no boat rather than one boat against three. Where a listing is a professional fleet — as the Staffordshire narrowboats appear to be — you are effectively booking a traditional hire firm through SamBoat's checkout, with SamBoat's cancellation terms and fee layered on top of the firm's own.

For a Mediterranean week, or for a catamaran in the Caribbean, the breadth is real and the comparison works in the platform's favour. For a week on the Llangollen Canal, check what the yard charges direct before you assume the marketplace is cheaper.

pros: Very large choice abroad — more than 50,000 boats and 1,400 destinations, with or without a skipper
Owner commission is published at 20%, and 10% on extras, so the economics are not hidden
Clear damage tariff: €175 exterior, €155 interior, €40 plus €2.50 a litre for fuel, so there is little to argue about
Deposit and cancellation cover are cheap for what they hold — €5,000 from €30 and €20,000 from €20
Owners are paid within 24 hours of the first day, and an owner who cancels pays a penalty of 50% with a €200 minimum
Plenty of English canal listings need no licence at all, and several ask for no security deposit
cons: The fee you pay as a renter is never expressed as a percentage or an amount anywhere in the terms — only as a line on the checkout total

The default ZEN policy keeps 30% of the rental even when you cancel five days ahead, and SamBoat's own fees may come back as a credit note that is "personal, non-transferable, non-refundable" rather than as money
You have 24 hours from taking possession to complain; a fault found midweek is already out of time
Safety compliance rests entirely with the owner — the platform publishes no check on hire boat safety certificates, Canal & River Trust business licences or MCA coding
No UK company stands behind the booking: Dream Yacht Charter UK Limited was dissolved on 26 December 2023, and the contract, mediator and courts are French
The fleet is quoted at over 50,000 boats by SamBoat and over 30,000 by its own parent, and the UK choice is thin at 161 boats — one of them on Ullswater
verdict: For a week in the Mediterranean or a catamaran somewhere warm, SamBoat is a genuinely broad market and the published 20% commission, the fixed damage tariff and the cheap deposit cover make it easy to work out what you are paying. In the UK it is a different proposition: 161 boats, a single Staffordshire fleet carrying most of the canal listings, and a contract that sits under French law with no British company behind it. Read the cancellation policy on the individual listing rather than assuming the default, ask an owner of a private sea boat about coding and hire-and-reward insurance, pay by credit card for the Section 75 cover, and compare the all-in checkout total against the yard's own price before you book at home.

faqs.q: Who am I actually hiring the boat from?
faqs.a: The boat's owner. SamBoat's terms say it "acts as a technical and commercial intermediary in putting Users in touch" and "is not a party to the Rental Agreements concluded between Users". The platform takes the payment, holds the deposit arrangement and offers to mediate, but the contract for the boat is between you and the owner, under French law.

faqs.q: What does SamBoat charge?
faqs.a: The owner pays 20% of the rental, reduced to 10% on extras such as paddleboards and snorkelling equipment. You pay a Renter Protection Fee covering payment security, assistance and booking management, which the terms do not express as a percentage or a sum — it appears in your checkout total. Both are due on confirmation, "regardless of the actual completion of the rental".

faqs.q: When is the security deposit taken, and what if there is damage?
faqs.a: It is debited 48 hours before the rental starts. If SamBoat has to use it, a handling charge of 5% of the deposit with a minimum of €100 is taken on top of the repair cost. Fixed charges apply for some things: €175 for abnormal exterior dirt, €155 inside, €40 plus €2.50 a litre for missing fuel, a minimum of €200 for breakages, and the hourly rate plus 50% for a late return. Deposit insurance covering up to €5,000 starts at €30.

faqs.q: Do I need a licence to hire a narrowboat through SamBoat?
faqs.a: Most of the English canal listings are marked "No licence", which reflects the ordinary position on inland waterways: the hire operator holds the Canal & River Trust business licence and the hire boat safety scheme certificate, and gives you a handover instead. At sea it is different — many listings require a pleasure boat licence, and where you take a skipper the Royal Yachting Association's guidance is that a boat operated for commercial gain should be commercially coded and the skipper commercially endorsed.

faqs.q: What protection do I have as a UK customer if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: Not ATOL or ABTA, neither of which applies to a boat hire. Your practical protection is the card: Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes a credit card provider jointly and severally liable with the supplier for misrepresentation or breach of contract where the item costs more than £100 and no more than £30,000. Beyond that, SamBoat offers to mediate, and French consumer mediation under Article R616-1 is free to use.

title: Santander Credit Cards Review: Five Cards, 34 Months at 0% and the Fee Arithmetic
meta_title: Santander Credit Cards: 34 Months at 0%, or No Transfer Fee
meta_description: Five cards compared: 34 months at 0% on transfers for a 3.15% fee, or 12 months with no fee at all. Plus 3% cashback on fuel, trains and eating out.
intro:
Santander's longest balance transfer runs 34 months at 0% for a 3.15% fee, and its five personal credit cards carry representative APRs from 24.9% to 49.8% variable. Every figure on this page was taken from Santander's own product pages, summary boxes and key facts documents on 12 September 2026, and the document references are given where they matter.

The lender is Santander UK plc, on the Financial Services Register under firm reference number 106054. Its range is unusually easy to read against itself, because it publishes a full summary box for each card with the same headings — the introductory periods, the fees, the default charges and the minimum payment rule all sit in the same place on every document. Three of the five cards charge nothing for spending abroad in local currency, which is rare on a mainstream range rather than a specialist travel card.

Entry is also set low. The stated requirement is an income of £10,500 a year, being 18 or over, permanent UK residence, a clean recent credit history and no bankruptcy, county court judgment or individual voluntary arrangement in the last six years. That is a modest income bar for a range that includes a 34-month transfer card, and it is published rather than left to the application to reveal.

headline.value: 24.9% to 49.8% variable across five cards

key_facts.value: Santander UK plc, Financial Services Register firm reference number 106054

key_facts.value: 34 months on the Everyday Long Term card, 3.15% fee (minimum £5)

key_facts.value: 24.9% on three cards, 29.8% on All in One, 49.8% on World Elite
