sections.heading: Five cards, and the three jobs they are built for
sections.html:
Two of the five are transfer cards. The Everyday Long Term Balance Transfer card gives 0% on transfers for 34 months from the day the account opens, for a fee of 3.15% with a £5 minimum, and 0% on purchases for three months. The Everyday No Balance Transfer Fee card gives 0% on transfers for 12 months with no fee at all, and the same three months on purchases. Both quote 24.9% APR representative on an assumed £1,200 limit with no monthly charge.

Two are spending cards. The Rewards card pays 3% cashback in the first twelve months on a defined list of everyday categories and 0.25% on everything else, at 24.9% APR representative and no monthly fee. The All in One card costs £3 a month and gives 0% on both purchases and balance transfers for 15 months with no transfer fee, plus 0.5% cashback capped at £10 a month; its purchase rate is 23.9% and the monthly fee lifts the representative APR to 29.8%.

The fifth is a premium card. The World Elite Mastercard costs £15 a month, has the lowest purchase rate in the range at 18.9%, the highest representative APR at 49.8%, and is closed to anyone who is not a Santander Select or Private Banking customer. Across all five, a balance transfer will only be processed if the card is activated within 45 days of arriving.

sections.heading: Thirty-four months at 0%, and what the 3.15% costs
sections.html:
Take a £2,000 debt to the Everyday Long Term card and the fee is £63.00, added to the balance at the point of transfer. Clearing £2,063 over the 34 interest-free months means paying about £60.68 a month, and nothing else is owed provided the payments land on time and the balance is gone before the promotion ends.

Set that against the no-fee card. Twelve months at 0% and no charge for the transfer means £2,000 clears for exactly £2,000 — but only if you can find £166.67 a month to do it. Fall short and the remainder starts attracting 24.9%. So the choice between Santander's two transfer cards is not really about the fee; it is about which monthly payment you can actually sustain. Above roughly £167 a month on a £2,000 balance, the free card wins outright. Below it, the £63 buys you nearly three years of protection and is cheap at the price.

Two details in the summary box are worth having before you commit. The 0% on purchases lasts three months on both cards, not the length of the transfer deal, so anything bought after that sits at 24.9%. And once the introductory period is over, a new balance transfer on the Long Term card attracts a 3% fee with no 0% attached to it. The document those come from is Santander's own summary box, reference ACS1 3417 OCT 25.

sections.heading: The £3-a-month card that undercuts the fee card
sections.html:
The most useful thing on this page is a comparison Santander's own marketing does not draw, because the All in One is sold as a cashback card rather than a transfer card. It gives 0% on balance transfers for 15 months with no transfer fee. The cost of holding it is £3 a month, so fifteen months of it comes to £45.

On that same £2,000 debt, £45 is less than the £63 the Long Term card charges, and it buys three more months than the free card gives. Clearing £2,000 across 15 months needs £133.34 a month. So the range actually offers three thresholds rather than two: £166.67 a month costs nothing, £133.34 a month costs £45, and £60.68 a month costs £63. Anyone who can manage the middle figure is paying less than the headline transfer card asks and finishing more than a year sooner.

The catch is that the £3 does not stop. It is a monthly account fee, not a transfer fee, so it keeps running for as long as the card is open — £36 a year, indefinitely, and 34 months of it would come to £102. The card only undercuts the fee card if you close it or clear it roughly on schedule. Against that, it is the only card in the range with 0% on purchases and transfers at the same time, for the same 15 months, and it pays 0.5% back on spending up to £10 a month.

sections.heading: Where 24.9% actually lands: £151.09 on £1,200
sections.html:
Santander publishes a worked representative example rather than leaving the reader to model it, and it is the clearest number on the whole range. Borrow the assumed £1,200 limit as a single purchase on the Rewards card and repay it in twelve equal monthly instalments at the standard rate, and the total payable is £1,351.09. The interest is £151.09 — about 12.6% of what was borrowed, on a card quoting 24.9%.

The gap is not a discrepancy. An APR describes the rate on money still outstanding, and a balance being repaid in equal instalments is only fully outstanding in the first month. It is worth stating plainly because a reader comparing a 24.9% card against a personal loan quoted at a similar rate is comparing two things that behave the same way, while a reader comparing it against a balance left to sit is not.

For scale, Bank Rate was 3.75% on 12 September 2026, held at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting of 30 July with the next decision set for 17 September. A 24.9% purchase rate is about six and a half times the cost of money, and 49.8% is over thirteen times it. The minimum payment rule is published too: the highest of £5, or the total of interest, monthly fee and default fees plus 1% of the remaining balance plus any arrears. Paying only that leaves most of the debt in place.

sections.heading: Cashback that runs for twelve months, and the list it applies to
sections.html:
The Rewards card pays 3% cashback during the first twelve months from account opening, and Santander publishes the qualifying merchant categories by code rather than by adjective — petrol, diesel and LPG stations, electric vehicle charging, trains, Transport for London and trams, buses, taxis, restaurants, cafés, coffee shops, takeaways and food delivery. Everything else earns 0.25%, and after twelve months everything earns 0.25%. The cashback terms carry no monthly or annual cap, which is unusual and worth checking against your own statement rather than assumed.

What does not earn cashback is set out in the same document: balance transfers, cash transactions, travellers' cheques, foreign currency, interest, account charges, fraudulent transactions, anything cancelled or refunded, and purchases made over the credit limit. Cashback is totted up each month and added on the following month's statement date. The reference is ACSMC1133, dated June 2026.

The other two cashback rates are capped and easy to size. All in One pays 0.5% up to £10 a month, so the cap bites at £2,000 of monthly spending and the £3 fee is covered by £600 a month. World Elite pays 0.5% up to £15 a month, so the cap bites at £3,000 a month.

sections.heading: £15 a month, and the spending it takes to earn it back
sections.html:
The World Elite Mastercard costs £180 a year. Its cashback is 0.5% capped at £15 a month, which is a maximum of £180 a year — so the cashback covers the fee only if you put £3,000 a month, £36,000 a year, through the card, and at any lower spend the card runs at a loss on cashback alone. The rest of the value has to come from the benefits, and those are real: LoungeKey access to over 1,400 airport lounges for the cardholder and additional cardholders, Mastercard Airport Security Fast Track, 3GB of free data roaming a year through Flexiroam across more than 150 countries with 15% off further plans, 40% off Santander travel insurance, and no foreign transaction fees on local-currency purchases.

Whether that beats £180 depends entirely on how often you fly. Guests and children are £24 a visit at the lounges, so a family is paying per head for everyone but the named cardholders.

The representative APR deserves a second look. At 49.8% it is the highest number on this page, and it is mostly the fee: the purchase rate is 18.9%, the lowest in the range. The £15 a month is folded into the representative calculation on an assumed £1,200 limit, which is what pushes 18.9% to 49.8%. A cardholder who clears the balance monthly pays the £180 and no interest; one who carries a balance pays 18.9% on it plus the £180. The card is also closed to anyone outside Santander Select or Private Banking.

sections.heading: The fees that are not in the headline
sections.html:
Default charges are £12 for missing a minimum payment and £12 for being over the credit limit on the statement date, on each card. Cash withdrawals cost 3% of the amount with a £3 minimum, and interest runs from the day of the withdrawal rather than from the statement — on the All in One that cash rate is 29.9% a year, above its own 23.9% purchase rate.

Spending abroad is where the range contradicts itself. The Rewards card, the All in One and the World Elite charge nothing for purchases made in the local currency. The two Everyday cards charge 2.95% of the transaction. Two cards sold under the same brand, from the same lender, on the same application journey, and the traveller who happens to have picked the transfer card pays £29.50 on every £1,000 spent abroad while the cashback customer pays nothing. Nothing on the product pages flags the difference.

One more piece of timing to watch: a balance transfer is only processed if the card is activated within 45 days of receiving it. Miss that and the transfer does not happen, while the introductory clock on the Everyday Long Term card runs from the day the account opened rather than from the day the transfer lands.

sections.heading: 57,274 complaints, and a £107.7m penalty
sections.html:
Santander publishes its own complaints return twice a year, which is a better source than any summary of it. For the six months from 1 January to 30 June 2026 it opened 57,274 banking and credit card complaints, a rate of 2.4 per 1,000 accounts. It closed 54% within three days and 46% between three days and eight weeks, and upheld 47%. The largest single cause was recorded as other general administration and customer service.

Nearly half of complaints being upheld is a figure worth sitting with. It means that when a Santander customer takes the trouble to complain, the bank agrees with them about as often as not — which cuts both ways, since a bank that upholds nothing is not necessarily doing better. The 54% closed inside three days is the softer number: it is below what the strongest performers in retail banking report on the same measure.

The regulatory record behind the licence is heavier. On 9 December 2022 the FCA fined Santander UK plc £107,793,300 for serious and persistent anti-money-laundering control failures between 31 December 2012 and 18 October 2017, affecting more than 560,000 business customers, with around £298 million passing through accounts the bank had failed to manage properly before they were closed. The penalty was reduced by 30% for early settlement, from £153,990,400. It concerns business banking rather than credit cards, and it is nearly four years old — but it is the largest published finding against the entity that would be lending you the money, and it belongs on the page.

sections.heading: Who can apply, and where a complaint goes
sections.html:
The published criteria are the same across the range: 18 or over, a permanent UK resident, an annual income of £10,500 or more, a good credit history, no bankruptcy, county court judgment or individual voluntary arrangement in the past six years, and not already holding the card applied for. The World Elite adds the Select or Private Banking requirement on top; Santander states plainly that it cannot accept applications for it from anyone else.

The lender is Santander UK plc under firm reference number 106054, and that reference is what a complaint attaches to. Santander's own complaints process runs first; an unresolved complaint can be taken to the Financial Ombudsman Service free of charge, normally after eight weeks or once a final response has been issued. Purchases between £100 and £30,000 made on any of these cards also carry the statutory joint liability that comes with paying by credit card, which is a protection the card gives and the debit card in the same wallet does not.

The 0% on purchases on the two Everyday cards can be extended to 56 days if the full statement balance is paid on time, which is the standard interest-free window rather than a promotion, and it is the cheapest way to use any card in this range: clear the statement in full and the only card here that costs anything to hold is the one with a monthly fee.

pros: 34 months at 0% on balance transfers, the longest in the range, for a 3.15% fee with a £5 minimum
A 12-month 0% transfer with no fee at all on the Everyday No Balance Transfer Fee card
All in One gives 0% on purchases and transfers together for 15 months with no transfer fee, for £3 a month
3% cashback for the first twelve months on petrol, EV charging, public transport, taxis and eating out, with no cap stated in the cashback terms
No foreign transaction fee on local-currency purchases with the Rewards, All in One and World Elite cards
A published income requirement of £10,500 a year, which is low for a range including a 34-month transfer card
A full worked representative example: £1,200 repaid over 12 months totals £1,351.09
A summary box per card with the same headings, so the five can be compared directly against each other
cons: The World Elite costs £180 a year and caps cashback at £15 a month, so £36,000 of annual card spending is needed before the cashback covers the fee
The two Everyday cards charge 2.95% on non-sterling transactions while the other three charge nothing, and the product pages do not flag the difference
The All in One's £3 monthly fee continues indefinitely after its 15-month 0% period, reaching £102 over 34 months
0% on purchases lasts only three months on both Everyday cards, against 34 and 12 months on transfers
A missed minimum payment costs £12 and going over the limit costs £12, on every card
Cash withdrawals cost 3% with a £3 minimum and attract interest from the day of withdrawal — 29.9% a year on the All in One, above its own purchase rate
The Rewards card's 3% cashback drops to 0.25% after twelve months, on the same spending
Santander upheld 47% of the 57,274 banking and credit card complaints it opened in the first half of 2026, and closed only 54% within three days
Santander UK plc was fined £107,793,300 by the FCA on 9 December 2022 for anti-money-laundering failures between December 2012 and October 2017
A balance transfer is lost if the card is not activated within 45 days of arriving, while the 0% clock runs from account opening
verdict: Santander's range rewards reading the summary boxes side by side, because the best transfer deal is not the card sold as one. On a £2,000 balance the 34-month card costs £63 and the All in One costs £45 for 15 months with no transfer fee, so the answer turns on whether you can find £133 a month or only £61. The Rewards card is a decent first-year cashback card on a published category list, and the World Elite needs £36,000 a year of spending before its cashback covers its £180 fee, which makes it a lounge card rather than a value one. Check the 2.95% foreign transaction fee on the two Everyday cards before taking either abroad.

faqs.q: Which Santander card gives the longest 0% on a balance transfer?
faqs.a: The Everyday Long Term Balance Transfer card, at 34 months from the day the account opens, for a fee of 3.15% of the amount transferred with a £5 minimum. On £2,000 that fee is £63.00. It gives only three months at 0% on purchases, and after the introductory period new transfers attract a 3% fee with no 0% attached.

faqs.q: Is the fee-free transfer card actually cheaper?
faqs.a: Only if you can clear the balance inside twelve months. The Everyday No Balance Transfer Fee card gives 0% for 12 months and charges nothing, so £2,000 costs £2,000 — but that needs £166.67 a month. At £60.68 a month the same debt takes 34 months, which only the Long Term card covers, and its £63 fee is far cheaper than paying 24.9% on the remainder. The middle option is the All in One: 15 months at 0% with no transfer fee for £3 a month, £45 in total.

faqs.q: What is the representative APR on Santander credit cards?
faqs.a: 24.9% variable on the Rewards, Everyday Long Term Balance Transfer and Everyday No Balance Transfer Fee cards; 29.8% variable on the All in One, whose purchase rate is 23.9% with a £3 monthly fee on top; and 49.8% variable on the World Elite Mastercard, whose purchase rate is 18.9% with a £15 monthly fee. All are quoted on an assumed credit limit of £1,200.

faqs.q: How much cashback does the Santander Rewards card pay?
faqs.a: 3% for the first twelve months from account opening on a published list of categories — petrol, diesel and LPG, EV charging, trains, Transport for London and trams, buses, taxis, restaurants, cafés, coffee shops, takeaways and food delivery — and 0.25% on everything else. After twelve months everything earns 0.25%. Balance transfers, cash, foreign currency, interest, charges and refunded purchases earn nothing.

faqs.q: Do Santander credit cards charge for spending abroad?
faqs.a: It depends which one. The Rewards, All in One and World Elite cards charge no foreign transaction fee on purchases made in the local currency. The Everyday Long Term Balance Transfer and Everyday No Balance Transfer Fee cards charge 2.95% of the transaction. Cash withdrawals cost 3% with a £3 minimum on every card, with interest running from the day of withdrawal.

faqs.q: What do I need to earn to be accepted?
faqs.a: Santander publishes a minimum income of £10,500 a year, along with being 18 or over, a permanent UK resident, having a good credit history and no bankruptcy, county court judgment or individual voluntary arrangement in the past six years. The World Elite Mastercard additionally requires you to be a Santander Select or Private Banking customer, and Santander states it cannot accept applications from anyone else.

title: Santander Edge Current Account Review
meta_title: Santander Edge Review: £3 a Month, 6% on £4,000
meta_description: Santander Edge costs £3 a month, pays 1% on household bills to £10, and opens a 6.00% AER saver on £4,000. Checked 23 September 2026.

headline.label: Interest, first 12 months
headline.value: None on the account; 6.00% AER on up to £4,000 in the linked Edge Saver, including a 2.50% bonus that runs for 12 months

intro:
The Santander Edge current account charges £3 a month and hands back 1% of what you pay on household direct debits, capped at £10 a month. Sitting beside it is the Edge Saver at 6.00% AER on balances up to £4,000. Every figure on this page was read off Santander's own product pages, its Edge key facts document and its savings rate sheet on 23 September 2026.

Santander UK plc has run a British branch network since it bought Abbey National in 2004, and it grew sharply this year. The TSB purchase completed on 30 April 2026, brought about four million customers with it, and left the group the country's third largest bank measured by personal current accounts, with 480 branches across the two brands. Its half-year statement to 30 June 2026 reported £227.2bn of customer deposits, £69.1bn of that held in current accounts.

One quirk of the fee works in your favour and one condition of the switching offer does not. The £3 is not taken until the month after you first meet the cashback conditions, so an account opened and left alone costs nothing. The £240 switching payment Santander opened on 1 September 2026, though, is payable only on the Everyday Current Account. Edge does not qualify for it.

key_facts.label: Provider
key_facts.value: Santander UK plc, FRN 106054, 2 Triton Square, Regent's Place, London NW1 3AN

key_facts.label: Monthly fee
key_facts.value: £3, first charged the month after you meet the cashback conditions for the first time

key_facts.label: Cashback
key_facts.value: 1% of selected household bills paid by direct debit, capped at £10 a monthly period

key_facts.label: Monthly conditions
key_facts.value: £500 paid in and at least 2 active direct debits, in every monthly period

key_facts.label: Credit interest on the account
key_facts.value: None, at any balance

key_facts.label: Linked saver
key_facts.value: Edge Saver (Issue 5), 6.00% AER / 5.84% gross variable on £1–£4,000, including a 2.50% bonus for 12 months; 3.50% after that; nothing paid above £4,000

key_facts.label: Arranged overdraft
key_facts.value: Representative 39.94% APR/EAR variable; switchers get 4 months interest free

key_facts.label: Spending abroad
key_facts.value: No Santander currency conversion fee on debit card use outside the UK

key_facts.label: Eligibility
key_facts.value: 18 or over, living in the UK permanently, signed up to online banking; maximum of two Edge accounts

key_facts.label: Deposit protection
key_facts.value: FSCS £120,000, shared with cahoot, Santander Business and Santander Corporate & Commercial

sections.heading: The £300 of direct debits that pays for the account
sections.html:
The cashback is 1% of what leaves the account by direct debit for a defined list of bills: council tax, gas and electricity, water, mobile and home phone, broadband and paid-for television packages. The cap is £10 in a monthly period, so the rate stops mattering once qualifying bills pass £1,000 a month. At £300 a month you earn exactly the £3 the account costs, and a full year of fees is £36 against a theoretical ceiling of £120.

What is left off the list matters as much as what is on it. Santander excludes TV licences, LPG and Calor gas, maintenance contracts and anything paid for commercial use. The payment method counts too: the same bill settled by standing order or card earns nothing, because only direct debits qualify.

Two conditions must both be met in each monthly period before any cashback is paid. You have to put £500 into the account, and you have to keep at least two active direct debits running from it. Santander counts every payment in towards the £500 except refunds on card purchases and money moved from another Santander account in your own name, so wages, benefits and transfers from a different bank all count. The account pays no interest on its own balance at any level, which is the trade for the cashback rather than an oversight.

sections.heading: Six per cent on four thousand pounds, with a clock running
sections.html:
The Edge Saver is why most people open the current account. Issue 5 pays 6.00% AER / 5.84% gross variable on £1 to £4,000, and that figure is a 3.50% underlying rate with a 2.50% bonus stacked on top for the first twelve months from opening. Santander's savings rate sheet effective 3 September 2026 sets out both halves separately, which is more candid than most banks manage with a bonus product.

Do the arithmetic before moving money. A full £4,000 held for the whole bonus year returns about £240. The same balance in year two, at 3.50%, returns about £140 — and 3.50% is a quarter of a point below the 3.75% Bank Rate the Bank of England set on 18 December 2025 and has left alone since. Nothing at all is paid on the part of a balance above £4,000, so this is a bucket rather than a home for savings.

The practical limits: the saver runs through online or mobile banking only, it has to be in a sole name, the minimum balance is £1, and you can hold up to three of them, one attached to each Edge or Edge Explorer current account you have.

sections.heading: Eight per cent that comes to about £104
sections.html:
Santander also offers a Regular Saver at 8.00% AER / gross variable, made up of a 3.00% underlying rate and a 5.00% bonus for twelve months. It takes up to £200 a month, has no minimum, and needs a Santander current account behind it.

Paying in the full £200 every month for a year puts £2,400 through the account and returns roughly £104 in interest, not the £192 that 8% of £2,400 suggests. That is not a trick. The first £200 earns for twelve months and the last for one, so the average balance across the year is a little over £1,300. Santander publishes the rate and the monthly limit plainly, and the total falls out of them.

The Regular Saver has a second role. Funding one with at least £200 is one of the five conditions attached to the £240 switching payment, alongside a full switch through the Current Account Switch Service, £1,500 paid in and two active household direct debits, all inside 60 days of the switch request.

sections.heading: Edge Up at £5, Edge Explorer at £17
sections.html:
Edge Up is the same idea with the dials turned up. It costs £5 a month, asks for £1,500 paid in monthly and two active direct debits, lifts the cashback cap to £15 and pays 2.10% AER / 2.08% gross variable on balances up to £25,000. A full £25,000 earns about £525 a year against £60 of fees, which is the strongest case in the range for anyone who genuinely parks that much in a current account. It is also 1.65 points below Bank Rate, and the rate used to be 2.50%.

Edge Explorer sits above both at £17 a month, or £204 a year, and is a packaged account rather than a banking one. It carries worldwide family travel insurance excluding Cuba, UK and European breakdown cover, mobile phone cover for the family, round-the-clock remote GP access, 1% on household bills to £10 a month and a second 1% at supermarkets and on travel costs to a further £10. Its age limits are tighter, 18 to 73, and joint applicants must live at the same UK address. Whether £204 is good value turns entirely on what those travel and breakdown policies would cost bought separately, and the policy documents are the ones to read before signing.

sections.heading: Whose licence your money is sitting on
sections.html:
Deposits are held by Santander UK plc, firm reference number 106054, and covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme to £120,000 per person. The bank is explicit that the same single limit covers its cahoot, Santander Business and Santander Corporate & Commercial trading names, so holding savings under two of those brands does not double the cover.

TSB is the interesting case. Santander bought it outright and completed on 30 April 2026, but on the bank's own wording dated 27 July 2026 the two still operate under separate banking licences, and protection applies to each separately. Someone with money in both currently has two £120,000 limits rather than one. That is a temporary position by definition — the licences will not stay apart forever — and it is worth rechecking before leaning on it. The same page carries a firmer promise: no further branch closures before 2028.

sections.heading: What the bank's own returns say about its service
sections.html:
The August 2026 service quality results, from the survey every large provider must publish, put Santander on 55% for overall service quality in Great Britain, ranked 13th of 17. Online and mobile banking scored 68% and also came 13th; overdraft services scored 57% for another 13th place. Branches were the exception, at 63% and 7th. In Northern Ireland it scored 55% overall, 10th of 12.

The complaints return is both more flattering and more detailed. For 1 January to 30 June 2026 Santander opened 57,274 banking and credit card complaints, a rate of 2.4 per 1,000 accounts. It closed 54% within three working days and the remaining 46% inside eight weeks, and upheld 47% of them. The largest single driver was general administration and customer service. Home finance was the weaker book, at 4.1 complaints per 1,000 balances and 66% upheld.

The branch network has been shrinking faster than that 2028 promise suggests. Santander closed 95 branches in 2025 and a further 40 during 2026, with four more going in early 2027, leaving 305 of its own sites: 244 full service, 36 on reduced hours and 19 without counters. It says every closing branch is within about 1.4 miles of a Post Office, and is expanding community banking points in libraries and local venues.

sections.heading: £32.8m for the accounts of customers who had died
sections.html:
On 19 December 2018 the Financial Conduct Authority fined Santander UK plc £32,817,800 over its probate and bereavement process: £20,217,800 for breaches of Principles 3 and 6 between 1 January 2013 and 11 July 2016, and £12,600,000 for a Principle 11 breach in failing to tell the regulator. The notice found 40,428 deceased customers affected and over £183m that should have been passed to their estates and was not. A remediation programme covered 36,059 customers and assets valued above £160m. The penalty carried a 30% settlement discount; without it the figure would have been £46,882,500.

A second and larger notice followed on 9 December 2022, £107,793,300 for anti-money-laundering failures in business banking between 31 December 2012 and 18 October 2017, discounted 30% from £153,990,400. That one concerns business customers rather than personal ones. Both sit on the public register, both predate the current management team, and neither appears anywhere in the marketing for this account, which is exactly why they are worth reading.

sections.heading: The cashback that was here two years ago
sections.html:
Until 9 September 2025 the Edge accounts paid 1% on debit card spending at supermarkets, on fuel, on public transport and travel, and at electric vehicle charge points, on top of the bills cashback. Santander withdrew it, citing wider market conditions, and put nothing in its place.

The effect on the ceiling is straightforward. Edge went from a possible £20 a month to £10, or £240 a year down to £120. Edge Up went from £30 to £15, £360 a year down to £180. Both fees stayed where they were. Edge Up's credit interest has since come down as well, from 2.50% to 2.10%. Anyone reading an older review of this account is reading about a materially better product than the one on sale, and the sums in those reviews no longer hold.

sections.heading: Questions Santander leaves unanswered in writing
sections.html:
Three gaps are worth a phone call before committing. Santander states the £500 pay-in and the two-direct-debit test clearly, but publishes nothing about a month in which you miss either one — whether cashback is simply lost for that month, and whether the £3 is still taken. The key facts document says the fee begins after you first meet the conditions and is silent on what happens once you stop meeting them.

An independent product rating could not be verified for this review either: the ratings tables on Fairer Finance's Santander page would not load on 23 September 2026, so no star rating is quoted here rather than one being carried in from elsewhere. And while the Edge Saver appears in the savings rate sheet effective 3 September 2026, the Regular Saver does not, so its 8.00% rests on the product page alone and should be confirmed at application.

Borrowing, at least, is fully documented. The arranged overdraft is a representative 39.94% APR/EAR variable, more than ten times Bank Rate, while unarranged borrowing carries 0% and no fees for paying or refusing a payment. Anyone switching in from another bank gets four months of the arranged overdraft interest free, which is a real concession and also a reminder of what the rate returns to afterwards.

pros: The £3 fee does not start until the month after you first qualify for cashback, so a dormant account costs nothing
1% on council tax, energy, water, phone, broadband and paid-for TV covers the fee at £300 a month of qualifying bills
The linked Edge Saver pays 6.00% AER on £4,000, which is 2.25 points above Bank Rate
No Santander conversion fee on debit card spending or cash withdrawals outside the UK
Complaints run at 2.4 per 1,000 accounts, with 54% closed inside three working days
Santander has committed to no further branch closures before 2028, and kept 305 of its own branches after the 2026 programme
cons: The current account itself pays no credit interest at any balance
The 1% cashback on supermarket, fuel, travel and EV charging spending was withdrawn on 9 September 2025, halving the Edge cap from £20 to £10 a month
The £240 switching payment is restricted to the Everyday Current Account, so Edge customers cannot have it
Edge Saver's headline 6.00% is a 3.50% rate plus a bonus that stops after 12 months, and 3.50% is below the 3.75% Bank Rate; nothing is paid above £4,000
Santander placed 13th of 17 providers for overall service quality in the August 2026 survey, on 55%
The arranged overdraft is a representative 39.94% APR/EAR, and Edge Up's credit rate has been cut from 2.50% to 2.10%
Santander does not publish what happens to the cashback or the fee in a month you miss the £500 pay-in or drop to one direct debit
verdict: Edge is a bills account with a savings account bolted to it, and the sums only work if your direct debits are large and your savings balance is close to £4,000. At £300 a month of qualifying household bills you break even on the fee; at £1,000 a month you clear £84 a year after it. Add £4,000 in the Edge Saver and the first year is worth roughly £324 against £36 of fees, which is a strong return. The second year is the one to watch, because the bonus expires, the saver drops to 3.50% and the cashback cap is half what it was two years ago. Anyone whose main interest is the £240 switching payment should look at the Everyday account instead, and anyone with more than £4,000 to hold should keep the surplus somewhere it earns.

faqs.q: Is the £3 monthly fee charged if I never use the account?
faqs.a: No. Santander's key facts document says the fee starts after you meet the conditions for earning cashback for the first time, so an Edge account opened and left idle does not cost £3 a month. What the bank does not publish is the reverse case, once you have qualified and then stop meeting the £500 pay-in or the two-direct-debit test, so check that before relying on it.

faqs.q: Can I get the £240 switching payment with an Edge account?
faqs.a: No. The offer that opened on 1 September 2026 applies to a new or existing Santander Everyday Current Account only. You also have to switch in fully through the Current Account Switch Service, pay in £1,500, hold two active household direct debits and fund a Santander Regular Saver with £200, all inside 60 days. Anyone who held a Santander current account on 1 January 2026, or who has taken a Santander switching incentive before, is excluded, as is a switch from Santander, cahoot or Cater Allen.

faqs.q: What happens to the Edge Saver rate after the first year?
faqs.a: The 6.00% AER is a 3.50% underlying rate plus a 2.50% bonus that runs for twelve months from opening. Once the bonus ends the balance earns 3.50% AER, below the 3.75% Bank Rate set in December 2025. Both halves are variable, and no interest is paid above £4,000, so a balance of £6,000 earns on £4,000 of it and nothing on the rest.

faqs.q: Does my money have extra protection now that Santander owns TSB?
faqs.a: For the moment, yes, if you bank with both. Santander says that because Santander UK and TSB still hold separate banking licences, FSCS protection of £120,000 applies to each bank separately. Within Santander UK plc itself the limit is shared across cahoot, Santander Business and Santander Corporate & Commercial. The separate-licence position is stated as correct at 27 July 2026, and it is the kind of thing that changes once an acquisition is integrated.

faqs.q: Which bills count towards the 1% cashback?
faqs.a: Council tax, gas and electricity, water, mobile and home phone, broadband and paid-for TV packages, and only when paid by direct debit from the Edge account. TV licences, LPG and Calor gas, maintenance contracts and anything used commercially are excluded. The cap is £10 a month, reached at £1,000 of qualifying bills, and £300 a month is the point at which the cashback covers the £3 fee.

title: Santander Personal Loan
meta_title: Santander Personal Loan: 6.4% APR, Rates Published Upfront
meta_description: Santander prints four loan rates by amount borrowed: 10.5%, 8.0%, 7.5% and 6.4% APR. Rates, thresholds and settlement terms checked 5 October 2026.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 6.4% APR representative — £7,500 to £25,000 over 1 to 5 years, with 10.5% below £3,000 and a 29.9% ceiling

intro:
Santander sets its personal loan price by how much you borrow, and it publishes the whole ladder before you apply: 10.5% APR on £1,000 to £2,999, 8.0% on £3,000 to £4,999, 7.5% on £5,000 to £7,499 and 6.4% APR representative on £7,500 to £25,000. Those four rates were read off Santander's own loan pages on 5 October 2026, alongside a stated ceiling of 29.9%.

That is more than most of the big banks put on the shelf. A searcher can work out the likely rate on a £6,000 loan without handing over a single detail, and the table applies to new and existing Santander customers alike – there is no requirement to bank with Santander first. The eligibility checker runs a soft search that leaves no mark on a credit file, an online decision usually arrives within five minutes, and approved money reaches a nominated account within two working days.

Two rules decide whether any of it is available. Santander lends on personal loans from age 21, not 18, and it wants a regular yearly income of at least £10,500 for loans up to £19,999, rising to £20,000 of income for anything between £20,000 and £25,000. No bankruptcy, County Court judgment or individual voluntary arrangement in the previous six years, and repayment has to be by Direct Debit.

key_facts.label: Lender
key_facts.value: Santander UK plc, Financial Services Register firm reference number 106054

key_facts.label: Published rate ladder
key_facts.value: 10.5% APR on £1,000–£2,999; 8.0% on £3,000–£4,999; 7.5% on £5,000–£7,499; 6.4% APR representative on £7,500–£25,000

key_facts.label: Maximum APR

key_facts.value: 21 or over; £10,500 a year up to £19,999 borrowed, £20,000 a year for £20,000–£25,000

key_facts.value: Unlimited, at no extra cost; the term shortens unless you ask to keep it and pay less each month

key_facts.value: 14 days from the day after the loan opens, with no interest payable

key_facts.value: Separate product from £500, paid straight to the card accounts named in the agreement, open from age 18

key_facts.value: Decision usually within 5 minutes online (6.30am–11.30pm); funds within 2 working days, or instantly in branch on accounts over 60 days old

key_facts.value: 1,132 credit-related complaints opened, 2.9 per 1,000 loans, 45% upheld

sections.heading: The ladder, priced in pounds
sections.html:
Percentages hide the size of the decision, so here are the same four rungs as monthly payments and total cost, worked from Santander's published APRs on a loan with no arrangement fee.

Borrow £3,000 over five years at 8.0% APR and the repayment is about £60.43 a month, £3,625.75 all told, of which £625.75 is interest. Take £10,000 over four years at 6.4% and it is roughly £235.86 a month and £11,321.21 in total; stretch the same £10,000 to five years and the monthly figure drops to about £194.35 while the total rises to £11,661.05. At the top of the range, £25,000 over five years costs in the region of £485.88 a month and £29,152.62 overall, with £4,152.62 of interest.

The ceiling matters as much as the ladder. Santander states plainly that "the maximum APR we could offer is 29.9%", so the advertised rung is where pricing starts rather than where it lands. A rate between 6.4% and 29.9% is a spread of more than 23 points, and which end of it you see depends on the credit and affordability assessment behind the application.

sections.heading: Where borrowing one pound more makes the loan cheaper
sections.html:
A price list arranged in bands has edges, and Santander's edges sit at £3,000, £5,000 and £7,500. Cross one and the rate on the entire balance falls, which produces an outcome worth checking before you type an amount into the calculator: on the published rates, borrowing slightly more can cost less.

Take a five-year term. £2,999 at 10.5% comes to roughly £3,825.51 in total. £3,000 at 8.0% comes to about £3,625.75. One extra pound of borrowing, £199.76 less to repay. The same thing happens, more mildly, at £5,000: £4,999 at 8.0% totals around £6,041.71 against £5,000 at 7.5% at £5,976.36, a £65.34 difference. And at the top edge, £7,400 at 7.5% over five years runs to about £8,845.02 at £147.42 a month, while £7,500 at 6.4% runs to £8,745.79 at £145.76 a month – a hundred pounds more borrowed, £99.23 less repaid, and a smaller payment every month for five years.

None of that is a trick in the pricing; it is the arithmetic of banded rates, and the bands are published so anyone can do the sum. It does mean the sensible move is to price the amount just above each edge as well as the amount you had in mind, and it is the single most useful thing this page can tell a reader who has already decided to borrow from Santander.

sections.heading: A second loan that pays your card companies instead of you
sections.html:
Alongside the main product, Santander runs a separate agreement called the Personal Loan to pay off your credit card(s), and its Key Facts Document, effective 4 November 2024, describes something built differently. The money does not arrive in a current account: it is "paid directly to your existing credit card account(s) shown in your credit agreement", and it "cannot be used for any other purpose".

Two of its terms are more generous than the main loan's. It starts at £500 rather than £1,000, and it opens at 18 rather than 21. The eligibility list also asks only that an applicant has not been declared bankrupt or had an individual voluntary arrangement in six years, where the main loan's list adds a County Court judgment. The upper limit is the same £25,000 and the rate is fixed for the life of the agreement, with the document noting that the rate offered "may differ from the advertised Representative APR".

Because Santander settles the card balances itself, the borrower never has the cash in hand to spend elsewhere, which is the whole point of the design. It is a narrower product than a general-purpose loan and it is easy to miss on the main loans page.

sections.heading: Five minutes, two working days, a search that leaves no mark
sections.html:
The mechanics are quick and documented. Santander's own wording on the checker is that "using our checker will give you an idea of whether we'll accept you for a loan. It won't leave a record on your credit file" – a soft search, with the hard one attached to the full application. Online applications made between 6.30am and 11.30pm typically get a decision within five minutes.

After approval, "once released, your loan funds will be in your chosen bank account within 2 working days". Applying in a branch can be faster still: Santander says an approved branch application on an account more than 60 days old can be funded instantly, and a phone application usually lands the next working day. Terms run from 12 to 60 months in six-month steps, and the rate is fixed – "the rate you pay is fixed and will remain so for the life of your loan".

The statutory escape hatch is spelled out too. Withdrawal is available "within 14 days, starting the day after your loan has been opened", and the document is explicit that "you won't need to pay any interest if you change your mind during this time". Up to two applicants can go on one agreement.

sections.heading: A £3.2bn loan book inside a £238.9bn bank
sections.html:
Santander UK plc reported a profit before tax of £528m for the six months to 30 June 2026, down from £764m a year earlier, on customer loans of £238.9bn and customer deposits of £227.2bn. Banking net interest margin was 2.25% against 2.26%, and the CET1 capital ratio stood at 14.2%.

Inside that, the unsecured personal loan book was £3.2bn. Mortgages were £204.7bn, and credit cards £3.7bn – so Santander has more money out on plastic than on loans, and both are rounding errors beside the mortgage book. A reader deciding whether to borrow here is dealing with a mortgage bank that also writes loans, which is worth knowing mainly because it explains why the loan proposition is priced to compete rather than designed to dominate.

The shape of the bank changed this year. Santander completed its purchase of TSB on 30 April 2026, bringing in around five million customers and roughly 174 branches to make a combined network of about 480, with a commitment that no further Santander or TSB branches will close before 2028 at the earliest. TSB continues to trade under its own brand for now, and existing TSB loan and mortgage terms are fixed, so nothing about an in-force agreement changes on acquisition.

For market context, the Finance and Leasing Association reported £10.3bn of new consumer credit advanced by its members in July 2026, 1% below July 2025, with credit card and personal loan new business together 2% lower than the same month a year before and the first seven months of 2026 running 4% ahead of 2025. Demand is flat rather than falling away.

sections.heading: 1,132 complaints, and roughly 390,000 loans behind them
sections.html:
Santander publishes its own complaints return, and the figures for 1 January to 30 June 2026 are specific enough to be useful. Across the bank it opened 62,497 complaints. The Credit Related line – which is where a personal loan grievance goes – accounted for 1,132 of them, at a rate of 2.9 per 1,000 loans, with 45% upheld.

Set that against the bank's other product lines in the same return. Banking and credit cards drew 57,274 complaints at 2.4 per 1,000 accounts, 54% closed within three days and 47% upheld. Home finance drew 3,878 at 4.1 per 1,000 balances with 66% upheld. Insurance and pure protection managed 82 complaints at 0.2 per 1,000 policies and 24% upheld. The lending line is therefore running barely above the everyday banking line on frequency and slightly below it on uphold rate, which is not what a borrower braced for an argument about a declined decision might expect.

The rate also gives away a number Santander does not otherwise publish. If 1,132 complaints represent 2.9 per 1,000 loans, there are roughly 390,000 live loan accounts, which against a £3.2bn book implies an average balance somewhere near £8,200 – comfortably inside the 6.4% rung. That is derived arithmetic rather than a disclosed figure, so treat it as an estimate.

Independent ratings are thinner. Smart Money People shows the Santander loan at 3.20 out of 5 from 57 reviews, last reviewed 22 January 2026. No Defaqto star rating or Fairer Finance score specific to the personal loan could be found, which needs confirming rather than reading as an absence of quality.

sections.heading: Fifty-eight days, and Santander prints the number itself
sections.html:
The sales pages lead with "overpay at no extra cost" and "you can make unlimited overpayments at any time before your final repayment is due or you can repay your loan in full". The Key Facts Document, effective 4 November 2024, is where the second half of that sentence gets priced: on settling in full, Santander says it will "assume that you'll repay your loan in full within 28 days so it will include interest over that period" and that "you'll also be charged an extra 30 days' interest. That means you'll be charged up to 58 days' interest in total".

Credit where it is due: Santander does the addition for the reader and prints the total, which not every lender bothers to do. The charge itself is an allowance the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004 give every creditor, not something Santander invented, and taking the full allowance is normal practice.

What the sales pages do not do is flag that "no extra cost" and "up to 58 days' interest" are answers to two different questions. Chipping away at the balance while keeping the agreement running is free. Closing the agreement is not. On £5,000 still outstanding the extra works out at roughly £49.53 at 6.4% APR and about £79.96 at 10.5%, so it is tens of pounds rather than hundreds – but a reader who plans to clear the loan with a bonus should ask for a settlement figure, on 0800 028 4055, rather than assume the headline covers them. A partial overpayment shortens the term by default; keeping the original term and paying less each month is available on request.

sections.heading: What the rulebook makes a lender do once the money has gone
sections.html:
Most of the attention on consumer credit rules goes on the decision to lend. The obligations that run for the next five years sit in CONC 6.7 of the FCA Handbook, and they are short enough to quote. CONC 6.7.2R, in force since 1 March 2018, requires that "a firm must monitor a customer's repayment record and take appropriate action where there are signs of actual or possible repayment difficulties". That is a standing duty, not a response to a phone call.

The refinancing rules are the ones worth reading before consolidating anything. CONC 6.7.17R, from 25 November 2020, defines refinancing to include extending a repayment period by agreement, by contractual power or by waiver. CONC 6.7.18R, in force since 1 April 2014, is blunt: "a firm must not encourage a customer to refinance a regulated credit agreement if the result would be the customer's commitments are not sustainable." CONC 6.7.19R bars refinancing without the customer's request or consent unless the firm is exercising forbearance, and then only where it reasonably believes it is in the customer's interests.

Santander's debt consolidation page sits squarely in that territory and does not oversell itself. Its own caveat is that "we can't guarantee that this type of loan will reduce your overall cost of borrowing", with a prompt to compare existing rates against what is offered. A longer term at a lower rate can still cost more in total, and the bank says so.

The other end of the same chapter is less comfortable reading. If payments stop, the Key Facts Document says Santander can "ask you to repay the remaining loan amount back straight away", "charge you our reasonable costs in trying to collect the loan amount from you, including legal costs and costs finding you", and "give information about you and how you've managed your account to licensed credit reference agencies". The collection costs are described as reasonable rather than listed, which is a real gap: there is no published schedule putting a number on them.

sections.heading: One £1,000 loan, as an ombudsman read it
sections.html:
Published Financial Ombudsman Service decisions are the closest thing to seeing a lender's affordability process tested by somebody outside it. Decision DRN-5688533, decided by ombudsman Robert Walker, concerns a £1,000 Santander personal loan taken in March 2019 at 24.89% APR.

The bank statements Santander itself collected showed the customer paying nearly £800 a month to eight loan providers, four of them payday lenders. The ombudsman found that "the bank statement shows that Mr G was likely dependent on payday lending" and that new borrowing was going on living costs, and concluded that Santander had lent anyway despite holding evidence that contradicted its credit check. The complaint was upheld. Santander was told to remove £672.20 of interest, fees and charges, refund anything paid above the original £1,000 with 8% simple annual interest from the date of payment, and delete the adverse entries from the customer's credit file.

Two things in that for a reader today. The affordability assessment is a check Santander can get wrong, and the Ombudsman will unwind the cost of the credit when it does. And 24.89% on a £1,000 loan is a reminder of how far the price can sit from the bottom rung: that rate is well inside the 29.9% ceiling, on an amount whose advertised rate today is 10.5%.

sections.heading: The figures Santander does not serve
sections.html:
For a product where the law is built around a worked example, the example is the hardest thing to read. On the main loans page and on the car, home improvement and debt consolidation pages, the representative example renders as labels without values – "APR representative", "Monthly repayment", "Total amount repayable" – because the calculator fills them in by script, with the note that "these figures will change every time you make changes to the calculator". A visitor using a browser normally almost certainly sees the numbers appear, so this is a rendering matter rather than a missing disclosure, and it is stated here as unestablished rather than absent. It still means the one passage designed for comparing lenders side by side cannot be read without running the page.

The newest Key Facts Document that could be located is effective 4 November 2024, which was almost two years old at the date of checking. Whether a 2025 or 2026 version exists behind the application journey could not be confirmed, so every quotation above is attributed to that document and that date. Santander's money worries page would not open on the day of checking, so the forbearance options it describes and the free debt advice organisations it names could not be verified first hand – worth a call to 0800 171 2171 if arrears are the reason for reading.

There is also no fee schedule anywhere in the open material. Beyond the 58-day settlement allowance and the undefined "reasonable costs" of collection, a prospective borrower cannot find out what anything else costs until the agreement is in front of them.

pros: Four rates published by loan size before you apply, rather than a single representative figure with nothing behind it
No requirement to bank with Santander – the same ladder applies to new and existing customers
Soft-search eligibility checker that leaves no mark on a credit file, with an online decision usually inside five minutes
Unlimited partial overpayments at no charge, and the choice of a shorter term or a smaller monthly payment
The Key Facts Document prints the full 58-day settlement figure instead of leaving the reader to add it up
A separate credit-card payoff loan from £500, open from age 18, paid straight to the card providers
Funds within two working days, and potentially the same day on a branch application
Lending complaints run at 2.9 per 1,000 loans with 45% upheld, barely above the bank's everyday banking line
cons: The 6.4% headline covers only £7,500 to £25,000; the ceiling is 29.9%, a spread of more than 23 points with no published table of who gets what
"Overpay at no extra cost" sits on the sales pages while the Key Facts Document charges up to 58 days' interest to settle in full, and neither page cross-refers to the other
The representative example renders as empty labels on all four loan pages, so the one legally mandated comparison passage is unreadable without running the page's script
Minimum age 21 and an income floor of £10,500, rising to £20,000 of income above £20,000 borrowed, rules out a slice of borrowers other lenders will quote
No published fee or charge schedule: collection costs are described only as "reasonable", with no figures attached
The newest Key Facts Document findable is effective 4 November 2024, and no later version could be confirmed
An ombudsman found in DRN-5688533 that Santander lent £1,000 at 24.89% to a customer its own bank statements showed to be dependent on payday lending
No Defaqto or Fairer Finance rating specific to the loan could be found, and Smart Money People has only 57 reviews behind a 3.20 out of 5
verdict: Santander is one of the few large UK lenders that tells you the price before it tells you about itself: 10.5%, 8.0%, 7.5% and 6.4% APR, set by how much you borrow, published openly and open to people who bank elsewhere. That makes it unusually easy to check, and the banded structure throws up a genuinely useful quirk at £3,000, £5,000 and £7,500, where borrowing a pound or a hundred more drops the rate on the whole balance and cuts the total cost. The caveats are the ones that come with any bank loan priced on a ladder: the advertised rung is a starting point against a 29.9% ceiling, settling early costs up to 58 days' interest even though the sales page says overpayments are free, and the detail thins out fast once you go looking for a fee schedule or a current Key Facts Document. Worth a soft search if you are borrowing £3,000 or more, and worth pricing the amount just above the nearest band edge before you commit.

faqs.q: What rate will Santander actually give me?
faqs.a: The advertised rate depends on the amount: 10.5% APR on £1,000 to £2,999, 8.0% on £3,000 to £4,999, 7.5% on £5,000 to £7,499 and 6.4% APR representative on £7,500 to £25,000. Those are starting points. Santander states a maximum of 29.9%, and the rate offered follows its credit and affordability assessment. The eligibility checker uses a soft search, so it costs nothing on a credit file to find out.

faqs.q: Do I need a Santander current account to get a loan?
faqs.a: No. The published rate table applies to new and existing Santander customers alike, and there is no requirement to hold a Santander account first. You do need to be able to repay by Direct Debit, be 21 or over, live permanently in the UK, and have a regular yearly income of at least £10,500 for loans up to £19,999 or £20,000 for loans of £20,000 to £25,000.

faqs.q: Is it really free to overpay?
faqs.a: Partial overpayments are. Santander says you can make unlimited overpayments at any time at no extra cost, and the term shortens unless you ask to keep it and pay less each month. Clearing the loan in full is different: the Key Facts Document effective 4 November 2024 assumes settlement within 28 days and adds an extra 30 days' interest, up to 58 days in total. On £5,000 outstanding that is roughly £49.53 at 6.4% APR. Ask for a settlement figure on 0800 028 4055 before you pay it off.

faqs.q: How quickly does the money arrive?
faqs.a: An online application made between 6.30am and 11.30pm typically gets a decision within five minutes, and approved funds reach your chosen account within two working days. A branch application on an account more than 60 days old can be funded instantly, and a phone application usually lands the next working day. You then have 14 days from the day after the loan opens to withdraw, with no interest to pay.

faqs.q: Who regulates Santander, and where does a complaint go?
faqs.a: Santander UK plc is on the Financial Services Register under firm reference number 106054, checkable at fca.org.uk/register. Complaints go to the bank first, on 0800 171 2171, and can then be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service if you are unhappy with the answer. Between 1 January and 30 June 2026 Santander opened 1,132 credit-related complaints, 2.9 per 1,000 loans, and upheld 45% of them.

faqs.q: Is a Santander consolidation loan cheaper than my credit cards?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, and Santander does not claim it is: its own wording is that it cannot guarantee this type of loan will reduce your overall cost of borrowing. A lower rate over a longer term can still cost more in total interest. CONC 6.7.18R forbids a lender from encouraging refinancing where the result would be unsustainable commitments, but the sum itself is still yours to do. There is also a separate Santander loan from £500 that pays your card balances directly and cannot be spent on anything else.

title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance Review
meta_title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance: What It Costs
meta_description: Simply Business quotes tradesman cover from £5.40 a month across a panel of 19 insurers. The prices, the limits, the excesses and the fees, checked.
intro:
Simply Business started in 2005 as a team of five people trying to sell business insurance online at a time when almost nobody did. It now covers more than one million small businesses and landlords across roughly 1,500 trades, employs over 900 people from offices in London and Northampton, and paid out £57 million in claims during 2025 — an average of about £156,000 a day. On the tradesman side alone it puts the figure at more than 253,000 tradespeople on cover. Quotes start at £5.40 a month and the site reckons on about seven minutes to complete one.

It does not carry the risk itself. Simply Business is the trading name of Xbridge Limited, an insurance broker, and the policy you end up with is written by one of the insurers on its panel — AXA, Aviva, Zurich, Allianz, QBE, Covéa, Hiscox, Markel, Churchill or AIG among them. That is a point in its favour rather than against it: a sole trader paying £7 a month is getting paper from companies that would not normally quote a one-person business directly. The whole operation has been owned by the American insurer Travelers since 2017, which bought it from Aquiline Capital Partners for around $490 million when it had 425,000 customers and had placed £93 million of premium in 2016.

What follows is what the cover actually contains, what the excesses look like on the two wordings the site publishes openly, what paying monthly adds, and where the paperwork runs out.
