key_facts.value: Rail Ombudsman, named in Trainline's own terms; 40 working days with Trainline first, then a decision binding on Trainline

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: None found — no ratings agency scores rail ticket retailers

sections.heading: Two numbers for the same question
sections.html:
Trainline's own about page gives two counts of the same thing on the same screen. It says the company aggregates data from "over 70 carriers across Europe", and a few lines away it says it works with "270+ rail and coach companies". Both cannot be a count of the same set. The likeliest reading is that the smaller number counts carriers wired directly into the booking engine and the larger one counts every company whose tickets can appear in a search, but Trainline does not say so, and it is the sort of figure worth asking about rather than assuming.

What is not in doubt is the shape of the business. Net ticket sales split three ways in the year to 28 February 2026: £4,135m from UK consumers, up 6%; £1,104m from international consumers, up 5%; and £1,081m from Trainline Solutions, the business travel and white-label arm, up 15%. The fastest-growing third of the company is therefore the part most travellers never see.

sections.heading: The fee, to the penny
sections.html:
The booking fee "will vary between a minimum of 59p and a maximum of £2.79", and Trainline says it is calculated from the booking itself — the ticket price and the date of travel. It is shown in the basket before payment, which is a change the regulator pushed for rather than a courtesy. The app is treated differently: book in it on the day you are travelling and there is no booking fee, and the app charges no delivery fee on any ticket at any time.

On the website, delivery is free for digital tickets, £2.99 to collect from a station machine and £12.99 for a paper ticket by Royal Mail Special Delivery. That last figure is worth pausing on — it is more than many advance fares cost, and it exists because Special Delivery is a tracked, insured service rather than a stamp.

The comparison a reader will want is with buying the identical ticket somewhere else. Rail fares are set by the industry, not the retailer, so the ticket is the same ticket and the price of the travel is the same price. LNER's own site tells customers they can "[b]ook train tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales through LNER and pay no bookings fees". On a £60 journey a fee of up to £2.79 is noise. On a £9 advance single it is nearer a third of the saving that made the advance worth booking.

sections.heading: How the money actually reaches Trainline
sections.html:
Put the two headline numbers side by side and the business model falls out of them. £6,319m of tickets sold produced £453m of revenue, which is a little over seven pence in every pound. Most of that is commission paid by the train and coach companies for selling their seats; the booking fee is the part the passenger sees. Trainline's terms put it plainly enough: "some of the fees come straight from the operators, so we have to charge them to you."

It is a profitable arrangement. Operating profit reached £122m in the year to 28 February 2026, up 43%, on adjusted EBITDA of £177m, up 11%, with basic earnings per share of 19.4p and £66m of adjusted free cash flow. The company has bought back £294m of its own shares since starting in September 2023, about 23% of its issued share capital, and had completed £94m of the current £150m programme by 30 April 2026. A retailer buying in a quarter of itself is a retailer with more cash than it has uses for.

sections.heading: Changing your mind costs money twice
sections.html:
Trainline runs two separate fee ladders, and they are its charges, levied on top of whatever the train company itself deducts. Refunding a UK ticket is free below £2, then £1 on a ticket costing £2 to £2.99, £1.50 from £3, £2 from £4, £3 from £5, £4 from £6 and £5 on anything from £7 upwards. Exchanging is dearer: free below £2, then £1 up to £4, £2.50 up to £6, £3 up to £8, £5 up to £11, £7.50 up to £13, £8.50 up to £15 and £10 above that. A Season Ticket refund costs a flat £10, though changing an eligible one is free.

Two details sit underneath the ladders. The booking fee itself is never returned — "booking fees cannot be refunded" — so a cancelled £8 ticket can lose its £5 refund fee and its booking fee together. And on European journeys the exchange fee is not Trainline's to set at all: it "vary[s] by carrier" and only appears during booking.

sections.heading: What changed on 1 April 2026
sections.html:
The biggest shift in years landed this April and it has nothing to do with Trainline's own charges. For Anytime tickets, Off-Peak tickets, Day Travelcards, Rovers and Rangers bought on or after 1 April 2026, a refund must be requested "before 23:59 on the day before your ticket becomes valid". Ask afterwards and it is "only considered in exceptional circumstances", with evidence that the ticket went unused. Tickets bought before that date keep the terms they were sold under, however far ahead the journey.

The industry administration fee sits on top: up to £5 a ticket and up to £10 a Season Ticket, and where the fee would swallow the refund, nothing is paid at all. Three things survive untouched, and they are the ones most often forgotten — a cancelled train still means a full refund, Delay Repay is a separate scheme that these rules do not reach, and the outward half of an Open Return cannot be refunded on its own once it becomes valid.

sections.heading: Delay Repay is the train company's job
sections.html:
Compensation thresholds are set by each operator and most follow the same shape: 25% of the fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes, and the full fare at 60 minutes and beyond. Some operators pay nothing below 30 minutes. Trainline's part is to watch the journey and tell you: "We'll track your journey and let you know if you're eligible... we'll send you a push notification or email with a link to the train operator's website, where you can submit your claim."

That handover is not a design choice. In its own full-year statement Trainline told investors that operators are offering "1-click delay-repay, a feature third party retailers are expressly prohibited from providing to their customers". A company flagging its own competitive disadvantage in an investor document is as close to an unvarnished fact as this market produces, and it is the single clearest reason a frequent claimant might book on the operator's own app instead.

sections.heading: The regulator has already done the arithmetic on refund fees
sections.html:
The Office of Rail and Road studied refund administration across a full year to 31 March 2020: 341 million tickets issued and 5.8 million refunded. It found the average fee charged, where one was charged at all, was £6.96 a ticket, against an average cost of processing a refund — staff, systems, bank charges — of £3.77. Because 28% of fees were waived, the average across every refunded ticket came out at £4.64. The industry cap is £10, and the ORR has been working with the Department for Transport and the Rail Delivery Group on whether that cap should come down.

Read Trainline's £10 Season Ticket refund fee against those numbers and it sits precisely at the ceiling, at something under three times the regulator's estimate of what the work costs. That is legal, it is what the rules allow, and it is also the kind of figure a passenger only discovers at the moment they need the money back.

sections.heading: Who you are buying from, and who is watching
sections.html:
The contracting party for a British booking is Trainline.com Limited, company number 03846791, incorporated on 17 September 1999 and registered at 1 Stonecutter Street, London EC4A 4AH under SIC code 62090. Its last accounts were made up to 28 February 2025 and its next confirmation statement is due on 23 January 2027. A booking made in France is with Trainline SAS instead, trade register 512 277 450 in Paris, under French law and with a French tourism mediator rather than an ombudsman.

British customers get the Rail Ombudsman, named in Trainline's own terms. Give Trainline 40 working days to resolve a complaint — or less, if it sends a deadlock letter — and the Ombudsman can then take the case and issue a decision binding on Trainline, free to the passenger except for incidental costs. The ORR polices the selling itself. It reviewed 40 online rail ticket retailers in December 2023 and wrote to seven about how clearly they displayed booking, finder's, fulfilment and refund fees; Trainline was one of the seven. By March 2025 the regulator recorded that all of them had made changes, and the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has since required fees to be folded into the total price at the earliest opportunity.

sections.heading: A state-owned rival is being built, and Trainline told its shareholders so
sections.html:
The government announced in January 2025 that Great British Railways would sell tickets, and the Railways Bill sets out how. Fourteen separate operator websites are to be folded into a single GBR app and site, alongside ticket offices, machines and onboard sales. Independent retailers are promised continued access — "[i]ndependent retailers, open access operators and devolved operators... will also be able to retail to passengers, just as they do today" — and a code of practice, owned and administered by the ORR, is meant to keep the state's retail arm at arm's length from the state's wholesale arm. Breaching that code will be a licence breach.

The detail that matters most to a retailer is quieter. The retail industry management functions the Rail Delivery Group performs today — setting commission rates, running technical standards, licensing retailers — move into a GBR back office. The body setting Trainline's commission will be part of the group competing with it. Trainline's own full-year statement records the company working on "development of the Code of Practice for GBR" and engaging with government on the Bill. None of this changes what a ticket costs this month, and all of it explains why the company is arguing publicly about fair retail market practices.

sections.heading: Where the savings are real
sections.html:
Two Trainline features genuinely move money, and both are worth naming precisely. SplitSave finds legal split tickets for a journey — you stay on the same train, it simply has to stop at each split point — and Trainline puts the average saving at £13 a trip for bookings between 1 July 2024 and 30 June 2025, measured against the next cheapest fare a Trainline customer could have bought. It is the company's own measurement against its own baseline, so treat it as a fair indication rather than an audited number, but split ticketing is real and most travellers never do it by hand.

The second is railcards. Trainline sells 2.7 million digital railcards, up 16% year on year, and holds 45% of the 16 to 30 market — a £30 card that takes a third off most fares pays for itself in two or three journeys, and the digital version cannot be left at home. Neither feature is exclusive to Trainline, but both are easier to find there than on most operator sites.

pros: No booking fee at all in the app on the day of travel, and no delivery fee on any app booking
One account covers more than 40 countries and, on Trainline's own account, the majority of Europe's rail and coach operators
Fees appear in the basket before payment, so the total is visible before you commit
SplitSave automates split ticketing — an average £13 a trip on Trainline's own 2024-25 measurement
2.7 million digital railcards sold, including 45% of the 16 to 30 market, and a digital card cannot be left in a drawer
The Rail Ombudsman is named in Trainline's own terms, and its decisions bind Trainline
Financially solid — £122m of operating profit and £66m of adjusted free cash flow in the year to 28 February 2026
cons: The booking fee of up to £2.79 buys nothing the train company would not sell you itself — LNER, for one, advertises no booking fees on tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales
Booking fees are never refunded, so a cancelled cheap ticket can lose the fee and the £5 refund charge together
Trainline's refund and exchange ladders are its own charges and sit on top of whatever the train company deducts — up to £5 to refund and up to £10 to exchange
The £10 Season Ticket refund fee sits exactly at the industry cap, against the ORR's estimate of £3.77 as the average cost of processing a refund
No one-click Delay Repay: Trainline is, in its own words to shareholders, "expressly prohibited" from offering it, so every claim is handed to the operator's own form
£12.99 to post a paper ticket, which is more than many advance fares
Its own about page gives two irreconcilable counts of the operators it works with — "over 70 carriers" and "270+ rail and coach companies"
No independent rating exists for rail ticket retailers, so there is no Defaqto, Which? or Fairer Finance score to check this against
verdict: Trainline is the most complete rail shop in Europe and it charges between 59p and £2.79 for the privilege, which is a fair price for one account covering 40-odd countries and a poor one for a single advance single from Leeds. The honest way to use it is the way its own pricing points: search in the app, let SplitSave and the railcards do their work, and book on the day in the app where the fee disappears. For a regular commuter on one line, or anyone who claims Delay Repay more than occasionally, the operator's own app is the better tool — no booking fee, and a compensation claim that takes one tap rather than a link to somebody else's form. Nothing here is hidden; the fees are all published and the basket shows them before you pay. What the page above should change is when you use it, not whether.

faqs.q: Does Trainline charge a booking fee on UK train tickets?
faqs.a: Yes, on most bookings — "a minimum of 59p and a maximum of £2.79", worked out from the ticket price and the travel date, and shown in your basket before you pay. The exception is the app: book in it on the day you travel and there is no booking fee. The fee is never refunded, even when the ticket is.

faqs.q: Is a ticket cheaper if I buy it from the train company instead?
faqs.a: The fare is the same, because fares are set by the industry rather than by the retailer. What differs is the booking fee. LNER, for example, advertises that you can book tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales through its own site and "pay no bookings fees". On a £60 fare the difference is trivial; on a £9 advance it is not.

faqs.q: What does it cost to refund or change a ticket bought on Trainline?
faqs.a: Trainline's own refund fee starts at nothing below £2 and rises in steps to £5 a ticket on anything costing £7 or more, with a flat £10 on Season Tickets. Its exchange fee runs from nothing below £2 up to £10 on fares of £15 and above. Those are Trainline's charges; the train company may deduct an administration fee of up to £5 a ticket as well, and since 1 April 2026 Anytime, Off-Peak, Day Travelcard, Rover and Ranger tickets must be refunded before 23:59 the day before they become valid.

faqs.q: Who pays me if my train is delayed?
faqs.a: The train operator, not Trainline. Most operators pay 25% of the fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes and 100% at an hour or more, though the thresholds vary. Trainline tracks the journey and sends a link to the operator's claim form, but it cannot process the claim — it told its own shareholders that third-party retailers are "expressly prohibited" from offering one-click Delay Repay.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if Trainline gets it wrong?
faqs.a: Trainline first. If it has not resolved matters after 40 working days, or it sends a deadlock letter sooner, the Rail Ombudsman can take the case — it is named in Trainline's own terms, it is free to passengers apart from incidental costs, and its decisions bind Trainline. The Office of Rail and Road handles the fee-transparency side; it wrote to Trainline and six other retailers about fee display in December 2023 and recorded the changes as complete by March 2025.

faqs.q: Will Great British Railways replace Trainline?
faqs.a: Not directly. GBR is folding fourteen train operator ticket websites into one app and site, and the Railways Bill says independent retailers "will also be able to retail to passengers, just as they do today". The part worth watching is that the body setting retailers' commission rates and licensing them moves inside GBR, and an ORR-administered code of practice is supposed to keep those decisions separate.

title: Tyres.net Review: What 750 Prices for One Tyre Size Leave Out
meta_title: Tyres.net: 750 Prices for One Tyre Size, Compared
meta_description: Tyres.net lists 750 offers for a 205/55 R16, from £35.58. What the price covers, who you actually buy from, and the fitting charge nobody shows.

headline.label: Cheapest 205/55 R16 tyre listed
headline.value: £35.58 for a 91V Dovroad Zyphira — one of 750 offers in that size, delivered price, fitting not included

intro:
Search Tyres.net for a 205/55 R16, the size on more British family cars than any other, and it returns 750 separate offers running from £35.58 to £150.11 a corner. Figures checked on 20 September 2026 against the site's own search pages. It is a price comparison platform rather than a tyre shop: it gathers what other retailers are charging, sorts it, and hands you over to them.

The engine belongs to TyresNET GmbH, registered at Franz-Joseph-Straße 11 in Munich under HRB 221425 at the Amtsgericht München, VAT number DE301419717, with Andreas Prüfer and Nina Andree as managing directors. The same platform runs in 64 countries and 12 languages off a product feed of more than 10,000 items, and its UK callers get an 0330 number rather than a German one.

What it does well is show you the same tyre at several sellers on one line. Ask for a Continental ContiEcoContact 5 in 205/55 R16 91H and three shops come back at £70.48, £70.60 and £71.41 — a spread of 93p that would take three browser tabs to find anywhere else. Every listing also carries the tyre label grades: fuel efficiency, wet grip and the external noise figure in decibels, so a Bridgestone Turanza 6 in that size shows as B, A and 69 dB before you click anything.

key_facts.label: Who runs it
key_facts.value: TyresNET GmbH, Franz-Joseph-Straße 11, 80801 Munich — Amtsgericht München HRB 221425, VAT DE301419717

key_facts.label: Directors
key_facts.value: Andreas Prüfer and Nina Andree

key_facts.label: What it is
key_facts.value: A price comparison platform and marketplace, live in 64 countries and 12 languages; it sells nothing itself

key_facts.label: Catalogue
key_facts.value: More than 10,000 items in the product feed — car, van, motorcycle, truck and bicycle tyres, plus wheels, oils and accessories

key_facts.label: Offers in one common size
key_facts.value: 750 for 205/55 R16, spread across 38 pages of results, cheapest £35.58 and dearest £150.11

key_facts.label: Who you buy from
key_facts.value: The listed shop, not Tyres.net — contracts are 'concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops'

key_facts.label: Cancellation
key_facts.value: 14 days from delivery under the site's own withdrawal notice, with TyresNET collecting the goods and paying the return carriage

key_facts.label: Governing law
key_facts.value: German law, per clause 8.3 of the general terms

key_facts.label: Dispute route named in the terms
key_facts.value: The European ODR portal — switched off on 20 July 2025

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: None found. Defaqto rates insurance, Fairer Finance does not cover retail, and no ratings agency scores tyre comparison sites

sections.heading: 750 offers in one size, and who is actually behind them
sections.html:
The breadth is real. A 205/55 R16 search runs to 38 pages at roughly 20 products a page, and the budget end goes a long way below what a fitting chain will quote: Dovroad Zyphira at £35.58, Comforser PureSpeed at £36.19, Lanvigator Comfort 1 at £36.31, Tracmax F-109 at £36.75 and Saferich FRC16 at £37.65, all 91V or 94V and all from the same seller, tyresdirect. Move up to the names most drivers recognise and the ladder runs Continental ContiEcoContact 5 at £70.48, Continental UltraContact at £76.72, Continental PremiumContact 7 at £78.91, Bridgestone Turanza T005 at £83.24, Pirelli Cinturato P1 at £85.61, Bridgestone Turanza 6 at £88.96 and Michelin Primacy 5 Energy at £95.16. Continental alone accounts for 53 of the offers in that one size.

The seller names repeat: onlinecarparts.co.uk, tyres-outlet.co.uk, mytyres.co.uk and tyresdirect carry most of the listings on the front pages. Mytyres.co.uk is worth knowing about, because it is not an independent shop. It belongs to Delticom AG of Hedwig-Kohn-Straße 1, Sehnde, which by its own account runs over 300 online stores in more than 70 countries, carries 600-plus tyre brands and over 40,000 tyre models, and has served more than 17 million customers. A German platform comparing prices is therefore partly comparing the prices of another German group that sells the same tyres under a dozen different shopfronts. Nobody hides this — both companies publish it — but it is worth understanding that the number of shop names on a results page is larger than the number of businesses behind them.

sections.heading: The charge that never appears on the results page
sections.html:
A tyre bought this way arrives at your door. Getting it onto the car is a separate transaction with a separate business, and that is where a large part of the real cost sits. Kwik Fit publishes the number on its own site: all tyre discounts 'apply to the cost of the tyre only and exclude charges for fitting, balancing, valve and disposal', quoted at £20.00 per tyre in its tyre FAQ and at £20.50 in the footnote on the same page. Take the lower figure and a set of four is £80 before anyone touches a tyre; take the higher one and it is £82.

Run that against the headline. The £35.58 tyre becomes roughly £56 on the car if a fitter charges what Kwik Fit charges, and four of them come to about £222 rather than £142 — a 56% increase on the number that won the comparison. The £70.48 Continental goes to about £90. The gap narrows as the tyre gets dearer, which is why the saving on a premium tyre bought this way is usually genuine and the saving on the cheapest one on the page is usually a good deal smaller than it looks. Tyres.net does not raise fitting anywhere. Its FAQ covers searching, delivery, who the contract is with and how to contact a seller, and the word does not appear.

Delivery is the other absentee. Listings show a tyre price and nothing else; the site says only that 'each shop listed on Tyres.net has different delivery options' and that it 'does not carry the transport risk. The retailer is always responsible.' Since 6 April 2025, section 230 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has required a trader inviting a UK consumer to purchase to give the total price, meaning 'any fees, taxes, charges or other payments that the consumer will necessarily incur', and either to state any freight, delivery or postal charges not included in it or to say that such charges may apply. A comparison layer that passes you to a checkout where the carriage is finally revealed is exactly the shape that provision was written about, and a reader is entitled to treat the ranked price as incomplete until the basket confirms it.

sections.heading: Whose customer are you?
sections.html:
The general terms are blunt about it. Clause by clause they place Tyres.net outside the sale: 'the contracts about the products or services on the websites are concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops', and 'TyresNET in this case is not representative of one contracting parties'. Liability is excluded 'regardless of the legal basis' apart from death or personal injury, product liability, intent or gross negligence, and breach of what the terms call cardinal duties. Warranty questions are pushed to the partner shop's own conditions, cancellation rights to 'the GTC of the online shops (including their cancellation policies)'. German law applies under clause 8.3.

Set that beside the site's return policy and the picture stops being consistent. That document is written in the first person by the platform itself: 'You are entitled to cancel this contract within fourteen days without having to state your reasons', addressed to 'TyresNET GmbH, Franz-Joseph-Str. 11, 80801 Munich Germany'; refunds 'without delay and no later than within fourteen days from the date of our receipt of your cancellation notice', by the same means of payment, with no extra charges; and, unusually generous, 'We collect the goods from you. We bear the cost of returning the goods.' Those are a seller's obligations, not an introducer's. The FAQ explains why both can be true — buyers either click through to a retailer or 'purchase directly via the marketplace' — but no page tells you which set of rules is governing the order you are about to place, and the difference decides who you chase when four tyres turn up in the wrong size.

sections.heading: What British law gives you here, whatever the terms say
sections.html:
A German choice-of-law clause does not strip a UK buyer of UK protection. Section 74 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says that where the law of another country 'is chosen by the parties to be applicable to a consumer contract, but the consumer contract has a close connection with the United Kingdom, this Part applies despite that choice'. A platform trading at uk.tyres.net in sterling, with an 0330 phone number and a product feed of British sellers, is about as close a connection as a website gets. The 14 days in the return policy also match what the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 would give a UK buyer anyway.

The weak point is what happens when a complaint goes nowhere. Clause 10.1 of the terms directs unhappy customers to the European Commission's online dispute resolution portal at ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr. That portal stopped operating on 20 July 2025; the Commission has redirected the address and the underlying regulation has been repealed. It had not been open to UK consumers since Brexit in any case. No UK alternative dispute resolution scheme is named anywhere on the site, and there is no UK-registered company to complain to — the registered office, the commercial register entry, the VAT number and the bank account are all German. What is left is the seller's own complaints process, a card chargeback, or section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974, which makes a credit card provider jointly liable on a single purchase of more than £100 and up to £30,000. Four tyres at £70 clears that bar comfortably; one budget tyre at £35.58 does not.

sections.heading: The label data is there, and it is doing more work than it looks
sections.html:
Credit where it is due: the grades are on every row, and that is a legal duty rather than a courtesy. The government's guidance for tyre suppliers and distributors tells anyone selling where the customer cannot see the tyre before buying to 'give the information on the fuel efficiency, wet grip (where applicable) and external noise during the buying process'. Tyres.net does exactly that — the Bridgestone Turanza 6 in 205/55 R16 94V shows B for fuel, A for wet grip and 69 dB for noise before you leave the results page, which is more than several high-street sellers manage on a quotation. The guidance also expects the downloadable product information sheet to be available on a website selling tyres; whether the platform offers that, as opposed to the three grades, could not be confirmed and is worth checking on the product page before ordering.

One caution on the letters themselves. The government's own guidance page describes Great Britain as grading car tyres A to G while Northern Ireland uses A to E, which is not how the assimilated tyre labelling regulation reads, and the two have not been reconciled publicly. Treat the relative position as reliable — an A wet grip really does stop shorter than a C — and do not read anything into the letter at the bottom of whichever scale a given page is using.

sections.heading: How the site is paid, and why it does not say so
sections.html:
Nothing on Tyres.net explains its revenue. The FAQ covers searching, retailers, delivery and contact, and stops short of the commercial arrangement. The Awin affiliate network fills the gap: programme 12715, listed as Tyres UK, pays publishers 4% of a sale and 10p for a clickout, with a 30-day cookie and an average transaction value of about £115 net, across 64 countries and 12 languages. That is an ordinary arrangement and there is nothing improper in it — a comparison site has to be funded somehow, and this one is funded per click and per sale.

It does mean two things worth holding in mind as you read a results page. The platform earns whether or not you get the best tyre, provided you click; and a shop that is not part of the commercial arrangement has no obvious route onto the page at all, so 'the cheapest price' is the cheapest among participating sellers rather than the cheapest in Britain. Neither the ranking method nor the participation rules are published. Compare100 is itself an affiliate of this programme, which is the same disclosure being asked of them.

pros: Genuine breadth — 750 offers in a single common size, 53 of them from one premium brand, across 38 pages of results
Several sellers' prices for the identical tyre on one line, including margins as fine as 93p between three shops on a Continental ContiEcoContact 5
Budget tyres from £35.58 in 205/55 R16, well below anything a fitting chain advertises
Tyre label grades — fuel efficiency, wet grip and noise in decibels — shown on every listing, which satisfies the distance-selling duty in the government's guidance
A 14-day cancellation right with return carriage paid and collection arranged, which is better than the law requires
Covers wheels, oils and accessories as well as car, van, motorcycle, truck and bicycle tyres
cons: Fitting is never mentioned anywhere on the site, yet at Kwik Fit's published £20.00 to £20.50 a tyre it adds roughly £80 to £82 to a set of four — turning £142 of budget tyres into about £222 on the car

Delivery cost does not appear in the listings, so the ranked price is not the price you pay; section 230 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has required total pricing since 6 April 2025

The only dispute route named in the terms is the European ODR portal, which was switched off on 20 July 2025 and was closed to UK consumers before that; no UK alternative dispute resolution scheme is named

The general terms say the contract is 'concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops', while the return policy is written in TyresNET GmbH's own name and promises to collect the goods and pay the carriage — nothing tells a buyer which applies to their order
No UK company, registered office or register entry; the registered office is in Munich, the commercial register is the Amtsgericht München and the bank account is with Commerzbank in euros
The site never discloses that it earns 4% of a sale and 10p a clickout, and publishes neither its ranking method nor the terms on which a shop gets listed
No independent rating exists for a tyre price comparison platform, so there is no external check on service quality
verdict: As a way of seeing what a tyre costs before you walk into a garage, Tyres.net earns its place: 750 offers in one common size, the label grades on every row, and several sellers priced against each other on a single line. Treat the number it gives you as the cost of the rubber and nothing else. Add £20 a tyre for fitting, balancing, a valve and disposal, add carriage, and then compare it with a fully fitted price — on a £35.58 budget tyre that arithmetic closes most of the gap, and on a £95 Michelin it does not. The paperwork is the part to go in with your eyes open: a Munich company, German law, a dispute portal that has been dark since July 2025, and a set of terms that cannot decide whether it is the seller or the introducer. Buy on a credit card, keep the order confirmation from the shop rather than the platform, and the risk is manageable.

faqs.q: Does Tyres.net sell the tyres itself?
faqs.a: Its general terms say no: contracts are 'concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops'. Its own return policy says something closer to yes, promising a 14-day cancellation, collection of the goods and payment of the return carriage in TyresNET GmbH's own name, and the FAQ mentions buying 'directly via the marketplace' as well as clicking through to a retailer. Check the order confirmation to see whose name is on the sale.

faqs.q: Is the price shown the price I pay?
faqs.a: No. The listing price is for the tyre. Delivery is settled at the retailer's checkout and fitting is a separate job at a garage — Kwik Fit publishes £20.00 to £20.50 a tyre for fitting, balancing, a valve and disposing of the old one, so a set of four typically adds £80 to £82.

faqs.q: What can I do if something goes wrong with the order?
faqs.a: Start with the retailer, since the contract is most likely with them. Section 74 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 keeps UK protection in place despite the German choice of law where the contract has a close connection with the UK. The European ODR portal named in the terms has not operated since 20 July 2025, and no UK dispute scheme is offered in its place, so a card chargeback or a section 75 claim on a credit card purchase over £100 is the practical backstop.

faqs.q: Why does the same tyre appear at four different prices?
faqs.a: Because several retailers list the same product. A Continental ContiEcoContact 5 in 205/55 R16 91H came back at £70.48, £70.60 and £71.41 from three shops on the same row. Some of those shopfronts belong to the same group — mytyres.co.uk is one of the 300-plus stores run by Delticom AG — so the number of names is not the number of businesses.

faqs.q: Are the tyre label grades on the site reliable?
faqs.a: They come from the manufacturer's declared figures and showing them is a legal duty for distance sellers under the government's guidance, so the fuel efficiency letter, wet grip letter and decibel figure on each listing are the same data a shop would have to hand you. Use them comparatively: an A wet grip stops shorter than a C in the wet, which matters more on a British winter road than the fuel letter does.

title: Voyager Travel Insurance Review
meta_title: Voyager Travel Insurance Review: Limits, Tiers & Fees 2026
meta_description: Voyager Plus in full: four tiers, a £150 excess falling to £50, £10m medical, 100+ activities as standard and a high-risk sister brand.
intro:
Voyager includes more than 100 sports and activities as standard, each published with its own depth, altitude or river grade rather than hidden behind the phrase ‘hazardous activity’. The firm has been arranging travel cover since September 1996, and for most of that time it did not sell to the public at all — it placed wholesale schemes for tour operators, which is why the policy wording reads like something written for people who already know what a grade 3 river is. Its retail brand, Voyager Plus, now sells single trip, annual multi-trip and long stay cover directly, and in February 2024 it bought Navigator Travel Insurance, a specialist it had worked alongside for more than twenty years.

The numbers at the top end are competitive. Emergency medical expenses run to £10 million on the two upper tiers, the excess on the highest tier is £50, and single trip cover carries no upper age limit. Long stay policies run to 24 months for travellers under 50. Buying or amending online carries no administration fee at all.

What sets Voyager apart is the edge of its appetite. Where a supermarket policy stops at a vague exclusion, Voyager publishes the metre and the grade — and it runs a separate brand, High Risk Voyager, for people travelling to countries the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office tells them to avoid. That is a narrow specialism, and it is worded and priced as one.

sections.heading: The four tiers, side by side
sections.html:
Voyager Plus is one product sold at four prices, and the gap between cheapest and dearest is wide enough that the tier matters more than the brand. Reading across Standard, Enhanced, Prime and Supreme in the 2025/26 wording, which covers departures up to 30 September 2027:

  • Excess per claim: £150, £100, £75 and £50
  • Cancellation and curtailment: £1,000, £2,500, £5,000 and £10,000
  • Emergency medical expenses: £5 million, £7.5 million, £10 million and £10 million
  • Baggage: £1,000, £1,500, £2,500 and £3,500, with single article caps of £100, £200, £300 and £400
  • Personal money: £350, £750, £1,250 and £1,500
  • Missed departure: £250, £500, £750 and £1,000
  • Travel delay: £100, £200, £250 and £500 per full 12 hours
  • Personal liability: £1 million, £2 million, £2 million and £3 million
  • Legal expenses: £10,000, £10,000, £20,000 and £35,000
  • Personal accident on death: £5,000, £7,500, £10,000 and £15,000, rising to £10,000–£35,000 for loss of limb or sight

Emergency dental is capped at £500 for the immediate relief of pain on natural teeth, and that ceiling barely moves between tiers. The single article cap is what catches people out: £400 on Supreme is generous by market standards but still short of a camera body or a laptop, and gadget cover is a separate option that cannot be added to a long stay policy running beyond 120 days.

sections.heading: Where the activity list actually stops
sections.html:
Those 100-plus activities come with their limits attached, which is more useful than a marketing claim. Scuba diving is covered to 15 metres as standard, 30 metres with the Action option and 40 metres with Action Plus. Hiking and trekking reach 4,250 metres. Glacier walking is covered below 2,000 metres as standard and between 2,000 and 4,000 metres on Action. Canoeing, kayaking and white water rafting are grades 1 to 3 as standard, with grade 4 and above needing Action. Bungee jumping runs to three jumps. Sailing is covered within 60 miles of a safe haven, and small boating within the 12-mile limit on craft up to 10 metres.

Action Plus reaches further again, adding canyoning, heli-skiing and cat-skiing, non-racing horse riding, rugby, American football, hurling, competitive cycling other than BMX, and judo, karate, kendo and kick boxing. Winter sports run to 21 days a year on an annual multi-trip policy and up to 31 days on single trip and long stay cover, both for extra premium.

Some things sit outside the appetite altogether. Downhill and competitive mountain biking, horse racing, hunting on horseback, BMX and stunt cycling, mixed martial arts and any professional participation are not covered at any price. Nor, specifically, is scuba diving in Cyprus. Motorcycling can be arranged but drops the personal accident section. Anyone buying on the strength of the headline count should read the entry for their own sport rather than the total.

sections.heading: Going where the FCDO says not to
sections.html:
Voyager Plus follows the market on government advice: there is no cover for travel to an area the FCDO has advised against all, or all but essential, travel. Belarus, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Syria and Ukraine are excluded outright under sanctions wording.

The unusual part is that Voyager sells the answer to its own exclusion. High Risk Voyager is a separate brand, underwritten by the same insurer, written for aid workers, missionaries, journalists, volunteers and contractors heading to Iraq, Nigeria, Libya, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and similar. It adds political and natural disaster evacuation, hijack and mugging benefits and post-traumatic stress counselling to the usual medical and repatriation sections. Israel, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sudan, South Sudan, Syria, Ukraine, Venezuela and Yemen are assessed case by case rather than quoted online; India needs a referral within 10 kilometres of the Pakistan border and in Jammu and Kashmir; and Belarus, Russia, Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson stay excluded. Annual multi-trip cover on that brand stops once anyone on the policy reaches 70.

It carries its own exclusions worth knowing about: nothing where vaccination requirements were not met, nothing for armed forces on operational duty, nothing for a newly declared infectious disease once the World Health Organization designates a public health emergency of international concern, and no pregnancy or childbirth claim where the expected date of birth falls before or within eight weeks of travel. The insurer also reserves the right to require repatriation if an epidemic is declared at the destination.

sections.heading: Who is actually behind the policy
sections.html:
Voyager arranges; it does not carry the risk. Policies for UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man and Gibraltar residents are underwritten by Starr International (Europe) Limited, firm reference 472977, regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. EEA residents get Starr Europe Insurance Limited, supervised in Malta. Starr’s insurance subsidiaries hold an A (Excellent) financial strength rating and an a+ long-term issuer credit rating from AM Best, most recently affirmed on 19 December 2023.

The arranging firm has changed hands. The company incorporated on 19 September 1996 as Voyager Insurance Services Limited was acquired by Caledon Group in July 2024 and renamed Caledon MGA Ltd on 19 June 2025, keeping Voyager as a trading style. Caledon Group was formed in 2023 by David Whitaker, Andrew Cross and Paul Davies, and also holds Somerville Group, the 75 per cent shareholder of record since April 2016. The firm reference number, 305814, has not changed and is verifiable on the FCA Register — but anyone searching that register for ‘Voyager’ will find the entry filed under Caledon.

The sale is non-advised. Voyager states plainly that it gives no personal recommendation, acts as agent of the insurer, and is paid a percentage of premium plus a bonus if the book hits profit targets; customers can ask what that commission is at any time. Complaints go first to the Managing Director on 01483 806 680 with a 20 working day target, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567, and the firm is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

sections.heading: What the claims data says about buying travel cover in 2026
sections.html:
Travel is one of the harder personal lines to claim on, and the regulator’s own figures show it. The FCA published its general insurance value measures for calendar year 2025 on 21 July 2026: travel products accepted between 83 and 86 per cent of claims, against 99 per cent for motor and 62 to 71 per cent for home combined. Claims complaints ran at 5 to 6 per cent of claims registered, high for a retail line. Claims costs rose to 44–48 per cent of premium from 31–37 per cent the year before, with payouts up 47 per cent against premiums up 12 per cent.

The Financial Ombudsman Service took 4,451 new travel insurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 36 per cent of those it decided, against an average of 30 per cent across all financial products; the figure for the first quarter of 2026/27 was 32 per cent. Declined claims are the single largest cause, and under-declared medical history is the most common reason a travel claim fails.

Set against that, the Association of British Insurers reported £472 million paid on more than 500,000 travel claims in 2024, published on 21 November 2025. Medical expenses took 34 per cent of the money — some £262 million — at an average of £1,528 a claim. That average is the number to hold next to Voyager’s excesses: on Standard, a £150 excess removes roughly a tenth of a typical medical payment before anything else is argued about. Pre-existing conditions have to go through Voyager Healthcheck, online or on 01483 806 666, and cover for anything undeclared simply is not there.

sections.heading: The costs and cut-offs to check before you buy
sections.html:
None of this is hidden, but several of these appear only in the terms of business rather than on the quote page. Buying online is free of administration charges. Buying or renewing by telephone costs £12. Changing a policy by telephone outside the 14 day cooling-off period costs £12, and cancelling outside that window costs £12 as well. The cooling-off period is 14 days, shortened if departure falls inside it and gone entirely once travel has begun. Cancel a single trip policy after that and the refund is 50 per cent; cancel an annual multi-trip policy and the refund slides from 100 per cent before it starts to 60 per cent within two months, 50 within three, 40 within four, 30 within five, 25 within six and nothing thereafter.

The age and duration ceilings do a lot of the underwriting. Single trip cover has no upper age limit, but the trip caps at 62 days, dropping to 31 days for travellers over 74 and 31 days to every destination once anyone is 85 or over. Long stay cover stops at 69 at departure and runs to 24 months for under-50s and 18 months for those aged 51 to 60, with up to five home visits of two weeks each allowed. Annual multi-trip is available up to 79 at inception, with 45 days per trip as standard and 62 days available to under-70s for extra premium.

Covid-19 cover is narrower than the length of the wording suggests. It reaches only cancellation under section 1.2, emergency medical expenses, hospital stay benefit and the cruise rejoin cover, so pandemic disruption and curtailment largely sit outside the policy. There is also a broadly drawn excessive alcohol exclusion — defined as drinking enough to notably impair faculties or judgement — which is a common ground for declining a claim after an accident abroad.

pros: Over 100 sports and activities included as standard, each published with its own depth, altitude or grade limit rather than a vague exclusion
Emergency medical expenses of £10 million on the Prime and Supreme tiers, with the Supreme excess at £50
No upper age limit on single trip cover, and long stay policies running to 24 months for under-50s
High Risk Voyager gives a route to cover for FCDO-advised destinations that most insurers refuse outright
Underwritten by Starr International (Europe) Limited, rated A (Excellent) by AM Best
No administration fee on anything bought, amended or cancelled online
cons: The Standard tier is thin for the price of a holiday: a £1,000 cancellation limit will not cover many package trips, and its £150 excess removes about a tenth of the £1,528 average travel medical claim
The sale is non-advised, so choosing the wrong tier or missing an activity limit is entirely the buyer’s problem, and Voyager is paid a share of premium plus a profit bonus by the insurer
A £12 fee applies to buying, renewing, amending or cancelling by telephone, which falls hardest on customers who would rather not transact online
Long stay cover cuts off at 69 and annual multi-trip at 79, so older travellers making long trips are pushed onto single trip policies capped at 31 days once past 74
Scuba diving is only 15 metres as standard and is not covered at all in Cyprus, while downhill mountain biking, MMA and any professional participation are uninsurable at any price
Covid-19 cover is limited to four named sections, and the trading name no longer matches the legal entity, so the FCA Register entry appears under Caledon MGA Ltd rather than Voyager
verdict: Voyager Plus is a specialist product sold at retail, and it suits people whose trips do not fit a supermarket policy: trekkers at altitude, divers, long stay travellers and anyone whose destination carries FCDO advice. The published activity limits and the £10 million medical ceiling on the upper tiers are genuinely strong, and the £50 excess on Supreme is among the lowest in the market. Take the Standard tier only for a cheap trip you could afford to lose, because a £1,000 cancellation cap and a £150 excess do not stretch far. Buy online rather than by phone, put every medical condition through Healthcheck before you travel, and read the entry for your own activity rather than trusting the headline count.

faqs.q: Who underwrites Voyager travel insurance?
faqs.a: Starr International (Europe) Limited, firm reference 472977, underwrites policies for residents of the UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man and Gibraltar, regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. EEA residents are covered by Starr Europe Insurance Limited, supervised in Malta. Starr’s insurance subsidiaries carry an A (Excellent) financial strength rating from AM Best, affirmed on 19 December 2023.

faqs.q: Is Voyager Insurance Services FCA authorised?
faqs.a: Yes. The arranging firm holds firm reference number 305814 and company number 3251842. The legal entity was renamed Caledon MGA Ltd on 19 June 2025, after Caledon Group acquired the business in July 2024, with Voyager kept on as a trading style — so the FCA Register entry appears under the Caledon name.

faqs.q: What excess does Voyager charge?
faqs.a: £150 per claim on Standard, £100 on Enhanced, £75 on Prime and £50 on Supreme. It applies per person per section claimed, so a couple claiming for medical costs and lost baggage on the same trip will meet it more than once.

faqs.q: Does Voyager cover travel against FCDO advice?
faqs.a: Not under the mainstream Voyager Plus policy, which excludes any area where the FCDO advises against all or all but essential travel. High Risk Voyager is a separate purchase, underwritten by the same insurer, covering destinations such as Iraq, Nigeria, Libya, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Israel, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sudan, South Sudan, Syria, Ukraine, Venezuela and Yemen are quoted case by case, and Belarus, Russia and the occupied Ukrainian oblasts stay excluded.

faqs.q: How deep can I scuba dive on a Voyager policy?
faqs.a: Fifteen metres as standard, 30 metres with the Action option and 40 metres with Action Plus, always on an amateur basis and within your certification or with a qualified instructor. Diving in Cyprus is not covered on any level.

faqs.q: How do I complain about Voyager?
faqs.a: Complaints go first to the Managing Director on 01483 806 680, with a stated target of 20 working days for a final response. If you are unhappy with the outcome you can take the case to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. The service upheld 36 per cent of the 4,451 travel insurance complaints it handled in 2025/26.

title: Wicked Quotes Motorbike Insurance Review
meta_title: Wicked Quotes Bike Insurance: Aviva and AXA Behind It
meta_description: Wicked Quotes is the retail arm of Novitas, an underwriting agency using Aviva and AXA paper. Nine-question quotes, £20m cover and the fees to know first.
intro:
Wicked Quotes sells one thing, motorcycle insurance, and it has sold it under that name for more than fifteen years from an office at 28 Station Close in Potters Bar. The quote form is about as short as they come: nine questions, no name and no phone number required, and a rough price on screen before you have given anything away. Sales lines are open 9am to 5pm Monday to Friday and 9am to 1pm on Saturday on 0344 8800 962, and the staff answering them are described as riders themselves.

The firm behind the brand has rather more history than the name suggests. Wicked Quotes is a trading name of Novitas Underwriting Agency Limited, company 03106533, incorporated on 26 September 1995 and trading since 1996. Novitas is an underwriting agency rather than a high-street broker: it holds authority to price and arrange cover on insurers' behalf, and describes itself as acting for “a number of market leading UK insurers including Aviva and Markerstudy”. Its own published product assessment maps its motorcycle schemes to Aviva and AXA. For a rider, that is the part worth knowing — the paper behind the policy comes from large, familiar names.

Novitas also supplies more than 150 brokers and intermediaries across the UK, so the same underwriting may well sit behind quotes you have been given elsewhere. Cover runs from third party only through third party fire and theft to comprehensive, with separate routes for modified bikes, high-value machines, multi-bike households and couriers, food delivery excepted. The firm is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 307931, which anyone can check on the FCA Register.

sections.heading: Nine questions and a price on screen
sections.html:
The Quick-Quote form asks for the bike's make, model and registration, the licence you hold and how long you have held it, your no-claims years, postcode, date of birth, whether the bike is garaged, its value and what you use it for. Email is optional. The site promises a quote in about 30 seconds and is honest that what comes back is “a simple rough estimate” built on stated assumptions, with a fuller quote behind it. That is a genuinely low-friction way to find out whether a specialist is even in the right ballpark before you start handing over personal details to comparison sites.

The site also sets out six levers it will price against: no-claims bonus, agreeing a mileage limit, garaging the bike, fitting extra security, dropping pillion cover and holding an advanced riding qualification. Two of those are worth thinking about before you accept the cheapest number. The mileage endorsements in the policy wording are hard cut-offs rather than sliding scales — endorsement J voids cover for any accident, loss or damage once the bike has passed 5,000 miles in the year, and endorsement L does the same at 3,000 miles. If you agree to one of those to shave the premium, the odometer becomes part of your contract.

sections.heading: Who actually carries the risk
sections.html:
An underwriting agency sits between you and the insurer. Novitas designs the product, sets the price within limits agreed with the insurer, binds the cover and handles much of the administration; the insurer supplies the capital that pays claims. Its published fair value assessment of 25 August 2023 names six schemes and, unusually, says which insurer stands behind each: Novitas Standard on Aviva paper, and Novitas Select, Novitas Bike and Novitas Basic on AXA. Two further schemes, Novitas Bikmarque and Novitas Palamon, are recorded as being in run-off with West Bay, meaning closed to new business and simply seeing out the policies already written. The assessment describes Novitas and the insurer as co-manufacturers of the product, which is the regulator's language for shared responsibility.

The corporate trail is straightforward enough to follow. The company was incorporated on 26 September 1995 as Whittington Underwriting Agency PLC, took the Novitas name on 28 February 1997, and converted from a plc to a limited company on 17 September 2015. Since 30 June 2016 it has been controlled by Daly Holdings Limited, which holds 75% or more of both the shares and the voting rights. Its registered office is 167 Turners Hill, Cheshunt EN8 9BH, while the working address on every customer-facing page is Potters Bar. Older policy paperwork also points to Lloyd's, and the complaints procedure still carries a separate escalation route for policyholders whose cover sits with a Lloyd's syndicate, so ask which insurer your own certificate names.

sections.heading: What the wording pays, and the conditions attached
sections.html:
The liability limits are generous and worth setting against the legal floor. The policy caps damage to other people's property at £20,000,000 for any one occurrence, with a further £5,000,000 for claimants' costs and expenses. The Road Traffic Act only obliges an insurer to provide £1,200,000 of third party property cover, so this is well beyond the minimum. There is also up to £5,000 towards legal representation if you face proceedings for manslaughter or dangerous riding arising from an accident.

Damage to your own bike is settled at market value at the time of loss, capped at the value you last declared — which makes keeping that figure current your job, not the insurer's, on a machine that has been rebuilt or has appreciated. Permanently fitted accessories are limited to £100 for any one claim unless separately declared. Riding another person's motorcycle, where that extension applies at all, gives you third party cover only; nothing pays for damage to the borrowed bike.

Theft cover carries the sharpest condition on the page, and the wording capitalises it: a secondary security device such as a D-lock, disc lock, chain and padlock or immobiliser is compulsory, and theft while the bike is unattended and unprotected by one is excluded outright. Leaving the bike also means removing the ignition keys and setting whatever security is fitted. Track days, competitions, rallies, trials, performance tests and speed trials are all excluded, as is food delivery work. European riding is capped at 30 days in any one trip and 90 days in total across the year, over the UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man, Republic of Ireland and 31 listed European countries, and needs telling in advance.

sections.heading: The fees, and what they do to a small premium
sections.html:
This is where a rider should slow down. The terms of business set out a charge of “£150 for setting up or renewing an insurance policy on selected products”, £50 for a mid-term adjustment whether temporary or permanent, £50 for any cancellation per policy, and £5 for duplicate documents. A £150 arrangement fee is at the very top of the range charged by UK insurance intermediaries, and it is charged again at renewal on the products it applies to. The wording “on selected products” is doing a lot of work and the site does not say which ones, so the only way to know what your quote carries is to ask before you pay.

Scale it against a premium. The ABI's motor premium tracker put the average private car policy at £566 in the second quarter of 2026, up £6 on the quarter and £14 on the year in cash terms though £14 lower once inflation is taken out. Motorcycle premiums are not tracked separately in that release, and a commuter bike or a small scooter frequently costs a good deal less than a car to insure. On a policy in the low hundreds, a £150 fee is not an administrative detail; it is a material part of what leaves your account, and it is not the bit that pays claims.

Two further wrinkles. There is a 14-day cooling-off period, but a refund is net of the insurer's charge and the firm's own fee, and after 14 days Novitas keeps its commission on any return premium; if a claim has been made in the policy year there may be no refund at all. And the policy wording itself carries a separate £25 administration charge plus insurance premium tax, along with a £15 charge for cancelling inside the cooling-off period. That wording dates from May 2018 and the terms of business are current, so the larger figures are the ones to work from — but the overlap is confusing enough that it is worth having the total spelled out before you commit.

sections.heading: The paperwork is published, just not on this site
sections.html:
Wicked Quotes does not publish a policy wording, an insurance product information document or a specimen schedule anywhere a shopper can find them before buying. Novitas does, on its own trade-facing site, and the two are the same company — so the documents exist and are free; they are simply on the other brand. Its legal page carries the motorcycle wordings before and after May 2018, the IPID, a target market statement and the fair value assessment. Anyone taking a quote from Wicked Quotes should read them there first, because that is the paperwork they will be sold.

The dates on those documents are less reassuring than their existence. The IPID is referenced 01/01/2018 and the current wording is version 2.01 of May 2018, both now more than eight years old. The fair value assessment is dated 25 August 2023 and states in terms that “the next FVA will be conducted within the next 12 months”; no later version is published, which leaves the visible assessment two years past its own stated review date. Its conclusion is that the core range “does provide fair value to customers”, while flagging concerns about add-on products, fees and the effect of premium finance — the assessment is candid that Novitas neither supplies the add-ons nor sets their selling price, which means the extras you are offered at the quote stage are priced by somebody else.

sections.heading: How bike cover looks in the official figures
sections.html:
No independent rating of Wicked Quotes could be verified: there is no Defaqto award on the site, no entry on the consumer rating panels that cover most brokers, and the firm is too small to appear in regulatory data under its own name. The claim on the homepage to be “one of the UK's largest independent motorbike insurance providers” is not one an outsider can check.

The sector-wide numbers do give a frame. The Financial Ombudsman Service's annual data, published on 21 May 2026, records 13,420 new complaints about car and motorcycle insurance at a 35% uphold rate, against 214,600 complaints and a 30% average across every financial product it covers. Motor sits above the average, and the gap is mostly about how claims are handled rather than how policies are sold. The FCA's general insurance value measures data of 21 July 2026 shows motor claims acceptance at 99% and claims costs at 59% of premium for 2025, up from 54%; motorcycle is not broken out separately in that release, so there is no bike-specific acceptance rate to quote and anyone offering you one is borrowing the car figure.

The market itself is growing. Motorcycle Industry Association registrations were 13% up in June 2026 against the same month a year earlier and 15.2% up year to date, with adventure bikes 23.8% ahead for the year and modern classics 23.1% up in the month. More bikes on the road tends to mean more competition for the business, which is an argument for taking two or three quotes rather than one.

sections.heading: Complaining, and who stands behind the policy
sections.html:
The complaints procedure is clear and the timescales are written down. Complaints go to the Potters Bar office in writing, by email, or by telephone on 01707 708262; an acknowledgement follows within five business days, with an aim to resolve on the spot or within three business days where possible, and a response within eight weeks at the outside. After that, or after a final response, you have six months to take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. Eligibility extends beyond private customers to micro-enterprises, charities with income under £6.5m, trusts with net assets under £5m, buy-to-let customers and small businesses under £6.5m turnover. Where the cover sits with a Lloyd's syndicate there is a parallel route to Lloyd's own complaints team.

On money, the terms of business say premiums are held in a trust account as agents of the insurers, which is the arrangement that protects your money if the firm fails before passing the premium on. They also confirm Financial Services Compensation Scheme protection applies, though the percentage differs by type of business and the exact level for your policy is worth confirming with the firm. Claims are reported to Wicked Quotes on 0344 8800 967 rather than direct to an insurer, and the site says your insurer, solicitor and repairer are instructed from there; no approved repairer network or courtesy bike arrangement is described.

pros: Nine-question quick quote gives an indicative price in about 30 seconds without asking for your name or number
Underwriting sits with Aviva and AXA on the current schemes, named openly in the firm's own fair value assessment
£20,000,000 third party property limit and £5,000,000 for claimants' costs, far above the £1,200,000 legal minimum
Genuine specialism in modified, high-value, multi-bike and courier risks that mainstream insurers price badly or decline
Policy wording, IPID, target market statement and fair value assessment are all published free on the Novitas site
Complaints timescales are spelled out, with a five business day acknowledgement and a named phone line
cons: A fee of up to £150 to set up or renew, charged again each year, with no list of which products it applies to
£50 to make any mid-term change and £50 to cancel, on top of whatever the insurer charges
No policy wording, IPID or specimen schedule published on the Wicked Quotes site itself — you have to know to look on the Novitas site
The current wording and IPID both date from 2018, and the published fair value assessment is two years past its own stated review date
Theft cover is void if the bike is left unattended without a secondary security device, and mileage endorsements cut off cover outright at 3,000 or 5,000 miles
No verifiable independent rating, and the claim to be one of the UK's largest independent bike providers cannot be checked from outside
verdict: Wicked Quotes is a specialist worth a quote if your bike is modified, valuable, one of several, or used for courier work, and the underwriting behind it is better than the modest branding suggests — Aviva and AXA paper, arranged by a firm that has been doing this since 1996 and supplies 150 other brokers. The liability limits are strong and the quick quote costs you nothing to try. The reservation is the fee schedule: up to £150 to arrange or renew, £50 to change anything and £50 to cancel are large numbers against a typical bike premium, and they are easy to miss until the paperwork arrives. Ask what fee your quote carries and read the Novitas wording before you buy, and you will know exactly what you are getting.

faqs.q: Who underwrites a Wicked Quotes policy?
faqs.a: Wicked Quotes is a trading name of Novitas Underwriting Agency Limited, which arranges cover on insurers' behalf rather than carrying the risk itself. Its 25 August 2023 fair value assessment places the Novitas Standard scheme with Aviva and the Select, Bike and Basic schemes with AXA; two older schemes sit in run-off with West Bay. The insurer that applies to you is named on your certificate of motor insurance, so check it there.

faqs.q: What fees does Wicked Quotes charge?
faqs.a: The published terms of business list up to £150 for setting up or renewing a policy on selected products, £50 for any mid-term adjustment, £50 for cancelling, and £5 for duplicate documents. Commission from the insurer is taken on top. The firm does not say which products attract the £150, so ask for the fee in writing with your quote.

faqs.q: Do I have to fit a lock for theft cover?
faqs.a: Yes. The policy wording states in capitals that a secondary security device — a D-lock, disc lock, chain and padlock, immobiliser or similar — is compulsory, and theft of a bike left unattended without one is excluded. Leaving the bike also means removing the ignition keys and activating any fitted security.

faqs.q: Can I ride in Europe on the policy?
faqs.a: Cover extends to the UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man, Republic of Ireland and 31 listed European countries, but foreign use is capped at 30 days in any one trip and 90 days across the year, and needs to be notified in advance. Longer touring needs a different arrangement.

faqs.q: Where do I find the policy documents before buying?
faqs.a: Not on the Wicked Quotes site, which publishes none of them. The same company's Novitas site carries the motorcycle wordings from before and after May 2018, the insurance product information document, a target market statement and the fair value assessment, all as free downloads. Read those before you pay.

faqs.q: How do I complain, and how long does it take?
faqs.a: Complaints go to the Potters Bar office on 01707 708262, by email or in writing. You should get an acknowledgement within five business days and a response within eight weeks; the firm aims to settle straightforward cases within three business days. If you are still unhappy, you have six months from the final response to refer it to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567.
